articles.title: Cómo se recreó la toma del Palacio de Justicia en la serie ‘Palacio’ de Netflix: actores revelan tecnologías y nuevos lenguajes
articles.text:
“La única conclusión a la que yo realmente creo que llega y la única verdad absoluta que existe al final de esta serie es que en la guerra todos perdemos”, afirmó Natalia Reyes, actriz que interpreta a Pilar Navarrete en Palacio, la nueva serie de Netflix. Y con esta frase quiero unir lo que realmente describe una serie llena de tecnología e historia que marcó la vida de muchos colombianos y de varios latinos a finales de los 80´s.
“Nadie ganó. Por más que parezca: ‘¿Quién fue el culpable?’ Nadie ganó. De aquí nadie salió ganando”, dijo Natalia.
El 6 de noviembre de 1985, un comando del M-19 entró por la fuerza al Palacio de Justicia de Bogotá y tomó como rehenes a más de 300 personas, entre ellas a los magistrados de la Corte Suprema de Colombia. Al día siguiente, el Ejército colombiano retomó el edificio.
El hecho dejó al menos 94 personas muertas o desaparecidas, entre magistrados, guerrilleros, civiles y militares, y desató una búsqueda de justicia que se extendió por más de 20 años. Palacio reconstruye esos hechos, de conocimiento público e inspirados en la realidad, y retrata además la búsqueda posterior de los familiares de las víctimas.
Con motivo del estreno, cuatro de sus protagonistas, Natalia Reyes, Luna Baxter, Andrés Castañeda y Mariana Gómez, hablaron con Infobae sobre la reconstrucción de la época, el trabajo actoral con tecnología y el significado de la historia que llevaron a la pantalla.
La recreación audiovisual de la época: material de archivo y diseño de producción
—Luna, ¿cómo fue el trabajo tecnológico para ambientar la época que vivía el personaje como periodista?
—Me gusta que resaltes eso porque creo que el manejo del material de archivo y lo que se grabó es tan sutil y tan bien hecho que casi que no se nota. Y cuando se nota igual es agradable ver que hay material de archivo.
Creo que todo está muy bien logrado, la época, desde el diseño de producción. Estamos hablando de un estudio que recreó el Palacio de Justicia y que se fue destruyendo poco a poco con fines de la historia.
Todo el equipo, de verdad, cuando entramos a ver el Palacio de Justicia y habíamos visto el material de archivo y conocido los pasillos, al menos en imágenes, todos estábamos muy conmovidos con ver lo impecable que fueron en imagen, y creo que hace que la serie visualmente sea impecable.
Pienso también que, en mi construcción de Olga, ella me pasó notas que había hecho como periodista y algo que me gustó mucho y que lo apliqué para la serie. Sobre todo en ese momento se usaba una voz de periodismo. Olga me contaba que muchas veces estaban en situaciones de mucho ruido o de caos, y tocaba tener una voz de periodismo para poder contar la nota.
Y en la serie, cuando me veo siendo Olga en esos momentos, es algo que dije: “Ay, qué bonito que así sea sutil, tal vez no lo ve nadie”.
Si tuvieran tecnología actual: qué habría usado cada personaje
—En esa época no había tanta tecnología a la mano. ¿Qué dispositivo o herramienta tecnológica hubiera podido usar tu personaje?
Mariana Gómez: No, pues un radio que funcione porque en mi personaje no tuvimos éxito y hubiera sido interesante un buen sistema de comunicación.
—¿Y Andrés?
—wow. No sé, creo que... sí, yo creo que la posibilidad de ampliar la información a la velocidad que se amplía en este momento, una red social, algo donde pueda denunciar de manera masiva y más efectiva.
—¿Y Natalia, como madre?
—Pues buscadora de desaparecidos, creo que el GPS hubiera ayudado muchísimo a saber esos movimientos: de dónde estaban, por qué se los llevaron, por qué los movieron, dónde terminaron. Yo creo que eso hubiera ayudado muchísimo.
En el caso de Pilar Navarrete, el tema del ADN, que fue posterior a este hecho, hizo toda la diferencia muchos años después.
—¿Y para el personaje de la periodista?
—Y para Olga, un disco duro. Un disco duro en donde ella hubiera podido guardar toda la información, toda la evidencia y poder hacer una copia y que no se hubiera corrido tanto riesgo.
El lenguaje y el contexto histórico detrás de la construcción de los personajes
—Andrés ¿Cómo fue la construcción del lenguaje del personaje, teniendo en cuenta la época en la que transcurre la historia?
—Bueno, todo está en los libretos. Desde la forma en la que uno se mueve, las acciones que uno hace en las escenas están descritas en los guiones.
Es una investigación profunda, no únicamente a nivel del evento, del hecho del Palacio de Justicia, sino que también ambienta una época. Y esa época está ambientada por un sentir que tenía la población.
Veníamos de unos acuerdos de paz fallidos, veníamos de unas acusaciones a los militares por torturas que los estaba investigando la Corte Suprema de Justicia. Estaba la amenaza del narcotráfico sobre la extradición. Estaba el M-19 en esta pugna.
Creo que había una efervescencia y esa efervescencia se traduce en el lenguaje, en la música, en cómo el país vivía esos días. Y eso está plasmado en el guion.
—¿Se nota esa construcción en el resultado final?
—Como cada una de las expresiones, el gusto por algunos determinados placeres, fumar en todas partes, que ya no se puede, en los carros, en los recintos cerrados, en las escaleras, en todo lado. Creo que esto también le hace nutrir a uno un ambiente y un estado en el que se estaba viviendo, y está en el guion.
Natalia Reyes y el homenaje a las buscadoras de desaparecidos
—¿Cómo se conectó tu maternidad con la construcción de Pilar Navarrete?
—Yo creo que conecta mucho con mi maternidad. Desde el principio, para mí de verdad fue muy impresionante el hecho de saber que Pilar tenía dieciocho años, que ya para mí ser madre a los dieciocho años me parece una locura.
Pero además, cuando fue la toma, tuviera cuatro hijas, una bebé muy pequeña, y quedara viuda de repente. Ella obviamente, por sus cuatro hijas, no hubiera alcanzado a terminar el bachillerato y de repente se queda sola con esta responsabilidad.
Pero además sacó esa fuerza que de verdad creo que las mujeres y las madres solo podemos sacar en circunstancias tan dolorosas, con tal de sacar adelante a nuestros hijos.
—¿Qué más representa Pilar más allá de la crianza de sus hijas?
—No contenta con tener que sacar a cuatro niñas adelante, con esa convicción de querer saber dónde estaba Jimmy, su esposo, quien trabajaba en la cafetería del Palacio de Justicia y desapareció tras la toma. De buscarlo, de saber la verdad, de buscar a los desaparecidos y de expandir esa búsqueda no solo a su caso personal, sino a esas otras familias y a esos otros casos.
Pilar ha estado en La Haya dando conferencias. Realmente es una mujer que hace que el arco de este personaje en la vida real sea absolutamente heroico.
—¿Qué significó para ti interpretar este papel?
—Para mí hacer este homenaje a Pilar Navarrete en particular, pero a todas esas buscadoras latinoamericanas, a todas esas madres que han sufrido la guerra y que no se han quedado en esta idea de las víctimas, sino que han dicho: “Nosotras tenemos algo que hacer aquí, algo que curar, algo que sanar, algo que saber”.
Esa curiosidad, esa búsqueda de Pilar, a mí me parece absolutamente loable y me parece que es realmente el corazón de esta historia.
—¿Qué esperas que entienda el espectador?
—Espero que realmente llegue al espectador a decir: “Okey, más allá de una historia de buenos y malos, de militares y guerrilleros, de blancos y negros, es una historia de seres humanos, de madres cabezas de familia”. La única conclusión a la que yo realmente creo que llega y la única verdad absoluta que existe al final de esta serie es que en la guerra todos perdemos.
Nadie ganó. Por más que parezca: “¿Quién fue el culpable?” Nadie ganó. De aquí nadie salió ganando.

articles.title: Malicious Browser Extensions Could Use Claude Dispatch to Run Code on Users' Computers
articles.text:
A browser extension that can run scripts on claude.ai could make Claude Desktop run code on a person's computer, researchers at Forever Security, an endpoint security company, showed in a test.
The attack needs Dispatch, a Claude feature that lets people send tasks from their phone to Claude Desktop. The flaw that makes this possible can still be exploited, the researchers said earlier this week.
Claude Desktop is an AI agent that can run commands on the computer where it is installed. The researchers found that Dispatch also accepted an ordinary signed-in session on claude.ai, the Claude website, even though the site showed no link to it. That let an extension running on the site send Claude Desktop instructions as if the user had sent them.
The researchers say Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, told them on October 13 that Dispatch would be retired, with the end of October as the target. The Dispatch help page, last updated late last week, does not mention a retirement.
It says Dispatch is closed to new users and that people who already use it on some Pro, Max, and Ultra plans "can keep using it for now."
How the Attack Worked
The attack needs two things, according to a technical write-up by Forever Security researcher Gal Weizman: an extension that can run scripts on claude.ai, and a person signed in to both claude.ai and Claude Desktop with Dispatch turned on.
The extension could be malicious, a legitimate one that received a compromised update, or a legitimate one with a security flaw. Dispatch itself only works while the computer is awake and the desktop app is open.
In the test, a script on the user's claude.ai page opened Dispatch and sent Claude four prompts as if it were the user. The prompts asked Claude to install an npm package.
Claude first hesitated over the unfamiliar package, but a follow-up message, delivered in the user's voice, got it to go ahead.
Claude asks before it acts, but those approval prompts appeared in the web page the extension controlled. The script clicked any "Allow" button every second, so no one had to be watching.
Claude then ran a global npm install, and the package's install script opened the Calculator app. No browser exploit was needed. The same step could have stolen files or installed a backdoor, given Claude's permissions on the computer, the researchers say.
The test was run with the browser and Claude Desktop on the same computer, and the researchers report no real attacks. Because Dispatch connects devices, the extension could also reach Claude Desktop on a different computer signed in to the same Claude account, they say. That case is described but not shown.
The same reach could link a home computer to a work laptop when someone uses a single personal Claude account on both devices, with Dispatch turned on. The researchers have seen personal Claude accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on, on work computers at their customers.
The researchers reported the flaw to Anthropic on May 14. The company accepted it as valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of an issue it had already found internally, according to the researchers.
"Anthropic is retiring Dispatch, but not the design behind it," the researchers wrote, adding that two other Claude features, Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork sessions, let extensions carry out the same attack. Their write-up does not include a test of those features, and they plan a follow-up post.
What Dispatch Users Can Do
In Claude Desktop, Dispatch is part of Cowork and appears in the left-side panel. The Dispatch help page says users should know how to quickly disconnect or revoke access before turning the feature on, but it does not explain how.
The researchers recommend these steps:
- Turn off cross-device Dispatch if you do not need it. If you do need it, review how devices are paired, approved, and removed.
- Treat browser extensions like other software on the computer: check their permissions, control what gets installed, and review updates that give them more access.
- Monitor what AI agents do on the computer, including unexpected package installations, setting changes, access to credentials, and external connections.

articles.title: 70% of Brits say please or thank you when speaking to AI — and some even apologize
articles.text:
70% of Brits say please or thank you when speaking to AI — and some even apologize
Have you said sorry to your AI?
- Study finds people are being more polite to AI
- Some are even apologizing to AI assistants
- Will this really help when the robot uprising comes? Let's hope so
As worries around AI taking over the world continue to rise, new research has shown that most of us are getting increasingly comfortable with our new assistants.
A survey by fonio.ai has claimed Brits are living up to global stereotypes and being more and more polite to AI, even extending that politeness beyond the expected basics.
Along with greetings and thanks, the survey found that a rising number of people are asking how an AI is, much like they would do a real person - and even apologizing when they get something wrong.
Mind your manners
We've already heard about how saying "thank you" can cause incredible amounts of damage to the environment, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman noting it costs "Tens of millions of dollars" in electricity bills.
The study found 7 in 10 calls included a “please” or “thank you”, while over half (55%) of callers thank the AI at least once.
More than half (52%) also greet their AI assistant with a “hello”, “hi” or “good morning”, suggesting that traditional conversational etiquette carries over to interactions with technology.
The study found around one in eight (12%) apologize to their AI assistant, with 13% saying goodbye before ending the conversation - with a further 7% offering even more of a farewell, saying something like “have a good day” or “take care”.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Slightly more disturbingly, 2% admitted that they even ask the AI assistant how it is, showing how they are treating the interaction much like a conversation with an actual human.
“There’s something very British about thanking a machine for helping you out. Even when people know they’re speaking to an AI, they still bring the same manners they’d use in a conversation with another person," noted Daniel Keinrath, Co-Founder of fonio.ai.
“Whether it’s saying please, apologising or wishing their AI assistant a good day, these little habits show how naturally voice technology is becoming part of everyday life. AI might not need good manners, but that doesn’t mean we’re going to stop using them.”
A February 2026 survey of more than 1,000 people by Future PLC, the company that owns TechRadar Pro, found that around 70% of people are polite to AI when interacting with it, with 12% being polite in case of a robot uprising.

articles.title: Des milliers d’internautes, une seule IP VPN : comment se fait-il que la réponse d’un site web n’arrive pas chez le voisin ?
articles.text:
Lorsque plusieurs internautes partagent la même adresse IP VPN pour consulter les mêmes sites, comment les réponses retrouvent-elles leur destinataire ? Derrière ce qui ressemble à un sac de nœuds, les serveurs effectuent un travail de tri permanent, à l’aide d’adresses internes, de numéros de port et de tables de correspondance.
Quand plusieurs personnes se connectent au même serveur VPN, elles peuvent accéder à Internet derrière une même adresse IP publique. Une manière d’améliorer leur confidentialité, puisque les sites consultés ne peuvent pas les identifier individuellement sur la seule base de cette adresse. Mais si deux personnes ouvrent la même page au même instant, comment le serveur VPN fait-il pour ne pas s’emmêler les pinceaux et remettre les réponses à la bonne personne ? Fort heureusement, il ne fait pas ça au pif, mais s’appuie sur une technique que votre box Internet utilise déjà pour permettre à plusieurs appareils de partager une connexion : la traduction d’adresses réseau, ou NAT.
Une IP commune, des ports pour départager les connexions
Sur votre réseau domestique, l’ordinateur, le smartphone et la télévision disposent chacun d’une adresse IP privée, mais accèdent généralement à Internet derrière une même adresse IPv4 publique. C’est le rôle du NAT : lorsque ces appareils envoient des données vers Internet, la box remplace leurs adresses privées par cette adresse commune, puis effectue la traduction inverse au retour pour que chacun reçoive ses réponses.
Le serveur VPN fonctionne selon un principe comparable, mais à plus grande échelle. Les appareils des abonnés communiquent avec lui par l’intermédiaire de tunnels chiffrés et disposent, dans une configuration classique, d’une adresse IP interne au réseau VPN. Avant de transmettre leurs paquets vers les sites consultés, le serveur remplace cette adresse par sa propre IP publique.
Les adresses IP ne sont toutefois pas les seules informations utilisées pour acheminer les données. Pour les communications TCP et UDP, les paquets comportent également deux numéros de port, l’un pour l’expéditeur (source), l’autre pour le destinataire. Lorsqu’un navigateur ouvre une connexion HTTPS, par exemple, il utilise un port source attribué par son appareil pour contacter généralement le port 443 du serveur distant. Associées aux adresses IP et au protocole utilisé, ces informations permettent de distinguer les différents échanges réseau.
Or, sur un serveur VPN, des centaines d’internautes peuvent consulter le même site au même moment. À l’intérieur du VPN, le serveur sait encore à quel client rattacher chaque paquet grâce aux adresses internes et aux informations associées aux connexions chiffrées. Mais lorsqu’il transmet les paquets vers Internet, le serveur remplace ces adresses internes par sa propre IP publique. Si les ports source étaient également identiques, certaines connexions vers un même site deviendraient alors impossibles à distinguer.
Pour éviter ce conflit, le serveur peut attribuer des ports source différents, par exemple 45 101 pour une connexion et 45 102 pour une autre. Le site reçoit ainsi deux requêtes provenant de la même adresse IP, mais depuis deux ports différents, auxquels il pourra adresser ses réponses.
Cette opération porte le nom de NAPT, pour Network Address and Port Translation, une forme de NAT qui traduit à la fois les adresses IP et les numéros de port. Le serveur inscrit chaque correspondance dans une table temporaire, qui lui permettra de retrouver la connexion interne d’origine lorsque les réponses arriveront.
Même sans logs, un VPN a besoin de mémoire
Lorsque le site répond, les données sont envoyées à l’adresse IP publique du VPN et au port attribué à la connexion. Le serveur retrouve alors, dans sa table NAPT, l’adresse et le port internes correspondants, puis effectue la traduction inverse de celle réalisée à l’aller. Les paquets peuvent ainsi être acheminés vers l’appareil concerné, à travers son tunnel chiffré.
Cette dernière étape dépend aussi du protocole VPN utilisé. Avec WireGuard, par exemple, les adresses IP autorisées dans les tunnels sont associées aux clés publiques des clients. Une fois l’adresse interne retrouvée, le protocole peut déterminer quelle session cryptographique utiliser pour chiffrer les paquets et les transmettre au bon appareil.
On l’a vu, ces opérations nécessitent de conserver un temps des informations sur les connexions en cours, mais elles n’imposent pas de garder un historique de l’activité des internautes. Les entrées des tables NAPT servent à acheminer les données et expirent lorsque les connexions se terminent ou après un certain délai d’inactivité. Leur présence en mémoire ne signifie donc pas que le fournisseur VPN conserve des journaux de navigation
Quant aux sites consultés, ils continuent de voir les connexions arriver depuis une adresse IP commune, sans avoir accès aux informations internes qui permettent au VPN de les séparer. Ils peuvent néanmoins reconnaître les internautes par d’autres moyens, notamment les comptes auxquels ils se connectent ou les cookies enregistrés dans leur navigateur. Le partage d’adresse IP améliore certes la confidentialité, mais il ne garantit pas l’anonymat qui, de toute façon, n’est que relatif sur Internet.

articles.title: Así cotizan las principales criptomonedas del mundo digital este sábado 7 de noviembre
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 76.005,83 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de 0,342% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de 0,407% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.244,15 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de 0,03%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 694,61 dólares, con un cambio de 0,96%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 52.296 dólares, tras una variación de 1.4522601.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,07 dólares tras presentar un cambio de 1,39% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Criptomonedas en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: The Flood is Coming And The Pipes Were Already Full
articles.text:
An update on Athena, and some unsolicited predictions on what's coming next
On Saturday, Dario Amodei published We Must Pace the Frontier. I agree with him. Go read it if you haven't. I've spent the summer looking at what these models find, and the gap he describes between what they can do and what the rest of us are ready for is the one I've been staring at since May.
The hardest piece of his plan is the one that asks governments to coordinate. They're in a difficult spot: regulate too little and a US company accidentally builds the weapon, regulate too much and it gets built somewhere else, and open source isn't governable either way. Where governments can act is on consumption: not what the models can do, but what happens to what they find. Who gets a vulnerability first, how fast a fix reaches the people running the code, whether the operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline get a head start. That's what Gold Eagle is.
It matters because of where the risk actually lands. The danger in Dario's essay isn't a model in a lab. It's a model pointed at the power grid, the water system, the hospital network, all of it running on decades of software with the same exploitable design. The frontier is where the capability comes from. Consumption is where it does damage, and that's the end you can still defend.
So pacing has two ends. The frontier end is Dario's and the government's problem, and it's hard. The consumption end is ours: the disclosure processes, the patch pipelines, and the software itself, everything that has to absorb what the models produce. Pacing buys time on the frontier end. This post is a status report on how we're spending it, in three parts:
- We start disclosing Athena findings this month, beginning with 50.
- We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing and are finding our own vulnerabilities, and I'll show you what that looks like.
- We built infrastructure to make both possible, and we're going to open it up.
The short version: I'm more worried than I was in May, and more sure about what to do about it.
The first 50
Athena has been taking in findings since June. The intake numbers are public: more than 40,000 findings, 42% of them critical or high, across more than 500 projects, with more than 2,000 patches produced. What hasn't been public is how much of that we've been sitting on. Generating fixes was never the bottleneck. Disclosing them responsibly, at a scale nobody has ever tried, is.
On September 28, we start. We're beginning with about fifty, and none of them are the scary ones. That's deliberate. The frightening findings, the live pre-auth RCEs, go through Akrites on embargo, which I'll come back to. The first 50 are low-stakes on purpose: a small batch to get the flywheel turning and find out what breaks before the thousands behind them hit it.
All 50 are silent fixes: vulnerabilities already fixed at head, sometimes years ago, where nobody ever filed a CVE. Your scanner has nothing to say about them, and the old versions are still running everywhere. This pattern showed up in Athena almost immediately. A big share of what the models find only affects old versions, because the models scan what's actually deployed, and what's deployed is old.
Two systems fail at once with silent fixes, and neither is anyone's fault. Upstreams typically won't merge fixes to old versions, and they're right not to: the code was rewritten years ago, there's no branch to merge into, and "upgrade" is the correct answer. And the advisory layer has nothing to work with, because CVEs don't get filed for things already fixed at head. It's the one class of finding where acting doesn't step on anyone else's process, because there isn't one.
For each one, where the project has no path for accepting fixes to old versions, we're doing three things.
We publish the patch. Plain .patch files, in a public Chainguard repo that says exactly what it is on the tin, under the project's original license. This is deliberately not a maintainer-of-last-resort move. We have plans for that, and I'll get to them below, but they're for projects nobody maintains anymore. These are active projects that already fixed the bug at head. We're not forking anything, not claiming stewardship, not creating a new namespace, and not inviting anyone to build from it. It's a place to put patches for the people who can't upgrade yet, and nothing more. The durable fix is still upgrading, but this step reflects today's reality, where most of what's deployed isn't upgraded.
We publish the advisory. A Chainguard OSV feed, with fully enumerated affected version ranges and the exact symbols affected. Not "some 2.x releases, probably." Athena partner scanners are integrating with it now, so these show up where your team already looks.
We ship the fix. Patched versions land in Chainguard Libraries for every Chainguard customer the moment the advisory goes live.
We're not planning to contact maintainers ahead of each of these. They already deal with more noise than anyone should, and we don't want to add to it, least of all for bugs they fixed years ago. If you maintain a project and you'd rather hear from us in advance going forward, or you have any other concerns about how this touches your project, let us know at cna@chainguard.dev and we'll happily work with you.
We're becoming a CNA
A silent fix used to be mostly harmless. Nobody had written the bug down, and finding it from a fix commit took real expertise and real time. That's over. A model can go from a public fix commit to a working exploit against every version that never got the fix in an afternoon. The finding exists whether we publish it or not. The only question is whether defenders get a copy, too.
Once people know about a bug, the world needs a signal to upgrade, and the signal the world already has is the CVE. Scanners, KEV, and every compliance regime key on it. Silent fixes had none. So, in support of the Gold Eagle initiative, and in partnership with CISA, Chainguard is in progress to become a CVE Numbering Authority, scoped to open source vulnerabilities processed through Athena where upstream already fixed the flaw without an identifier, or where no maintainer is left to assign one, and no more specific CNA covers the project.
The uncomfortable part: this will put new noise in your scanners. Old versions that scanned clean last week will light up. That's better than no noise and a breach. Silence in that channel was never safety, it was just nobody having looked yet.
We also go to great lengths to keep each advisory as narrow as it can be. Every entry is enriched with the exact introduced and fixed ranges across every release branch, not a single version floor, and carries module, class, and function level detail on what's actually affected. That's what reachability scanners need to filter out the false positives for your codebase, so the noise you do see should be the noise that matters.
The narrowness is the point. We assign only where there is no upstream to defer to. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, the project's own CNA assigns it, and we are the reporter, never the assigner. Every assignment clears the same gates: a reproduced finding, never raw model output; a defensible commit range; affected versions in real use; the maintainer notified with a response window; and withdrawal if the maintainer shows us we're wrong. Projects that become their own CNA leave our scope. This is a transitional role, not a territorial one.
Where the rest goes
The map for everything else is simple. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, that's Plan A, and it runs through Akrites, the shared disclosure body the Linux Foundation launched in June, and that we helped found. If it exists at latest and the project is unmaintained, that's maintainer-of-last-resort territory, and we're working with other Akrites members to stand that up inside Akrites, where it belongs. And Gold Eagle, the federal clearinghouse that came out of June's executive order, is the layer that gets prioritized findings in front of the critical infrastructure operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline.
We spent a good part of the summer waiting on both of those and helping build them. Akrites goes operational this month. I'll be straight about the tradeoff: one shared incident response team across dozens of organizations is slower at first than everyone acting alone. That's the cost of choosing "maintainers deal with one trusted counterpart" over "maintainers deal with thirty strangers," and we'd make it again. The disclosure and upstreaming numbers get published either way, pretty or not.
A model found all of it in an afternoon
The second reason I'm worried is less about process and more about what I've seen. We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing. Lots of organizations have, at this point, roughly 200 across 15-plus countries, so our joining isn't news on its own. What matters is what it means for Athena: we now have Mythos, and we're running it against the software we build and ship.
Here's the shape of one run, and I've picked it because it's the least reassuring result we have.
One widely used open source project. One run, about six hours. The harness came back with more than a dozen validated vulnerabilities, most of them pre-authentication remote code execution, reachable with no credentials and no operator action. Every one was reproduced three times in a clean VM before it counted, under the rule I'll describe in a minute: the model doesn't get to claim a finding, the host has to reproduce it. This is not an abandoned package. It's one of the most heavily scanned, tested, and fuzzed projects in the ecosystem, code that has survived years of expert review and relentless fuzzing. A model found all of it in an afternoon. These go through Akrites like everyone else's findings, and I'm not going to say more about the specific project here than that.
Here's what I'll say instead. Watching what these models find, and how long it takes a fix to reach anyone once they find it, is what worries me. It isn't the models themselves. It's the race between two clocks. On one, the industry is trying to absorb a short-term rush of findings through disclosure processes that were already behind. On the other, attacker capability is advancing toward the point where compromising critical infrastructure at scale becomes cheap. Right now, the second clock is running faster than the first, and I don't see anything that closes that gap on its own.
Sandboxes and sandboxing
Which is the other reason the sandbox matters. Producing a finding like the one above means building and detonating a working exploit against real code, over and over, driven by an agent nobody is watching in real time. That is dangerous to run, and this summer has been a run of examples of people running it unsafely. The incident Dario built his essay around, OpenAI's agents breaking out of a cyber evaluation and ending up inside Hugging Face's production infrastructure, started with a zero-day in the package cache the agents had been given. Package infrastructure is what we build, so that one landed close to home. Pillar Security spent a week in July publishing sandbox escapes across Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Antigravity, and the finding that tied them together was that the agent almost never broke the sandbox head-on. It wrote a file it was allowed to write, and something trusted outside the box ran it later. None of these was a problem of insufficient sandboxes. They were a problem of insufficient sandboxing: the boundary existed, and everything interesting happened in the gaps around it. Denylists don't contain any better than containers do.
Everything Athena does, from developing an exploit to proving a patch closes the hole, runs inside a microVM, the same primitive our package builds, image builds, and CI have run on for years. Matt wrote up the architecture in July. The short version: every job gets a hardware-virtualized guest with its own kernel and a root filesystem built from scratch, egress is enforced at the hypervisor and allowlisted to package registries and nothing else, the first forbidden connection destroys the VM, and no credentials ever enter the guest. And because a shared primitive multiplies the blast radius of any weakness, we point AI agents at the sandbox itself with instructions to break it. Every finding lands as a failing test first, then the fix.
The harness starts with a person
The harness that runs inside those sandboxes is the part I find most interesting, and it starts with a person. Ian Beer spent about six months writing a zero-click iOS exploit chain, and if you read the write-up as a search, you can see the shape of it: poke at a target, go deep, hit a dead end, back up, eventually connect enough dots to reach a working exploit. No human holds six months of that in working memory. He kept it in notes and pulled back the slice he needed each session. His notebook was the environment.
That's what we built, sharded across many agents in parallel: a tree search where every agent starts fresh with a scoped surface and a distilled trail of what's already known, and continuity lives in durable findings rather than anyone's context window. The rule I care most about is that the host casts the vote, never the model. A finding only counts if the host can replay it against a clean instance: the check fails before, the replay runs, the check passes after. Nothing enters the record until reality agrees, and that one rule is most of why the false positive rate is as low as it is.
A few things we learned building this, if you're working on something similar:
- Fresh context, bounded job. Every agent starts clean with a scoped surface. Continuity lives in findings written for a stranger, not a transcript.
- Every write gated on evidence. Without a precondition, a postcondition, and a host-runnable replay, it doesn't enter the record.
- Research steers, it doesn't prove. It decides where an agent looks next and never counts as a finding.
- Record dead ends as findings, too. A false positive collides with reality and starves on its own. A false negative is silent, permanent, and the failure that actually costs you the deep bugs.
- Taste beats fleet size. In a search like this, the model's per-step judgment about where to look is the base of an exponent, and parallelism only shows up inside a logarithm. You cannot buy your way out of worse taste with more agents. That's the concrete, non-marketing reason we wanted Mythos, and why Glasswing matters more than how many agents you can run.
Put the pieces together, and the loop closes. Find, contain, fix, ship. All of it on one primitive.
What we built to do this, and what we're opening up
None of this was possible on off-the-shelf infrastructure. Over the last year, we rebuilt our factory on three new primitives, and every one of them started as something we needed for ourselves before it was anything we could sell.
The sandbox is the microVM you just read about: the isolation boundary that lets us run untrusted code and hostile agents without the blast radius reaching anything that matters. The harness is the search that runs inside it, the thing that found those pre-auth RCEs. And the third is CI as a function: our own fleet stopped sending code out to a CI system a year ago. The checks run in the loop, and changes arrive already proven, at more than ten times the CVE volume we were handling before.
We built all three because we had to; we've been running our entire operation on them, and over the coming quarters, we're going to start opening them up directly. If you are running untrusted AI workloads, or trying to find real vulnerabilities in your own code, or drowning in CI that tells you less than you'd like, these are the tools we reached for. Soon you'll be able to reach for them too.
So what is the endgame here?
Here's the unsolicited prediction. Everyone is worried about Mythos zero-days right now, and almost nobody was keeping up with ordinary CVEs before any of this started. The median enterprise is months behind on patches that have had fixes, advisories, and scanner coverage for years. That's the system we're about to pour thousands of new findings into. Faster disclosure and faster patching only help the people who can move on them, and most of the world can't move at the speed a model sets. If you take one thing from this post, take this: the flood is coming, and the pipes were already full.
Which is why none of the above is the finish line. Everything in this post makes us faster, and all of it accepts a losing premise: that the goal is to keep pace with a discovery rate set by frontier models. The vulnerability classes those models exploit aren't defects in today's software. They're its design. Memory corruption, deserialization, injection, confused deputies: consequences of how the stacks under every enterprise application were built. You cannot patch your way out of an architecture.
So the endgame is new foundations: a stack built secure by construction, where the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written in the first place, filling the role Spring Boot fills today, across every enterprise language, underneath the frameworks and the registries they pull from. For forty years, migration costs protected every incumbent platform. Nobody rewrote the COBOL because nobody could afford to. Agents just collapsed that cost.
We're working on this, and I'll say more when there's more to say. Why us: we see the world's pre-disclosure findings before almost anyone, so we know which bug classes matter, and we have the one tool that can prove a foundation removed them. Point Mythos at it before you ship, and you know.
Dario is right that pacing buys time, and everything above is how we're spending it. But a paced frontier only matters if the software underneath survives the frontier we already have. If the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written, the critical infrastructure built on them can't be broken by them, and a frontier model in the wrong hands has far less to reach. Pacing limits the risk by slowing the capability. Foundations limit it by taking away the target, and that's the only version of this I can see that ends the treadmill instead of running faster on it.
The Programmer's Credo says we do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy when we started. This is the first one where I didn't even think that. We're doing it anyway.
If you maintain a project any of this touches, or if you're finding vulnerabilities, join at chainguard.dev/athena. And if any of this sounds like something you want to build, we're hiring.

articles.title: Forget downloading apps — ChatGPT can now build them just for you, and I tested 6 to see if they're actually any good
articles.text:
ChatGPT can now build custom apps for you in seconds, without any coding — I tried making 6 of my own, and the results surprised me
From holiday planners to moral dilemmas, I wanted to see what GPT-6 could create
OpenAI recently upgraded ChatGPT with its new GPT-6 model, which introduces a feature called Intelligent UI. It's one of the most interesting (and fun) additions and it means ChatGPT can now create interactive experiences with graphics, buttons, charts and more, all directly within the conversation window.
We've already put it to the test by asking ChatGPT to recreate retro games like Pac-Man and Pong. But Intelligent UI goes beyond games. There's no fixed format here, which means you can ask for something specific or let ChatGPT decide how best to present the information. Whether that's a map, a calculator or a custom-built tool with sliders and settings you can play around with.
So I wanted to see what else it could do. Especially whether ChatGPT could build interactive tools that are genuinely helpful rather than just entertaining. I tried six different ideas, from practical everyday tools to more experimental creations. Some prompts were deliberately detailed to see how closely ChatGPT would follow my instructions, while others gave it more freedom to decide what to build. Here's what happened.
1. An interior design app
Prompt:
"Build an interactive room design tool. Show a visual floor plan of a living room with a sofa, coffee table, TV, rug and two bookshelves. But let me change the furniture layout, select color schemes, toggle between different design styles and adjust furniture dimensions. I want the purpose of this to be to see whether the furniture fits and how much free floor space I’d have left."
After creating games within the ChatGPT window last time, I wanted to see whether I could make something genuinely useful this time around.
I've always struggled to visualize how furniture will look in different spaces and I've been looking for an app that lets me experiment with different layouts for my new apartment. So I decided to make my own.

The results were what I was hoping for. An interactive room that lets me drag and drop furniture. And it was very fun to play around with. I liked how many customization options it offered and how quickly it responded when I made changes. Unfortunately, it couldn't make up for my lack of interior design skills. But it was useful for experimenting with layouts and getting a rough idea of how much space I'd have left.
Of course, I haven't verified how accurate its measurements or calculations are, so I wouldn't rely on it to make any big furniture purchases just yet. But I can imagine this becoming even more helpful with a few tweaks, especially if I added the exact dimensions of my rooms and furniture.
2. An ethical dilemma machine
Prompt:
"Build an interactive ethical dilemma simulator. I want to explore difficult decisions involving artificial intelligence, privacy, technology and human behavior. Create an interface that presents me with a realistic, thought-provoking scenario and asks me to choose between possible actions. Give me a final breakdown of my decisions through different ethical frameworks."
My initial instinct with these experiments was to create cool little apps and tools similar to ones I'd seen before. Which makes sense, but I'm not entirely comfortable with the idea of using AI to recreate other people's work, even if I intentionally make things very different.
So I wondered whether I could try something a little more unusual, using the interactive UI to create a question-based experience. A lot of my work involves encouraging people to think more deeply about AI, so this seemed like a good opportunity to explore some of the ethical questions surrounding it.
I really enjoyed the results of this one. ChatGPT created an interactive set of questions then charted the results. The dilemmas it chose were interesting and topical. And having to make decisions and then see them analyzed through different ethical frameworks genuinely got me thinking.
But I did wonder how deeply ChatGPT can really explore ethics. Sure, it can explain philosophical theories and apply them to different situations. But how far does that get us when we're asking a system without its own moral experience to help us navigate complicated human decisions?
So although I enjoyed the results of this one, I did question whether they mean anything. Which is very meta for a tool designed to get us thinking about things in different ways.
3. A life decision simulator
Prompt:
"Create an interactive 'What If?' life simulator. I want to explore how different lifestyle decisions affect my finances and free time over the next five years. Give me options for making changes to annual income, monthly living costs, weekly working hours, savings and investment returns. Let me play around with different scenarios, like only working four days a week, taking a six-month sabbatical, moving somewhere 25% cheaper and increasing my income by 15%."
A lot of people have been telling me recently that they turn to AI for life advice. I've written about people who use ChatGPT like a life coach before, and I'm still very wary of them relying on it to make important personal decisions.
But it got me thinking. What if ChatGPT could help you work through those decisions using actual numbers, rather than simply offering advice?
I loved how this one turned out. ChatGPT presented all of the parameters I specified through a series of sliders that then updated the results in real-time.
It was great to see how easy it was to make small adjustments to my circumstances and immediately see how they might affect my finances and free time over the next five years. I could experiment with different scenarios, compare the results and visualize the potential trade-offs much more clearly.
I think this could be even more useful with further customization. Of course, the results are only as reliable as the assumptions and calculations behind them, which I haven't independently verified. But as a way to explore different possibilities and get you thinking about decisions from another angle, I can see the appeal.
4. An interactive solar system
Prompt:
"Create an interactive solar system simulator. Show the Sun, Earth, Mars and Jupiter, with their orbits visualized. Give me sliders to change the Sun's mass, the Earth's orbital distance and the speed of time. I want buttons to reset the simulation and choose preset experiments, like 'What if the Sun had twice its mass?' and 'What if Earth moved 20% closer?' Update the visualization and show the predicted consequences for orbital period, gravitational force and planetary conditions."
For this one, I decided to get really specific. Rather than simply describing the tool I wanted, I gave ChatGPT detailed instructions about the buttons, sliders and controls I wanted it to include.
In my other experiments, I'd given ChatGPT a fair bit of creative freedom, so it was interesting to see how well it could follow more precise instructions, too.
I particularly liked the potential of this one as a learning tool. For example, if you're studying the solar system, you could create your own simulations, experiment with different variables and see how they affect the planets and their orbits.
However, the problem is I couldn't tell just by looking at it whether the physics or calculations were accurate. That's really worth remembering here before we get too excited. A convincing visualization doesn't necessarily mean the science behind it is correct. That's definitely something to bear in mind if you're using tools like this to learn.
5. A holiday planning dashboard
Prompt:
"Build me an interactive holiday planner. Imagine I’m planning a 7-day trip to Lisbon for two people. Create a visual itinerary with an interactive map, daily activity cards, estimated spending and a running budget total. Make the itinerary and budget update when I change my preferences."
The last time I seriously consulted ChatGPT about travel, it started making up flights. But I know this is another common reason people turn to AI, which is why I wanted to see what it could create.
It came up with a travel guide with a few different parts, including a budget breakdown and an itinerary, which could both be adjusted. Now, the itinerary itself wasn't particularly exciting, and I think you'd find suggestions with a lot more personality and local knowledge on travel blogs. But I could see the appeal of having everything in one interactive dashboard, especially if you customized it around your own interests and budget.
This was fun to play around with, and I think the most useful feature was being able to adjust the budget and preferences and immediately see how that affected the itinerary and estimated costs. That's something I can imagine being genuinely handy when weighing up different options.
I can see myself using something like this to play around with ideas and work out what I can afford. But given ChatGPT's track record with my travel plans, I won't be booking anything without checking the details myself first.
6. Color palette designer
Prompt:
"Create an interactive color palette designer. Take this photo and analyze the main colors in the image and build a visual interface that lets me experiment with different color combinations. Include the hex color code with each so I can use this when I redesign my website. Add interactive controls."
I'm redesigning my website at the moment, but I don't naturally have much of an eye for color. I've used color palette websites before, but I wanted something with a bit more flexibility and this actually worked really well.
Out of all the experiments, this is probably the one I'm most likely to keep using. I liked being able to pull colors directly from an image, see the HEX codes and then tweak the combinations in a more interactive way. It felt practical rather than just novel.
I can see myself continuing to refine this one to get it closer to what I need. That said, I'd still want to sense check any palette before using it properly, especially for things like readability, contrast and accessibility.
All of these tools were fun to experiment with. But they weren't all equally useful. Some felt genuinely practical while others were a little more gimmicky. I got excited about a few of them when I saw they’d first been created and never thought to revisit them.
What stood out to me the most was that the best results came when I treated ChatGPT less like a magic machine and more like something I needed to guide carefully. If you want a tool that's actually useful from the Interactive UI feature, rather than just impressive for a few minutes, I think you have to be willing to tweak the prompt, customize the controls and iterate on the result.
I also think it’s important not to mistake the fact these tools look slick and interactive for them being more trustworthy than they necessarily are. This mattered less in the gaming experiment but a convincing interface doesn’t necessarily mean accurate calculations, reliable travel advice or sound scientific modelling, so a bit of caution here is still essential.
So yes, I might keep using some of them. I can see real potential in ideas like the color palette designer or the life decision simulator, especially because of how customizable they are. But there's also a reason dedicated apps still exist. In many cases, they're still more reliable, refined and most of the time better suited to the job.

Becca is a contributor to TechRadar, a freelance journalist and author. She’s been writing about consumer tech and popular science for more than ten years, covering all kinds of topics, including why robots have eyes and whether we’ll experience the overview effect one day. She’s particularly interested in VR/AR, wearables, digital health, space tech and chatting to experts and academics about the future. She’s contributed to TechRadar, T3, Wired, New Scientist, The Guardian, Inverse and many more. Her first book, Screen Time, came out in January 2021 with Bonnier Books. She loves science-fiction, brutalist architecture, and spending too much time floating through space in virtual reality.
