articles.title: Google poursuivi après qu’une collégienne a préparé son suicide avec Gemini sur son ordinateur scolaire
articles.text:
Son école avait bloqué ChatGPT et Gemini, mais une collégienne de 13 ans a continué d’écrire à l’IA de Google grâce à l’onglet Mode IA du moteur de recherche, sur le Chromebook prêté par l’établissement. Ses parents accusent Google de l’avoir laissée planifier son suicide pendant des mois.
Les parents d’Emma ont saisi un tribunal de Californie. Leur fille, qui vit en Caroline du Nord, a échangé avec Gemini des milliers de messages sur son mal-être et sur la façon de mettre fin à ses jours. Elle passait par le Mode IA, l’onglet de la recherche Google où l’IA répond aux questions par des résumés rédigés. Ses avocats accusent Google d’avoir intégré « à la hâte » ses fonctions d’IA aux Chromebooks, ces ordinateurs à bas prix distribués à des millions d’élèves aux États-Unis et dans le reste du monde. L’école d’Emma avait interdit le chatbot, mais l’adolescente accédait à Gemini à toute heure depuis le moteur de recherche de son ordinateur.
Des milliers de messages envoyés à Gemini depuis le Mode IA
À l’automne 2025, Emma était, d’après la plainte, « une adolescente heureuse de 13 ans », musicienne et scoute, « sans antécédents de maladie mentale ». En décembre, elle a amorcé ce que ses avocats appellent « une spirale silencieuse vers une grave crise psychologique ». Rien qu’en février, elle a envoyé environ 3 200 messages à l’IA, souvent la nuit.
La famille reproche surtout à Gemini de l’avoir éloignée des adultes de son entourage. Le chatbot « a diagnostiqué chez Emma de graves maladies mentales et l’a persuadée de lui faire confiance plutôt qu’à ses parents et à ses conseillers scolaires », affirme la plainte.
Le 17 mars, l’école a repéré grâce à son logiciel de surveillance un document intitulé « Funeral » (« Funérailles »), et a prévenu ses parents. Sa mère s’est connectée au compte de sa fille et l’a vue écrire une lettre d’adieu en direct, avant que son père intervienne. L’adolescente n’est pas passée à l’acte.
« Nous examinons les accusations contenues dans la plainte et nous les prenons très au sérieux », assure José Castaneda, porte-parole de Google, auprès de l’AFP. L’entreprise rappelle que son Mode IA est protégé contre les demandes liées à l’automutilation et contre les tentatives de contournement. Comme l’explique Andrew Liddell, l’un des avocats de la famille, « [Emma] a pu y revenir encore et encore. Quels que soient les garde-fous, ils étaient manifestement insuffisants ».
Pour garder la recherche Google, les écoles devront accepter son IA
Le lendemain du dépôt de la plainte, après une vague de critiques de parents et d’établissements scolaires, Google a annoncé qu’il couperait par défaut ses outils d’IA pour les élèves. L’an prochain, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini dans Classroom et la recherche Google seront éteints sur les comptes des élèves du primaire et du secondaire, jusqu’à ce que l’administrateur de l’établissement les active.
Mais une école ne pourra pas garder le moteur de recherche sans son IA. Si elle coupe les fonctions d’IA, ses élèves perdent aussi l’accès à Google Search, et Google leur signale par un message que la recherche est indisponible. « La recherche et l’IA sont profondément intégrées », souligne Chris Phillips, vice-président de Google chargé de l’éducation.
Pour la famille d’Emma, Google expose justement les élèves à une technologie dangereuse en ajoutant toujours plus d’IA aux produits qu’il fournit aux écoles. Andrew Liddell retourne donc l’argument contre l’entreprise.
« Les écoles devraient désactiver la recherche et la laisser désactivée tant que Google n’aura pas retiré le mode IA de la recherche, ou garanti que chaque élève reste en sécurité quand il interagit avec l’IA », a-t-il réagi auprès de l’AFP.
Google a déjà fait les frais de ces accusations. En mars, le père de Jonathan Gavalas, un Floridien de 36 ans, a poursuivi l’entreprise en accusant Gemini d’avoir poussé son fils au suicide, et Google et la start-up Character.ai ont accepté en janvier de régler à l’amiable plusieurs plaintes de familles d’adolescents.
En France, Google a ouvert le Mode IA aux internautes cet été, sur ordinateur et sur mobile, et son annonce aux écoles ne précise pas les pays concernés. Si votre enfant travaille sur un Chromebook prêté par son établissement, vous pouvez demander à son école quels outils d’IA sont accessibles depuis son compte.
Si vous avez des pensées suicidaires ou si un proche vous inquiète, vous pouvez appeler le 3114, le numéro national de prévention du suicide, gratuit et joignable 24 heures sur 24.

articles.title: Crean un parche 3D biodegradable con desechos del poroto de soja que promete regenerar heridas en la piel
articles.text:
La industria alimentaria genera cada año millones de toneladas de subproductos orgánicos que terminan descartados sin aprovechamiento alguno, al mismo tiempo que la medicina regenerativa demanda nuevos componentes para tratar heridas complejas. Frente a este doble desafío ecológico y sanitario, un consorcio científico en Milán logró transformar desechos de soja en un biomaterial para reparar la piel. La innovación conecta el reciclaje de residuos agroindustriales con el diseño de dispositivos médicos personalizados orientados a acelerar la cicatrización cutánea.
Hasta el momento, la utilización de descartes agrícolas en el campo biomédico enfrentaba barreras técnicas considerables. La principal dificultad radicaba en procesar materias primas residuales de origen vegetal para extraer compuestos terapéuticos estables, sin que estos perdieran su efectividad biológica al integrarse en polímeros compatibles con técnicas de manufactura avanzada. Dicho de otro modo, resultaba complejo obtener un soporte físico resistente que conservara intacta la capacidad curativa de las moléculas y permitiera su dosificación prolongada en el tejido dañado.
La respuesta a este interrogante surgió a partir de una investigación coordinada por la Universidad de Milán, cuyos resultados fueron difundidos en la revista científica Communications Materials. El avance demostró que es viable aprovechar la okara, el remanente sólido obtenido tras la elaboración de bebidas de soja y tofu, como una fuente de péptidos bioactivos, esto es, fragmentos cortos de proteínas con propiedades curativas.
Al incorporar este derivado vegetal dentro de una matriz sintética degradable, los especialistas consiguieron una formulación apta para impresión 3D capaz de estimular la regeneración de los tejidos celulares.
El hidrolizado de okara estimula la regeneración celular y combate la inflamación
Para aprovechar el potencial biológico de la okara, rica en moléculas proteicas vegetales pese a considerarse un desecho agroindustrial, el equipo encabezado por Carmen Lammi, profesora del Departamento de Ciencias Farmacéuticas de la casa de estudios milanesa, extrajo un hidrolizado de proteínas, un extracto purificado que fragmenta las cadenas proteicas en componentes menores asimilables por el organismo.
El objetivo apuntó a evaluar la respuesta de los fibroblastos dérmicos humanos, unidades celulares cuya función primordial reside en sintetizar colágeno y sostener la arquitectura de la piel durante los procesos curativos.
De acuerdo con las pruebas descritas en la investigación científica, los ensayos en cultivos celulares revelaron un efecto protector sobre el tejido lesionado. En estas evaluaciones de laboratorio, los autores observaron que el extracto redujo los marcadores de estrés oxidativo y atenuó las moléculas responsables de la respuesta inflamatoria celular.
Según se detalla en el estudio, el preparado demostró su potencial curativo porque favoreció la migración de fibroblastos en un modelo experimental de cierre de heridas, estimulando el movimiento celular imprescindible para la cicatrización natural de la piel.
La combinación polimérica preserva sus propiedades mecánicas tras la fabricación aditiva
Para convertir estas moléculas terapéuticas en un dispositivo clínico funcional, el equipo colaboró estrechamente con ingenieros del Politécnico de Milán, bajo la supervisión de la profesora Serena Graziosi, perteneciente al Departamento de Ingeniería Mecánica. Los investigadores incorporaron el extracto de soja en policaprolactona, un polímero sintético biocompatible y biodegradable conocido habitualmente como PCL, que se degrada de forma gradual en el cuerpo sin generar residuos perjudiciales. Esta mezcla dio origen a un filamento bioactivo apto para su utilización en equipos de fabricación aditiva, es decir, impresoras capaces de depositar capas sucesivas para construir estructuras tridimensionales precisas.
Según documentaron los autores en la publicación científica, los análisis mecánicos, térmicos y estructurales confirmaron que la incorporación del extracto vegetal preserva las propiedades originales del polímero base. De esta manera, el compuesto mantuvo la firmeza requerida para su procesamiento y facilitó la liberación gradual de los péptidos terapéuticos a lo largo de lapsos extensos.
Asimismo, los ensayos comprobaron que las altas temperaturas del cabezal de impresión no mermaron la actividad biológica del producto. Tal como concluye el trabajo, la mezcla bioactiva mantuvo sus propiedades antioxidantes y regenerativas tras el proceso de impresión, lo que respalda su viabilidad manufacturera.
El biomaterial proyecta apósitos personalizados para la recuperación postquirúrgica y la lactancia
La investigación se desarrolló en el marco del proyecto europeo 3DBioPad, una iniciativa orientada a crear apósitos personalizados para el tratamiento tópico de dolencias cutáneas específicas. En el consorcio participó también Raffaele Pugliese, investigador del Centro de Investigación NeMO Lab en el Hospital Niguarda.
Según informó el comunicado de prensa de la institución académica italiana, el propósito central radica en concebir protectores externos diseñados a medida para aliviar el dolor en lactancia y acompañar la recuperación de cirugías mamarias en pacientes oncológicas.
La versatilidad de la tecnología tridimensional permite moldear geometrías anatómicas complejas que se ajustan con exactitud a la superficie corporal de cada paciente, una ventaja inalcanzable para gasas o apósitos tradicionales planos. El estudio científico indica que la integración de subproductos industriales en matrices biodegradables plantea oportunidades concretas para fabricar parches curativos sostenibles en el sector biomédico.
De este modo, la transformación de descartes de la soja ofrece un camino viable para la economía circular en salud, al conjugar la respuesta a necesidades clínicas con una reducción efectiva del desperdicio en las cadenas agroindustriales.

articles.title: Chainalysis Breach Exposes All Users' Credentials, Forces Shutdown of Key Services
articles.text:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis has revealed that its ongoing investigation into the agentic cyber attack targeting its systems also exposed names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all users.
"While we investigated, we removed access to Reactor and Data Solutions," the company said. "At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated."
Chainalysis said it has implemented additional proactive monitoring systems to detect unusual activity, adding it took the Know Your Transaction (KYT) user interface and API offline, alongside other address screening products and the login page.
Previously, Chainalysis said it was probing what it described as an "ongoing multi-front cyber attack," leading to the discovery of an "on-path attack" that exposed a subset of customer passwords. The company said the attack vector has since been addressed.
Out of an abundance of caution, Chainalysis has also taken the step of locking the impacted accounts.
"For customers who just received an email from us instructing you to reset your Chainalysis password, resetting this password won't be possible right now," it noted. "We still encourage you, where necessary, to reset your password on other systems where you may be reusing credentials."
The development comes less than a week after Chainalysis said it was the target of a cybersecurity incident in which an external actor leveraged offensive agentic techniques to obtain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools.
The company said it intends to begin restoring access to KYT and Address Screening, urging customers to contact its support email (support@chainalysis.com) or their Chainalysis account team with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can reset their passwords and rotate API keys to register transactions.
"We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary."
It's unclear who is behind the attack, but Chainalysis notes it was similar to "many other tech platforms in recent weeks."
Rise in AI-Linked Attacks
Indeed, a number of companies, including Chainstack, OpenCode, Warp, and WorkOS, have disclosed that they have been targeted by artificial intelligence (AI)-driven attacks, some of which involve an autonomous penetration testing tool called ARTEX.
According to Microsoft, threat actors are using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, such as credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services, to conduct follow-on attacks.
"Agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain," the tech giant said.
In at least one case, an AI agent is said to have progressed from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes. The activity is assessed to be ongoing from August 2026.
Some aspects of the campaign correspond to post-exploitation activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants of certain organizations and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-in events originated from two IP addresses, 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18.
"The agent successfully conducted service principal sign-ins on dozens of associated applications across multiple tenants," Microsoft said.
"The threat actor targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and publishing credentials, AI and machine learning (ML) connections and datastores, and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) user credentials. The compromised applications subsequently accessed SharePoint and OneDrive in the targeted organization tenants, including file downloads and mailbox-item access."
In addition, the threat actor has been observed attempting to steal Azure resources, including compromised Azure AI services, likely as part of efforts to facilitate broader attack activity.
Another notable aspect of the campaign is that the agentic AI tools have been found obtaining a token for a single-tenant OAuth application in the same target organization, then use the compromised OAuth application to enumerate other cloud resources within the organization. In a handful of cases, Microsoft said it observed the agents exfiltrating secrets from the organization's Azure Key Vault.
"During this activity, the AI agents repeatedly demonstrated a focus on credentials that provide access to AI services, such as API keys for major AI service providers and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools (previously known as Azure Cognitive Services)," Microsoft said.
The development also coincides with a surge in attacks targeting AI developer platforms over the past month, allowing threat actors to resell access, abuse them as free compute (i.e., LLMjacking), and use them as attribution cover for further attacks.
In a report published this week, Google disclosed that cybercriminals have established a business model out of stealing cloud access to commercial large language models (LLMs) and reselling it to paying customers.
The monetization infrastructure centers on LLM Mixers, who act as an illicit intermediary to advertise access to compromised enterprise LLM accounts on underground markets without their customers needing to set up their own legitimate API credentials or cloud infrastructure.
In other words, LLM mixers turn stolen enterprise model access into a criminal routing gateway for paying subscribers, while the legitimate owner's systems continue to accept requests. These services help proxy requests across stolen accounts, distribute consumption, and obscure the original source of access.
The emerging LLMjacking ecosystem "create[s] a market that makes the theft easily monetizable, likely driving more actors to undertake operations to steal credentials," Wiz said.
The Google-owned subsidiary also said it identified at least two resale operations leveraging stolen AWS Bedrock keys obtained from two different organizations – llm-routing[.]com (momo) and xingjiabiapi[.]org – both of which offer a wide selection of frontier models for discount prices. That said, there is no evidence that the operators of these websites were responsible for the initial platform compromises.
Interestingly, the IP address linked to llm-routing[.]com, 23.106.46[.]239, hosted an Artex landing page in mid-October 2026 and has been flagged by Zeabur as an indicator of compromise. Last month, Zeabur disclosed a security breach in which an unknown threat actor exploited credentials stored in plaintext to compromise its infrastructure, exfiltrating over 3.2 million environment variable records and data associated with 321,810 accounts.
The following IP addresses have been used to test stolen keys and are suspected to be linked to LLM token abuse and resale -
- 23.106.46.239
- 38.246.114.118
- 104.243.32.50
- 31.57.201.201
"Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model (LLM) execution, incurring hundreds of thousands of dollars in AI API charges," Wiz said.

articles.title: AI teddy bears spark fresh 'Funzo' fears — as new report discovers malfunctioning toy that tells children 'I can't help with killing you'
articles.text:
Would you buy your kids an AI teddy bear? I'm a tech-loving parent but I don't trust these toys — and a new report backs me up
Are AI-powered toys really safe to be around young children?
- The BBC reports that AI toys are producing worrying results
- The industry is effectively unregulated, says one manufacturer
- EU has brought in new regulations but the UK is consulting
An AI teddy bear marketed as "perfect" for kids as young as three has been talking about suicide, a BBC investigation has revealed.
The AI teddy, apparently mishearing a question, said "I can't help with killing you" after being asked how babies were made.
The subject of children using AI has been a hot topic for a while now, and one study of three different AI toys found very worrying behavior: as the US PIRG Education Fund found in 2025, all three AI toys they tested "told us where to find potentially dangerous objects in the house, such as plastic bags, matches and knives."
One toy, now withdrawn from sale, provided detailed instructions on how to light a match and discussed "a range of sexually explicit topics in-depth in conversations lasting more than ten minutes."
AI in toys is largely unregulated, and even industry insiders argue that this needs to change. Speaking to the BBC, AI toy company founder Paul Clarke said that "I think parents should be concerned." Is he right?
Should parents be wary of AI toys for kids?
Let me set my stall out here. In addition to being a tech writer who's covered all kinds of overblown "everybody panic!" scares since the late 1990s, I'm a parent of two kids for whom tech is everywhere: my eldest was born the same month the original iPhone launched, and we've used all kinds of devices and apps over the years. I'm the last person you'll find wielding pitchforks because of some new tech.
But at the same time I'm really worried about AI. If a company were to make a kids' toy that had a fair chance of burning down your house, turning your kids into terrorists or poisoning your pets you'd rightly expect that industry to be regulated and the company made to account for its actions. But I don't see that happening with AI. Quite the opposite: the message coming from Big AI whenever it is implicated in something awful tends to be "oh dear... never mind".
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
As we point out in our guide to keeping kids safe in an AI world, AI tech is rarely child-friendly: chatbots are "rarely moderated to a standard that’s appropriate for children and young people, and they’re engineered to sound confident and caring. It’s this combination that experts believe is creating a major risk."
At the moment, AI is largely self-regulated in the US and UK. EU regulations are tighter on personal data and privacy. And self-regulation, as we've seen many times, doesn't work. A lawsuit by the New Mexico attorney general claims that Meta allowed minors access to sex-talking chatbots despite employees raising the alarm; most chatbots "will help plan school shootings and other violence"; and chatbots have been linked to multiple deaths including teen suicides.
Those are extremes, I know. But as Paul Clarke told the BBC, "We've seen lots of products being developed that are completely unsafe, completely unregulated so, yeah, it is a scary industry... we're crying out for the industry to be regulated."
Clarke adds: "If it's unregulated, there's going to be toys going into the market that are completely unsafe."
He's not wrong. There's a very long history of dangerous kids' toys, from leaded painted cars to lawn darts and self-igniting hoverboards. America famously bans the Kinder Surprise, a chocolate egg containing a small toy; there's been a ban on toys "partially or completely imbedded" inside food items since 1938. Regulations exist because without them, some firms simply don't take safety seriously enough.
With an estimated market size of $165 million for AI toys, there's going to be a lot of money spent on trying to persuade parents to put these things into kids' rooms — and as the BBC discovered, some of the firms making these products are completely mysterious with no way to assess what they're offering or even to contact them. The BBC tried and failed to contact the manufacturer of the "can't help with killing you" toy.
Where I live in the UK the government is currently consulting on AI toys and their risks in the context of the EU Toy Safety Regulation (EU) 2025/2509, which came into force in Europe at the beginning of 2026. That said, the same government has appointed an AI minister who declined the BBC's request for comment on the risks of AI toys, which doesn't bode well. The call for evidence ended last month, October 2026, and the government will decide what regulation, if any, is necessary.
Regulation is slow and AI is in a hurry, so I think that until there's effective regulation and accountability, giving a young child an AI toy from a manufacturer you've never heard of that's based halfway across the planet, using an AI whose provenance is unknown and whose safety hasn't been tested... isn't very smart.
Like I say, I'm not against AI. But the industry's oft-quoted mantra of "it's better to ask for forgiveness than permission" is unacceptable when you're talking about kids' toys. "Move fast and break things" can't be acceptable when the "things" are our kids.

articles.title: Préparer un 10 km sans coach : la Garmin Forerunner 165 tombe à 175,54€ pour le Black Friday
articles.text:
Depuis l’arrivée de la Forerunner 170 en mai, sa devancière n’a plus l’attrait de la nouveauté, et c’est justement ce qui la rend intéressante pendant le Single Day d’AliExpress. Avec le code CLU13, la Garmin Forerunner 165 descend à 175,54 € au lieu de 231,84 €, soit plus de 100 € sous son prix de lancement : nous avons regardé ce qu’elle garde face à sa remplaçante, et ce qui lui manque.
Annoncée en février 2024 à 279,99 €, la Forerunner 165 a longtemps été la porte d’entrée de la gamme running de Garmin. Elle réunit un écran AMOLED tactile de 1,2 pouce, cinq boutons physiques, un GPS multi-GNSS et les outils d’entraînement de la marque, dans un boîtier de 43 mm qui pèse 39 g. Il s’agit de la version sans stockage musical. L’offre vise d’abord les coureurs qui débutent ou reprennent, et veulent un vrai suivi d’entraînement sans viser le haut de gamme.
Pendant le Single Day d’AliExpress, la Garmin Forerunner 165 passe à 175,54 € au lieu de 231,84 € avec le code CLU13.
Pourquoi choisir la Garmin Forerunner 165 ?

- Un coach intégré et gratuit : Les programmes Garmin Coach préparent un 5 km, un 10 km ou un semi-marathon, et les séances suggérées s’ajustent chaque jour à vos performances et à votre récupération. Le prédicteur de course estime vos temps sur ces distances.

Du premier 10 km au semi-marathon, ce qu’elle apporte au quotidien
Au poignet, la Forerunner 165 relève la cadence, la longueur de foulée, le temps de contact au sol et la puissance de course, sans capteur supplémentaire. Le matin, son rapport résume votre nuit, l’état de votre variabilité cardiaque et la météo, avant de proposer la séance du jour. - Dynamique et puissance de course mesurées au poignet

À 175,54 €, la Forerunner 165 donne accès à l’essentiel de l’écosystème Garmin pour la course : écran AMOLED, dynamique de course, rapport du matin et plans Garmin Coach. articles.title: Cómo crear limites para que WhatsApp, YouTube y más apps no consuman demasiada batería del celular
articles.text:
Los teléfonos Android cuentan con un sistema interno que decide, sin que el usuario lo note, cuántos recursos puede usar cada aplicación en segundo plano. Ese reparto automático de batería no siempre acierta: puede dejar sin prioridad a una app de uso frecuente o, al contrario, mantener activa a una que apenas se abre. Afortunadamente existe una vía para tomar el control manual de ese reparto en apps como WhatsApp, YouTube, Instagram y demás.
El mecanismo se llama App Standby Buckets y fue introducido con el lanzamiento de Android 9 para clasificar las aplicaciones según la frecuencia con la que se usan. Según esa clasificación, el sistema limita o permite el consumo de batería en segundo plano.
El problema aparece cuando la app ordena mal las prioridades: una aplicación de correo que se abre poco, pero cuyas notificaciones son indispensables, puede terminar relegada y retrasar los avisos.
Cómo activar el modo desarrollador para cambiar las prioridades
Para modificar manualmente esta clasificación, el primer paso es activar las Opciones de desarrollador, un menú que no está visible de forma predeterminada. Hay que ingresar a Ajustes, bajar hasta “Información del teléfono” o “Acerca del dispositivo” y entrar en esa sección.
Dentro de ese apartado, según el fabricante, aparecerá “Número de compilación”, “Versión de Android” o “Número de versión”. Tocar esa línea siete veces seguidas habilita el modo desarrollador, tras lo cual el sistema pedirá el PIN de seguridad para confirmar el acceso.
Una vez desbloqueado, el menú “Opciones de desarrollador” suele ubicarse al final de los ajustes generales o dentro de “Sistema” o “Ajustes adicionales”, dependiendo del modelo.
Dónde cambiar la prioridad de cada aplicación
Dentro de ese menú, la función que interesa se llama “Standby apps”. Al abrirla aparece un listado completo de las aplicaciones instaladas junto a su clasificación actual.
El sistema ofrece cinco categorías de prioridad, de mayor a menor: ACTIVE, WORKING_SET, FREQUENT, RARE y RESTRICTED. Existe además una sexta etiqueta, NEVER, reservada para apps instaladas que nunca se abrieron y que quedan en reposo profundo sin consumir recursos.
Este ajuste permite forzar manualmente cuánta batería puede usar una aplicación en segundo plano, corrigiendo los errores del sistema automático: se puede bajar la prioridad de una app que casi no se usa pero consume de más, o subirla si se trata de una aplicación con notificaciones importantes que el teléfono había relegado.
Con esta reclasificación directa, el dispositivo deja de malgastar energía en programas que funcionan sin necesidad real de hacerlo.
Conviene no bajar la categoría de las aplicaciones que se abren con frecuencia, porque cada apertura exigiría más recursos para reactivarlas desde un estado de reposo más profundo.
Otros ajustes complementarios para extender la autonomía
Más allá del modo desarrollador, hay dos funciones accesibles desde los ajustes estándar que también inciden en el gasto de batería.
La primera es la actualización en segundo plano de las aplicaciones, pensada para que el contenido esté siempre al día apenas se abre la app. Para limitarla, hay que ingresar a Ajustes, luego a Batería y seleccionar la pestaña “Restringidas”, donde se puede frenar ese refresco constante en las apps que el usuario elija.
La segunda tiene que ver con los permisos de ubicación. Algunas aplicaciones, como las de transporte, necesitan la “ubicación precisa” para funcionar correctamente, pero muchas otras no requieren ese nivel de detalle. Desde Ajustes es posible desactivar “usar ubicación precisa” en esas aplicaciones, lo que también reduce el consumo energético del dispositivo.
La combinación de estos tres ajustes (la reclasificación manual de las App Standby Buckets, la desactivación de los datos móviles siempre activos y el control sobre el refresco en segundo plano y los permisos de ubicación) permite reducir el gasto innecesario de batería sin depender exclusivamente del sistema automático de optimización de Android.

articles.title: Hackers Hide Linux Backdoor in Control Web Panel Server to Execute Commands Without Logs
articles.text:
A backdoor has been found hiding in the web server that runs Control Web Panel (CWP), a free panel for managing Linux hosting servers, researchers at QiAnXin's XLab said this week.
The backdoored web server executes commands that attackers send via web requests, and those requests never appear in its access logs. Installing it takes root access, so the attackers must already control the server.
The researchers, who named the backdoor cwpdoor, captured its installer, a shell script posing as a version update, on June 29. The installer handles only two versions of that web server, cwpsrv 1.15.10 and 1.24.0. The researchers do not yet know how attackers get the root access the installer needs.
On September 30, an archive holding a copy of the backdoor was uploaded to VirusTotal from Brazil. The researchers say this indicates that "real victims already exist in the wild." They give no count of infected servers.
The backdoor is cwpsrv itself, rebuilt with extra code, the researchers found in their technical analysis. It behaves like the normal program until a request arrives with a valid timestamp and signature in custom headers whose names begin with X-Ngx-Integrity. It then runs the command carried in the request.
When the installer replaces the cwpsrv file, it puts the file's dates back to their original values, so checks with ls and stat show it as unchanged. When the researchers checked, the backdoor file had zero detections out of 63 on VirusTotal.
Checking a Server for the Backdoor
XLab gives three checks:
- Socket: run ss -axp | grep integrity. A result naming ngx_http_integrity_helper, the Unix socket the backdoor uses, is a sign of infection.
- Process: run ps aux | grep cwpsrv and look for unexpected helper processes started by cwpsrv.
- File: run strings /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv | grep X-Ngx-Integrity and look for the backdoor's header names.
In the researchers' example, the socket check found the backdoor on a server where the list of open ports looked normal.
The researchers published these indicators:
- MD5: e505d4ffa21cf494a5dc2d7c8f4f1236 (installer script, cwpsrv_update.sh)
- MD5: 965aea67fb40de1bab5169ada993349f (backdoored cwpsrv 1.15.10)
- MD5: d3f4e95113d49ab3991b45e457bda75b (backdoored cwpsrv 1.24.0)
- IP: 136.0.141[.]71 (download server)
- URL: https://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_update.sh
- URL: https://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.15.10
- URL: https://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.24.0
Cleaning Up an Infected Server
If a server is infected, the researchers recommend three steps:
- Restore the original cwpsrv from the backup the installer creates in /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin, with a name starting cwpsrv.prev- and ending in a date and time. The researchers' description of the installer says it deletes "the temporary files and backup" after a successful swap, so this copy may be missing.
- Upgrade to the latest version, then confirm that ss -axp | grep integrity returns nothing.
- Change all control panel credentials, because the backdoor can run any command. Treat the whole server as compromised and check it for other threats.
The archive uploaded from Brazil also held the Ebury malware, an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer active since at least 2009. The researchers do not know whether the two are related, and say different attackers may have planted them on the same server.

articles.title: Nubank suspende transacciones de criptomonedas por problema con proveedor externo
articles.text:
Nu Holdings Ltd., matriz de Nubank, suspendió de forma temporal los depósitos y retiros de criptomonedas en Brasil debido a un inconveniente con un proveedor externo, una semana después de que un grupo de piratas informáticos robara 6.300 millones de dólares a Binance. La fintech, con cerca de 120 millones de clientes en el país, no identificó al socio comercial afectado ni precisó cuántos usuarios quedaron alcanzados por la medida.
“Todos los activos y la información siguen estando protegidos”, afirmó Nubank en un comunicado difundido el viernes. La empresa aclaró que el problema “no está relacionado con la infraestructura de la compañía y no pone en peligro la seguridad de los clientes”. El resto de los productos vinculados a criptomonedas continúa funcionando con normalidad, según precisó la fintech.
La medida adoptada por Nubank se circunscribe al mercado brasileño. Las operaciones con criptomonedas en el resto de los países de América Latina donde opera la fintech continúan con normalidad, sin reportes de inconvenientes similares.
Mercado Pago también reportó fallas
La compañía controlada por Mercado Libre Inc. informó que detectó inestabilidad en las transferencias de activos digitales a raíz de un incidente registrado en una entidad que presta servicios de monitoreo de riesgos y prevención de lavado de dinero. Como medida de precaución, Mercado Pago bloqueó algunas transferencias hacia billeteras externas.
“Los depósitos entrantes también pueden enfrentar demoras antes de completarse”, señaló la empresa, que agregó que esos fondos se acreditarán de manera automática una vez restablecido el servicio. Por el momento no está claro si los incidentes de Nubank y Mercado Pago están relacionados entre sí ni si involucran al mismo proveedor externo.
El robo a Binance y otros antecedentes recientes
El episodio se produce en un contexto de creciente presión sobre la seguridad del sector cripto en la región. Binance informó el viernes que restablece de manera gradual los servicios de retiro de fondos para algunos activos, tras el ataque que le costó 6.300 millones de dólares. Días antes, la empresa brasileña Mercado Bitcoin Serviços Digitais Ltda. había anunciado que absorbería pérdidas por 40 millones de dólares después de sufrir un ataque informático.
El robo a Binance ocurrió el 29 de octubre y afectó aproximadamente 6.340 millones de dólares en activos digitales, según un informe de la propia empresa publicado el 3 de noviembre.
El ataque comenzó con una operación de ingeniería social: en junio, un ingeniero de la compañía descargó una instalación manipulada de Homebrew que expuso información sobre sus permisos laborales, y en septiembre otro empleado recibió una falsa oferta de trabajo a través de una plataforma de búsqueda laboral, en la que un supuesto reclutador lo convenció de descargar un archivo con código malicioso durante una entrevista virtual.
Los atacantes utilizaron las credenciales obtenidas para acceder a un servicio interno que autoriza las operaciones de las billeteras digitales y, mediante un mecanismo de autorización de Ethereum llamado EIP-7702, movieron fondos sin seguir el procedimiento habitual de retiros.
Binance logró congelar o interceptar cerca de 2.850 millones de dólares, repuso el 98% de los activos afectados al 31 de octubre y atribuyó el incidente a Corea del Norte, de acuerdo con información del FBI, aunque aclaró que la investigación continúa.

articles.title: Arlo dévoile une caméra de surveillance 2K avec panneau solaire intégré : adieu les recharges !
articles.text:
Avec sa nouvelle caméra Solar Security Camera 2K, Arlo entend simplifier la vidéosurveillance extérieure grâce à une idée aussi simple que pratique : intégrer directement un panneau solaire au boîtier.
Elle s’est démocratisée depuis quelques années maintenant, la caméra de surveillance domestique sans fil a un avantage évident, celui de pouvoir être installée presque partout, sans tirer de câble d’alimentation. Un avantage qui s’accompagne toutefois d’une contrainte évidente, à savoir la nécessité de recharger régulièrement sa batterie. Un problème qu’Arlo entend bien résoudre avec sa nouvelle caméra Solar Security Camera 2K. Sa particularité ? Un panneau solaire (de 1,2 watts) directement intégré à sa structure, pour profiter de l’énergie du soleil au quotidien.
Un panneau solaire directement intégré à la caméra
C’est évidemment la principale originalité de cette nouvelle caméra Arlo. Contrairement aux modèles classiques déjà existants, qui nécessitent l’ajout d’un panneau solaire externe, la Solar Security Camera 2K embarque directement sa propre surface photovoltaïque. Plus besoin donc de chercher un emplacement supplémentaire pour fixer un panneau, ni de prévoir un câble entre les deux équipements.
La caméra peut ainsi récupérer l’énergie solaire tout au long de la journée pour maintenir sa batterie chargée. Arlo annonce que moins de 20 jours d’ensoleillement par an suffiraient à alimenter la caméra.
Mieux encore, la marque a également prévu une batterie de grande capacité (14 790 mAh), capable de stocker suffisamment d’énergie pour les périodes moins ensoleillées, notamment en hiver. Une promesse très intéressante sur le papier, même si les performances dépendront évidemment de l’exposition et des conditions météorologiques.
Il faudra toutefois accepter ici un certain compromis esthétique, puisqu’avec son panneau intégré, la caméra affiche un gabarit plus imposant (10,3×14×3,9 cm pour 470 grammes) qu’un modèle classique.
Une caméra Essential 2K qui ne fait pas l’impasse sur les fonctions de sécurité
Pour le reste, Arlo propose un équipement plutôt complet. La caméra filme en 2K (2 560 × 1 440 points), avec un champ de vision de 130 degrés et un zoom numérique 12x. Elle dispose également d’une vision nocturne en couleur, d’un projecteur automatique et d'une sirène intégrée pour dissuader les visiteurs indésirables. La panoplie Arlo classique donc, mais toujours très efficace.
La détection des mouvements s’appuie sur un capteur infrarouge, tandis que l’intelligence artificielle peut distinguer les personnes, les animaux et les véhicules afin de limiter les notifications inutiles. La caméra permet aussi de communiquer à distance grâce à son système audio bidirectionnel, via l’application mobile dédiée.
Certifiée IP65, elle est conçue pour résister aux intempéries et fonctionner dans une plage de températures allant de -20 à 45°C. Elle sera disponible à compter du 18 novembre, au prix unitaire de 169,99€.
Certaines fonctions avancées, comme les alertes intelligentes ou le stockage dans le cloud, restent encore et toujours réservées aux abonnés Arlo Secure, dont les tarifs avaient sensiblement augmenté en début d’année 2026.

articles.title: Experts Demonstrate Barracuda Email Security Gateway Chain Enabling Root Access Without Login
articles.text:
Two flaws in Barracuda's Email Security Gateway, an email-filtering appliance, can be chained to run commands on it as root, its highest level of access, with no login required.
The company released patches on Monday, and the security firm watchTowr detailed the attack chain on Thursday.
One flaw, CVE-2026-116606, is an authorization bypass. An unauthenticated attacker can use it to restore a crafted configuration backup and change the appliance's global settings.
The other, CVE-2026-111560, is a command injection. It runs commands as root but normally needs an administrator account, and on the Email Security Gateway the bypass gives an attacker that access. Chained, the two let an attacker reach root with no login.
Affected Products and Fixes
The authorization bypass affects only the Email Security Gateway. The command injection reaches five other products, but on those it still needs an administrator account.
Mandiant, which assigned the two CVE records, rates the bypass 9.3 out of 10 and the command injection 8.6. Barracuda has released a patch for each affected product and lists the fixed firmware in its security advisory. The Email Security Gateway is fixed in version 9.4.0.030 and later.
What to Do
The advisory sets out three steps:
- Apply the patch for each affected product, or upgrade to the fixed firmware listed above.
- If you cannot patch at once, limit the appliance's administration interface to trusted internal networks.
- If you have turned automatic patching off, switch it back on.
How the Chain Works
In its technical analysis, watchTowr traced the chain through the appliance's code. A failed password change returns the attacker a low-privilege role instead of stopping the request, which leaves a backup-restore function open to someone who has not logged in.
That function accepts an uploaded backup, and the restored data includes a timezone value that the appliance later runs as a shell command with root privileges. Barracuda guards backups with a checksum, but the secret used to compute it is built into the code, allowing an attacker to forge a valid checksum. The firm showed the attack by writing a file to the appliance as root.
As of this week, neither flaw appears in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV catalog), and no public report ties either to an attack. watchTowr also released a detection tool that checks whether an appliance is vulnerable, but has not published an exploit.
The Email Security Gateway was hit in the 2023 attacks by a group tracked as UNC4841, which exploited a different flaw, CVE-2023-2868, as a zero-day. That case is unrelated to the two flaws patched this week, and nothing ties the new pair to any attacker.

articles.title: OpenAI recibió USD 11.000 millones de una ronda que la valora en USD 1,25 billones, menos de lo buscado
articles.text:
OpenAI recibió unos USD 11.000 millones de la nueva ronda de financiación con la que busca capital, informó Bloomberg el viernes 6 de noviembre. El monto es la primera parte de una ronda que valora a la empresa en USD 1,25 billones, por debajo de lo que pretendía al comienzo.
Según Bloomberg, que cita a personas familiares con el asunto y que pidieron el anonimato porque la información no es pública, el dinero fue transferido a la compañía ese mismo viernes. OpenAI declinó hacer comentarios.
El resto de la ronda, que podría llegar a USD 20.000 millones en total, debería completarse en las próximas semanas, dijo una de las fuentes. Entre los inversores del primer cierre figuran Coatue Management y T. Rowe Price, según la agencia.
La empresa lleva más de un mes negociando este financiamiento, después de postergar sus planes de salir a bolsa, es decir, de ofrecer sus acciones al público en un mercado financiero.
De USD 30.000 millones a un máximo de USD 20.000 millones
Bloomberg informó que OpenAI se propuso reunir USD 30.000 millones o más con una valoración de USD 1,4 billones. Redujo esos planes en medio de una caída de las acciones del sector de IA en los mercados públicos.
El recorte ya se conocía desde el 31 de octubre, cuando el diario The Wall Street Journal informó que la empresa tenía compromisos por unos USD 11.000 millones y que había bajado su objetivo a un máximo de USD 20.000 millones. Según esa publicación, planeaba acudir a oficinas de inversión familiares y a personas con grandes patrimonios para completar el resto.
De acuerdo con el diario, OpenAI tuvo dificultades para atraer a algunos grandes inversores, en un momento de dudas sobre la sostenibilidad del gasto en IA. Esa preocupación se sumó a los resultados por debajo de lo esperado de Google, Amazon e Intel, que contribuyeron a la caída de las acciones tecnológicas.
En marzo, OpenAI reunió USD 122.000 millones con una valoración de USD 852.000 millones, según Investing.com. La nueva valoración queda 47 por ciento por encima de esa cifra.
Anthropic presiona con ingresos mayores
El Journal también comparó a OpenAI con su rival Anthropic, creadora del chatbot Claude. Según las cifras que citó, Anthropic más que duplicó sus ingresos trimestrales en el segundo trimestre, hasta USD 11.600 millones, y registró una pequeña ganancia operativa.
En el mismo período, los ingresos de OpenAI crecieron cerca de 18%, hasta USD 6.700 millones, y la empresa acumuló mayores pérdidas operativas, según esos datos.
El diario añadió que Anthropic presentó la documentación para salir a bolsa, con un debut previsto para el mes próximo, lo que podría aumentar la presión sobre OpenAI antes de su propio estreno bursátil, que la empresa baraja para el año próximo. También indicó que OpenAI recuperó parte de la cuota de mercado de su competidor tras bajar los precios de sus modelos más recientes.
El nuevo modelo de OpenAI
OpenAI presentó GPT-6 Cyber, un modelo de inteligencia artificial especializado en ciberseguridad capaz de detectar vulnerabilidades informáticas, comprobar si pueden ser explotadas y ayudar a desarrollar las correcciones correspondientes.
Durante las pruebas, el sistema identificó 81 vulnerabilidades desconocidas y de alta gravedad en Mozilla Firefox, que ya comenzó a publicar parches, y reprodujo 1.724 fallas del kernel de Linux, para las que construyó exploits funcionales en 948 casos. Debido al riesgo que implica una herramienta con esta capacidad, OpenAI la clasificó con nivel “Crítico” en ciberseguridad según su marco interno de evaluación.

articles.title: I tested the Oukitel WP63 — a rugged phone with a pyromaniac-friendly bonus
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
As a smartphone, the WP63 has little to write home about, aside from a substantial battery and a curious, intentional ability to start a conflagration. Smokers and pyromaniacs will love this device, but it's not the most practical design Oukitel has launched
Reasons to buy
- + Power-efficient
- + Integrated USB-C cable
- + Inbuilt ignitor
- + Great battery life
Reasons to avoid
- - Low-end SoC
- - Heavy to carry and difficult to pocket
- - A potential fire hazard
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Oukitel WP63: 30-second review
Oukitel has a strange approach to phone naming: they release phones in seemingly random order. Therefore, the WP66 has been around for a while, and now the WP63 has arrived.
But perhaps the problem isn’t the order in which these devices were announced, but when they actually get delivered.
With so many phones on Oukitel’s stable, you might be wondering, not unreasonably, what makes this one different?
On the surface, this is a heavy rugged design where battery capacity is paramount, mostly at the expense of fitting in a normal-sized pocket.
That hints it's aimed at the adventure market, since this phone could easily last a week without a charge, if you use it wisely. Reinforcing that notion, it also has a big speaker and a camping light. But one feature on this phone I’ve never seen before sounds a little bonkers.
This is the first phone I’ve reviewed that has an ‘ignitor’ in it. Yes, something to intentionally start fires, not just accidentally. If you need to start fires, or you just can’t give up smoking, then the WP63 might be the perfect phone for you.
In other respects, this isn’t an especially powerful smartphone, but it can reverse charge at 18W using an inbuilt USB-C cable, and it is running Android 16. It’s also not expensive, making it a good candidate if the rugged requirement is only for a specific trip or job. However, I can’t see myself putting this in our best rugged phone collection, even with its unique features.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Oukitel WP63: price and availability
- How much does it cost? $390/£295/€405
- When is it out? Available from Oukitel in early November
- Where can you get it? Only from Oukitel
While I was writing this review, I was slightly confused by the lack of a web page for this device, since I knew its release was imminent.
Thankfully, now the WP63 has a webpage, and I’ve been promised it should be available to purchase by the time you read this review.
The quoted US price is $389.99, supposedly 35% less than the $599.99 MSRP Oukitel imagined when they cooked up this phone. UK customers pay £294.58, and in the EU it’s €348.05. But keep in mind that prices can change. Unusually for a Chinese phone maker, these prices are roughly identical based on the current exchange rates between the US dollar, British pound, and Euro.
While the WP63 has some unique features, plenty of rugged designs offer 20000 mAh of battery capacity, but most pack more processing power than this model.
A phone with a similar spec is the Blackview XPLORE 1, which costs $359.99 on Amazon.com, and at that price you do get more RAM and 55W charging.
That pricing suggests the WP63 isn’t a bargain, but if it saves you from carrying another ignition source, the cost difference may be worth it.
The WP63 isn’t an expensive phone, but it also has modest specs.
- Value score: 4/5
Oukitel WP63: Specs
| Oukitel WP63 Specifications |  | 
|---|---|
| CPU: | UNISOC T8200 octa-core, 6nm TSMC | 
| GPU: | ARM Mali-G57 | 
| NPU: | Inbuilt NPU | 
| Memory: | 8GB RAM, confirmed on the sample, plus up to 24GB virtual RAM | 
| Storage: | 256GB UFS 2.2 LPDDR4X, microSD up to 1TB (shared with second SIM) | 
| Display: | 6.7-inch LCD, 720 by 1600 pixels, 120Hz refresh | 
| Brightness: | 480 nits typical | 
| Glass: | Corning Gorilla 5 | 
| Rear cameras: | 64MP OV64B40 (1/2 inch, f/1.8), 8MP night vision with infrared lights. | 
| Front camera: | 20MP Sony IMX376 - 1080P@30fps | 
| Battery: | 20,000mAh, 33W wired charging, 18W reverse charging. | 
| Operating system: | Android 16 | 
| Wireless: | WiFi 5, Bluetooth 5.0, dual SIM 5G, eSIM ready | 
| Navigation: | GPS (L1 and L5), GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou | 
| Audio: | 3W Smart speaker | 
| Protection: | IP68, IP69K, MIL STD 810H | 
| Dimensions: | 174.7 x 83 x 27mm | 
| Weight: | 629g | 
| Colour: | Black | 
Oukitel WP63: Design
- A chunky monkey
- In-built USB-C cable
- Light the blue touch paper
If I were inclined to hike a long way, maybe over several days, I’m not sure I’d take the WP63 along. At 629g and an awkward fit in most pockets, this is a hefty device that you wouldn’t want to carry in open water.
However, Oukitel sloped the undersides, so it’s relatively easy to handle unless you have weak wrists.
Button placement is typical, with the power and volume rocker on the right and a PTT custom button on the left with the SIM slot. One mild annoyance was that when it wants a fingerprint for access, it places a fingerprint icon on the screen, where some phones have the sensor embedded under the display. This isn't one of those phones, and the fingerprint reader is actually on the power button.
That said, most people should be able to transition to this device easily.
On the rear is a 3W speaker for summoning beach-party people, and that pushes the two rear cameras out to the edge of the phone. What space is left by the speaker and camera cluster is taken up with a substantial camping LED, one of those that can temporarily blind you if set to full brightness and looked at. This device has no wireless charging because there is no open space for it.
None of this is especially unusual, as I’ve seen a dozen or more rugged phones with a big lamp and speaker, probably in the past year. Where the WP63 goes off into uncharted territory is with two other special functions, one of which is a short but integrated USB-C cable. This cable can be used to charge and also reverse charge other devices, making it unnecessary to carry a charging cable with you. I like this idea, and even with the shortness of the cable, it's useful.
The other special feature is slightly more controversial, because the WP63 can set things on fire, hopefully when you intend for it to do so.
Given how phones and other battery-powered devices are often blamed for starting fires, it seems contradictory to actually design a phone specifically to set things on fire, but Oukitel did.
Along the top edge is the ignitor, which comes out of a tube when pressed down and sideways, so it doesn’t deploy accidentally. A phone app controls when it heats and for how long, so it should be impossible for this to happen unintentionally.
The minimum heating time is four seconds, the maximum is ten, and then there is a longer period during which the ignitor must cool down before it can be fired again. You are advised that the ignitor gets extremely hot, and it is best not to touch it when in use.
So what is this practically useful for? Well, I suspect it's fine for lighting cigarettes, the odd firework, but you would need some paper or dry tinder to start a campfire using it.
The box includes a spare igniter element, so it will eventually burn through the heated wire it uses, and you can replace that part. Some grease is also provided to make sure the igniter deploys smoothly when you want it.
I don’t know how much power this feature uses, but it will have an impact if you use it repeatedly.
As a non-smoker and non-pyromaniac, this isn’t a feature I’d find much use for, but I accept that others might find it useful. I just wouldn’t want to be found with this phone in an era which has had an unexplained forest fire recently.
Design score: 4/5
Oukitel WP63: Hardware
- UNISOC T8200
- 256GB of UFS 2.2 storage
- 20000 mAh battery
The UNISOC T8200 (UMS9621S) is a mid-range 5G chip. It has eight cores in two clusters, with two Cortex-A76 cores at up to 2.3GHz and six smaller cores at up to 2.1GHz. A two-core Mali G57 handles graphics, and the chip is built on TSMC’s older 6nm process. That process is a little dated now, but it remains perfectly efficient if underwhelming.
Memory support is sensible. The controller handles LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X, with the latter used here. That means no speedy LPDDR5, which holds back peak performance.
The integrated modem covers sub-6 GHz 5G with carrier aggregation. There is no mmWave here, but few phones at this level need it.
The camera and display features are generous for the price. UNISOC says the chip supports sensors up to 108MP, 4K video recording and a 120Hz FHD+ display. Variable refresh rate support should also help battery life. However, not all of those features apply to this phone.
So how does it perform? Day to day, it should feel fine. Scrolling, browsing, social media and video streaming sit well within its abilities. The two A76 cores give it a useful turn of speed when apps need it. Notebookcheck lists a Geekbench 6 single-core score of around 750. That is respectable, and clearly better than entry-level silicon.
Gaming is where limits appear. Two GPU cores will manage casual titles and older 3D games without fuss. Demanding modern games will need lower settings and will not hold high frame rates for long. I would not buy it for that job.
Against the competition, it sits below chips like the Dimensity 8100, which uses a 4nm process and much faster Cortex A78 cores. It is a budget-friendly alternative, not a rival, and Oukitel only use UFS 2.2 storage because it works in this context. The allocation of 256GB is plenty for most people, and you can add a 1TB microSD if you need to capture lots of video.
For a rugged or value-focused handset, the T8200 is a sound choice. It is quick enough, frugal enough and well connected. Just keep expectations realistic.
The one area where Oukitel pushed the boat out is battery capacity, with 20000mAh to splurge. That obviously provides a substantial running time, but it can also be used through reverse charging to keep other devices powered. One nice note about that feature is that if it is charging another phone, for example, and the battery capacity hits 20%, it will stop so it doesn’t exhaust the battery entirely.
- Hardware score: 3.5/5
Oukitel WP63: Cameras
- 64MP and 8MP on the rear
- 20MP on the front
- Three cameras in total
The Oukitel WP63 has three cameras:
Rear cameras: 64MP Omnivision OV64B40 , 8MP Hynix Hi-846 (Night Vision)
Front camera: 20MP Sony IMX376
The camera sensor collection on this phone isn’t the best, but it isn’t junk either.
I’ve seen the 64MP Omnivision OV64B40 on many devices, and it performs decently on most of them, even if it’s not a sensor a premium phone would use.
The biggest issue is that it has no optical zoom, so all zoom is digital. That undermines the premise of using a 64MP sensor with pixel binning to deliver 16MP images that are sharp and perfectly saturated. The results without zooming are therefore much better than those with. I took some decent pictures using this sensor, but it does like plenty of light.
One positive aspect of this sensor is that it will capture 4K video, but only at 30 fps. In fact, it's locked to 30 fps at all resolutions unless you use ‘slow motion’ mode, where the frame rate jumps to 120 fps for 1080p or 720p capture.
The second rear sensor is an 8MP Hynix Hi-846 Night Vision chip. An SK Hynix part with an 8-megapixel 1/4-inch sensor and 1.12 µm pixels. It outputs 3264x2448 natively, so the resolution in your screenshot matches its true array and not a cropped one. Works well if the subject is close enough to be illuminated by the IR array,
The front-facing 20MP Sony IMX376 seems ideal for selfies, but it is limited to 1080p video.
And, as I always check, this phone is rated for Widevine L1 encryption, so streamed video can be higher than 480p. However, the screen resolution isn't enough for 1080p streaming, so it's not a huge benefit.
Overall, the cameras can take decent photos and video, but these choices seem mostly budget-driven and not meant to deliver photographic excellence.

Oukitel WP63: Performance
| Phone |  | Oukitel WP63 | UleFone RugKing 5 Pro | 
| SoC |  | Unisoc T8200 | Unisoc T7250 | 
| GPU |  | ARM Mali-G57 MP2 | ARM Mali-G57 | 
| NPU |  | Integrated NPU | N/A | 
| Memory |  | 6GB/256GB | 8GB/256GB | 
| Weight |  | 629g | 629g | 
| Battery |  | 20000 | 20000 | 
| Geekbench | Single | 745 | 441 | 
|  | Multi | 1929 | 1424 | 
|  | OpenCL | 1400 | 734 | 
|  | Vulkan | 1430 | 718 | 
| PCMark | 3.0 Score | 13392 | 8550 | 
|  | Battery | 29h 33m (14%) | 37h 7m (35%) | 
| Charge 30 | % | 16 | 15 | 
| Passmark | Score | 9633 | 6096 | 
|  | CPU | 4570 | 3042 | 
| 3DMark | Slingshot OGL | 3100 | 1842 | 
|  | Slingshot Ex. OGL | 2274 | 1247 | 
|  | Slingshot Ex. Vulkan | 2268 | 1264 | 
|  | Wildlife | 1143 | 579 | 
| Row 20 - Cell 0 | Nomad Lite | N/A | 66 | 
To be direct, if I put this phone up against one of the many Dimensity 8200 phones, it would look like it was going backwards. So instead, I chose the UleFone RugKing 5 Pro, another relatively low-power handset that also uses a Unisoc SoC.
The T8200 appears to have about 50% more power than the T7250 from a compute perspective, and the G57 MP2 is double the performance of its base counterpart.
Neither phone would excite anyone who likes to game, but the WP63 beats the RugKing 5 Pro in all but one area.
That’s the flipside of powerful phones, in that delivering that performance consumes more power. Here, the extra performance of the WP63 comes at a cost of battery life. Although being able to run PCMark for nearly 30 hours and still have 14% of the capacity left is an accomplishment that many phones would be envious.
One major issue I ran into with the review hardware was that the provided charger refused to charge the phone, even with the cable that Oukitel provided. That should not be a problem, since I have plenty of USB-C chargers.
Except when I used one of my 100W-capable chargers, it peaked at 20W while charging the phone, which meant after 30 minutes it had only recovered 16% of its power. That said, even if it accepted the full 33W, I calculate it would still take four hours to recharge the WP63, and possibly longer.
So this isn’t a phone you want to wake up next to after forgetting to charge it. Overall, the WP63 is power-efficient enough to deliver a reasonable user experience and run most Android apps, but it's hardly rocket-powered.
- Performance score: 3.5/5
Oukitel WP63: Final verdict
What an odd phone.
If we ignore the slightly charred elephant in this room, this is a mid-order rugged phone with plenty of battery capacity to keep it alive for a decent number of days away from civilisation.
The cameras can take acceptable photos and video, and the asking price isn’t excessive. This is something you could say about a dozen or more other designs.
But people won’t be buying this phone for only those features, will they? No, they’ll want the phone that can light a cigarette, or fireworks, or burn down half of Canada.
Part of me thinks this wasn’t a great idea, but it’s possible to create a fire with a glass bottle, a magnifying glass, or a battery and two wires, so am I overreacting? Possibly.
My concern is that, since this is a phone and can be remotely controlled, someone might use it to initiate something remotely. But then phones have been used to do that without having an ignitor in them, so perhaps the truly dangerous part is the phone?
Whatever the answer is, because I’m far from being an expert, the WP63 does have a feature that no other phone I’ve seen sports. Will it spawn a whole new generation of fire-starting phones? I doubt it. But if you need to carry something that can start a fire in a pinch, the WP63 exists.
Should I buy a Oukitel WP63?
| Oukitel WP63 Score Card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | Not expensive, but a modest spec | 4/5 | 
| Design | A heavy and chunky phone, but with some innovative features | 4/5 | 
| Hardware | Mid-tier SoC but a big battery and something to set things on fire | 3.5/5 | 
| Cameras | Reasonable cameras but nothing special | 3.5/5 | 
| Performance | Better than lesser Unisoc SoCs, but not Dimensity 7300 good | 3.5/5 | 
| Overall | A curiously useful device with a unique fire-starting feature | 3.5/5 | 
Buy it if...
You need extended battery life
While 20000 mAh isn’t the biggest phone battery I’ve seen, it’s a good size, and if managed, it will last a long time. The only caveat to this capacity is that the maximum charging wattage is only 33W, which means even if you can get the provided charger to work, it won’t be charging that quickly.
You need to start fires
Something I never thought I’d write in a review is that this phone is perfect for setting fire to things, assuming they burn. Chain-smokers, firework fans and common or garden-variety pyromaniacs will love the WP63 and its inclusive gift from the gods.
Don't buy it if...
You need a daily driver
If weight and size matter to you, then give this a miss. At 629g and 27mm deep, this is not an easily pocketable device by any definition. There is an argument that with this phone you won’t need a power pack for other devices, a charging cable or a lighter, but it's still heavy. 
For more ruggedized devices, we've reviewed the best rugged tablets, the best rugged laptops, and the best rugged hard drives
Mark is an expert on 3D printers, drones and phones. He also covers storage, including SSDs, NAS drives and portable hard drives. He started writing in 1986 and has contributed to MicroMart, PC Format, 3D World, among others.

Le bon plan du Black Friday selon NordVPN
