articles.title: GlobalFoundries VP details FDX Fusion technology, sporting 7nm-class performance without the need for EUV tools — company targets 2030 for high-volume manufacturing, with planar transistors in tow
articles.text:
GlobalFoundries VP details FDX Fusion technology, sporting 7nm-class performance without the need for EUV tools — company targets 2030 for high-volume manufacturing, with planar transistors in tow
Albeit at a low transistor density.
Eight years after GlobalFoundries abandoned the development of its 7nm FinFET technology, the company is preparing to return to 7nm-class performance, this time by going via a different route. Its FDX Fusion process, built on FD-SOI (fully depleted silicon-on-insulator) technology, promises 7nm-class performance using advanced planar transistors, with no EUV lithography necessary.
In an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium, GlobalFoundries' Sudipto Bose, vice president of the FD-SOI business unit, shared new details about its FDX Fusion technology, including its 8nm-class logic density, advanced planar transistors, manufacturing costs, and plans to begin commercial production in 2028. The company also explained how it intends to compete with conventional FinFET technologies and why it believes FD-SOI has a future beyond the 22nm-class generation. Some elements of this interview transcript have been edited for flow and clarity.
Sudipto Bose: I have been at GlobalFoundries (GF) for a little bit over six years, and I have been in the industry for 25+ years. I spent the rest of my career at Texas Instruments (TI), so it's really two jobs that I have done: TI and GF. Half and half engineering and business. I spent a lot of my business days in the automotive segment. This was what I was doing at GF when I joined, and now I have the FDX product line role.
Sudipto Bose: A little bit on the history of FDX at GF. GF has been investing in FD-SOI for a long time. It started [these efforts] before I joined. So I would say almost eight years now. And a lot of the investment thesis that drove us towards FDX Fusion is based on the traction that we have in the market today, right? We have quite a few customers who are ramping up. And I say quite a few; this is like high double-digit customers in the nineties that are ramping up right now.
Applications for FDX Fusion
Anton Shilov: What specific types of chips and devices is FDX Fusion designed for? Which application will benefit most from its capabilities?
Sudipto Bose: FDX Fusion will try to enhance the applications in which we play today. What do I mean by that? If you look at our current customers, they are designing chips, everything to do with connectivity. When I say connectivity, think of Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, satcom, all of that. So that is one class of customers.
There's another class of customers who are designing processors at the edge, so these are MCUs (microcontroller units) with some level of inference sitting inside. Think of customers like Alif Semiconductors. So that is another class: MCUs at the edge.
Then in automotive, we have a disproportionate exposure to radar, and this is because of the eighty-one gigahertz performance that FDX brings to the table. So we will engage with them as they try to enhance their portfolio. We also have an automotive MCU, but radar is where you will see a lot of press releases that we have done.
Last but not least, we also have exposure in the data center segment. This also goes back to the fT/fmax, the high-performance RF that we have, which is a good candidate for designing TIAs and clock recovery circuits.
Anton Shilov: By applications inside data centers, what exactly do you mean? CPUs?
Sudipto Bose: Not CPUs. It is in the connectivity space. So, if you think about GF's focus, we are very focused on two things in data centers: power and connectivity. So in the connectivity space, we have silicon photonics, or turning electrons into photons. But then when you receive them, you have the optical diode, again, a GF silicon photonics technology. After that, you need circuits that will amplify those weak electrical signals and drive them to the compute chip. This circuit, which amplifies the weak electrical signals, is right now being done by GF silicon-germanium, but once FDX Fusion is there, we'll offer them both [as] options. And so, to be very specific to your answer, these are data/signal paths inside the data center that feed into CPUs.
7nm-class FD-SOI node
GlobalFoundries' FDX Fusion is a new manufacturing technology that promises 8nm-class logic density and 7nm-class power and performance without EUV lithography or FinFET transistors, which greatly reduces design costs and manufacturing costs at the cost of significantly lower transistor density compared to 7nm-class nodes.
Instead, the process relies on advanced planar fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FD-SOI) transistors, strained silicon substrates, and aggressive optical patterning techniques to achieve transistor dimensions comparable to those of conventional 8nm-class FinFET nodes.
FDX Fusion also retains support for adaptive body biasing and combines high-density digital logic with RF, analog, and embedded memory capabilities. The technology will be manufactured using deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography, although its tighter gate and metal pitches will likely require extensive multipatterning for the most critical layers.
Anton Shilov: What are the key innovations of FDX Fusion compared to predecessors and other nodes that are currently used?
Sudipto Bose: The key things that we're improving from the current-generation FDX, the first one is fT/fmax, this is 500 GHz, or 0.5 THz fT/fmax. This helps the first segment that I talked about, which is connectivity. This helps automotive radar, and this definitely helps the data center segment as they try to improve data speeds. So this is not really competing with silicon germanium. Think of it as silicon germanium at the very high end, and FDX in the 100 – 200 Gb per lambda space. That is one. The second one is the inference at the edge. So we can call it physical AI, and we look at physical AI as sense, think, act, and connect. But the kind of feature set we are putting in starts with improving the digital gate density. This is 2.2 times more dense than the current generation FDX (22FDX and 22FDX+).
Sudipto Bose: We are putting in a lot of flavors of eNVM, a lot of flavors of SRAM, because in edge AI, and in fact for any AI, the real game is how much memory you can pack without increasing the cost. So we are adding a lot of flavors of those. The way we architected FDX Fusion is that we set a goal of how much performance we can deliver to our customer base without increasing their operating expenses.
If you look at classic 7nm, 6nm, they require EUV tools. The mask set is costly; the tool chain is costly. The FDX Fusion platform that we've built isn't going to use EUV tools. It is also based on planar technology. So there are two advantages to this. One is that we can support a much more competitive mask set price compared to 6nm. We can also offer [customers] a lot more flexibility in terms of cycle time and in how many places we manufacture, because FDX Fusion does not need EUV tools.
So, to summarize the answer? We are trying to improve RF and analog performance, digital gate density, and the classes of memory that we offer. What applications are we trying to target? It is connectivity, edge AI, high-frequency mmWave, automotive radar, and definitely applications inside data centers.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | FDX Fusion vs FDX22 | FDX Fusion vs 12LP+ | FDX Fusion vs N7 | FDX Fusion vs 8LPP | Notes | 
| Power | -40% | -20% | -5% | ? | At iso performance, ABB on for FDX | 
| Performance | 30% | 16% | 4% | ? | At iso power, ABB on for FDX | 
| Logic Density | ? | ? | ? | ? | - | 
| Transistor Desnsity (MTr/mm^2) | 2X vs 1X | 56 vs 30 - 40 | 56 vs 91.2 | 56 vs 61.2 | - | 
| Transistor Type | Planar vs Planar | Planar vs FinFET | Planar vs FinFET | Planar vs FinFET | - | 
| HVM | 2028 vs 2018 | 2028 vs 2017 | 2028 vs 2017 | 2028 vs 2018 | - | 
Anton Shilov: You just mentioned transistor density. The press release says that it has more than twice the transistor density of the original 22FDX process, but you never actually published a transistor density number for this. Could you share any numbers?
Sudipto Bose: I will share a number with you. But I will also give you a little bit of context on how our customers look at our technology portfolio. If you look at the current generation, the one that we are manufacturing today, the one where I said we have 90+ customers ramping. Not designing, ramping. This basically comes from the flexibility of FD-SOI. You have the box, the depleted channel, and you can use body bias. So we have customers who are able to achieve 16nm-class power and performance with 22FDX. What do I mean by 16nm-class power and performance?
It essentially means that although our gate density is not as close to 16mm, when you look at the system-level requirements like CPU clock, but think of it as TOPS per watt, we are matching 16nm; in some cases, we are matching 12nm-class.
[...] If I were sitting in a time machine and went back seven years, instead of calling it 22FDX, we could have called it 16FDX, right? Or we could have called it 16nm-class FDX. So with that analogy, if you come to FDX Fusion, our gate density of FDX Fusion will be exactly the same as the industry's 8nm standard today.
It is 14 million gates per square millimeter; that is the density.
Note: Assuming he uses a two-input NAND gate as its reference, each gate contains four transistors, which translates to 56 MTr/mm², which is comparable to what Samsung's 8nm-class nodes use.
Sudipto Bose: Now, why do we call it 7nm-class? Or we actually thought of calling it 6nm-class, but then we said, let's wait for some silicon before we go too far ahead. It is because digital gate density is one aspect of a solution. It defines your physical size, the die size, and that is great. But then you need power and performance. And with the adaptive body bias (ABB) capability that FD-SOI has, and with the standard cell metallization innovations that we have brought in FDX Fusion, once a device is done and you again look at TOPS per watt, it should be equivalent, if not better, than what 7nm can achieve. That is our product target. So for a customer, the value it brings [customers] is: 'I do not have to use an EUV tool line. I do not have to use a mask set that costs many millions of dollars.'
I have something which costs a few millions of dollars, has great cycle time, but at the same time, I am getting TOPS per watt, which is similar to or better than 7nm. The die size might be bigger, but again, it should not be no bigger than what 8nm is today. And that is the messaging to the industry; that is why we say 7nm-class instead of saying, 'Hey, this is 7nm density.' We are trying to reflect what our customers have told us. That in the edge world, in the physical AI world, the size of the die is one aspect, but if the die does not meet the power requirement of the application, then the whole system will not function. So that is the push.
Anton Shilov: That is perhaps why you actually called the technology FDX Fusion instead of using some fancy number.
Sudipto Bose: Yes, because the moment we put a number [out], people put us in a box. And we want to give customers the optionality of, 'Listen, you want to design a transimpedance amplifier using the fT/fmax that we have? That's an analog circuit. No one cares about digital gate density. Go build it.'
'You want to build a simple MCU, which is just SRAM and IOs? We have 14 million gates per square millimeter. Go build it.' 'You want to build a mixed-signal design like a single-chip radar, Wi-Fi, a satcom digital beamformer? Here are the few other knobs that you can turn to get the best PPA or the best system performance that you need.'
That is why we chose the name Fusion; we are trying to imply [that] we give you many options. It is the combination of all the good things the world needs to design the physical AI dream that we have put in front of ourselves, like the whole stack concept of 'sense, think, act, and connect'. Let us see if it sticks. I think it is a bold move for us to go against the grain of the way the foundry industry typically names its platforms, but we feel pretty strong about it.
Anton Shilov: So, you shared the gate density number, but could you maybe also share things like contacted gate pitch, metal pitch as well?
Sudipto Bose: In time. The reason I mention that is there is a little bit of IP involved. We want to get the first silicon out, engage with a few customers before we publish the CPP and the M(etal) layers. […] We are pushing the limits of patterning and coloring as well as gate oxide engineering to get the best CPP and metal pitches, which will enable this level of density of gates. That is, I would say in terms of R&D dollars just at a very high level, 50% of R&D dollars is on the transistor itself because we are doing strained substrates. There are multiple techniques we are using to improve the PFET and NFET performance. The other 50% is all on CPP and metal pitches.
Anton Shilov: So, are those contacted gate pitches and metal pitches comparable to conventional 7nm class FinFET process technologies?
Sudipto Bose: Comparable to 8nm.
Anton Shilov: When we talk about 8nm, basically speaking, there is only one company that actually produces chips using an 8nm-class technology. That is Samsung Foundry. TSMC and Intel Foundry do not have 8nm-class technologies. So I suppose that we should compare it to Samsung's 8nm node, right?
Sudipto Bose: That's a fair guess.
Anton Shilov: When it comes to power consumption improvements versus 22FDX and 22FDX+, how much lower power can we get using the new FDX Fusion node?
Sudipto Bose: It depends on the application, but I understand your question. So if you just normalize with [iso performance and iso power], I am giving you an answer with adaptive body bias included. If you consider current-generation FDX as the base point, the goal of FDX Fusion is to get 30% higher performance and 40% lower power. Again, it is really application-driven [in] how low you can go. But if you take the standard core, our goal is to get at least a 20% improvement.
Anton Shilov: What types of chips do you expect to benefit most from the FDX Fusion technology? You mentioned connectivity, edge AI, high RF, automotive radar, and connectivity applications inside data centers. What about application-specific AI accelerators, because you mentioned edge inference?
Sudipto Bose: From the STAC — sense, think, act, and connect — framework point of view, let me give you an example. Think of a humanoid, or a car — major applications that need to see. It needs to see and then infer what the environment is like. So the class of chips that do this vision processing at the edge to infer the surroundings will definitely be supported with FDX Fusion. The class of chips that will hear, do voice recognition, and, from voice recognition, draw conclusions, we definitely want to support [them]. Now, at the data center right now, as I said, our play is connectivity. Just translating optical to electrical signals.
If a customer wants to use a chiplet, which has a lot of memory, think of analog in-memory compute along with an inference engine, by all means we will support [such applications]. We will work with customers to see how we can play in that compute ecosystem in the data center. But in terms of pure focus, the first 10 customers that we are engaged with are either at the edge, or they are in the connectivity piece inside the data center.
Note: For those of our readers who are not familiar with ABB, this is a technique that dynamically adjusts a transistor's threshold voltage by changing the voltage applied to the transistor body. Forward body bias reduces threshold voltage to improve performance, while reverse body bias increases it to reduce power leakage. This enables chips to optimize performance and power consumption according to workload requirements. ABB is one of the key advantages of the FD-SOI technology.
Anton Shilov: Since you mentioned this, does FDX Fusion retain the active body biasing capabilities of its predecessors?
Sudipto Bose: It is an inseparable part of the platform, yes. We will launch this platform in a way that customers can use it.
New tools required
Anton Shilov: You also mentioned makers of wafer fab equipment. Will FDX Fusion use existing manufacturing equipment at the Dresden facility, or will it require substantial investments in new lithography, deposition, etching, and metrology tools?
Sudipto Bose: It will require new tools. Substantial is a relative term. If you see the amount of money being invested in semiconductors, the term 'substantial' has changed. We are going to get new tools, which is why we combined the FDX Fusion announcement event with the topping off of the Sprint expansion project. That's why we had all the luminaries from the German and the European government. There will be tool investment; we will be buying tools from the vendors. How much of it is going to be litho versus etching? Time will tell, but for sure we need new tools compared to what we have today.
Anton Shilov: But will you essentially need to completely re-equip the Dresden facility to use FDX Fusion? What percentage of the tools you have can be reused for FDX Fusion?
Sudipto Bose: We can get back to you on that exact answer because I do want to give you a proper answer, rather than a high-level answer. But I will tell you where the targets are. With the front end, the transistor fabrication tool chain, my target is to reuse as much as we can.
Anton Shilov: You also mentioned that you plan to begin manufacturing FDX Fusion in 2028. But does this refer to risk production, initial customer production, or high volume manufacturing?
Sudipto Bose: Initial customer production.
Anton Shilov: When do you expect the technology to reach mature yields and meaningful production volumes?
Sudipto Bose: I will give you my target, and then the industry will define it because we are a part of a bigger ecosystem. 2030 is when we want to get to high-volume manufacturing with FDX Fusion. But again, it depends on the first applications and the first few customers.
Readiness
Anton Shilov: Speaking of customers, you probably already have customers who are committed to production, haven't you?
Sudipto Bose: We have customers who are committed to building a chip. Of course, we have to deliver to their specs before they go to production.
Anton Shilov: I suppose the customers that you mentioned in the press release like BMW, Bosch NXP, Siemens, and Tesla, they are all plan to build chips on this technology.
Sudipto Bose: […] They have been pushing us for the last few years to do something like this, and they have given us requirements. Now we are doing it, and we have to show them what we can [deliver]. So there is a lot of push that we have received from the industry, from these companies. When I say these companies, the supply chain that leads into these companies to deliver something which will work at the edge. So we are racing against time to show them something that will meet the specs.
Anton Shilov: GlobalFoundries plans to release the initial FDX Fusion PDK in mid-2027. But when do you expect complete digital, analog, and RF design flows to become available from the three major EDA vendors?
Sudipto Bose: Yeah. I wish I could tell you… Right now we are in discussion with all the major primes, so we are in the request for information/request for quotation (RFI/RFQ) phase, but we have started discussions with the major EDA vendors. It has been almost six to nine months now.
Anton Shilov: But you do expect all the leading EDA vendors to support FDX Fusion in eight to nine months?
Sudipto Bose: Of course. We are going to engage with the whole ecosystem that we have, and once [the PDK is out], we have to support a proper flow not just for chip design, but also IPs that are required and everything else around it.
Anton Shilov: So how extensive will the initial FDX Fusion IP ecosystem be? Will customers have access to silicon-proven standard cell libraries, SRAM compilers, embedded non-volatile memory, interface IPs, maybe analog and radio frequency building blocks before 2028?
Sudipto Bose: Yes. In the first two years, we are going to engage with pilot customers. Think of these as early adopters. We have early adopters listed, and we will design standard cell, I/Os, and SRAM [...] needed for everything, so we will have those. But then the complex IPs, like PCIe Gen 4/5 or LPDDR6 or a DisplayPort, will be dictated by the first few applications that will ramp. FDX Fusion for us is the beginning of a journey. We have been on the journey of 22FDX for almost eight years. I envision FDX Fusion to be more than that. Even on our current platforms, we keep enhancing our IP portfolio. So I expect us to be adding IPs to FDX Fusion over the next ten years.
ARC, MIPS, and Fusion FDX
Anton Shilov: GlobalFoundries also highlighted its ARC and MIPS processor IP portfolios and RISC-V expertise as part of the FDX Fusion offering. Do you plan to develop processor cores and AI accelerators specifically optimized for FDX Fusion? IPs specifically optimized for FDX Fusion? Or will you primarily port existing IP to the new process?
Sudipto Bose: MIPS is an internal customer and a partner, and we will engage with them, and they will launch a platform for physical AI that is fine-tuned, in a combination of what they have and what FDX Fusion has. ARC and MIPS are key pieces of the strategy. Having an internal customer like that just enhances our development cycle by 5X because now they can start developing fast turns of test chips and give us feedback. We did not have this capability in the past. Now we do. Once they are ready, they will start announcing stuff.
Anton Shilov: So essentially, you will both port the existing IPs to the new node, but also MIPS will likely develop something brand new specifically for FDX Fusion.
Sudipto Bose: Yes.
Costs
Anton Shilov: How will the manufacturing complexity and cost per transistor of FDX Fusion compare to 22FDX+, your 12nm FinFET technology, and conventional 8nm FinFET technology?
Sudipto Bose: This would be the most advanced planar transistor that the world has seen, the most advanced non-EUV-based manufacturing line that the world has seen. So, I would say significantly more complex than our current 22nm-class FD-SOI line. More complex than what we have on the 12nm FinFET line. We are working with every tool vendor that you can think of as part of this program, and we have given them the challenges. It goes back to your question about our contacted gate pitch and metal pitch. So, we have had multiple workshops with them over the last few quarters, and each one of them is proposing a tool recipe that they think will get this to a nice and solid yield.
Sudipto Bose: So, I guess the answer to your question is: firstly, it is definitely complex, and secondly, we are really using the entire ecosystem available to us to come up with tool configurations that will deliver this. All of this is going to happen in Dresden. We have to be competitive, so price is always dictated by the market. Our goal is to have a running cost that is significantly better than a 7nm or a 6nm class of design (due to planar transistors and due to lack of EUV masks). After that, we will work with our customers to figure out what makes sense. But you are right, the value that we want to bring in is, 'dear customers, you do not have the same operating expenses load, meaning the cost of tape-out is less than 6nm.'
And you can do multiple tape-outs because this class of devices is not something where you can design one part and use it for 15 applications. You really need 15 devices for 15 applications. So, we definitely enable that. Then, when it comes to manufacturing cost, it is a discussion with our customers. We have various business models, but the goal is to make sure it is a win-win. At the end of the day, the lower the cost we are, the more flexibility we can provide to our customers. The non-EUV path is one of the things that was dictated by our decision that we must keep this a cost-competitive platform.
Anton Shilov: So, cost-wise you want to be competitive, but it's likely comparable to 8nm.
Sudipto Bose: I will have a better feel once we are complete with what we call our M-cycles inside the fab. But I would say my internal target is that we have to be better than that.
The future of FDX
Anton Shilov: GlobalFoundries describes upcoming technology as its 1st Generation of FDX Fusion. Does this mean that you envision subsequent generations with high transistor density and performance? Maybe you can share some preliminary targets or timelines for the next node?
Sudipto Bose: We have listed quite a few innovation steps that we want to enable on this platform. The FDX Fusion definition is based on the ones we believe we are more confident that we will be able to deliver in the timeframe that we have said. We have kept a few things in the innovation lab, and they are pushing the boundaries of a few things like eNVM, EDA routing, chip folding, 2.5D integration, which, once they mature, will define what the next version of FDX Fusion will look like. I do not have a timeline for the next version of FDX Fusion, though.
As we proceed through the development phase, I would say early 2028 to mid-2028 is when I expect to have a better view of when the next version will be launched. And this is also based on feedback we will get from customers. Because what we have right now is our first silicon, which is running in the lab, which we will show to customers. They will give us a lot of feedback. I am sure we will get a few things right, and at the same time, we will get a few things not so right. And that feedback, along with a few of the innovation topics I mentioned, will dictate what the next generation is going to look like. Stay tuned!
Anton Shilov: One of the reasons why I aksed about next-generation nodes is partly because TSMC typically shares its process technology roadmaps with new nodes well before it releases early PDKs for these nodes. Given that FDX Fusion is now GF's most advanced logic process, with capabilities comparable to 8nm-class technologies (i.e., more advanced than 22FDX or bulk 12nm FinFET), how frequently does GlobalFoundries plan to introduce new process technologies, and how far in advance will it disclose its roadmap?
Sudipto Bose: I would say, we are doing advanced development across the board. If you look at the work we are doing on silicon photonics, on packaging, on power transistors like GaN, RF GaN, Power GaN, these are all pretty advanced. But yes, you are right: in what the world understands as a classic, let's say, high-density process, FDX Fusion is the most advanced. We typically announce or update the industry about our roadmap every year at the GlobalFoundries Technology Symposium. Like this year at GTS, we announced FDX Fusion. So, I would say stay tuned for the GTS sessions that we have, and typically every year we do it in September or October.
CEA-Leti involvement
Anton Shilov: CEA-Leti describes FDX Fusion as a single-digit FD-SOI node. How closely is this new technology related to CEA-Leti's own research in 10nm and 7nm with their SOI nodes?
Sudipto Bose: The platform that we have right now is the outside of the substrate engineering work that we are doing with Soitec and CEA-Leti; the rest of it is GF inherent IP at this point in time. So we are bringing in the knowledge that we have from current-generation FDX, the knowledge that we have from the work that we did in 7nm before we stopped it, the work that we have done on 12nm. So it is bringing in all the innovations across all the GF fabs to figure out what is the best that we can offer. Does it mean that we will not look at what CEA-Leti has in the future? I do not have an answer right now. But for now, FDX Fusion is a very GF innovation-driven effort.
Anton Shilov: So you did not use pre-competitive IP from CEA-Leti to develop FDX Fusion? Is it a completely internally developed node?
Sudipto Bose: Correct.
Anton Shilov: The press release mentions innovations in substrate engineering along with endorsements from CEA-Leti and Soitec. What exactly does that involve, and how does it improve transistor performance? What role do Soitec and CEA-Leti play in developing FDX's strained silicon substrates, and how close is this technology to mass production?
Sudipto Bose: GlobalFoundries is working with CEA-Leti and Soitec under the FAMES program to develop strained silicon substrates for FDX Fusion. The goal is to improve charge carrier mobility and, consequently, transistor performance. Since FD-SOI technology relies on specialized silicon-on-insulator wafers supplied by Soitec, the three organizations are developing ways to introduce strain into these substrates and make the technology suitable for high-volume manufacturing. The approach has already demonstrated its viability in the laboratory, and the partners are now refining the manufacturing process to prepare it for commercial production.
[Session ends]
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Final Fantasy 10 a directement été inspiré par Star Wars et ses courses de pods
articles.text:
Sorti en 2001 au Japon sur PlayStation 2, puis en 2002 en Europe, Final Fantasy X reste l’un des épisodes les plus marquants de la saga de Square Enix. Ses décors entièrement en 3D, ses dialogues doublés (une première pour la série), son histoire d’amour entre Tidus et Yuna, sa musique et son système de progression par sphérier y sont pour beaucoup.
Final Fantasy X a également marqué les esprits grâce au Blitzball, ce sport aquatique qui occupe une place particulière dans l’aventure et qui fait office de mini-jeu. Un sport fictif qui doit une partie de son existence à une certaine galaxie très lointaine.
Yoshinori Kitase, producteur et réalisateur historique de la franchise, est revenu sur les inspirations de ses jeux dans un entretien accordé à IGN lors du festival Lucca Comics & Games, qui s’est tenu du 28 octobre au 1er novembre 2026 en Italie. Parmi elles, Star Wars occupe une place importante.
Le sujet est venu sur la table à propos de Clair Obscur : Expedition 33, le RPG du studio français Sandfall Interactive, sacré jeu de l’année aux Game Awards 2025, qui revendique l’influence de Final Fantasy. Yoshinori Kitase s’est dit « très heureux » que ses créateurs s’en soient inspirés, avant d’expliquer qu’il avait lui-même puisé dans les films de sa jeunesse, Star Wars en tête.
En évoquant la création du Blitzball dans Final Fantasy X, Yoshinori Kitase déclare s’être inspiré de la course de modules de Star Wars : Épisode I – La Menace fantôme, sorti en 1999. Il explique avoir repris directement l’idée de proposer une véritable discipline sportive dans un monde imaginaire. Une inspiration assumée, même si les deux activités n’ont finalement pas grand-chose à voir.
Final Fantasy et Star Wars : une histoire d’inspiration
Pour autant, la filiation est évidente quand on regarde de plus près : dans le film de George Lucas, la course de modules, ou pods, organisée sur Tatooine, constitue un véritable événement populaire et une parenthèse dans le récit. Les pilotes s’affrontent devant une foule venue assister au spectacle, dans une compétition avec ses enjeux, et qui fait tout de même progresser le jeune Anakin Skywalker dans son arc.
Le Blitzball est une sorte de mélange entre football, rugby et water-polo, disputé dans une gigantesque sphère d’eau suspendue dans les airs. Étrange sur le papier, le sport tient une place centrale dans le récit : Tidus, le héros, est lui-même une star du Blitzball. Le Blitzball donne de la consistance à l’univers et divertit les joueuses et les joueurs, un peu comme les courses de modules dans Star Wars.
Dans le même entretien, Yoshinori Kitase cite également une référence plus directe : Biggs et Wedge, duo récurrent de la saga depuis Final Fantasy VI, portent les noms de deux pilotes rebelles de Star Wars, Biggs Darklighter et Wedge Antilles. Il dit pourtant s’être longtemps méfié de tout emprunt trop visible à la saga de George Lucas, de peur que ses jeux passent pour des copies.
Final Fantasy XII, sorti en 2006, a lui aussi été régulièrement comparé à Star Wars pour son intrigue politique, ses conflits entre empires et ses personnages. Hideo Minaba, directeur artistique de Final Fantasy XII, s’était dit grand fan de Star Wars, tout en refusant d’y voir une influence directe, comme le rappelait GameSpot en 2016.

articles.title: Mars n’est pas morte, une sonde européenne détecte les signes d’un magma endormi sous ses volcans
articles.text:
Au-dessus de fissures volcaniques sur Mars, la sonde européenne ExoMars TGO a détecté du chlorure d'hydrogène, un gaz que rejettent souvent les volcans terrestres. Un indice que la planète rouge garde de la chaleur sous sa croûte, voire des refuges pour la vie.
Mars pourrait abriter une activité volcanique en sommeil, selon une étude internationale fondée sur les données de la sonde européenne ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO). À contre-saison, l'orbiteur de l'ESA a repéré du chlorure d'hydrogène au-dessus des mêmes fissures du volcan Alba Mons, un signal qui pourrait trahir un magma endormi sous la surface. La découverte relance l'éternel débat sur l'activité de la planète rouge, et pourrait bien indiquer aux scientifiques où chercher la vie.
Sur Mars, un gaz volcanique qui n'en fait qu'à sa tête
Le chlorure d'hydrogène (HCl), TGO l'a signalé pour la première fois dans l'atmosphère martienne dès 2021. Comme ce gaz s'échappe couramment des évents volcaniques sur Terre, donc par des fissures et des fumerolles, les chercheurs se demandaient s'il en allait de même là-haut. Mais pour l'essentiel, il suit un calendrier bien réglé, car il culmine pendant l'hiver de l'hémisphère nord puis disparaît presque entièrement l'été, un va-et-vient qui semble surtout lié aux cycles de la poussière et de l'eau. Presque, car une exception revient avec une régularité d'horloge.
Au début de l'été, dans l'hémisphère nord de Mars, des pics de chlorure d'hydrogène apparaissent au-dessus des fissures qui zèbrent les flancs d'Alba Mons. Ils ont été repérés par l'ACS (Atmospheric Chemistry Suite), un ensemble de spectromètres infrarouges embarqué sur TGO. Ces instruments analysent la lumière du Soleil qui traverse l'atmosphère martienne, où chaque gaz laisse sa propre empreinte, un peu comme une signature. Daniel Mège, co-auteur principal de l'étude publiée dans Science Advances, compare l'exercice à la recherche d'une aiguille dans une botte de foin. La sonde a détecté une poignée de molécules, venues d'une source qui ne s'active peut-être que par intermittence, alors qu'elle tourne sans cesse autour de Mars pour surveiller l'atmosphère de toute la planète.
Il fallait comprendre comprendre d'où venait ce gaz. La caméra CaSSIS, elle aussi à bord de TGO, a révélé à cet endroit des fissures fraîches et étroites, parfois longues de plusieurs centaines de mètres, associées à des changements de couleur du sol. L'hypothèse des chercheurs ? En hiver, quand le thermomètre descend jusqu'à −120 °C, la glace bouche ces fissures. Aux premiers beaux jours, elle se sublime (elle passe directement de l'état solide à l'état gazeux) et libère le gaz piégé.
Un volcanisme martien en sommeil… et peut-être des niches pour la vie
Pour l'équipe internationale menée par le chercheur Alexander Trokhimovskiy, ces émanations proviendraient d'un magma chaud en profondeur. Les fissures joueraient le rôle de fumerolles, ces évents dont nous parlions plus haut, par lesquels un volcan terrestre « respire », et les décolorations alentour pourraient être des dépôts laissés par les gaz. Selon Daniel Mège, la répartition du gaz évoquait d'emblée un volcan, mais il a fallu examiner toutes les réactions chimiques possibles de l'atmosphère pour le démontrer. Dans l'étude, les auteurs avancent l'idée d'une chambre magmatique en sommeil, une sorte de plomberie volcanique enfouie.
C'est tout le paradoxe martien. La planète abrite les plus grands volcans du Système solaire, sans qu'on sache à quel point ils sont encore actifs. D'après les images prises en orbite, certains semblent l'avoir été au cours des derniers millions d'années, et des sismomètres y ont enregistré des séismes. Pourtant, aucune éruption ni nouvelle coulée de lave n'a jamais été observée. « Nos résultats suggèrent que Mars a conservé assez de chaleur interne pour entretenir une activité volcanique jusqu'à récemment, et peut-être encore aujourd'hui », avance Daniel Mège, professeur au Centre de recherches spatiales de l'Académie polonaise des sciences.
Quant à la question de la vie… Par le passé, ces gaz venus du magma ont pu être bien plus abondants. Ils auraient alors contribué à épaissir l'atmosphère, qui retenait mieux la chaleur, à adoucir le climat et à permettre à l'eau liquide de couvrir une bonne partie de la surface. Et si de la lave remontant dans la croûte rencontre de l'eau souterraine, elle pourrait la réchauffer et créer des poches chaudes, propices à la vie. C'est ce qu'on appelle des systèmes hydrothermaux : sur Terre, des micro-organismes prospèrent dans ce type d'environnement. Pour Daniel Mège, chercher la vie dans les fissures d'Alba Mons aurait donc tout son sens. Si de tels systèmes y sont actifs, ils fourniraient aux micro-organismes les ingrédients et l'énergie nécessaires, tout en les protégeant d'une surface hostile et changeante. Colin Wilson, responsable scientifique de TGO à l'ESA, estime que ces résultats pourraient être le plus grand succès de la sonde à ce jour.

articles.title: Warum gute Texte in ChatGPT unsichtbar bleiben – und was hilft
articles.text:
KI-Suche statt Google: So schreibst du Texte für Sprachmodelle
Ich sehe das Muster in fast jedem GEO-Projekt: Die Texte sind fachlich korrekt, sie ranken bei Google auf der ersten Seite, und trotzdem nennt ChatGPT die Quelle nicht. Meistens liegt das am Aufbau des Textes.
Wie liest ein Sprachmodell deinen Text?
KI-Systeme lesen keine ganzen Seiten. Sie zerlegen Dokumente in Textabschnitte, sogenannte Chunks, und wählen daraus einzelne Passagen für die Antwort aus. Das Modell sieht also möglicherweise nie deinen kompletten Artikel, sondern nur einen Absatz daraus ohne den vollständigen Zusammenhang.
Der Begriff „LLM-Readability“ beschreibt, wie gut sich ein Text auf diese Weise zerlegen lässt. Klassisch zählt, ob ein Mensch einen Text versteht. Hier zählt aber, ob eine Maschine ihn eindeutig zerlegen kann. Weil Modelle einzelne Absätze statt ganzer Seiten lesen, ändert sich die Einheit, für die du schreibst: Bei der klassischen Google-Suche war das die Seite, in der KI-Suche ist es der Absatz. Ein Abschnitt, der seinen Sinn erst aus dem vorherigen bezieht, ist für ein Modell wertlos, selbst wenn der Gesamttext exzellent ist.
Jeder Absatz muss allein stehen können. Er braucht einen klaren thematischen Fokus, überprüfbare Aussagen und im Idealfall unter 250 Wörter. Ein Gedanke pro Absatz.
Die Antwort kommt zuerst. Sprachmodelle verlieren bei langen Dokumenten messbar an Genauigkeit, wenn die entscheidende Information in der Mitte steht. In der Praxis heißt das: Die wichtigste Aussage gehört in die ersten 350 bis 400 Wörter des Dokuments und in den ersten Satz jedes Absatzes. Danach folgen Erklärung, Belege und Kontext.
Vorher und nachher: Ein optimierter Absatz
Nimm einen (fiktiven) Softwareanbieter für digitale Zeiterfassung. Auf der Ratgeberseite steht ein Abschnitt, der so oder ähnlich in vielen Unternehmensblogs zu finden ist.
Vorher:
Zeiterfassung im Mittelstand
Die Digitalisierung der Arbeitswelt stellt viele Betriebe vor neue Aufgaben. Wer sich mit der Umstellung von Excel-Listen auf eine digitale Lösung beschäftigt, stellt sich zunächst die Frage nach dem Aufwand. Erfahrungsgemäß bewegt sich die Einführung zwischen zwei und acht Wochen, wobei die Zahl der Standorte und die Anbindung an die Lohnabrechnung eine Rolle spielen. Unsere Software wurde speziell für die Anforderungen mittelständischer Unternehmen entwickelt und bietet dafür alle notwendigen Funktionen.
Die Information steht da, aber die Überschrift nennt kein Problem, und die Antwort versteckt sich im dritten Satz hinter einer Einleitung.
Nachher:
Wie lange dauert die Einführung einer digitalen Zeiterfassung?
Zwei bis acht Wochen. Der Aufwand hängt an zwei Faktoren: der Zahl der Standorte und der Anbindung an die Lohnabrechnung.
Ein Betrieb mit einem Standort und weniger als 50 Beschäftigten liegt meist am unteren Ende. Die Installation selbst dauert wenige Stunden. Die Zeit geht dafür drauf, Altdaten zu übernehmen und sich mit dem Betriebsrat abzustimmen.
Die Überschrift ist jetzt die Frage, die jemand tatsächlich eingibt, und der erste Satz ist die Antwort. Der Absatz funktioniert isoliert, weil er nicht voraussetzt, dass man vorher etwas anderes gelesen hat. Wenn ein Modell eine Passage zur Einführungsdauer sucht, kann es diese verwenden. Mit der ersten Version ging das nicht.
Wie optimierst du Content für die KI-Suche?
Du musst dafür nichts neu schreiben. Die meisten Effekte entstehen durch Umbauten an vorhandenen Texten:
- W-Fragen als Zwischenüberschriften, formuliert wie eine echte Suchanfrage
- Die Antwort in den ersten Satz, Begründung danach
- Ein Gedanke pro Absatz, unter 250 Wörter
- Belege direkt am betreffenden Satz verlinken, statt gesammelt am Seitenende
- Für ein Konzept durchgängig denselben Begriff verwenden, keine Synonym-Variation
LLM-Readability wirkt erst, wenn die klassische Suchmaschinenoptimierung stimmt. Ein Text, den Google nicht indexiert oder den der Server nicht sauber ausliefert, landet gar nicht im Kandidatenpool, aus dem ein KI-System seine Antwort baut. Ein Text muss erst gefunden werden, bevor er verwertbar ist.
Für welche Texte gilt LLM-Readability?
Diese Regeln sind in erster Linie für Ratgeber- und Erklärinhalte gedacht, für Absätze, die eine Frage beantworten oder eine Entscheidung vorbereiten. Genau diese Absätze entscheiden am Ende, ob dein Content als Quelle zitiert wird. Für andere Textgattungen gilt das nicht in gleicher Strenge.
LLM-Readability ist eine von drei Disziplinen, mit denen Unternehmen ihre Sichtbarkeit in KI-Antworten steuern. Wie du deine Marke im semantischen Raum der Modelle verortest und Fortschritte messbar machst, zeigt Olaf Kopp im t3n-Onlinekurs „GEO statt nur SEO: So wird dein Unternehmen in der KI-Suche sichtbar“.
Datum: 15. Dezember 2026, 10 bis 12 Uhr Preis: 149,00 € t3n PRO-Member nehmen kostenlos teil. Alle Infos zum Onlinekurs findest du hier im Shop!
Olaf Kopp beschäftigt sich seit 2023 intensiv mit Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) und hat Konzepte wie LLM-Readability und Digital Authority Management mitgeprägt. Als Co-Founder und Head of SEO & AI Search bei der Online-Marketing-Agentur Aufgesang GmbH verbindet er konzeptionelle Tiefe mit handfester Praxis.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos de Amazon con implante capilar para verse más joven: las fotos que revelan cómo nos engañan
articles.text:
Dos fotografías de Jeff Bezos junto a su esposa, Lauren Sánchez, comenzaron a circular en redes sociales con una afirmación que despertó curiosidad: el fundador de Amazon se habría sometido a un trasplante capilar en Turquía. Las imágenes muestran al empresario con cabello corto y abundante, una apariencia diferente a la que suele exhibir en sus apariciones públicas.
Sin embargo, las publicaciones no presentan pruebas de que Bezos haya viajado a ese país ni de que se haya realizado una intervención para recuperar el cabello. Las fotografías virales fueron modificadas con inteligencia artificial (IA) y parten de escenas que sí corresponden a un viaje de la pareja a Italia en junio de 2023.
La comparación con los registros fotográficos de aquella visita permite identificar el origen de las imágenes y entender cómo una fotografía auténtica puede convertirse en contenido engañoso cuando se altera con herramientas de IA.
Las fotos de Jeff Bezos que se viralizaron en redes sociales
Las imágenes muestran a Bezos caminando junto a Lauren Sánchez, ambos vestidos con ropa informal. En una aparece con una camiseta blanca, pantalón celeste y gafas oscuras; en la otra, acompaña a su pareja durante un paseo. El detalle que llamó la atención de los usuarios es el cabello que se le observa en la cabeza.
A partir de esas fotografías, distintas publicaciones comenzaron a asegurar que el empresario se había sometido a un implante capilar en Turquía, un destino conocido por ofrecer procedimientos de restauración del cabello a pacientes extranjeros.
No obstante, no hay información verificable que respalde esa versión. Tampoco existe una declaración pública de Bezos o de sus representantes que confirme una operación de ese tipo.
El elemento central para desmontar el rumor está en el origen de las escenas. Las fotografías originales de la pareja fueron tomadas en Portofino, Italia, durante junio de 2023. La agencia Getty Images conserva registros del 12 de junio de ese año, cuando Bezos y Sánchez fueron fotografiados a bordo del yate Koru.
También existen imágenes del 13 de junio, cuando ambos fueron captados durante un paseo por las calles de esa localidad italiana. Fox Business publicó fotografías de aquella jornada, acreditadas a Splash News.
Cómo la inteligencia artificial puede alterar una fotografía real
El caso muestra una modalidad de desinformación que puede resultar difícil de detectar: utilizar una fotografía auténtica como punto de partida y modificar algunos de sus elementos mediante inteligencia artificial.
En este caso, las escenas corresponden a momentos reales de 2023, pero las versiones que circulan en redes presentan a Bezos con cabello. La alteración cambia un detalle físico del empresario y lo utiliza para construir una historia sobre un supuesto procedimiento médico.
La tecnología actual permite realizar este tipo de modificaciones sin necesidad de recrear una imagen desde cero. Algunas herramientas pueden añadir cabello, cambiar el rostro, modificar la ropa o alterar el fondo de una fotografía. El resultado puede conservar suficientes elementos de la imagen original para parecer una captura periodística auténtica.
Por eso, comprobar una fotografía no consiste únicamente en observar si parece real. También es necesario buscar su primera publicación, revisar los créditos, identificar la fecha y contrastarla con otras imágenes del mismo acontecimiento.
No hay pruebas de que Jeff Bezos se haya realizado un trasplante capilar
La circulación de estas fotografías no confirma que Bezos se haya sometido a una cirugía. Hasta el momento, no existe información independiente que demuestre que viajó a Turquía para realizarse un trasplante ni que haya pasado por un procedimiento de restauración capilar.
El rumor se sostiene en imágenes modificadas y en publicaciones de redes sociales que presentan como un hecho una afirmación sin respaldo documental.
La diferencia entre una fotografía original y una versión alterada puede cambiar por completo el sentido de una noticia. En este caso, un paseo de Jeff Bezos y Lauren Sánchez por Italia en 2023 fue utilizado como base para difundir una historia sobre una supuesta intervención capilar tres años después.
El episodio también deja una advertencia para los usuarios: antes de compartir una imagen que parece confirmar una noticia, conviene comprobar cuándo fue tomada y si existe una fuente confiable que respalde lo que se afirma sobre ella. En internet, una fotografía puede mostrar una escena real y, al mismo tiempo, transmitir una historia falsa.

articles.title: Bonne nouvelle, Nintendo assure que le prix de la Switch 2 ne devrait plus augmenter
articles.text:
Le 8 mai, Nintendo annonçait une hausse du prix de la Switch 2 dans plusieurs régions, en invoquant « l’évolution des conditions du marché ». En France, la console est passée de 469,99 à 499,99 euros le 1er septembre, quand les Américains la paient désormais 499,99 dollars au lieu de 449,99. À l’occasion de ses résultats semestriels publiés le 5 novembre, le constructeur affirme n’avoir aucun projet de nouvelle hausse.
À lire aussi : Il piratait des jeux Switch, Nintendo lui fait payer 4,5 millions de dollars de dommages et intérêts
Nintendo dit avoir mis sa mémoire à l’abri
L’annonce de mai était intervenue en pleine flambée des prix de la mémoire vive, tirée par la demande des centres de données dédiés à l’intelligence artificielle. Les coûts de transport et ceux des plastiques grimpaient eux aussi. Comme un smartphone ou un PC, une console embarque de la mémoire vive, et sa facture suit les cours de ces puces. Le Japon avait encaissé la plus forte augmentation, de l’ordre de 20 % sur certains modèles dès le 25 mai. La France s’en tirait avec 30 euros de plus, soit environ 6,4 %, et les États-Unis avec 50 dollars, soit environ 11 %.
Six mois plus tard, Nintendo déclare n’avoir « aucun projet d’augmenter à nouveau le prix de la Nintendo Switch 2 ». Le constructeur explique avoir pris les mesures nécessaires pour disposer de quantités suffisantes de mémoire, et se dit en position de sécuriser ses approvisionnements. Il ne précise ni jusqu’à quand ces réserves le protègent, ni à quel prix elles ont été constituées.
Des ventes en net recul, face à un été 2025 hors norme
D’avril à septembre, premier semestre de son exercice, Nintendo a livré 6,49 millions de Switch 2, un recul de 37,4 % sur un an, dont 2,67 millions sur le seul été, en baisse de 41 %. La période de référence englobe toutefois le lancement de la console, le 5 juin 2025, quand 3,5 millions d’exemplaires s’étaient écoulés en quatre jours. La hausse française n’est par ailleurs entrée en vigueur que le 1er septembre, au dernier mois du trimestre, ce qui rend hasardeux tout lien direct avec ce ralentissement.
En mai 2025, avant même la sortie, Shuntaro Furukawa, le président de Nintendo, reconnaissait déjà que la console était relativement chère comparée à la première Switch, et en tenait compte dans ses prévisions. Il tablait alors sur 15 millions d’unités pour le premier exercice.Sur la durée, la machine garde une avance confortable sur sa devancière : 26,35 millions de Switch 2 ont été livrées, contre 19,67 millions pour la première Switch au même stade. Nintendo maintient son objectif de 16,5 millions d’unités sur l’exercice, ce qui suppose d’en écouler une dizaine de millions d’ici fin mars, contre 6,49 millions sur les six mois précédents. Les jeux Switch 2, eux, ont atteint 15,03 millions d’exemplaires sur l’été, en hausse de 26 %.
Pour les acheteurs, la Switch 2 reste à 499,99 euros, sans nouvelle hausse annoncée ni baisse évoquée. Ceux qui la visent pour Noël savent au moins à quoi s’attendre, et Nintendo joue son objectif annuel sur ces quelques semaines de fêtes. Rappelons aussi que le prix n’est pas le seul changement que la Switch 2 a connu à la rentrée, puisqu’une révision est apparue sur les étales, avec la promesse d’un remplacement de batterie facilité.

articles.title: El aire acondicionado puede calentar mejor y más barato en invierno de lo que piensas: pero solo si lo ajustas de una manera
articles.text:
Cuando llega el frío solemos pensar en radiadores o estufas eléctricas para calentar nuestra vivienda, ya que el aire acondicionado está reservado para los meses de verano. Sin embargo, lo que algunos no saben es que los equipos actuales también funcionan como calefacción y pueden convertirse en una alternativa interesante para reducir el consumo eléctrico, sobre todo si solo necesitamos calentar una habitación.
Como explican en Ideal Home, la eficiencia depende del modelo, la temperatura exterior y el aislamiento de la vivienda. A diferencia de una estufa eléctrica convencional, los aparatos reversibles funcionan gracias a una bomba de calor que aprovecha la energía del aire exterior para calentar el interior. Así, en lugar de producir todo el calor a partir de la electricidad, lo trasladan de un lugar a otro.
Gracias a eso, algunos equipos proporcionan varias unidades de energía térmica por cada unidad de electricidad consumida, pero hay que tener en cuenta que su rendimiento disminuye si las condiciones exteriores son especialmente frías.
Subir el aire acondicionado a 26 grados no significa que caliente antes
Aumentar mucho la temperatura del mundo cuando sentimos frío es uno de los errores más habituales, ya que esto no calienta antes la habitación. Además, fijar 26 grados en lugar de 21 no garantiza que el aparato funcione más rápido, ya que estamos indicando la temperatura que queremos alcanzar.
Organizaciones como Energy Saving Trust recomiendan buscar una temperatura cómoda sin elevar el termostato y comenzar por unos 20 o 21 grados ajustándolo según nuestras necesidades. También conviene evitar encender y apagar constantemente el equipo cuando pasamos buena parte del día en casa, puesto que los modelos inverter pueden reducir su potencia al alcanzar la temperatura deseada.
Como el ahorro depende del tiempo y características de la vivienda, lo ideal no es mantenerlo funcionando durante nuestra ausencia. Así, antes de aumentar los grados, merece la pena comprobar si los filtros estén limpios, si no entran corrientes de aire y si el aparato tiene capacidad suficiente como para calentar el espacio.

articles.title: Varlock Releases Bumpy: A File-Based Versioning Alternative to Changesets
articles.text:
Bumpy, a modern monorepo-friendly version management and changelog tool from the team behind Varlock, has been gaining traction as a self-described successor to changesets. First unveiled in April 2026 via a Show HN post from creator Theo Ephraim, the project now ships under the @varlock/bumpy package and claims to address more than 120 open issues from its predecessor.
Bumpy follows the familiar changesets workflow. Contributors drop a small markdown "bump file" into .bumpy/ that declares which packages should be released, at what level, with a changelog description. The files are reviewable in the PR diff, consolidated into a release PR by CI, and consumed when that PR merges. An example looks like this:
---
'@myorg/core': minor
'@myorg/utils': patch
---
Added user lang prefs to core config.
Fixed locale fallback logic in utils.
Where the two tools diverge is beneath that surface. Bumpy ships with full support for workspace: and catalog: protocols across npm, pnpm, Yarn and Bun, per-package custom publish commands for VS Code extensions, Docker images or JSR targets, and a configurable three-phase dependency propagation algorithm that lets teams decide how peer dep bumps cascade through their graph. The CI story is leaner too, with two commands, bumpy ci check and bumpy ci release, running directly in a standard GitHub Actions workflow with no GitHub App to install or separate action repo to trust.
Version 1.14 added branch-based prerelease channels where prerelease versions are derived at publish time and never committed to git. The design targets complaints documented in the changesets own prerelease docs, which describe their pre mode as "very complicated" with states that are "very hard to fix". Another differentiator is AI integration. Bumpy ships an agent skill that teaches LLMs how to inspect git changes, identify affected packages and generate bump files via bumpy add. It installs through the Vercel Labs skills CLI, the GitHub CLI, or as a Claude Code plugin.
Getting started is a single install and an init that migrates existing changesets projects automatically:
bun add -d @varlock/bumpy
bunx bumpy init
A Show HN thread was candid that the project "was coded using AI, but carefully", and the team notes it is already being used to release Varlock alongside 25+ related libraries and plugins. In a separate thread on polyglot monorepos, bumpy was mentioned as a tool that "fixes a few things with changesets around custom publishing". Teams evaluating migration have opened issues flagging gaps such as Yarn 4.10 catalog detection.
Competition tightened with the changesets v3 release in August 2026, which closed many of the long-standing issues bumpy originally targeted. Bumpy's own differences doc now compares against v3 and credits it as "a substantial cleanup", while pointing out remaining gaps around configurable propagation, catalogs, custom publish targets and prerelease workflows. Relative to semantic-release, bumpy keeps the file-based model but adds a bumpy generate command that can produce bump files from branch commits when teams want to bridge both styles.
Bumpy is MIT-licensed, built in TypeScript, and available via the @varlock/bumpy package on npm, with the full source and documentation on GitHub.

articles.title: The wave of European fridge hacks has reached France's blood supply
articles.text:
What just happened? Refrigeration units operated by Établissement Français du Sang (EFS), France's national blood service, have been hit by a cyberattack. It is the latest in a series of intrusions targeting cold-storage controllers across Europe. No blood products or other biological materials were lost. The attack triggered EFS's alarm system, prompting staff to move the affected stock to functioning storage units before it could spoil.
The French Health Ministry said it is closely monitoring the situation and confirmed that no biological materials were lost. The intrusion appears to have targeted refrigeration equipment at three sites, reportedly including one in Burgundy-Franche-Comté.
The attackers did not breach EFS directly. The agency says the intrusion occurred at one of its service providers, which several outlets have identified as Coolworld, a refrigeration rental company. Coolworld has published a notice attributing the incident to "remote monitoring software" used in its systems. It traced the problem to "a component from a third-party supplier," but has released no further technical details.
Without those details, it is difficult to determine how the attackers gained access. In the earlier supermarket attacks, they targeted refrigeration equipment that was directly exposed to the internet. Coolworld may instead keep its controllers on a private network, which would have required the attackers to breach that network first. One detail stands out either way: EFS's monitoring and alarm system detected the breach, not the vendor's.
Coolworld has not disclosed which brand of controller it uses. The attacks so far appear to have targeted one manufacturer's equipment at a time. Danfoss controllers have featured most prominently, particularly in the attacks at the beginning of November, although they were not the only devices involved.
Copeland's Dixell controllers were also targeted in the attacks in mid-October. During the second wave of supermarket attacks, intruders raised freezer temperatures in Belgium and Sweden to 50 degrees Celsius, destroying food stocks.
The manufacturers' own documentation helps explain how the devices became accessible to attackers. A Danfoss datasheet says its controllers should be installed behind "appropriately configured firewalls and secure LAN" and should not be connected to "any public or non-secure network."
That wording leaves considerable room for interpretation. An installer who opens firewall ports to enable remote access can leave a device almost as exposed as one connected directly to the internet. Danfoss has since issued a support bulletin explicitly instructing customers to install the units behind a VPN. The bulletin appeared only in October 2026, and searches turned up no earlier version of this recommendation.
Copeland's guidance was even less restrictive. Installation manuals for its Dixell XWEB supervisory controllers instruct installers to forward port 80 (the web interface) and port 22 (Secure Shell) to the internet so the units can be accessed remotely. A VPN is mentioned only as an option. Copeland changed its guidance on October 14, following the first wave of attacks, when it published a security advisory stating that the controllers should only be accessible through a VPN.
Two Russia-aligned hacking groups, Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest, have claimed responsibility for the attacks. Several news outlets report having seen the claims in Telegram posts that have since been deleted. Z-Pentest reportedly published 2,500 lines of Danfoss code, although none of that material has been made publicly available. The groups say their goal is to expose poor cybersecurity practices.

articles.title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.
The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”
In a blog post, cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.
Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.
The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.
Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September. Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.
Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October, which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customers’ cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”
Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.
The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.
Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

O Galaxy Watch Ultra LTE de 47 mm está saindo por R$ 1.799,10 no Pix no Mercado Livre. O smartwatch premium da Samsung, com sensores que suportam diversos esportes e corpo de titânio, recebe desconto de 64% sobre o preço original de R$ 4.999 durante a Black November 2026.

O suporte ao 4G/LTE permite ao wearable ser útil em situações de risco. No caso de uma emergência médica, ele pode disparar alertas para contatos pré-programados e ligar para números como 190 (polícia) e 192 (bombeiros) sem depender de um celular, podendo assim salvar a vida do usuário.

O chip Exynos W1000, 2 GB de RAM e 64 GB de espaço interno permitem que o gadget instale e rode apps localmente. Sua bateria de 590 mAh resiste até 100 horas de uso no modo economia de energia, segundo a fabricante.
O Galaxy Watch Ultra de 47 mm (R$ 1.799,10 no Pix) suporta redes Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.3, o já mencionado 4G/LTE e GPS multibanda, que determina a posição do usuário em tempo real, essencial para esportes e outras aventuras.

articles.title: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
articles.text:
In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. “This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.”
In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth’s mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet’s interior.
Ice and sea
The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says.
The leading explanation was glaciation. Between roughly 720 and 635 million years ago, glaciers reached the tropics, and some scientists think the entire planet froze over, a scenario called Snowball Earth. “Ice sheets are very good at grinding, scouring, scraping the surface,” Flament explains. He said that glaciers are about 10 times more effective than rivers at eroding rock away. But if the whole planet froze, the Great Unconformity should be found everywhere. And it’s not.
Other explanations included rifting, pulling and stretching of Earth’s crust, and a global drop in sea levels. But rifting acts mostly on the edges of continents, and a sea level change should have affected all continents alike. “There’s no doubt that there was extensive glaciation. There’s no doubt that there have been sea-level changes throughout time. The question is, was that enough to put the Great Unconformity puzzle together?” Flament says.
A fourth idea held that the mantle itself was moving continents up and down, a process called dynamic topography. “It had been proposed, but it hadn’t been quantitatively tested,” Flament says. So, his team set out to do so.
Lava lamp planet
From roughly 100 to 200 kilometers beneath the surface down to nearly 3,000 kilometers, Earth’s mantle slowly convects. “An analogy would be a lava lamp, where some stuff comes up and some stuff comes down,” Flament explains. “Cold rock sinks and hot rock rises.”
The mantle is solid, yet a piece of rock can slowly travel from the surface to the deep Earth over some 200 million years. That motion tugs on the surface. Where cold slabs of ocean floor sink into the mantle at subduction zones, the ground gets pulled down; where hot mantle rises, it gets pushed up. The amplitude of this up and down motion is still debated, though. “The short of it is several hundreds of meters, and it’s still to be worked out exactly what that [precise value] is,” Flament says.
Dhungana and Flament ran six simulations of mantle convection going back 1 billion years, driven by reconstructions of how tectonic plates moved over that time. Then they grouped regions where the ground rose and fell in similar ways to find where the unconformity should have formed, and where it should have survived to the present. Flament, however, says the starting configuration of these simulations remains uncertain.
Magnetic records in ancient rocks reveal how far continents were from the equator, but not their longitude. “It’s possible that some continents may be in the wrong hemisphere,” Flament admits. The ancient ocean floor, long since recycled into the mantle, had to be invented entirely from scratch in the models. Still, the simulations produced a consistent story.
Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, had little or no subduction along its margins between about 930 and 510 million years ago, much like Africa today, so it sat above some rising mantle and was pushed up. Five of the six models showed this pattern of Laurentia seeing long uplift followed by sinking in the Cambrian. For northern Europe and North China, this pattern showed up in four.
But the uplift alone, Flament’s team concluded, was too gentle to strip away enough rock to create the Great Unconformity.
Glacial grind
“The uplift could create a tilt for the whole continent, but it’s not great at creating a steep slope,” Flament says. The missing piece of the puzzle, he argues, were glaciers that ground through rock even on low ground and gentle slopes. The models show the uplift was still building when Snowball Earth hit. “This gentle uplift that’s continuous, and then that glacial erosion that comes on top, work together,” Flament explains. “They’re not coupled. They just happen to coincide in time.” When the continents sank in the Cambrian, seas flooded in and buried the eroded surface.
The models made by Flament’s team also explain why the gap is so obvious in North America but hard to find elsewhere. Compared with records of sediment preserved on each continent, North America and Eurasia show one long rise followed by one long fall, which the researchers interpret as the ideal recipe for the Great Unconformity.
South America and Australia, on the other hand, went through two cycles. “This would form potentially two unconformities, and then the Great Unconformity would be more difficult to see,” Flament says. Africa was a different case altogether—hemmed in by mountain belts at the time, its erosion and sediment were shaped by the mountains rather than by the mantle beneath.
But if the mantle goes through such up and down cycles on a regular basis, the remaining question was why we can see only one Great Unconformity, and not many.
One of a kind
The team says the Great Unconformity is unique in the geological record because of a combination of a rise-and-fall cycle lasting over 900 million years, a near-global glaciation that happened at the right moment, and rock records that get harder to read farther back in time.
Flament suspects there may be an older candidate, tied to a glaciation 2.4 billion years ago, but rocks that old lack the fossils that make younger sediments easier to date. “Having life in sediments makes it a lot easier to have a sense of time,” he says. His work, however, may help explain what happens right after the Great Unconformity formed.
The intense erosion that carved the Great Unconformity washed rock material into the oceans, possibly fertilizing them just before the Cambrian explosion, when calcium became abundant in seawater. “That’s when life learns to mobilize calcium and create skeletons and shells,” Flament says. He admits, though, that mantle dynamics likely wasn’t the only process that enabled the Cambrian explosion. “I think it would be misleading to say the mantle set the pace here. But I think it was one of the forces that worked together.”
Jacek Krywko is a freelance science and technology writer who covers space exploration, artificial intelligence research, computer science, and all sorts of engineering wizardry.

articles.title: Tesla officially kills off the Cybertruck
articles.text:
The day you all have been waiting for is finally here – The Tesla Cybertruck is officially dead!
CEO (and mastermind of whatever that thing was) Elon Musk revealed the news on X, saying that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybertruck production.”
Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 6, 2026
To no surprise, the Cybertruck’s decline largely stems from weak sales over its first four years. WIRED notes that despite Musk’s claim that there were more than a million reservations, the truck sold fewer than 50,000 units in total by March, 2025.
According to Reuters, Kelly Blue Book data suggests Tesla sold only 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, which is down 48 per cent from the 38,965 sold in 2024. North of the border, data from Transport Canada suggested that Tesla had sold fewer than 2,000 between 2024 and 2025. Ironically, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.
The announcement also came only minutes after Musk raised the Cybertruck price in both the US and Canada, with the price rising to C$142,886.
Interestingly, former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer spoke to Reuters and quipped that “It doesn’t make sense to keep it going when it’s not meeting its targets. Every rational auto guy would say the same.”
To put it lightly, the Cybertruck has had a pretty tumultuous existence. When Elon Musk first stepped on stage to show off the Halo-looking thing, he tried to demonstrate the strength of the “unbreakable” glass by throwing a steel ball at it, and (shocker), it broke.
The Cybertruck has also had quite a few recalls throughout its history. The first recall was because the accelerator pedal was getting stuck due to an unapproved lubricant that reduced the pedal’s retention, and perhaps the most famous one was when the glued-on stainless steel trim on the front of the truck would just fall off after the elements got to it.
This is yet another move that signals Tesla is shifting away from being an automotive-only company, and towards being an AI and robotics company. Although the Cybercab is still a small project, Musk clearly sees this as the way forward for the company, and is scrapping his ridiculous fantasy truck to do it.
Rest easy, Cybertruck. You were strange, but fun to laugh at.
Sources: Elon Musk on X via WIRED, Reuters

articles.title: Climate protestors storm Microsoft AI data center construction site — Amsterdam reportedly first of many targeted actions across Europe
articles.text:
Protesters storm Microsoft AI data center construction site — Amsterdam reportedly first of 85 targeted actions across Europe
'Screw your data center.'
A Microsoft data center under construction in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, has been overrun by about a hundred protesters, with some carrying placards saying, “Screw your data center.” According to Reuters, the “Stop Dirty Data Centers” coalition is planning actions across 16 countries on November 6 and 7, 2026, including Amsterdam, Dublin, Warsaw, and another Microsoft site in Denmark.
Pure Data Centers, which owns the Amsterdam data center, said, “We respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have.” The report also quoted Microsoft saying that it understood the strong feeling that people have and respected their right to peaceful expression but says that it does not condone any unlawful action.
"On 6-7 November 2026 we are taking action across Europe to say Stop Dirty Data Centres," the group's website reads. "Local communities are rising up to stop dirty data centres where they live. We will unite and exercise our democratic rights to speak out, assemble, and protest to hold elected officials to account. We’re calling for an immediate moratorium on large data centres in Europe!" A map on the site shows actions planned at 85 locations across Europe over the coming days.
The group cited a list of concerns about "the explosion of AI data centres across our towns and cities," and claims to be joining to prevent "the irreparable harms data centres pose to the wellbeing of people and planet." They cite local communities, jobs, housing shortages and rising energy bills, the climate crisis, heatwaves and water shortages, big tech undermining democracies, the mental health crisis, increased surveillance and the erosion of privacy, securitization and militarization, and a toxic supply chain as motivations.
Data center opposition is one of the issues that has taken center stage in the U.S. midterm elections, with Americans overwhelmingly voting against them. It seems that resistance isn’t limited to the United States, though, as European countries take measures to limit their unlimited development. For example, Google has been hit with a criminal probe after its Finnish subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, allegedly destroyed 816 acres of forest without a permit. Denmark has also hit the brakes on data center grid connection requests as total applications exceed 60GW, more than eight times the country’s current peak power consumption. One Italian council also a 200% tax on data center development in agricultural land to encourage developers to reuse old industrial areas instead.
The Stop Data Center coalition claims that it isn’t against progress or that it wants to close down existing projects. Instead, it wants AI data center construction to be held until governments have established clearer rules on their development so that they do not have leave a negative impact on the environment and the people living around them. “AI, of course, is a super important technology and we need to have our own capacity,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told the publication. But she also added that “it's very important for citizens that they can trust that their energy bills are not skyrocketing and there are not electricity blackouts because of data centers, or they are not destroying the environment with these projects.”

Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.
