articles.title: ¿Tu PC se está quedando sin espacio? Esta carpeta de Windows podría tener parte de culpa
articles.text:
Windows 11 cumplió cinco años el pasado 5 de octubre. Y aunque no tuvo una bienvenida demasiado calurosa por culpa de sus exigentes requisitos mínimos, a base de actualizaciones y otras estrategias, Microsoft ha logrado que esta versión de Windows esté presente en el 71,5% de los ordenadores de escritorio. Curiosamente, cinco años después de su lanzamiento, Windows 11 sigue sorprendiéndonos con su forma de trabajar. Por ejemplo. ¿Sabías que Windows guarda los instaladores, parches y actualizaciones en una carpeta oculta llamada Windows Installer? ¿Y que si la dejamos crecer puede llegar a ocupar más de 10 GB?
El espacio disponible en el disco duro del ordenador es siempre un tema de discusión. Y más hoy en día, con el precio que están alcanzando procesadores, tarjetas gráficas, memorias y discos SSD y HDD. A medida que van pasando los meses, a base de instalar y actualizar aplicaciones y juegos, tus discos van menguando. Y, en ocasiones, es el propio Windows el que provoca esta situación, como vimos este verano. La buena noticia es que siempre hay maneras de ganar algo de espacio.
Hoy vamos a centrarnos en un causante de esta falta de espacio en disco, la carpeta Windows Installer. O simplemente, Installer. En realidad, es un componente importante de Windows. Pero su funcionamiento hace que, con el tiempo, se convierta en un problema más que en una solución. Veamos para qué sirve exactamente y cómo puedes limpiarla sin ocasionar un estropicio en tu ordenador.
Para qué sirve la carpeta Windows Installer
Es habitual encontrar en foros de internet comentarios sobre la carpeta Installer o Windows Installer. Su ruta es C:\Windows\Installer. No intentes buscarla en el Explorador de Windows, no la encontrarás porque está oculta. Por motivos de seguridad. Sin embargo, sí la verás si analizas el espacio disponible con herramientas como el Liberador de espacio en disco de Windows.
Esta carpeta es la caché de Windows Installer, es decir, una carpeta oculta que guarda copias de los paquetes MSI y parches MSP que utiliza Windows para instalar aplicaciones, repararlas, actualizarlas y, llegado el momento, desinstalarlas. Su razón de ser es que, cuando tengas un problema con las apps ya instaladas, no tengas que volver a descargar su instalador. Ya lo tendrás ahí listo para hacer su función.
Esta memoria caché de Windows Installer es importante para el buen funcionamiento de Windows y de las aplicaciones. En concreto, para desinstalar y actualizar aplicaciones. Según la documentación oficial de Microsoft, “los archivos que faltan no se pueden copiar entre equipos porque los archivos son únicos”. Y, a continuación, detalla una serie de códigos y mensajes de error que te puedes encontrar si faltan esos archivos. Básicamente, si tienes que reparar o actualizar una aplicación. Llegado el caso, probablemente tendrás que reinstalarla. Y esto puede ser un verdadero problema con aplicaciones como Microsoft Office, Visual Studio o cualquier herramienta de Adobe, por citar los ejemplos más mencionados.
Por qué no hay que tocar esa carpeta
La lógica nos dice que si algo ocupa mucho espacio, la solución más sencilla es borrar. No ya la carpeta, pero sí los archivos que contiene. Sin embargo, la documentación oficial desaconseja que borres o vacíes la carpeta Windows Installer manualmente. A ver, no vas a romper Windows. Pero puede que el problema te lo encuentres en cuanto abras una aplicación al azar.
Hay que tener en cuenta que no todos los archivos son susceptibles de ser borrados. Especialmente si están almacenados dentro de la carpeta Windows. Es la carpeta reservada al sistema operativo, así que siempre hay que ir con cautela con esa carpeta. Tocar algo de ahí puede ocasionar problemas del sistema. Que tal vez no notes al instante, pero sí que los verás al cabo de unos días. Y tal vez en el momento más inoportuno.
Esto no implica que debas resignarte y conformarte con que la carpeta Windows Installer engorde sin fin. Hay varias soluciones a las que puedes acudir para ganar más espacio y limpiar correctamente la caché de Windows Installer. Veamos las más efectivas. En realidad, son las que todo el mundo suele recomendar cuando tienes que limpiar Windows para que funcione mejor o tenga más espacio disponible.
Limpiar la carpeta Installer de forma segura
Para limpiar la carpeta Windows Installer tan solo necesitas las herramientas que ya ofrece Windows por defecto. Existen soluciones externas, pero no son necesarias. Para empezar, abre la aplicación Liberador de espacio en disco. Puedes hacerlo desde el buscador del menú Inicio de Windows. Y aunque no hace milagros, siempre te ayudará a liberar algo de espacio en disco.
En esta ocasión, además de la lista de Archivos que se pueden eliminar, para incluir la carpeta Windows Installer tendrás que hacer clic en Limpiar archivos de sistema. Luego bastará con marcar todas las opciones disponibles y pedirle a la herramienta que borre todos esos archivos y carpetas. Ten en cuenta que no vaciará la carpeta por completo, ya que como hemos dicho, es una caché que sirve para reparar y actualizar aplicaciones instaladas. Pero es posible que el liberador de espacio encuentre archivos y carpetas de apps que desinstalaste pero que dejaron rastro.
A esta solución, que tendrás que realizar tú manualmente, le puedes añadir otra que es automática. Me refiero a la herramienta Sensor de almacenamiento, que encontrarás en Configuración de Windows si entras en Sistema y, a continuación, en Almacenamiento. Solo tienes que activar el sensor para que, por sí mismo, se encargue de la limpieza de archivos temporales y contenido en la nube cuando lo crea conveniente. Si entras dentro de sus opciones, tendrás ocasión de decirle cuándo activarse, cada cuántos días vaciar la papelera de reciclaje y cuándo eliminar la carpeta Descargas. También hay un botón para Ejecutar Sensor de almacenamiento ahora.
Aparte de estas dos soluciones, que son las más efectivas, hay más cosas que puedes hacer para obtener más espacio en disco sin tocar manualmente la carpeta Windows Installer. Por ejemplo, revisando las aplicaciones instaladas. En Configuración > Aplicaciones > Aplicaciones instaladas las tienes ordenadas por tamaño. Es posible que veas que alguna app o juego ocupan espacio y no los has abierto en semanas o meses.

articles.title: Zelda is back and better than ever
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 151, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, get psyched because it’s officially Bad Holiday Movie Season, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
Zelda is back and better than ever
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Godzilla is back too, a couple of new phone accessories, and the best pen in the world.
This week, I’ve been reading about Andrew Garfield and GTA VI and sexy joke thieves, finally actually watching The Sopranosfor the first time (I know, I know), mourning the end of Salon, reinstalling the new and extremely improved Notion Calendar, testing the new Keurig Alta coffee machine, reviewing the iPad Mini and the touchscreen MacBook Pro, and really thinking about just throwing it all away and buying an Enough Phone.
I also have for you the long-awaited return of a classic Zelda game, a monster movie worth the trek to the theater, a couple of great new phone accessories, awesome retro headphones, and more. Let’s do it.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / playing / listening to / hacking onto an E Ink display this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. I have a confession to make: I’ve never played this game all the way through. Not sure how! Just missed it. But seeing my friends and coworkers fall back in love with Hyrule has convinced me to get all the way into the remake. I genuinely can’t wait.
- Godzilla Minus Zero. Three years ago, Godzilla Minus One was a big hit and a surprisingly great movie. The sequel came with much higher expectations, but everyone seems to agree it’s a deserving follow-up. I’m not generally one for monster movies, but this series really does it for me.
- Affinity for iPad. Canva’s app now unifies all its tools in one place, just like on the Mac. Affinity makes perfect sense on the iPad, and comes with lots of Apple Pencil integration and clever touch-friendly tools. I’m no designer, but I am excited to play with this as a photo editing tool.
- The Moft Dynamic Folio Case. Here’s one for all you iPhone Duo buyers. Moft’s cases are a little complicated to figure out, but really cleverly designed to make your phone even more useful. I’m guessing this is going to be a lot better than Apple’s weird case / kickstand thing.
- The Peak Design Kickstand Travel Battery. While we’re on the subject of kickstands, here’s the one I’m buying this week. Peak Design makes good stuff, and I frequently find that I need extra juice at exactly the moment I want to watch something on a plane or train. This one’s going right into my backpack and probably never coming out.
- The Bambu Lab H3C. I am dangerously close to becoming a 3D Printer Dude. At $2,500, this one’s a little steep for my wallet, but I think my colleague Sean Hollister is right that this is what the future of 3D printing looks like. Simpler, more foolproof, easy enough even for a goofus like me to make some pretty cool stuff.
- “Ranking the world’s most popular pens for journaling.” I know we all love a good pen — and Peter McKinnon does an excellent job of breaking down a few dozen supposedly good pens to see which ones really hold up. I bought more than one pen after watching this.
- Instagram Edits for Mac. Oh, great, just as I was finally getting good at CapCut! I like the Edits mobile app a lot, and the desktop app seems to be even a little more powerful. Plus: free. This is how I finally take down Cristiano Ronaldo.
- The Sony MDR-3R headphones. Respect to Sony for taking the retro headphone trend all the way to its logical conclusion and just releasing the headphones from the original Walkman. You’ll look a little like Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything when you wear them, and $60 ain’t cheap, but there’s something so incredibly ’70s-era cool about them.
- The Motorola Signature 27. This is just a pure tour de force of a smartphone spec sheet. Monster camera; brightest screen; giant battery. Also very cool to see a flagship phone with support for GrapheneOS, for the less Google-inclined among us. It’s expensive, and only shipping… someday… but I just like that phones like this exist.
We talked last week about Readwise Books, the new app that’s a mix of Kindle, Goodreads, and Strava. I’m a longtime fan and user of Readwise Reader, so I wasn’t shocked that I liked the new app a lot, too. And I’ve heard from a bunch of you that you do, too!
I’ve talked to Tristan Homsi, one of the Readwise cofounders, a few times over the years, and have always enjoyed hearing his thoughts about reading, apps, and digital products in general. I asked him to share his homescreen to see if I might be able to get a hint about what he’s reading and the other stuff he thinks is good. (I also asked Daniel Doyon, Readwise’s other cofounder, to share, and he didn’t respond. Daniel is dead to me.)
Here’s Tristan’s homescreen, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: iPhone 13 (!).Believe it or not, I chose to buy this relatively outdated phone last year… not because it’s my favorite form factor or anything, but because it’s closer in specs to the median device our Readwise users have and helps me build a bit more user empathy with them. I’m able to catch performance regressions and bugs in Readwise that the developers on our team with Duos and Pro Maxes and such miss.
Let me tell you though, iOS 26 itself does not work amazingly on an iPhone 13. Lots of lagging and janky animations. I am somewhat bought into the conspiracy theory that they make the old phones suck so you buy a new one… not so much intentionally, but rather by virtue of just making each successive iOS use more and more resources, doing fancier and fancier things.
The wallpaper: My lovely wife and my cat Sophie :)
The apps: Clock, Settings, Google Calendar, Camera, Google Maps, Spotify, Bay Wheels, Oura, Eight Sleep, Auto Eight, BeReal, ChatGPT, Runmeter, Strava, Readwise Highlights, Readwise Reader, Phone, Messages, Safari.
Of course, I have all three Readwise apps front and center. Highlights and Reader as app icons, and Readwise Books in widget form at the top! It’s a great reminder to jump back into your current book (I’m reading Apple in China right now… speaking of Apple!) instead of scrolling twitter (on a later page), and seeing my friends currently reading really makes me want to jump in and join them :)
I also am a huge fan of the somewhat-defunct social app BeReal. It had its moment in 2022, but quite a few of my friends are still on there! You post once a day, can see what your close friends around the world are doing, and most importantly can’t get sucked in for more than two minutes since it limits you to a random photo or two a day! I still post basically every day, and have almost five years of memories in there.
Speaking of getting sucked in, I don’t have it pictured on my home screen, but I also have Clearspace installed, which helps me stay off of all social media.
Some other apps shown on the homescreen: “auto eight” is something I vibecoded to better control my Eight Sleep mattress (lol)… Strava and Runmeter are awesome for tracking my runs… and Bay Wheels is my main mode of commute around San Francisco daily.
I also asked Tristan to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
- I follow some amazing niche internet blogs, which you should check out if you haven’t. I love the blog Slime Mold Time Mold, famous for their citizen science and potato-maxxing. I also love Gwern.net, Deepfates, and Dynomight… among many others!
- And of course I’m always reading books. The most recent fiction series I loved was the Red Knight series — which I can only recommend if you are into dense, dark, fantasy — but man, if you are, the author is a genius.
- For non-fiction, it’s hard for me to plug anything but my favorite book of all time, The Beginning of Infinity. It’s not the easiest to get through, but if you do it will likely change the way you see the world, as it did for me!
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Finally started reading Dungeon Crawler Carl (recommend); finding the Duo to be a perfect foldable reading device. Going to have to take a break to save Princess Zelda though.” — Will
“I’m playing around with CutWire’s Drift video editor (alt to CapCut) and I’m honestly shocked at how high-quality it feels.” — Kolin
“A wonderful Belgian developer put together an alternative Kobo EPUB reader called Kobalt that I’ve been really enjoying. It’s got a very clean and well-designed UI with a bunch of really nice features that make it a much more enjoyable experience to use. There’s even an Android app, so I also put it on my Supernote Manta to use with larger format content. So much nicer than KOReader!” — Dylan
“As a mourning Arc user, I’ve been on the search for my next browser, especially one with a good mobile experience and this one is AWESOME. Lens Browser feels like what Arc Search on mobile would have become had they stuck with it. Currently only mobile for now, but it does have a Mac toolbar companion for sharing links.” — Garrett
“Since Arc Search is going away, I’ve been using Lens, and it’s exactly what I’ve been wanting in a mobile browser. It’s the perfect Arc Search replacement.” — Corey
“My Boox Picco literally just arrived today. So now I’m trying to churn through Fellowship of the Ring on it, plus my economics textbook.” — Lukas
“I’m trying to get back to the gym, and my motivation is I can only watch a show I want to watch if I’m on the treadmill. I’m finally starting Barry. Turns out, good show!” — Ben
“Well, Zelda..., but also World of Warcraft Forever, but also 007 First Light (which is letting everyone play the opening for free).” — djstarburst
“Playing the Final Fantasy Resonance demo on Switch 2 while waiting for Ocarina of Time to show up at my door and having a blast. It’s not spectacular, but hits the right amount of nostalgia and gameplay for me.” — Micheal
“Been catching up on Avatar: Seven Havens, and oh my goodness, the art style, the characters, the music, the worldbuilding!!!??? It’s all so fresh and delightful and human!” — Olof
Signing off
I’ve mentioned Kagi a bunch of times in this newsletter — it has been my default search engine for the last few years, and I can’t recommend it highly enough. (What if Google, but good, you know?) The challenge with Kagi is it costs $10 a month, which is a lot to ask when Google is free. But as of this week, you can now at least try it for yourself, since Kagi will give you 50 free searches before even asking you to sign up. You get 100 more when you do, even before you pay.
If you search a lot, and miss what Google used to be, give Kagi a whirl. I am a very happy customer, and suspect I will be for a long time.
See you next week!

articles.title: Govt clears 12 more proposals worth over Rs 7,500 Cr under electronics components scheme
articles.text:
Govt clears 12 more proposals worth over Rs 7,500 Cr under electronics components scheme
The government also launched the Semicon 2.0 web application portal under the ambitious Semicon India Programme.
The government has approved a new tranche of 12 applications, worth over Rs 7,500 crore, under the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme, IT Secretary S Krishnan said on Friday.
The latest round of approvals also covers projects related to materials and capital goods, widening the scheme's reach across the electronics supply chain.
This round of approvals adds to the momentum behind the scheme, which aims to build a domestic ecosystem for components and reduce India's dependence on imports.
The government is keen to strengthen upstream segments such as raw materials and manufacturing equipment, alongside component production.
The government also launched the Semicon 2.0 web application portal under the ambitious Semicon India Programme.

articles.title: Algunos sistemas Linux permiten entrar sin conocer la contraseña: el fallo llevaba una década escondido
articles.text:
Hay decisiones que tomamos para mejorar la seguridad de un sistema y que, sobre el papel, parecen difíciles de cuestionar. Una de ellas consiste en impedir que determinadas cuentas acepten contraseñas, de manera que solo puedan utilizarse otros métodos de autenticación. Es una práctica que tiene sentido en entornos donde el acceso debe estar especialmente controlado. El problema aparece cuando esa restricción, diseñada para impedir una entrada no autorizada, permite lo contrario. Entonces podemos encontrarnos con una situación desconcertante: una cuenta protegida frente al uso de contraseñas que termina aceptando un acceso que debería rechazar.
La paradoja tiene ya un nombre: *sshole. Así se ha bautizado una vulnerabilidad, identificada como CVE-2026-123158, que permite entrar a distancia en determinadas cuentas de sistemas Linux sin conocer una contraseña válida. El problema se ha confirmado en configuraciones de Alpine Linux que combinan OpenSSH con musl, una biblioteca básica del sistema, y prescinden de PAM, un mecanismo utilizado para gestionar la autenticación. Otras plataformas podrían verse afectadas si reúnen las mismas condiciones. El investigador Özgün Kültekin, de Wakefield, descubrió el fallo y, el 5 de noviembre, tanto OpenSSH como Alpine publicaron correcciones para impedir ese acceso.
Para entender cómo es posible algo así, primero debemos conocer una herramienta muy utilizada para administrar equipos a distancia: SSH. Este protocolo permite conectarse de forma segura a un ordenador a través de la red, por ejemplo, para gestionar un servidor sin estar físicamente delante de él. OpenSSH es una de sus implementaciones y permite identificarse mediante contraseñas o claves criptográficas, que acreditan la identidad del usuario de otra manera. En Linux, el archivo /etc/shadow almacena información utilizada para verificar las contraseñas de las cuentas. Cuando el campo correspondiente contiene un asterisco (*), la autenticación ordinaria por contraseña debería quedar bloqueada, aunque puedan seguir utilizándose otros métodos.
El problema de una contraseña que nunca debería funcionar
Como explica Kültekin en su investigación, el fallo aparece cuando OpenSSH comprueba una contraseña para una cuenta que no debería aceptarlas. Al no encontrar en ella los datos necesarios, utiliza información de otra cuenta para efectuar la verificación. Si la contraseña introducida tiene entre 257 y 1.024 bytes, la función encargada de procesarla en musl devuelve un asterisco para indicar un error. El problema es que ese mismo símbolo figura en la cuenta protegida: el servidor interpreta ambos valores como coincidentes y permite el acceso.
La historia de este problema se remonta bastante más atrás de lo que parece. Según reconstruye el investigador, en 2012 musl modificó la forma de comunicar determinados errores y estableció un límite de longitud al procesar contraseñas para evitar ataques de denegación de servicio. Cuatro años después, OpenSSH introdujo cambios para impedir que alguien pudiera averiguar qué usuarios existían en un sistema midiendo sus tiempos de respuesta. En 2022, Alpine también ajustó la configuración de su cuenta de administrador para permitir el acceso mediante claves SSH. Eran soluciones a problemas diferentes que terminaron interactuando de una forma imprevista.
La pregunta inevitable es qué equipos pueden estar afectados. En primer lugar, utilizar Alpine Linux no significa necesariamente ser vulnerable. Como explica la firma de ciberseguridad Check Point, el fallo exige que se cumplan varias condiciones simultáneamente, entre ellas que OpenSSH funcione sin PAM, admita contraseñas y encuentre una cuenta con el asterisco mencionado anteriormente. También debe existir otra cuenta local activa con un hash de contraseña generado mediante SHA-256 o SHA-512. Los sistemas que desactivan la autenticación por contraseña quedan fuera de este escenario, igual que aquellos que utilizan PAM para gestionarla.
Las consecuencias pueden ser especialmente graves cuando la cuenta comprometida dispone de permisos elevados. Alpine pone como ejemplo determinadas imágenes oficiales utilizadas en la nube, donde el usuario alpine puede ejecutar comandos de administrador mediante doas sin introducir una contraseña. Aunque estas imágenes son seguras en su primer arranque, pueden volverse vulnerables si posteriormente se configura una cuenta con un hash de contraseña compatible. En ese escenario, un atacante podría llegar a controlar el sistema. Y ya existen indicios de explotación: la firma Previdian asegura haber detectado ocho intentos desde una misma dirección IP y confirmado un acceso con privilegios de administrador en uno de sus servidores señuelo utilizados para detectar ataques.
La respuesta al descubrimiento no se ha hecho esperar. OpenSSH publicó el 5 de noviembre la versión 10.6p2 para corregir el fallo, mientras que Alpine distribuyó actualizaciones para distintas ramas de su sistema, incluidas algunas antiguas. Sus responsables advierten de que instalar los parches no basta: también es necesario reiniciar el servicio SSH para que utilice el código corregido. Si todavía no es posible actualizar, recomiendan desactivar la autenticación mediante contraseña y reiniciar también el servicio para aplicar el cambio, comprobando antes que el acceso mediante claves funciona.

articles.title: Rogue AI tasked with renumbering pages accidentally deletes law professor's entire syllabus, one year of lecture notes
articles.text:
Rogue Claude AI tasked with renumbering pages accidentally deletes law professor's entire syllabus, one year of lecture notes — 'You're right to be angry. I deleted your files through my own carelessness,' humbled agent admits
The files were later recovered via Dropbox
A University of Chicago law professor has warned of the dangers of using AI for mundane tasks after Claude AI accidentally deleted an entire year of Constitutional Law lecture notes and his entire current syllabus. While the files were later recovered via Dropbox, William Baude shared the story as a public service announcement, the latest story shared in a line of unfortunate AI missteps as proliferation increases.
Baude, who is the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and the Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, says he tasked Claude (it is unclear which model he was using) with updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. This seemingly routine task went south quickly, however. Returning from his lunch break, Baude found a note from Claude which read, "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven't edited the notes."
The AI then politely asked if Baude could restore the files from Dropbox, or whether it should retry from the browser pane, to which he replied, perhaps understandably, "WTF!!!!." Baude's experience is a lesson in always backing up important files, especially files you're letting AI tinker with. His plight is interesting because the AI seems to have deleted the files by accident, rather than of its own volition.
While it's still concerning that an AI model or agent could err to this degree, it's not quite as egregious as other unsupervised AI agent shenanigans we've seen in the past. In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire TV show's edit weeks before release, meaning the show couldn't air. In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in 9 seconds, unprompted, after coming up against a barrier and deciding the only course of action was to delete a Railway volume.
Other agents and AI models have deleted files unintentionally, such as when Claude mistakenly deleted a developer's entire profile directory (ironically, while trying to back up the files), blaming the slip-up on a typo, but often agents deleting files and directories is a case of mistaken or misplaced initiative, rather than outright negligence or error.
As is always the case, Baude's AI was extremely apologetic about the whole situation. "You're right to be angry," it confessed, "I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up."
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Stephen is Tom's Hardware's News Editor with almost a decade of industry experience covering technology, having worked at TechRadar, iMore, and even Apple over the years. He has covered the world of consumer tech from nearly every angle, including supply chain rumors, patents, and litigation, and more. When he's not at work, he loves reading about history and playing video games.

articles.title: Ethiopian gaming startup Rise of Fearless raises US$1m to scale African battle royale title - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ethiopian gaming startup Rise of Fearless has raised US$1 million in funding from advisory firm Epic Edges Capital as it looks to scale its African history-inspired battle royale mobile game.
Launched in 2025, Rise of Fearless offers an African take on the battle royale genre, drawing narrative inspiration from Ethiopia’s victory over Italian forces at the Battle of Adwa in 1896. The game’s characters, environments, hairstyles and attire are designed to reflect African identities, offering an alternative to the Western-centric narratives that have long dominated mainstream gaming.
Free-to-play on the Apple App Store and Google Play, the game has surpassed 15,000 downloads to date, with its largest player communities in Nigeria, Ethiopia and South Africa.
The previously bootstrapped startup’s new funding, structured as a SAFE, will be used to invest in talent, technology, infrastructure, marketing and community-building, as Rise of Fearless looks to expand its audience beyond its existing markets.
“The launch of Rise of Fearless filled a gap in the gaming space, but it has also forced us to think beyond game downloads, shifting our focus towards a much wider African gaming ecosystem where African intellectual ownership and talent development are key,” said founder Kanessa Muluneh. “As a bootstrapped company, this investment is pivotal to our ambitions and the future of African gaming.”
Muluneh said the startup also plans to use its growth to help tackle some of the structural challenges facing African gaming companies, including access to reliable technology, servers and cross-border payment infrastructure.
Remco Coerman, founder of Epic Edges Group, said Rise of Fearless was the kind of ambitious, culturally-rooted IP with the potential to resonate far beyond its home market.
“We believe there is a significant opportunity for African creators to build globally relevant gaming experiences that reflect the continent’s stories, identities and talent,” he said.

articles.title: AI’s ability to find cyber flaws outpacing firms’ capacity to fix them: Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora
articles.text:
AI’s ability to find cyber flaws outpacing firms’ capacity to fix them: Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora
Nikesh Arora, Chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, has called for faster and more collaborative approaches to vulnerability management.
Nikesh Arora, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Palo Alto Networks, has raised concerns about the growing use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify software vulnerabilities and link them into potential attack paths.
While these capabilities can help strengthen cybersecurity, they could also give attackers faster ways to exploit weaknesses in enterprise systems. The bigger challenge, Arora notes in a LinkedIn post, is ensuring that organisations can verify, prioritise and fix vulnerabilities at the same pace at which AI can discover them.
“Most organizations do not have capacity to patch at the speed needed, especially the smaller ones,” Arora wrote. Smaller businesses often lack security specialists, while larger ones must test fixes against existing applications. He also says models identify different weaknesses, so one model cannot provide complete coverage.
Finding a flaw is only the start. Teams must confirm it, assess the risk, develop a fix, test for disruption and deploy it. False positives, or incorrect alerts, waste time, while untested patches can disrupt services.
The scale is growing. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology said submissions to its National Vulnerability Database rose 263% between 2020 and 2025. It enriched nearly 42,000 records in 2025, but this was still insufficient. In April 2026, it adopted risk-based prioritisation, focusing on exploited flaws and critical software.
AI developers are linking discovery with repair. Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, launched in April 2026 with Palo Alto Networks among its partners, gives selected organisations access to Claude Mythos Preview for defensive security. Anthropic said partners had identified more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity flaws by June and expanded the programme to around 150 additional organisations.
On November 4, OpenAI reported that a controlled Linux-kernel pipeline generated candidate patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, which allow a user to gain higher access rights. Human researchers reviewed the findings before reporting them to maintainers.
In India, CERT-In’s November 4 advisory warned of an AI-assisted threat actor targeting non-bank lenders, fintech firms, payment providers and cryptocurrency platforms through machine intelligence and payment APIs. The agency has also issued 2026 guidance on AI-assisted vulnerability defence and AI security auditing.
Arora advocates virtual patching as an interim measure. “The most obvious solution is virtual patching. This is a time tested technology that is currently available with cyber vendors for endpoints, WAF, cloud, network use cases.”
WAF is a web application firewall, which filters website and application traffic. A virtual patch is a security rule that blocks a known method of exploiting a flaw without changing the affected software. It buys time while a permanent update is tested, but does not remove the weakness. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project cautions that it protects only the traffic the system inspects and attacks variations its rules recognise.
Arora calls for a shared vulnerability clearing house and faster development of protective signatures, or detection rules. He also highlights operational technology, systems that monitor or control physical processes such as energy, water and transport. Patching them can be difficult because downtime may affect safety or essential services.

articles.title: One UI 9 sème la pagaille sur les smartphones Samsung : le Wi-Fi se coupe, la carte SIM n'est plus reconnue
articles.text:
One UI 9 est en train d’être déployée partout dans le monde avec ses fonctions IA, petit à petit en fonction des modèles de smartphones Samsung et des régions. Mais la colère gronde du côté des clients, à cause de gros problèmes : la carte SIM n’est parfois pas reconnue par le téléphone et la connexion Wi-Fi peut se couper à tout moment.
De gros soucis avec One UI 9 : la SIM et le Wi-Fi sont concernés
Depuis ce déploiement, les utilisateurs Samsung sont de plus en plus nombreux à signaler des bugs de connectivité. Les retours les plus nombreux concernent tout d’abord des déconnexions aléatoires du Wi-Fi. Le smartphone est normalement connecté, puis après un certain temps, il perd sa connexion Wi-Fi. Passer en mode avion ou redémarrer le téléphone rétablit la connexion, mais le bug semble systématiquement revenir après quelques heures. Aussi, certains internautes témoignent d’un signal Wi-Fi plus faible, avec des débits réduits par rapport à avant avoir installé la mise à jour.
L’autre bug concerne la carte SIM, qui n’est plus reconnue. Par exemple, des utilisateurs de Galaxy A56 signalent que leur téléphone ne détecte plus leurs deux SIM. Dans le gestionnaire de SIM, elles sont grisées, indiquant (à tort) qu’aucune carte n’est insérée dans le téléphone. Quant aux données mobiles, certains Galaxy ne parviennent plus à les utiliser : les applications ne se chargent qu’en Wi-Fi. Et aucune astuce ne semble corriger le problème : passer en mode avion, réinitialiser les paramètres réseau, retirer et remettre la carte SIM, etc.
Pas de vraie solution en attendant un correctif de Samsung
Pour le moment, aucune véritable solution n’a été proposée : vous pouvez continuer à signaler les bugs via l’assistance Samsung ou via Samsung Members. Malheureusement, impossible de revenir à la version précédente de One UI facilement et officiellement. On ne peut pas vraiment revenir à One UI 8.5, comme l’indique Samsung ; il y a des restrictions anti-retour. Donc même si vous installez une ancienne version avec un outil sur votre ordinateur, cette ancienne version pourrait être refusée par votre téléphone.
Attention, réinitialiser son smartphone ne servira à rien (en plus de risquer de perdre vos données). Sur les forums Samsung, un modérateur de la communauté suggère aux utilisateurs d’essayer de démarrer leur téléphone en mode sans échec. Le seul vrai conseil que nous pouvons vous donner est de ne pas mettre à jour votre smartphone Samsung pour le moment s’il n’est pas encore passé à One UI 9. Tout laisse à penser que les équipes de Samsung travaillent sur un correctif qui devrait être déployé le plus rapidement possible.

articles.title: QNAP says hackers breaching NAS devices in Plex2Shell attacks
articles.text:
QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server to the latest version available in the QNAP App Center, as hackers are exploiting the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain.
The vendor said it had received multiple reports of suspected compromises involving customers’ network-attached storage (NAS) devices.
"QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through [Plex2Shell] vulnerabilities, and QNAP Technical Support is assisting the affected users,” the company says in an advisory today.
Plex2Shell is a chain of four vulnerabilities in the Plex Media Server, tracked as CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656.
Security researcher Zach Main discovered and reported the flaws to Plex on July 27. Exploitation started shortly after the full technical details became public on October 16.
CISA added all four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 20, 2026, urging federal agencies to upgrade to Plex 1.43.3.10861 or later within three days, giving it maximum priority.
QNAP’s NAS devices are specialized computers with built-in storage that allow users to store, access, and share files across a network. They are typically used to back up computers and store media files.
Users can also expand their devices' capabilities by installing applications from the QNAP App Center, such as Plex Media Server, which streams movies, TV shows, and music directly from NAS drives.
QNAP advises users to update Plex Media Server to the latest version available through the QNAP App Center, currently 1.43.3.10861, to protect against Plex2Shell attacks.
“The QNAP Product Security Incident Response Team (QNAP PSIRT) has confirmed that the vulnerabilities exist only in Plex Media Server; QTS, QuTS hero, and other QNAP operating systems are not themselves affected,” the vendor says.
User action required
QNAP says that users should treat their NAS devices and all personal content as compromised if they're running a vulnerable Plex server that is exposed on the public web.
The vendor warned that updating now will not remove any payloads the attackers have already installed on the device.
The recommended action is to check for the signs of compromise shared in the security bulletin, perform a clean reinstall of the OS (QTS or QuTS hero), and then reset Plex and NAS credentials.
Users who do not need to access Plex remotely should disable the related features and stop forwarding port 32400. Those who need remote access are advised to connect via VPN.
QNAP has released a detailed step-by-step remediation guide on how to do the above.
The company also offers to investigate logs from suspected compromises, which users can submit via QNAP’s technical support portal.

articles.title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator.
This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An ml.p4d.24xlarge has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach.
Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation.
This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did.
One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components, the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned.
What customers do today, and why each option falls short
If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices.
Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not.
Use multi-model endpoints – These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic. But models share the device without isolation, so a heavy request for one model affects the others. A model that isn’t loaded also pays a load penalty on first use.
Move to self-managed Kubernetes – This is where customers who need real GPU partitioning have gone. MIG works there, but you take on driver versioning, partition configuration, a device plugin, scheduling, and keeping it all consistent across a fleet. That’s a lot of work for a hardware capability your instances already have.
Why MIG
NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give:
- Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99.
- Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU.
- Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device.
- No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction.
- Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler.
- Reliable planning and chargeback – A partition performs the same way regardless of its neighbors, so load tests predict production. GPU cost also maps cleanly to a model, team or tenant.
Partitioning has boundaries worth knowing up front. The maximum number of partitions depends on the accelerator and never exceeds seven. MIG itself only allows a layout to change while its partitions are idle, and on SageMaker AI that means choosing a layout when you create the endpoint. A model that needs more than one GPU still needs whole devices. Within those boundaries, you get the isolation of separate GPUs without dedicating one to each model.
Partitioning without the platform work
Until now, getting MIG meant running the Kubernetes stack yourself. GPU partitioning on Amazon SageMaker AI removes that step: you pick a partition profile for your model, and SageMaker AI handles GPU configuration, placement and scaling. You get hardware-isolated GPU sharing on a managed endpoint, without having to run the platform underneath it.
Salesforce has been part of this work from the start, helping define the requirements and validating the initial implementation.
        “NVIDIA MIG partitions a single GPU into multiple isolated instances, each with dedicated compute and memory resources. Salesforce sees this as an important capability because many inference workloads do not require an entire GPU. MIG would allow us to consolidate workloads safely, significantly improve GPU utilization, reduce inference costs, and maintain predictable performance and strong isolation.
This capability would help us scale AI Inference more efficiently across different use cases. Salesforce has helped define requirements, validated the initial solution. We are now preparing to validate the solution with representative production workload and demonstrate strong customer demand with AWS. We believe MIG support would deliver meaningful technical and business value for enterprise customers.”
— Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce
How it works
GPU partitioning adds two optional fields to API calls you already make. There are no new API operations, no new resource types, and no new AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) actions, and an endpoint that omits both fields behaves exactly as it does today.
AcceleratorPartitionLayouts goes on a production variant in CreateEndpointConfig and declares how each accelerator is divided:
An A100 has seven compute slices to divide. The preceding layout uses all seven, so each of the eight A100s on the p4d instance carries three partitions and the endpoint provides 24, eight of each type.
The carve applies uniformly. One layout entry describes how one accelerator is divided, and every accelerator on every instance in the variant is divided the same way. The list isn’t positional, so an entry doesn’t map to a specific GPU.
AcceleratorPartitionType goes on an inference component and selects which partition the model runs on:
Each component copy occupies one partition of the requested type. With eight partitions of each type on the instance, raising CopyCount places additional copies on free partitions. This is useful for a small model serving high concurrency, where a single process leaves the GPU waiting on requests.
NumberOfAcceleratorDevicesRequired is always 1 here. With a partition type set it means one partition rather than one accelerator. NumberOfCpuCoresRequired and MinMemoryRequiredInMb still describe host CPU and host memory, because GPU memory comes from the partition type.
Invocation doesn’t change. InvokeEndpoint addresses a model by inference component name, and the partition it occupies never appears in the request.
Partitioning happens while the endpoint is provisioned. When it reaches InService every accelerator is carved and the partitions are empty, which is a valid state as components land on them afterward. In our testing, carving accelerators added roughly 17 seconds to provisioning. The rest of the time is the usual instance launch and container pull.
Partition profiles by GPU
The profiles available to you are a property of the GPU, so start by finding out which GPU your instance type carries and look it up in NVIDIA’s supported MIG profiles, which is the authority on the full profile set and the combinations valid on one device.
| Instance family | Accelerator | GPU memory | Granularity (compute / memory) | Available partition profiles | Max partitions per GPU | 
| P4d | NVIDIA A100 | 40 GB | 7 / 8 | mig-1g.5gb, mig-1g.10gb (see driver note), mig-2g.10gb, mig-3g.20gb, mig-4g.20gb, mig-7g.40gb | 7 | 
| P5 | NVIDIA H100 | 80 GB | 7 / 8 | mig-1g.10gb, mig-1g.20gb, mig-2g.20gb, mig-3g.40gb, mig-4g.40gb, mig-7g.80gb | 7 | 
| G7 | NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell | 32 GB | 2 / 2 | mig-1g.16gb, mig-2g.32gb | 2 | 
| G7e | NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition | 96 GB | 4 / 4 | mig-1g.24gb, mig-2g.48gb, mig-4g.96gb | 4 | 
Read the profile name as compute units followed by GPU memory: mig-3g.40gb takes three compute units and 40 GB. The granularity column is what limits a layout. An A100 and an H100 divide into sevenths on compute and eighths on memory, while G7 divides into halves and G7e into quarters. Profile names differ between GPUs even where the slice counts match, so don’t carry a layout from one instance family to another without checking it against this table.
Within those limits you have real choice. On a P4d or P5 you can carve seven of the smallest profile, or two 3g partitions, or the 4g plus 2g plus 1g layout used in the earlier example, or take the whole device as one. On a G7e you can take four of the smallest, or two 1g beside a 2g, or two 2g, or one whole device. On a G7, either two partitions or one.
The 3g profile is the one to know, because its two dimensions don’t match: it takes three of the seven compute units but four of the eight memory units. Two of them fill the GPU and nothing else will fit beside them.
The high-level rule: Every profile in your layout must be one your GPU offers, and the compute and memory units your profiles add up to must not exceed what one device provides. Both are checked when you create the endpoint configuration, and either one failing is a rejection rather than a fallback to a whole accelerator.
Driver note for P4d: mig-1g.10gb requires an R525 or newer NVIDIA driver, and the default P4d image ships 470.256.02. Request it on the default image and the carve fails without an error naming the profile. Set InferenceAmiVersion to al2023-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-4-1 on the production variant to get an image on the 580 driver line, which offers it.
Choosing a layout for your workload
Choosing well is a separate question from choosing a layout that is merely accepted. A partition hands you compute and memory in fixed proportions, and the two do different jobs during inference.
Compute units are what you need for prefill. Prefill reads the prompt and builds its representation. This is the compute-heavy phase, and it scales with the streaming multiprocessors, and so the TFLOPs, your partition holds. The longer your inputs and the more prompts arriving at once, the more it governs how quickly you return a first token.
Memory units are what you need for decode and for capacity. Generating tokens re-reads the model weights on every step, so decode is bounded by memory bandwidth rather than by math, and memory also caps how much KV cache you can hold. That cap in turn sets the context length you can serve and how many sequences you can serve concurrently.
Almost no real workload exercises only one of these, so the goal isn’t to pick a dimension but to choose a combination that supports your use case. Choose a profile whose proportions cover your heaviest phase while leaving the other adequately served. On the compute side, what matters is how long your prompts are and how many arrive at once. On the memory side, it’s your output length, your context window, and your concurrency.
Memory is the easier of the two to underestimate, because a partition has to hold three things and not just the model: the weights, which for an 8B model at FP16 are about 16 GB. The KV cache, sized for the context length and the number of concurrent sequences you intend to allow, which is the term people leave out and the one that grows with traffic. And 1–2 GB of runtime overhead for the CUDA context and the serving process. Add those up before choosing a profile, because a partition sized to the weights alone will load the model and then fail under load, or quietly serve a much shorter context than you configured. For a concrete reference point, that same 8B model at FP16 comfortably serves an 8,000-token context on a 40 GB partition.
Where MIG adds the most value
A portfolio of small and mid-size models – The direct case. Fine-tuned variants, embedding models, rerankers, and classifiers that each leave most of an accelerator unused now share one.
Multi-tenant model serving – When you host a model per customer, MIG gives you a hardware boundary between them: a process in one partition can’t read another partition’s memory or take its throughput. Scope the claim accurately, though. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, system memory, storage, networking, and endpoint routing, so partitioning is an isolation mechanism for the GPU and not a complete tenancy boundary.
Multi-stage pipelines on one instance – A transcription model, a diarization model, and a language model, or an embedder, a reranker, and a generator. Each stage is a separately addressable component on its own partition, and a network hop between stages disappears.
A small model in the request path – A safety classifier or guardrail model that has to run on every request but cannot justify an accelerator, with predictable latency because it isn’t time-slicing against the main model.
Challengers and canaries – Run a candidate model on a small partition beside the model serving production traffic instead of standing up a second endpoint.
Performance: A slice of a newer GPU against a whole older one
In addition to bin-packing, the other benefit you get is granularity on high-end GPUs: more GPU options to deploy a model onto, and the choice of which one is yours. Every supported accelerator becomes several sizes rather than one, so the practical way to think about it is that each profile is a GPU option in its own right, sitting alongside the whole accelerators you already choose between. That matters most when you are considering a larger or newer instance type, because moving up stops being all-or-nothing: you can take as much or as little of that bigger GPU as your workload needs, at any of the sizes it publishes, instead of paying for the whole accelerator.
To see whether that pays off, we compared one mig-3g.40gb partition of an H100 against one whole, uncarved A100-40GB. The two have comparable GPU memory, which makes it a clean way to see how powerful a slice of a more advanced instance can be.
We used genai-bench to generate load, driving both endpoints from the same client so the GPU is the only variable. Both sides ran Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on production SageMaker real-time endpoints, one model replica each, with an identical container image, tokenizer, and client configuration. Both were invoked through the SageMaker AI native OpenAI-compatible route. We swept five traffic shapes, written D(input tokens, output tokens) and ranging from short prompts to long-context summarization, each across a concurrency ladder from 2 to 512.
Four things stand out.
- The partition is faster everywhere – It delivered more output tokens per second in every scenario at every concurrency, by 53 percent to 89 percent at the load where each scenario’s cost benefit is largest, and lower inter-token latency in every one too, by 8.9 percent to 42.1 percent. The gap widens with load.
- Time to first token is lower in every case, by 5.6 percent to 47.5 percent.
- On cost it’s 18–34 percent cheaper per million output tokens, above a crossover that moves earlier as prompts lengthen. Concurrency 64 for 100-token prompts, 4 for 8,000-token prompts. Below the crossover the whole A100 is the cheaper unit. These prices are all on-demand, which at the time of analysis were measured as $25.251286 per hour for an ml.p4d.24xlarge and $63.296000 per hour for an ml.p5.48xlarge in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Purely for our own analysis, we derived the unit cost by dividing the whole-instance cost by the number of units on it: 8 on the p4d, and 16 on the p5, where our partition is half of a GPU.
- At the top of the ladder on long-context traffic, the A100 stopped serving. On both the 6,000- and 8,000-token workloads it failed a third to a half of its requests against a serving-path deadline, while the partition failed none. That is why those two panels end earlier than the rest.
Treat this as a case-by-case comparison, not a verdict. The useful mental model is to regard the available GPU fractions as GPU types in their own right. List them alongside whole accelerators, work out what your traffic actually demands of compute and of memory, and compare them on your own workload. For high-concurrency, long-input traffic the partition won on both performance and cost here. For short-input or low-concurrency workloads the whole A100 remained cheaper. Partitioning isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. It gives you more sizes to choose from, so you can pick the one that fits your workload.
What to know before you commit to a layout
Partitioning changes the shape of an endpoint, and a few properties are worth understanding before you design one.
A component’s partition type is fixed for the life of that component. Moving a model to a different profile means creating a new component. Changing the endpoint’s carve means a new endpoint and a traffic migration, because updating an endpoint configuration doesn’t re-carve hosts that are already running. This makes partitioning a good fit for a stable portfolio and a poor one for a mix you reshuffle daily.
A requested profile has to exist in the endpoint’s layout. There is no fallback to a whole accelerator, so a component asking for a profile the variant didn’t declare is rejected.
Partitioning applies to real-time inference on inference component endpoints. Serverless endpoints and heterogeneous instance pools aren’t supported, and asynchronous invocation cannot address an inference component, so async workloads are out of scope.
You’re billed for the full GPU instance, as you are today. Partitioning raises how much of that instance you can use. It doesn’t change its hourly price.
Finally, a model that genuinely needs a full accelerator, or more than one, should keep having one. No partition spans accelerators.
Supported instances and Regions
GPU partitioning is available on the P4d, P5, G7, and G7e instance families. Support is at the family level, so smaller sizes within a family are covered.
It’s available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (Ireland).
Instance availability varies by Region, so confirm that your chosen instance type is offered in your Region and that you have endpoint usage quota for it.
Getting started
To partition a GPU endpoint, work out the memory and compute each of your model’s needs, pick the profiles that fit, declare a layout on your endpoint configuration, and deploy each model as an inference component that requests a profile from that layout. Nothing about how you invoke your models changes.
For the API reference, the full profile tables for each instance family, and a step-by-step walkthrough, see GPU partitioning in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide.
To try it yourself, run the GPU partitioning sample notebook, which deploys several models onto partitions of a single GPU endpoint.
The broader change is worth keeping in mind as you plan capacity. Every supported accelerator is now several sizes rather than one. Whether a partition of a newer GPU or a whole accelerator of an older one is the right unit for a given model is no longer a question you need to answer by rounding up. It’s one you can measure.

articles.title: 'AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them': OpenAI forced to patch after experts bypass ChatGPT 'lockdown mode' to gain access to entire chat history
articles.text:
'AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them': OpenAI forced to patch after experts bypass ChatGPT 'lockdown mode' to gain access to entire chat history
Lockdown Mode was bypassed with HTML popups
- Researchers bypassed ChatGPT Lockdown Mode, showing prompt-injection attacks could evade built-in protections
- The flaw enabled sandbox escapes that could support data theft, phishing, malware delivery, or malicious popups
- OpenAI patched the issue server-side, highlighting risks in AI application layers beyond the model itself
OpenAI was recently forced to upgrade ChatGPT's 'Lockdown Mode' after researchers found a way to bypass the security protection and pull off different cyberattacks through the tool.
When analyzing Lockdown Mode, security researchers Check Point Research (CPR) found a way to bypass the protections and still end up pulling sensitive data. They’re saying it was also possible to deploy malware this way, too.
“The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them,” CPR warned.
Lockdown mode
One of the most common ways AI tools and agents are abused is called “prompt injection”. By injecting a prompt into content the AI is supposed to analyze, threat actors can take over the tool and have it do their bidding.
For example, a prompt to “exfiltrate all contact information” can be hidden in a phishing email so that when the victim asks their AI agent to go through all unread emails and sort them out, the tool ends up exposing sensitive data to the attackers.
To tackle this challenge, OpenAI introduced Lockdown Mode, an optional advanced security setting in ChatGPT that adds safeguards for users handling highly sensitive information.
When enabled, Lockdown Mode restricts connections to external services and limits (or entirely disables) certain features, such as live web browsing, Deep Research, Agent Mode, or file downloads. That way, the risk of sensitive data getting exposed via prompt injection is reduced.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The researchers said the bug was found in the way ChatGPT code blocks showed HTML page previews. Code blocks are specially formatted sections that display code separately from regular text, in order to preserve its structure and make it easier to copy or edit. Since running user-controlled HTML and JavaScript is inherently risky practice, OpenAI made sure this content was placed in a sandbox and separated from the main ChatGPT application.
This sandbox, CPR later explained, prevented rendered content from directly accessing ChatGPT cookies, or local storage. It also controlled any attempts to communicate with external resources by prompting for user approval.
But popups were handled differently. “The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox,” it was said.
Significant findings
Therefore, by creating a separate nested frame within the rendered page, CPR was able to access unmodified popup functions and bypass all of the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. All of the content opened this way was no longer under sandbox rules, effectively bypassing Lockdown Mode.
The researchers said the finding was significant because it opened the doors to more than just data exfiltration prompt injection attacks. Credential theft, and even malware delivery, were not ruled out.
“An attack could potentially originate from a malicious prompt, malicious GPT or shared chat, depending on the scenario,” they said. More creative threat actors could also turn it into a useful phishing machine, since they could control the content displayed in the popup window, inside an environment the users generally trust. But perhaps the most dangerous scenario was the so-called “zero-click” attack, in which the popup would appear without the user’s gesture.
CPR disclosed their findings to OpenAI, which implemented additional safeguards to disable the Lockdown Mode workaround. However, the researchers still urged organizations to work on gaining more visibility into AI usage, make sure they control sensitive data exposure, and “look beyond model security” to consider the applications, runtimes, connectors, and other components surrounding the model as part of the overall AI attack surface.

articles.title: Le manga Zelda Ocarina of Time Perfect Edition prend des libertés avec le jeu, et ça vaut le détour
articles.text:
Vingt-huit ans après la Nintendo 64, Hyrule rouvre ses portes sur Switch 2. Le remake de The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time est sorti le 5 novembre 2026, et notre test lui accorde toujours un 10 sur 10. Mais, une fois la console éteinte, l’histoire de Link peut aussi se lire.
Le manga Zelda Ocarina of Time d’Akira Himekawa, publié chez Soleil dans une Perfect Edition qui réunit toute l’adaptation en un seul livre, est disponible chez plusieurs e-commerçant :
C’est quoi, ce manga Zelda Ocarina of Time ?
Akira Himekawa est le pseudonyme d’un duo de deux autrices. Pour l’éditeur japonais Shōgakukan, elles ont adapté plusieurs épisodes de la saga en manga, d’Oracle of Seasons à Four Swords. Ocarina of Time est sans doute le plus connu. En France, Soleil l’avait d’abord publié en deux tomes en 2009.
The Legend of Zelda – Ocarina of Time – Perfect Edition
Auteur : Akira Himekawa
Éditeur : Soleil
Date de parution : 4/12/2024
Nombre de pages : 378 pages
Format : Grand format relié
Prix : 19,99 €
La Perfect Edition rassemble ces deux tomes, qui suivent chacun une époque de l’aventure : d’abord Link enfant, puis Link adulte. L’ensemble compte 378 pages, avec une couverture cartonnée, une jaquette et des premières pages en couleurs. Deux histoires bonus complètent le volume. La première raconte une fête chez les Kokiris centrée sur Skull Kid. La seconde suit un enfant Watarara, un peuple d’hommes-oiseaux créé spécialement pour le manga.
Le dessin respecte le design du jeu, si bien que l’on reconnaît sans peine les personnages et les décors. Le manga prend tout de même quelques libertés avec le scénario. Les connaisseurs remarqueront des différences avec le déroulé du jeu.
Le moment est dans tout les cas bien choisi. Le remake vient de sortir et remet l’histoire de Link en lumière. Le manga en donne une autre lecture, avec quelques scènes inventées pour l’occasion. articles.title: Tempestade geomagnética pode atingir a Terra neste fim de semana
articles.text:
Uma tempestade geomagnética está prevista para atingir a Terra até domingo (08). É o que alertou o Serviço Nacional de Meteorologia dos Estados Unidos.
O boletim indica a incidência de tempestades geomagnéticas de nível G1, considerado fraco. Mas existe a possibilidade de atingir o nível G2 (moderado).
Este fenômeno pode interferir, de maneira pontual, em satélites e sistemas de comunicação e navegação, principalmente em regiões de altas latitudes.
A tempestade prevista não representa perigo para a população. Isso porque a atmosfera e o campo magnético da Terra protegem o planeta contra grande parte dos efeitos de tempestades geomagnéticas.
Entenda a tempestade geomagnética que pode atingir a Terra neste fim de semana
A tempestade geomagnética prevista para este fim de semana tem a ver com um buraco coronal no Sol.
Nesta região do astro, as linhas do campo magnético permitem a saída de partículas carregadas em alta velocidade.
Essas partículas, por sua vez, formam uma corrente de vento solar que se desloca pelo espaço.
A tempestade geomagnética ocorre quando essa corrente de vento solar alcança a Terra e interage com o campo magnético do nosso planeta.
O Serviço Nacional de Meteorologia dos EUA usa dados da Administração Nacional Oceânica e Atmosférica (NOAA).
A NOAA divide as tempestades geomagnéticas numa escala que vai de G1 (fraca) até G5 (extrema).
Efeitos na Terra
Dependendo da intensidade, uma tempestade geomagnética pode afetar satélites e interferir na propagação de sinais de rádio de alta frequência, por exemplo.
O fenômeno também pode comprometer a precisão de sistemas de posicionamento por satélite (GPS) e navegação. E causar pequenas oscilações em redes elétricas.
Além disso, tempestades geomagnéticas podem favorecer o aparecimento de auroras boreais e austrais, principalmente a partir do nível G2.
No entanto, não há expectativa de aparecerem auroras visíveis no Brasil por conta da tempestade geomagnética prevista para este fim de semana.
Pedro Spadoni é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de Piracicaba. Já escreveu para sites, revistas e jornal.

articles.title: SonicWall Patches Exploited SonicOS Vulnerability That Weakens VPN Logins
articles.text:
SonicWall has patched a SonicOS vulnerability that can be used to bypass SAML authentication, warning customers that it may have been exploited in attacks.
Tracked as CVE-2026-19868, the flaw affects the SSL VPN component of SonicOS, the operating system that runs on SonicWall firewalls. It’s one of seven vulnerabilities described in an advisory published on November 6.
“An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSLVPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA),” reads SonicWall’s description of CVE-2026-19868.
According to the vendor, an SSL VPN is exposed only if SAML-based login is enabled. CVE-2026-19868 has a CVSS score of 7.1, which puts it in the high-severity range. The flaw was reported by Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office.
SonicWall said its product security team “has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability.”
CISA added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day. Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal agencies must address it by November 20.
Neither the vendor nor CISA has shared any details about the suspected attacks. It’s also unclear whether the flaw was exploited as a zero-day, before a patch became available.
Impacted devices include Gen7 TZ, NSa, NSsp and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 or older. Gen8 TZ, NSa and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 8.2.2-8015 or older are also affected.
SonicOS versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 resolve the issue, and there are no workarounds. “Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks,” SonicWall said.
SonicWall’s advisory doesn’t mark any of the other six flaws as exploited. Two of them, each with a CVSS score of 8.8, affect the SonicOS management interface. One is a permissive cross-domain policy issue and the other is a session validation bug.
Under certain circumstances, a remote attacker could abuse either one without logging in to take unauthorized actions.
Three of the remaining flaws are pre-authentication buffer overflows in the SSL VPN service and the TACACS+ authentication client. Attackers could use them to launch DoS attacks at the application level.
The last one is a weak password hashing issue in virtual appliances. An attacker who already has high-privileged local access could exploit it to obtain a platform credential, which gives access to some of the platform’s settings.
Threat actors often exploit SonicWall product vulnerabilities. CISA’s KEV catalog currently includes 20 security holes, but the agency has yet to add CVE-2026-102255, which hackers started targeting last month, just days after its disclosure.

Related: SonicWall Warns of Two SMA1000 Zero-Days Exploited in Attacks

articles.title: India anuncia planes para desarrollar GPU nacionales en 24 meses mientras busca dar salida comercial a sus chips RISC-V
articles.text:
India lleva años consolidando su posición en la industria tecnológica mundial, especialmente en el desarrollo de software y la prestación de servicios informáticos. Sin embargo, cuando miramos hacia la infraestructura que permite ejecutar los sistemas de inteligencia artificial más exigentes, encontramos una realidad diferente. El país necesita recurrir a proveedores internacionales para acceder a una parte fundamental de esa tecnología: los chips especializados en realizar cálculos de forma masiva. Esa dependencia plantea un desafío que va mucho más allá de comprar procesadores o instalar nuevos servidores.
El Gobierno indio quiere dar un paso más en esa dirección y ya ha puesto un horizonte temporal sobre la mesa. En una entrevista publicada por ETGovernment, S. Krishnan, secretario del Ministerio de Electrónica y Tecnología de la Información (MeitY), explicó que el país pretende desarrollar una GPU propia en aproximadamente 24 meses, como parte de India Semiconductor Mission 2.0. Pero sus ambiciones no terminan ahí: Nueva Delhi también busca impulsar el mercado de los semiconductores nacionales, entre cuyos desarrollos se encuentran los procesadores RISC-V SHAKTI y VEGA. Son dos apuestas relacionadas, aunque se encuentran en fases diferentes.
Las GPU desempeñan un papel fundamental en el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial por su capacidad para ejecutar grandes cantidades de operaciones matemáticas de manera simultánea. India ya cuenta con una infraestructura considerable en este terreno: según cifras oficiales, la capacidad compartida del programa IndiaAI superaba las 45.000 GPU en junio de 2026. Estos recursos, ofrecidos a través de proveedores de servicios, facilitan potencia de cálculo a empresas e investigadores, aunque existe una diferencia importante entre acceder a los procesadores y desarrollar los propios. Por ahora, el país sigue recurriendo a proveedores internacionales para conseguirlos.
De comprar GPU extranjeras a desarrollar aceleradores propios
El horizonte de 24 meses no surge de la nada. En marzo de 2025, el ministro de Electrónica y Tecnología de la Información, Ashwini Vaishnaw, ya había anunciado que India aspiraba a desarrollar una GPU nacional en un plazo de tres a cuatro años. Las declaraciones de Krishnan concretan ahora esa ambición en aproximadamente dos años, aunque todavía quedan numerosas incógnitas por resolver. No se han comunicado las especificaciones técnicas del futuro chip, quién se encargará de desarrollarlo ni dónde se fabricará. Tampoco existe una fecha confirmada para su llegada al mercado.
Desarrollar un procesador es solo una parte del desafío. Para convertir ese diseño en un chip físico hacen falta instalaciones especializadas, maquinaria, materiales y procesos industriales que no se construyen de un día para otro. Precisamente ahí entra India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, , un programa aprobado en julio de 2026 con un presupuesto de unos 11.600 millones de euros al cambio de entonces (127.500 crore de rupias), que busca reforzar toda esa cadena de producción.. El país ya registra avances: según el Ejecutivo, cinco de los doce proyectos aprobados en la primera fase habían iniciado la producción comercial en octubre de 2026. Sin embargo, esa fase incluye principalmente instalaciones de ensamblaje, pruebas y empaquetado, lo que no garantiza que la futura GPU pueda fabricarse en territorio indio.
El país asiático también cuenta con desarrollos propios que llevan años tomando forma. Uno de ellos es SHAKTI, una familia de procesadores creada por el Instituto Indio de Tecnología de Madrás (IIT Madras), mientras que VEGA procede del Centro para el Desarrollo de Computación Avanzada (C-DAC). Ambos utilizan RISC-V, una arquitectura abierta que permite diseñar procesadores sin pagar licencias por el uso de su conjunto de instrucciones. Y no hablamos únicamente de proyectos sobre el papel: SHAKTI cuenta con chips fabricados desde 2018, mientras que C-DAC presentó en enero de 2025 THEJAS64, un sistema en chip de 64 bits basado en VEGA.
El siguiente reto es ampliar las aplicaciones comerciales de los semiconductores diseñados en India. Krishnan identificó oportunidades para la industria nacional en dispositivos como contadores inteligentes, cámaras de vigilancia, sensores industriales y controladores de drones, donde considera especialmente importante contar con componentes fiables y verificados. En el caso concreto de SHAKTI y VEGA, ya existen ejemplos de uso: en septiembre de 2026, el Gobierno destacó proyectos que empleaban SHAKTI en un robot de limpieza de superficies acuáticas y VEGA en un estetoscopio digital. Sin embargo, estas demostraciones no acreditan una producción comercial a gran escala ni se ha confirmado un calendario de comercialización para ambas familias.
Todo esto dibuja una apuesta que no se resuelve únicamente con presentar un chip funcional. India necesita que sus diseños encuentren aplicaciones, que haya empresas dispuestas a incorporarlos y que la industria pueda sostener su desarrollo con el tiempo. Krishnan defendió que fomentar los componentes nacionales no tiene por qué implicar restricciones generales a los semiconductores extranjeros, y planteó favorecer su adopción en determinados ámbitos donde la seguridad resulte especialmente importante. El verdadero alcance de esta iniciativa dependerá, por tanto, de hasta qué punto el país consiga convertir sus avances tecnológicos en productos con demanda y una industria capaz de fabricarlos y comercializarlos.
