articles.title: Nigeria is rewriting its cyber laws, can it stop hackers?
articles.text:
Nigeria is reviewing its cybersecurity laws to counter mounting threats as artificial intelligence (AI) makes fraud, digital deception, and attacks on critical infrastructure harder to detect.
AI was linked to 55% of cybercrime incidents recorded across Africa last year, while deepfake cases increased sevenfold between the second and fourth quarters of 2024. Cybercriminals are using AI to automate scams, create convincing fake identities, and more quickly identify weaknesses in critical systems. This means attackers are adopting the technology faster than institutions can strengthen their defences, leaving existing security systems and laws struggling to keep up.
This growing technology gap is the primary driver behind the current legislative review, as the Nigerian government acknowledges that existing frameworks fail to provide adequate guardrails or align with international best practices.
Nigeria is also considering a national cybersecurity architecture to establish baseline security standards for organisations nationwide. However, unless these reforms improve enforcement, fortify vulnerable infrastructure, and foster local technical expertise, they risk expanding state surveillance powers without making Nigeria’s digital economy any safer.
Nigeria’s cybersecurity reforms are progressing along three distinct tracks. The Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015 was amended in February 2024, while a broader policy review convened lawmakers, government agencies, and industry stakeholders in Lagos. The National Cybersecurity Policy and Strategy, first introduced in 2014 and revised in 2021, is due for its five-year review in 2026. Meanwhile, the proposed National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill 2025, which underwent a public hearing in November 2025, aims to establish a comprehensive legal framework for digital services and e-governance.
Together, these initiatives address cybercrime enforcement, institutional security, and the governance of Nigeria’s expanding digital economy.
What is the government trying to fix?
The government says it has advanced work on a draft executive bill designed to strengthen the nation’s legal protections against cyber threats.
In October 2026, Adedeji Stanley Olajide, Chairman of the House Committee on ICT & Cybersecurity, told TechCabal on the sidelines of the International Cybersecurity Conference in Abuja that “the timeline is immediately after the election…” because not much can happen during political campaign season.
The lawmaker, however, expressed confidence that between January and June 2027, “the cybercrime, cybersecurity, and digital economy bills” would all be enacted into law.
He maintained that, once enacted, these laws would curb cyberbullying and other cyber threats and enforce stricter compliance and security standards across the financial sector.
The urgency for reform is evident: nine in ten Nigerian children face risks of cyberbullying, harassment, and online exploitation.
Financial institutions under siege
Nigeria’s financial sector also faces pressing vulnerabilities. In 2025, Nigeria lost ₦25.85 billion ($19.2 million) to electronic payment fraud. In September 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) cautioned banks, fintechs, and payment service providers that cyber risks and AI-driven vulnerabilities pose direct threats to financial stability.
These warnings align with findings from TC Insights’ report: “The Compliance Reckoning: Regulating Financial Services in the Age of AI.” The study notes that while gross fraud losses decreased in 2025, AI-powered attacks have grown considerably more sophisticated, with escalating regulatory fines underscoring systemic compliance risks.
In 2025 also, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) fined MultiChoice Nigeria ₦766.24 million ($568,630) for data protection breaches and unauthorised cross-border transfers of personal data. Also, the Commission launched investigations into 1,369 organisations across the banking, insurance, pensions, and gaming sectors
In a separate case, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) investigated a ₦3 billion ($2.23 million) fraud scheme that targeted First City Monument Bank customer accounts through unauthorised access.
These incidents demonstrate how systemic cyber vulnerabilities leave consumers exposed, compromise sensitive records, and erode trust in public institutions.
Even the government is not safe
Nigeria’s cybersecurity risks also extend to public institutions as government infrastructure has proven vulnerable. The AI-generated photo controversy involving the Independent National Electoral Commission’s voter register revealed that suspicious voter records entered the commission’s database through authorised registration terminals operated by its own officials, rather than via an external hack. It exposed a weakness in how public institutions control access, monitor staff activity, and verify data before adding it to their systems.
The Corporate Affairs Commission experienced a major breach exposing over 15 million corporate documents and beneficial ownership records. Meanwhile, Remita—the central payment gateway for Nigeria’s Treasury Single Account—suffered a data exposure due to a misconfigured cloud storage bucket that leaked nearly three terabytes of financial data.
Vincent Olatunji, NDPC National Commissioner, at a five-day hands-on cybersecurity training for technical personnel in government ministries, departments and agencies, in June, disclosed that the commission faced over 2,000 cyberattack attempts on its portal in one week.
These incidents highlight the growing threats facing institutions responsible for protecting Nigerians’ personal data, even as e-governance expands.
Across Africa, the case is not different: detecting intrusions is now harder as AI transforms routine cybercrime into automated reconnaissance, synthetic identity fraud, and credential hijacking.
Findings from Esentry and Darktrace—a cybersecurity intelligence partnership focused on enterprise threats—reveal that modern attackers rarely force their way in through software flaws; they enter via compromised credentials and weaponised internal trust that slip cleanly past conventional security alerts. According to the report, West Africa lost over ₦1 billion ($742,104) in fraudulent transactions that slipped past legacy security controls in the first half of 2026 alone.
This dynamic hits Nigeria with disproportionate severity. While South Africa accounted for 45% of Darktrace-observed incidents (20% ransomware), Kenya accounted for 6% (33% ransomware), and Nigeria accounted for only 5% of regional volume. However, ransomware was present in 80% of the investigated Nigerian cases, with data exfiltration in 40%—proving that Nigeria’s cyber risk far outstrips its visibility, masking high-impact extortion behind low detection numbers.
Rather than breaching perimeter walls, threat actors now leverage AI-enabled behavioural evasion to mimic legitimate user actions and quietly hijack authorised workflows—rendering static government firewalls and manual compliance audits obsolete.
Breaches of this magnitude undermine public trust in official registries and jeopardise data essential for corporate verification and anti-money laundering enforcement.
These failures highlight a critical requirement for new cybercrime legislation to establish clear accountability and enforce proper configuration standards for critical data infrastructure.
As legislative frameworks expand, lawmakers must balance state oversight with the protection of privacy and civil liberties. The true efficacy of these reforms will lie in whether they yield higher prosecution rates, fewer systemic breaches, and stronger data protection.
Building local capacity, not foreign dependence
For Nigeria, meaningful investment in cybersecurity sovereignty requires building internal capabilities to secure critical infrastructure, safeguard citizen data, investigate cybercrimes, and maintain vital digital services. Crucially, it also means curbing reliance on external vendors for system maintenance and incident response.
The government’s National Digital Cloud Policy attempts to address these challenges by granting tax and duty waivers on servers and data centre infrastructure to attract private investment. In return, the policy directs federal agencies to migrate legacy systems to the cloud while mandating that sensitive national data—including biometric and healthcare records—remain hosted within Nigerian borders.
Official reports state that over ₦4.5 trillion ($3.34 billion) was allocated to Nigeria’s information technology sector between June 2023 and June 2026.
Additionally, Nigeria aims to attract $250 million in private investment within 12 months and $750 million within 24 months. However, capital targets alone do not guarantee enhanced security capacity. The ultimate test remains whether these capital flows translate into resilient infrastructure, institutional capability, and skilled local talent.
As Abdul-Hakeem B.D. Ajijola, Chair of the African Union Cyber Security Expert Group, noted at the international cybersecurity conference mentioned earlier that the value of security investments must be measured by the capabilities that remain after vendor contracts expire. Procuring third-party software provides temporary protection, but without skilled local engineers to maintain and defend these systems, Nigeria risks trading technological vulnerability for vendor lock-in.
AI is shifting from an advantage for attackers to a standard part of offensive infrastructure. Essentry and Darktrace’s forecasts for the second half of 2026 point to an acceleration in deepfake-driven executive fraud, software supply chain compromises, and automated ransomware targeting cloud assets.
Progress must therefore be measured by operational outcomes: faster threat detection, prompt vulnerability patching, mandatory breach disclosure, rapid service recovery, and strict accountability for non-compliance with minimum standards.
Updating legislative frameworks can clarify agency responsibilities and expand investigative mandates. However, reforms should not be judged merely by the scope of powers granted to the state, but by whether citizens’ data is protected, financial infrastructure remains resilient, and public services can withstand sophisticated attacks.
Ultimately, Nigeria’s success will not depend on passing stricter cybersecurity laws, but on building a digital ecosystem capable of defending itself, recovering from security incidents, and safeguarding the public.

articles.title: Un cocinero italiano se negó por tercera vez a poner piña en una pizza y acabó despedido
articles.text:
Davide Tamburella era el jefe de cocina de La Costa, un restaurante italiano que se anunciaba como un rincón de la Riviera en pleno Fortitude Valley, el barrio de ocio nocturno de Brisbane, capital de Queensland y que es el estado donde se cultiva el 99 % de la piña australiana. Cuando un cliente que había contratado un evento de más de 15.000 dólares australianos pidió pizza de jamón y piña, Tamburella se negó a prepararla porque, como italiano, consideraba que ponerle esa fruta encima era "un insulto a su cultura", de modo que era la tercera vez en cuatro años que rechazaba la misma petición.
Se le pasó la pasta (y la paciencia del jefe)
En la resolución que publicó este martes la Fair Work Commission, el tribunal laboral de Australia, también aparece que el cocinero llegó a pedirle a su jefe que se informara de lo importante que es para los italianos que la pizza no lleve piña. Lo despidieron el 20 de mayo, dos semanas después de que el dueño, Elliot Ingram, lo citara a una reunión sobre su rendimiento en la que, además del episodio de la piña, salieron el lenguaje malsonante que el propio cocinero reconoció, su manera de comunicarse con el equipo y varios momentos de frustración en la cocina que se sumaban a un aviso previo por escrito.
Ingram explicó en redes sociales que la petición del cliente le pareció razonable y que la piña influyó en la decisión, aunque pesó más lo que venía arrastrándose de antes, y a The Guardian le contó que en sus 17 años en hostelería ha aprendido a elegir sus batallas. Reconoce que la hawaiana no es su favorita, aunque llegaron a tenerla en el menú infantil porque en Australia es de lo más corriente.
Fuori tempo massimo: por qué perdió el cocinero su reclamación
Tamburella acudió al tribunal con una reclamación por "protecciones generales", una vía que sirve para denunciar que te han despedido por un motivo que la ley prohíbe, y sostenía que en su caso había influido la lesión que sufrió en el trabajo cuando, al golpear una barandilla metálica, se fracturó dos huesos de la mano derecha. Como esa reclamación hay que presentarla en los 21 días siguientes al despido y él dejó pasar el plazo, la comisionada Jennifer Hunt, que no encontró motivos excepcionales para ampliarlo, archivó el caso sin llegar a pronunciarse sobre si la negativa a poner piña estaba justificada.
Tempo scaduto también para el visado
Donde el despido le ha salido más caro es en su situación en el país, porque llevaba más de tres años tramitando el visado 186, que permite obtener la residencia permanente con el patrocinio de la empresa. Ingram dice que retrasó todo lo que la ley le permitía el aviso a las autoridades con la esperanza de que el visado se aprobara antes, pero no llegó a tiempo y el cocinero tendrá que empezar el trámite desde cero. La Costa cerró en julio, cuando venció el contrato de alquiler, por lo caro que resulta mantener un local en la zona, y Tamburella, que no ha respondido a la prensa, trabaja ya en otro restaurante italiano de Brisbane en cuya carta no aparece la piña.
Una hawaiana con pasaporte canadiense
La pizza hawaiana, que inventó en 1962 Sam Panopoulos, un inmigrante griego que vivía en Canadá, lleva desde entonces dividiendo a los aficionados, y ni siquiera en Italia hay unanimidad: Gino Sorbillo, uno de los pizzeros más conocidos de Nápoles, la incorporó a finales de 2023 a la carta de su local de la Via dei Tribunali, en una versión blanca con tres quesos y piña caramelizada que le valió una buena ración de críticas en redes. En el extremo contrario está Lupa Pizza, una pizzería de Norwich (Reino Unido) que cobra 100 libras a quien quiera ponerle piña a una pizza que normalmente cuesta unas 12.

articles.title: Google, Meta, and TikTok sue California over law banning addictive social media features for children
articles.text:
What just happened? Google, Meta, and TikTok are taking California to court over its latest attempt to keep children from getting hooked on social media. The companies have filed separate lawsuits challenging a law that restricts addictive features for children under-16, arguing that the state is interfering with free speech and parents' authority.
The complaints, filed Wednesday, target Assembly Bill 1709. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the measure on September 10 as part of a broader package covering social media and AI chatbot safety. It's scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027.
The restrictions cover personalized feeds, endless scrolling, and autoplay videos, all defined as "psychologically exploitative features." Platforms must also take reasonable steps to verify users' ages. The aim is to stop companies from pushing features designed to keep children scrolling long after they intended to put their phones down, which sounds like a good thing.
According to Reuters, the companies argue that California is dictating how they present content and replacing parents' judgment with its own. Their challenges invoke the First Amendment and the often-used Section 230, which broadly protects platforms from liability for user-generated content.
Meta says the state cannot override its editorial decisions about organizing and displaying posts. Google argues that the restrictions could undermine systems that help children find appropriate videos, while TikTok says they interfere with free expression and parental choice.
Google also says parents are the ones who should decide what is appropriate for their families, pointing to its existing parental controls and protections.
"Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we've built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos," Google spokesman José Castañeda said.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office told The Guardian it was reviewing the lawsuits and would defend the state's child-protection laws.
It's not just the social media giants expressing opposition to the law. The Electronic Frontier Foundation warns that age checks could push everyone to hand over more personal information. It also argues that removing recommendation tools could effectively shut young people out of online communities.
The fight follows Meta's August agreement to pay up to $18 billion and change how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram to settle states' child-safety claims. Those changes include default time limits and mandatory scrolling breaks.
Much of the world is now introducing restrictions or bans on social media use for young people. In Australia, which was the first country to introduce such a law, Reddit challenged its under-16 ban in the High Court, arguing that it restricts political communication and that the platform isn't actually a social media site.

articles.title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick
Over the past year, as we built Amazon Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user.
Take the user who says “monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice.
This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When?, What?, Who?, and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it.
The framework at a glance
A trigger starts the work and carries the task (When and What), an agent takes it on (Who) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task (How). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more.
Triggers: What causes work to begin
Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task.
- Human-initiated: A person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something. Interactive, synchronous, conversational.
- Agent-delegated: One agent, mid-task, invokes another to handle a sub-problem. Programmatic, composable, potentially recursive.
- Scheduled: Time-based activation, like “run financial research every Monday at 9am.” Deterministic, with the same standing instructions applied across runs.
- Event-driven: A signal from an external system, such as a new email, a Slack mention, a file change, or a webhook.
The type of trigger conditions the execution: a scheduled background task might stay conservative (for example, do nothing if uncertain), while a human-initiated one would be responsive (for example, ask rather than stop).
Agents
We define an agent as a persistent, learning actor. It’s the Who? in any execution, and the anchor against which learning accrues. Two agents given identical input can differ, because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories. The agent isn’t the instructions it follows. It’s the entity that interprets them. It consists of three things:
- Instructions: Standing guidance defining persona, role, context files, and operating principles. A Finance Agent behaves differently from a general assistant primarily because of this.
- Capabilities: The tools, skills, workflows, and sub-agents available for use, updated dynamically. A charting library can be added in one session and removed the next.
- Learned context: Memory that accumulates through use: the queries that work for a tool, the formatting users prefer, the edge cases they care about. This is how the tenth execution beats the first without anyone changing the instructions.
Everything else is extrinsic: the large language model (LLM) underlying the agent is a swappable model parameter, conversation history is per-session state, and triggers belong to the platform.
A consequence of this definition is that a user request “I want an agent that monitors my Slack and sends a digest every morning” is usually a trigger added to an existing agent, not a new agent or workflow. With this framing, we can merge chat, scheduled, and “autonomous” agents into one actor that you can converse with, schedule, and that can orchestrate and inspect its own past work.
Capabilities
Capabilities are How an agent acts, spanning a spectrum from fully agentic to fully deterministic. That axis is really a confidence contract: how much latitude the agent keeps versus how much the user fixes in advance.
Tools are atomic operations with a typed schema: send an email, query a database, read a file. Whether a local function, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, or another agent behind a protocol boundary, the caller sees the same interface: name, description, parameters, result.
Skills are structured guidance with room for judgment: instructions bundled with resources (templates, scripts, examples) that describe an approach rather than a rigid sequence. They load through progressive disclosure, so the agent sees only names and short descriptions until one becomes relevant, then reads the full instructions in. A skill can therefore bundle arbitrary depth of expertise without a constant cost.
Workflows are deterministic coordination: declared steps, control flow, branching, and error handling that execute in fixed order, with decision logic in code rather than model inference. Think of a purchase-approval route: budget check, manager sign-off, then finance, each recorded. The route is fixed, but the judgment inside a step is still the agent’s.
Why skills and workflows outlast model improvements
A natural question arises: if models keep improving, won’t skills and workflows become unnecessary? We don’t think so, because each holds value independent of model capability. Skills are the unit for capturing, versioning, and sharing institutional expertise, while workflows deliver auditability, step-wise visibility, and deterministic multi-service coordination. Nor are they fixed: a well-understood skill can tighten into a workflow (crystallization), a workflow that keeps hitting edge cases can loosen back into a skill (dissolution). This is done in Quick through our continuous learning framework, which we will describe in a future post.
What this means in practice
Return to “monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest”. Because these primitives compose, the same request can be met several valid ways:
- A scheduled task with a one-line instruction, leaving the agent to figure out the rest.
- The same task backed by a skill with explicit formatting rules and channel priorities.
- The same task invoking a workflow with deterministic steps and error handling.
All three produce a daily digest on a schedule. What differs is the confidence contract. A user who trusts the agent wants the first, one burned by inconsistency the second, one running a compliance-sensitive process the third.
Learning shifts that trajectory over time. A task that starts as one sentence (“check my email for urgent items”) accumulates domain-bound learnings: effective queries, preferred formatting, and which senders matter. The tenth run is markedly better, with no one encoding that by hand. The right design is the simplest option that meets the user’s confidence requirement, with a path to graduate through autonomous learning when they need more.
Conclusion
The value of this agentic primitive taxonomy is that four plain questions, When, What, Who, and How, are enough to place any piece of agentic work, from a one-line chat request to a scheduled, compliance-grade process. Sharing one vocabulary lets builders reason about the system and lets the product hide complexity. Best of all, the user never has to learn any of it. They say what they want, and the system assembles the appropriate primitives to do their job.
Next in the series: the agentic operating system that builds on these primitives and powers Amazon Quick.

articles.title: AWS Ships Continuum for Code Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
AWS recently made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon), four months after announcing it in gated preview. The pricing page, which the announcement does not mention, shows a model that charges by the finding as well as by the codebase.
Principal solutions architect Esra Kayabali describes a service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches that can be automated or as pull requests in the connected repositories. It builds a context graph from those repositories and the surrounding AWS environment, with an optional collector supplying resource and network context from wherever the code runs.
Swami Sivasubramanian, VP of Agentic AI, and Christopher Rae, who leads AI security go-to-market at AWS, both framed the problem as volume rather than detection. Sivasubramanian wrote that most organizations running large application estates see thousands of findings a day; Rae put it more bluntly, saying scanners find thousands daily and "most becomes noise that doesn't matter in your environment."
The validation step is the answer to that: rather than ranking by severity, Continuum confirms which findings are reachable by running the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaching proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. Findings carry an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path, and the output is an attack path and "a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone."
Pricing has two dimensions: a context fee covers lines of code protected per month, starting at $200 per million and tiering down to $100 above ten billion. An inference fee charges $10 per Continuum inference unit, consumed as findings are worked. AWS’s worked examples show the interaction: one million lines with 100 vulnerabilities at one unit each comes to $1,200, while 100 million lines with 10,000 vulnerabilities at two units each reaches $218,200. Context accounts for $18,200 of that and inference for the remaining $200,000, or roughly $20 per validated finding. The thousands of daily findings both executives describe, and the per-finding fee, measure the same workload from opposite ends.
Responding on LinkedIn, Bernardo Meireles Correa, an engineer working on non-human and agent identity at Avatier, welcomed the ranking and named two things to watch:
A proof in an isolated sandbox says the code is exploitable. It does not say the path to it exists in your environment, and the findings it cannot prove still need somewhere to go, or they quietly become the safe pile.
The product partly answers the first question: the optional collector gathers AWS resource and network configuration to judge reachability, though as additional setup rather than a default. The second goes unaddressed, since AWS documents what happens to findings it can prove and says nothing about the rest.
Where the announcement points is autonomy. For now, "every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships," and the console warns that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed, but AWS plans to let Continuum apply classes of fix on its own once confidence criteria such as test coverage and historical success rate are met.
(Source: AWS News Blog post)
Jorg Huser, a CTO and former AWS principal, replied to Rae by questioning what should unlock that:
The move from approving each merge to approving a class of fixes deserves its own acceptance test. An overloaded review queue can otherwise become the reason to grant more autonomy. I’d want evidence that the fix removes the vulnerability and preserves expected application behavior. What would qualify a fix class for autonomous merging, and what would send it back to human review?
Google's CodeMender ships something close to that evidence. It also proves exploitability by running an exploit and declines to apply patches itself, and it then validates each patch with an LLM-as-a-judge framework that tests for program equivalence, so the fix resolves the root cause "without altering the application's intended behavior." That is the step AWS's console caveat concedes Continuum does not perform.
The product boundary InfoQ reported in July, when AWS serverless hero Yan Cui said "we have the same capabilities, two product names, and no clarity on which one you should use," is still visible in the documentation: the Continuum user guide covers code vulnerabilities itself and sends readers to a separately titled AWS Security Agent User Guide for penetration testing and threat modeling. Only the code vulnerabilities capability reached general availability. Penetration testing remains separately priced at $50 per task-hour, and threat modeling, announced in preview in June, carries no published pricing.

articles.title: "Most apps never make it off localhost": Cursor takes on Lovable and Replit with fully managed app deployment
articles.text:
“Most apps never make it off localhost”: Cursor takes on Lovable and Replit with fully managed app deployment
AI coding agents have certainly made it easier to transform an idea into a working application. However, getting that application off a local machine and into the hands of real users remains a hurdle, requiring essential infrastructure steps spanning everything from hosting and database provisioning, to critical security checks.
Cursor, the AI coding platform acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX for $60 billion back in August, acknowledged the problem in an X post published on Thursday.
“Agents have made it easier to write code, but most apps never make it off localhost,” the company notes.
To address this, Cursor is introducing new app-building and deployment functionality, designed to take AI-generated applications from development to a live, shareable URL, without users having to even think about the underlying infrastructure themselves.
“Agents have made it easier to write code, but most apps never make it off localhost.”
Built on cloud agents
The new feature is built around cloud agents, which Cursor introduced last year as a way for developers to run multiple AI coding agents remotely without having to keep their laptops engaged. At the time, the company highlighted their ability to fix bugs, handle smaller coding tasks and implement some complex features.
With this latest update, those same agents can now take applications all the way through to deployment, handling the important steps needed to make them accessible to other users. The functionality is only available through cloud agents, though, which means it can’t be used with agents running locally.
Users start by describing the application they want to build in natural language, with Cursor managing the code generation and development process as usual.
From there, the agent creates the application and sets up the underlying project, including the necessary components to get it running.
Once the application is ready, users can preview the result before deciding whether to hit publish.
Publishing makes the application accessible through a live URL, allowing users to share it with colleagues or other users without having to configure hosting themselves.
It’s worth noting that there are two ways to get started. Users building an application from scratch will automatically have a new repository created on Cursor Origin, the company’s Git-based code-hosting platform launched in August as an agent-centric alternative to GitHub.
Alternatively, users can deploy applications from an existing GitHub repository. This means developers who already have an application under development can use Cursor’s cloud agents to prepare and publish it, without having to move their code to Origin or set up deployment infrastructure manually.
Judging by Cursor’s own examples, the feature seemingly targets employees who need to create internal business applications, such as sales dashboards, onboarding programs, customer presentations and developer portals. So in that regard, it could prove a boon for non-developers who have an idea for a tool but lack the technical nous to get it running themselves.
Of course, there’s nothing restricting the feature to business applications. An aspiring vibe coder could just as easily create a neighbourhood football league tracker or interactive family holiday planner. And because individual subscribers can publish apps publicly, those creations can be shared with anyone who has the link.
Under the hood: hosting, databases and security
Cursor had actually begun closing this gap, when in August it introduced the ability to preview cloud-agent projects and publish them to a live URL. However, users still needed to connect their own Vercel accounts.
The latest release removes that requirement while introducing various new smarts to the mix.
Behind the scenes, Cursor now takes care of several infrastructure requirements, including hosting, databases, and authentication.
For hosting, Cursor automatically creates a dedicated account for each team or individual subscriber, isolated from other customers. While Cursor’s announcement doesn’t identify the underlying hosting provider, Vercel revealed in a separate response on X that the new functionality is built on its Vercel for Platforms infrastructure. This basically allows users to deploy applications without having to create their own Vercel accounts or configure hosting themselves.
If an application needs a database, Cursor provisions one using PostgreSQL, while private and team applications are protected by Cursor’s existing sign-in system. Individual subscribers can also make their apps publicly accessible.
Applications can connect to external services, such as company databases or data warehouses, with users supplying the necessary credentials. Cursor says these secrets are managed separately, meaning the AI agent never sees their actual values.
Then there’s the thorny issue of security. When users choose to publish an application, Cursor says it runs “a series of deterministic and agentic security checks” before allowing it to go live. These include mandatory checks for exposed credentials, secrets and sensitive files, alongside an AI-powered review intended to identify more serious vulnerabilities.
However, it’s unclear how reliably these automated checks can identify more complex problems, such as incorrectly configured database permissions or application-level access controls. This is an important consideration for organisations contemplating connecting AI-generated applications to sensitive internal systems, where additional security scrutiny would still be advisable.
There is precedent for such concerns, too. In May last year, Semafor reported that two Replit employees examined 1,645 Lovable-built applications and discovered that 170 of them exposed sensitive information. The problems involved incorrectly configured database permissions, highlighting the difficulties of securing applications created through AI tools. Lovable says it subsequently introduced further security checks to identify potential vulnerabilities before applications are published.
Cursor moves onto Lovable and Replit’s turf
Of course, Cursor is entering territory already occupied by the likes of Lovable and Replit, which allow users to create and publish applications through natural-language prompts.
While Cursor’s latest announcement emphasizes internal business tools, Lovable and Replit have traditionally appealed to a broader audience of aspiring application creators. Still, the overlap is clear, and Cursor’s move into deployment has already caught the attention of developers.
“Cursor just came for the localhost graveyard.”
One software engineer writes on X that “cursor just came for the localhost graveyard,” riffing on Cursor’s own messaging about AI-generated applications that never make it beyond local development.
There’s also an interesting overlap with Grok Build, particularly given SpaceX’s acquisition of Cursor in August.
SpaceXAI introduced Grok’s Build Mode in July, before expanding it to all Grok plans the following month. The feature allows users to create apps, games and websites directly inside a Grok conversation, then publish them to shareable grok.me links.
That bears something of a resemblance to Cursor’s latest offering, although Cursor is approaching it through its established coding environment and cloud agents, and with a stronger emphasis on business applications and managed infrastructure.
The overlap hasn’t gone unnoticed though. One X user responded to Cursor’s announcement by asking, “so cursor is now properly replacing grok build?”
There’s no indication that Grok Build is being replaced, but the two offerings now cover some notably similar ground, raising questions about how SpaceXAI intends to distinguish them going forward.
For those wanting to check out Cursor’s new functionality, it’s available on all paid Cursor plans with cloud agents enabled.
With deployment increasingly becoming part of the AI coding experience, Cursor’s latest move could put further pressure on dedicated app-building platforms as the distinction between tools aimed at professional developers and those targeting aspiring vibe coders continues to narrow.

articles.title: Japan Announces Emergency Cybersecurity Package Following a Wave of Attacks
articles.text:
Japan on Friday announced an emergency cybersecurity package that includes the use of artificial intelligence and cyber rescue teams after a wave of massive data breaches hit major companies and government agencies.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told a ministerial meeting Friday that a rapid response to potential attacks is essential in the era of AI-generated attacks. She urged both government agencies and companies to step up their preparedness.
The emergency package comes after dozens of companies and government agencies were hit by unauthorized access to their systems and leaks of client data, prompting uneasiness across Japan.
“At this very moment, cases of unauthorized access and data breaches are occurring, causing a major impact on daily lives of the people and corporate activities,” Takaichi said. “Let us increase the response capability across Japan by devoting all government resources.”
Measures in the 10 billion yen ($63 million) package are designed to build a resilient society in which the public and private sectors share information, provide swift assistance to the affected and recover from damage.
It aims to acquire one of the world’s highest levels of cybersecurity.
The government will enhance its capability to access servers used by hackers as a preemptive measure known as “active cyber defense,” which was legalized in October.
In case of a possible challenge to Japan’s national security, the government will deploy a support team of officials from the Defense Ministry, the National Police Agency and the National Cybersecurity Office.
Under the measures in the package, a “top gun” team of cybersecurity experts will be set up by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry by the end of November. Team members will use AI to counter hackers and detect weaknesses in network systems. They are to cooperate with technology companies and advanced AI developers of friendly nations to keep Japan’s security expertise up to date.
There will also be a “cyber rescue team” of experts from the public and private sectors to provide initial responses to companies affected by cyberattacks. A separate team will help vulnerable companies to strengthen their defenses.

articles.title: PlayStation 5 Slim enfim volta a entrar em promoção em até 12x sem juros • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
PlayStation 5 Slim enfim volta a entrar em promoção em até 12x sem juros
PS5 Slim Edição Digital possui SSD veloz interno e controle DualSense; oferta do Magalu no AliExpress oferece console da Sony com desconto de 18% no prazo com cupom
O PlayStation 5 Slim Digital está saindo por R$ 3.750 com cupom AFFNOV09 em até 12x sem juros na loja do Magalu no AliExpress. O console da Sony, com SSD veloz e que traz um controle DualSense, recebe desconto de 18% sobre o preço base de R$ 4.599, reajustado recentemente.
Esta é uma rara chance de adquirir o modelo base do atual sistema da Sony com desconto no Black November 2026, já que ele não tem aparecido em promoções no varejo nos últimos meses.
O PS5 Slim é o modelo revisto do console lançado em 2020, com design compacto, mas a mesma performance. Seu SSD interno de 825 GB e os 16 GB de RAM garantem o carregamento quase instantâneo dos jogos, enquanto é possível expandir o espaço interno com um SSD externo e/ou um M.2.
Seu controle sem fio DualSense possui feedback háptico avançado, que oferece tensão e resistência nos gatilhos conforme a interação, enquanto respostas táteis e de áudio via alto-falantes embutidos fazem o jogador se sentir na pele do personagem no game.
O sistema reproduz gráficos em 4K a uma taxa de até 120 fps em TVs compatíveis. A tecnologia de ray-tracing entrega renderização de reflexos e sombras mais realistas, tornando a jogatina mais imersiva.
O PS5 Slim roda todos os jogos do PS4, mas não possui um leitor de mídia física. O acessório, também compatível com o PS5 Pro, precisa ser comprado à parte.
Este console suporta Wi-Fi 6 e Ethernet para acesso à PlayStation Store, que oferece jogos digitais e acesso a apps de streaming, como Apple TV e Spotify.
O PlayStation 5 Slim Digital (R$ 3.750 com cupom AFFNOV09 em até 12x sem juros) traz duas portas USB-C e duas USB-A, e inclui um cabo USB-C duplo para carregar o DualSense.
Black November é o mês da Black Friday 2026, que acontece no dia 27 de novembro, mas o varejo se antecipou e já oferece ofertas em eletrônicos com diversos cupons e condições exclusivas durante o período.

articles.title: The feds plan to merge BDC and EDC. What might that mean for Canada’s largest VC investor? | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada is combining the two Crown corporations most directly involved in financing Canadian startups and promoting trade, a complex process that raises questions about downstream impacts on the innovation economy.
The consequential announcement was buried at the back of Thursday’s federal budget document. Following a review of the effectiveness of financing Crown corporations, the feds are launching a transition process to merge the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) and Export Development Canada (EDC) into a single federal development bank.
If combined today, the Crown corporations would total approximately 5,000 employees and more than $120 billion in assets
The budget document said the new institution would “build on the strengths, expertise, and strong teams” of BDC and EDC to provide a “more integrated suite of financing solutions” for Canadian businesses.
The decision was part of an effort, originally referenced in the Spring Economic Update, to review the effectiveness of Canada’s financing Crown corporations, which also include Canada Infrastructure Bank, the Canada Growth Fund, and a forthcoming sovereign wealth fund called the Canada Strong Fund.
With little detail out so far, questions abound about how the merger process could change financing options for entrepreneurs, or whether it might address some of the historical gripes about BDC’s role in the market.
EDC is Canada’s export credit agency, which generally serves larger Canadian businesses selling internationally. BDC is a development bank for Canadian entrepreneurs, typically serving smaller businesses. Separate from BDC’s large loan and financing business, BDC Capital is Canada’s most active venture capital investor, acting as both a limited partner (LP) in many funds and a direct investor across major sectors. If combined today, the Crown corporations would total approximately 5,000 employees and more than $120 billion in assets.
Merging these organizations won’t be a light task and will certainly take years, said Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy and a former special advisor to the prime minister. A “specially constituted” board of directors will be formed to oversee the transition, and the government will have to figure out a plan before amending two pieces of legislation: the BDC Act and the Export Canada Act.
There will also be leadership questions about who will lead the combined entity and how it could impact staff with overlapping roles.
More on #Budget2026
“You have to be very careful to make sure you’re not interrupting the delivery of services while this is happening,” Mullin said in an interview. According to the feds, “existing products and services will be fully maintained throughout the transition.”
In response to questions from BetaKit about potential staff cuts, possible program interruptions, and government guidance, both BDC and EDC pointed to official statements on the planned merger. BDC’s statement said the organization “welcome[d] this decision with openness” and that its priorities for supporting entrepreneurs remained unchanged.
“We don’t have all the answers today, but what I do know is that both organizations bring complementary strengths, deep expertise, talented people, and a strong commitment to helping Canadian businesses succeed,” EDC president and CEO Alison Nankivell wrote in a LinkedIn post on Friday.
A spokesperson for the Department of Finance told BetaKit in an email that this proposed merger was “subject to budget secrecy” until the budget was tabled. Since Thursday, the government has been working with both organizations on the transition, and both will continue to operate under their existing mandates, the spokesperson said.
A new future for BDC?
The feds framed the proposed merger as a way to reduce overlap and improve the efficiency of federal financing bodies.
“In the economy of 2026, their distinct roles—one focused on export markets, one focused on growing businesses at home—probably don’t make sense anymore to have as two separate organizations,” Mullin said, as a key growth driver for most companies now is selling abroad.
Notably, the budget document said it expects these Crown corporations to “have a greater risk tolerance than private sector peers” and to complement, instead of replicate, investments that could come from the private sector.
BDC has previously been told via legislative review to refine its risk appetite. Canadian VCs have suggested that the Crown corporation should play less of a role in the direct investing market and skew its activity toward investing in funds. Current CEO Isabelle Hudon told BetaKit earlier this year that the bank is increasingly taking that approach.
RELATED: Canada’s early-stage investment gap “now a sovereignty issue,” BDC says
John Edgar, a Montréal-based partner at cross-border fund Maple VC, told BetaKit that combining the two Crown corporations and changing their focus could be a boon for Canadian venture if they focus less on direct investing and prioritize coinvesting with fund managers. “If they could do that, that would be great for Canada,” Edgar said in an interview.
“Those types of organizations should focus on market making instead of direct investing in the market,” Edgar said.
Chris Arsenault, co-founder and partner at Inovia Capital—one of Canada’s largest venture firms, with BDC in its LP pool—called it a “courageous move” given the size and activity of both organizations.
“I think it makes sense to become more efficient and offer Canadians a single access for all things capital, equity, debt, and global export support,” Arsenault said in a text message. However, he added, some entrepreneurs and GPs could see the combined organization as one less LP to potentially fundraise from.
Some founders were optimistic about the planned consolidation. “In my recent experience with both, it’s blurry trying to understand their separation of roles,” Rivercity Innovations CEO Jeff Shirley wrote in an X post. “All great services and people, but having them under one banner makes sense from my user perspective.”
Feature image courtesy BDC and EDC.

articles.title: Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo | TechCrunch
articles.text:
AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer.
One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large.
The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models.
You can interact with the typewriter and music tuner.
You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music.
All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download.
While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts.
This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark, a 167MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation.
Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog, told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data.
“I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto.
In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.

articles.title: Intel’s next-gen Nova Lake needs new motherboards — what we expect from Nova Point and Z990, Z970, and B960 chipsets
articles.text:
Intel’s next-gen Nova Lake needs new motherboards — what we expect from Nova Point and Z990, Z970, and B960 chipsets
More PCIe 5.0 lanes, Thunderbolt 5 support, faster memory speeds, and the potential of active chipset cooling highlight the list of Nova Point chipset features.
Intel’s new Nova Lake-S CPUs are rumored to be on track to start mass production in Q4 2026, with a launch expected in Q1 2027. Unlike previous launches, we’re supposed to see mid-range SKU(s), supposedly an unlocked 28-core product(s), first in Q1, followed later in 2027 by flagship-class models that allegedly use two compute tiles and feature up to 52 cores.
Lip-Bu Tan, Intel CEO, said earlier this year that Nova Lake is “coming at the end of 2026.” Despite the growing number of rumors and statements, we still don’t have a concrete date, but we can expect to see the CPUs soon, and with them, a brand-new socket and motherboard chipsets.
Regardless of how many cores they have or when they arrive, you will need a new motherboard for Nova Lake. The LGA 1851 socket is at the end of its life with the release of Core Ultra Series 2 processors like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus, released earlier in 2026; that means no more new processors and a dead end. A new socket, LGA 1954, is necessary because Nova Lake CPUs have a significant increase in I/O and power needs. It’s also Intel’s first bLLC (big last-level cache) intended to take on AMD’s X3D CPUs.
We haven’t seen many details about the boards themselves, like pricing, official configurations, or product stacks, and we've only caught glimpses of one or two early models at Computex. Still, we have seen a few interesting platform details and rumors. To that end, we’ve put together a table of what we know so far about the specifications. Some things aren’t official yet and are noted by the tilde (~). We’ve also listed last-gen equivalents for reference.
| 900 Series Chipset, “up to” | B960 (Mainstream) | B860 (Mainstream) | Z990 (Enthusiast) | Z890 (Enthusiast) | Z970 (Enthusiast) | 
| Total PCIe Lanes | 34 | 34 | 48 | 48 | 34 | 
| Processor TB4/USB4 | 1 (TB5, 80Gbps) | 1 | 2 (TB5, 80Gbps) | 2 | 1 (TB5, 80Gbps) | 
| DMI Gen5 Lanes | 2 | 0 (4x G4) | 4 | 0 (8x G4) | 2 | 
| Chipset PCIE 5.0 Lanes | 0 | 0 | 12 | 0 | 0 | 
| Chipset PCIe 4.0 Lanes | 14 | 14 | 12 | 24 | 14 | 
| SATA 3.0 (6G Lanes) | 4 | 4 | 8 | 8 | 4 | 
| USB2 Ports | 12 | 12 | 14 | 14 | 12 | 
| USB3.2 (20G) Ports | ~2 | 2 | ~5 | 5 | ~2 | 
| USB3.2 (10G) Ports | ~2 | 4 | ~10 | 10 | ~4 | 
| USB3.2 (5G) Ports | ~6 | 6 | ~10 | 10 | ~6 | 
| IA OC | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| BCLK OC | No | No (board discretion) | Yes | Yes | No | 
| Memory OC | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Processor PCIE 5.0 Slot Lane Config | 1x16 | 1x16 + 1x4 | 1x16 or 1x8 + 2x4 or 2x8 or 4x4 | 1x16 + 1x4 or 2x8 + 1x4 or 1x8 or 3x4 | 1x16 | 
| Processor PCIE 5.0 Storage Lane Config | 1x4 | 1x4 | 1x8 or 2x4 | 1x4 | 1x4 | 
| ECC | No | No | No | No | No | 
| Simultaneous Displays Supported | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 
| PCIE RAID 0/1/5/10 Support | No | No | Yes | Yes | No | 
| SATA RAID 0/1/5/10 Support | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Intel vPro + Standard Manageability | No | No | No | Yes | No | 
The new lineup consists of five different chipsets. You get Z990 and Z970 for the enthusiast class, B960 for the Mainstream, W980 for workstations, and Q970. You may notice it’s missing the ‘H910’ platform for entry-level PCs, and now we see a second enthusiast-class platform, the Z970, wedged between the B960 and Z990. Z990 is still the flagship, offering more PCIe lanes, a DMI Gen5 x4 link, and 12 Gen5 lanes from the chipset. Z970 is the less expensive enthusiast option and is reportedly built on the same silicon as B960. You get CPU multiplier overclocking, but no BCLK adjustment, and of course fewer ports and lanes than the flagship.
The chipset package itself, internally codenamed “Nova Point,” will also differ slightly and is smaller than Z890 (600 mm² vs 658 mm²). The die-on-package shrinks to 72.5 mm² (11.15 x 6.5mm) compared to 92.9 mm² (11.15 x 8.33 mm), or roughly 22% smaller. Base power increases to 7.9 Watts, up from 6 W on the Z890, with a maximum of 14 W while working.
That power-density increase explains Intel’s rumored active-cooling guidelines for the chipset. When you start connecting components that use the chipset, think some PCIe slots and M.2 drives, the chipset raises its working voltage to maintain signal integrity for all of the bandwidth it now has to provide for the attached devices. Hopefully this is only needed in the high-end Z990/970, where it has a lot more lanes/bandwidth to support, as some of the fans on the chipset (remember early X570?) could get loud.
What to expect from Nova Point motherboards
Beyond the new LGA 1954 socket, not much information has been released about what to expect from motherboard partners. We know the platform's base memory speed is a smoking-fast DDR5-8000, up 800 MT/s over the Arrow Lake refresh chips. And if you don’t have a kit that can run those speeds and want to, it will cost at least $700 from any reputable brand. So the platform's cost of entry will be high unless you’re starting with compatible RAM. That said, you can run slower speeds if you already have DDR5, which would save money, but it could create a performance ceiling.
We’ll also see more abundant PCIe 5.0 connectivity. The upcoming Nova Lake CPUs are said to offer 36 PCIe Gen5 lanes. You get 16 lanes dedicated to graphics, eight lanes to storage, eight lanes to Thunderbolt 5 controllers (4x ea.), and four lanes for the DMI. That said, speeds are the same as the previous generation, since PCIe 4.0 x8 matches PCIe 5.0 x4. The chipset now has 12 dedicated PCIe 5.0 lanes, so motherboard manufacturers can include multiple PCIe 5.0 NVMe slots without sharing bandwidth from the primary PCIe slot or stealing USB4 bandwidth. In theory, you can have five PCIe 5.0 M.2 sockets between the CPU's native lanes and the chipset without sharing bandwidth among PCIe slots or M.2 sockets—a significant upgrade over Z890.
| Lane Category | Lane Count | Type | Functionality | 
| Graphics | 16 Lanes | PCIe 5.0 | Primary GPU Slot (x16) | 
| Storage | 8 Lanes | PCIe 5.0 | Two dedicated M.2 NVMe sockets (4x ea.) | 
| Thunderbolt Reserved | 8 Lanes | PCIe 5.0 | Dual Thunderbolt 5 Controllers (x4 ea.) | 
| DMI Reserved | 4 Lanes | PCIe 5.0 | DMI 5.0 x4 Link to Chipset | 
| Total CPU Native | 36 Lanes | Gen5 | Total Lanes | 
Thunderbolt 5 (TB5) is another feature we’ll see more of on some of these new boards, offering baked-in support via a controller chip, typically the Intel JHL9580. We’ve seen at least one Z890 board (Asus ProArt) already using it, but it should be more prevalent in this generation.
TB5 speeds hit 80 Gbps (bidirectional) or up to a wicked-fast 120 Gbps in single-direction boost mode. TB5 also supports DisplayPort 2.1, USB4, and USB PD 3.1(100-130W depending). So for anyone who needs fast external storage, a board with TB5 plus an appropriately speedy M.2 external drive means transfers will be much faster.
On the networking side, expect another round of 2.5-5GbE on most boards, with the cheapest options opting for the less expensive 1GbE. Premium boards, on the other hand, will work in dual Ethernet connections and 10 GbE. We’ll see a lot of Realtek 8125/8126 (2.5/5GbE) chips, along with some Killer E3100G, and perhaps Killer’s E5000 mixed in, too. 10GbE will still rely on the Marvell AQtion, like the AQC113C.
Integrated Wi-Fi support will vary, with most SKUs opting to use Wi-Fi 7. You’ll see a smattering of the ‘slower’ 160 MHz Wi-Fi 7 which, in reality, is plenty fast and will not be a choke point for most users on less expensive boards. The faster 320 MHz widens the bandwidth highway from four lanes to eight, so you can move twice as much data simultaneously. We expect chips from MediaTek (MT7927), Intel (BE200/202), and Realtek (RTL9822AE) to dominate the Wi-Fi 7 scene for Nova Point boards. Just remember: to take advantage of Wi-Fi 7, you need a Wi-Fi 7-capable router in the first place.
What motherboards can we expect to see?
We’ve seen leaks from the Eurasian Economic Union database Gigabyte (via Videocardz), listing a whopping 24 SKUs. We’ve also seen leaks about several ASRock motherboards via shipping records (via Club386). So far, there's not been a peep from MSI or Asus, but you can bet they’ll have a full complement of new boards of all shapes, sizes, and price points. But remember, just because something is listed in the EEU database doesn’t mean it will be released, or released in the U.S. So until we see an official list from the board partners, take this with a pinch of salt.
For Gigabyte, we see a lot of familiar faces in the list, including the flagship Aorus Xtreme, Aorus Master (now in three different SKUs), Aorus Pro and Elite (six total SKUs), and it even looks like they are planning multiple rear-connect Aorus Stealth options. We’ll also see several Aorus Elite and more affordable Eagle SKUs, along with more Duo X boards (this time from different families), all presumably using a 2-DIMM topology that supports high-density CQDIMMs. Micro ATX and Mini-ITX boards are also listed along with the wood-accent Aero models that made a splash this year.
ASRock is offering six different models, from the flagship-class Taichi (White) and Taichi Creator to the budget Pro RS Wifi and Z990 Challenger SKUs. In between, they have multiple variants of the Steel Legend Wi-Fi. What we don’t see from here are Micro ATX or Mini-ITX form factors, or any Z970 or B960 offerings out of the gate. We'll almost certainly be seeing those before long.
Asus has been tight-lipped, and as of this writing, we haven’t heard a peep about their boards. I’m confident we’ll see the usual ROG Maximus, ROG Strix, ProArt, TUF, and Prime lines (among others), with their typical Asus flair and value-add features like AI-assisted functionality (automating performance, optimizing cooling, managing network traffic, etc.).
MSI has also kept its cards close to the vest, and we haven’t seen much from them yet. But we do expect to see the company's lineup in full force. We expect to see the flagship Godlike board from the MEG series, high-end Ace, and mid-range MPG offerings like the Carbon and Edge, along with the MAG value series like the Tomahawk. I’d also imagine we’ll see some small-form-factor offerings, too, like a Z990 Edge Ti Wifi. In short, motherboard partners won’t miss the boat for a fresh revenue stream, and we’re sure to see a lot of options available come launch day.
Pricing for these future motherboards hasn't been listed. Still, you can imagine, with the increase in PCIe 5.0 bandwidth available and the copper needed to support it, hardware upgrades, and other external factors, it's safe to assume most SKUs will increase in price, or, with some luck, be the same as previous-gen versions. Either way, this is the start of a new platform, and those looking for a long-lasting socket should get in on the ground floor, assuming the performance is good, of course.
Final thoughts
So who are these motherboards for, really? With the cost of video cards, storage, and, of course, RAM through the roof, upgrading to the new platform isn’t going to be cheap, especially if you want to get the most out of it. While RAM speeds tend not to make a significant difference in many cases, it can in others. So reaching the base memory speeds of this new platform will cost an arm and a leg. As mentioned earlier, it will run with existing RAM below that value. Still, performance losses will range from negligible to notable, depending on differences in speed and timings, as well as the work being executed and the application used.
Nova Point-based motherboards are shaping up as a meaningful step for Intel’s new platform: a new LGA 1954 socket, 12 PCIe 5.0 lanes attached to the chipset for Z990, Thunderbolt 5 support, and increased base memory speed to DDR5-8000. We even saw Intel add another enthusiast chipset to bridge the gap between enthusiast and mainstream in these trying times. Most of this information comes from leaks and rumors, and without a firm launch date from Intel, details and lineups could change before the Nova Lake CPUs arrive, supposedly in early 2027. We expect to see a lot of boards at CES 2027, with launches following soon after.
If the new CPUs are competitive with AMD's X3D offering, we can imagine those also costing more than the Arrow Lake refresh chips. If you already have a capable system, waiting to see the official lineups, performance, and pricing is the smarter move. But if you want the most PCIe 5.0 storage and the fastest external connectivity with TB5, this platform is built for you. Otherwise, you can likely make do with what you have for a little while longer, hopefully until inflated prices on at least some major components drop.
Joe Shields is a staff writer at Tom’s Hardware. He reviews motherboards and PC components.

articles.title: El próximo iPhone podría quedarse sin su botón más útil
articles.text:
Apple prepararía un importante cambio para sus próximos iPhone, que perderían su botón físico más útil. Según recoge MacRumors, una nueva filtración apunta a que los de Cupertino podrían eliminar el botón de acción de los iPhone de 2027.
De acuerdo con el rumor en cuestión, la eliminación del botón de acción del iPhone no implicaría la quita de las funciones que este actualmente alberga. Lo que Apple haría sería unificarlas con el Control de Cámara, la tecla dedicada para funciones fotográficas y de inteligencia artificial.
Como siempre decimos cuando surgen informaciones de este tipo, hay que tomarlas con pinzas porque son extraoficiales. Dicho esto, es muy probable que si al público le dieran a elegir qué tecla física del iPhone eliminar, la mayoría elegiría el Control de Cámara por sobre el botón de acción.
Desde su introducción en 2023 de la mano de los iPhone 15, el botón de acción se ha vuelto una de las características más útiles del dispositivo. La posibilidad de personalizar su funcionamiento para disparar distintos atajos configurables le ha permitido convertirse en una de las funciones preferidas de los usuarios.
La filtración no indica los supuestos motivos por los que Apple eliminaría el botón de acción a partir de los iPhone de 2027. Tampoco hace referencia a si la medida impactará en todos los modelos que llegarán el próximo año, o si esto impactará exclusivamente en una parte de la gama.
Apple podría quitar el botón de acción de los iPhone de 2027
Respecto de la fusión del botón de acción y el Control de Cámara del iPhone, la filtración indica que se podría invocar uno u otro con la misma tecla dependiendo del tipo de interacción. Un toque simple abriría la cámara del móvil, mientras que al mantenerlo presionado se dispararía el atajo configurado en el botón de acción.
Esto genera algunas dudas respecto de qué pasaría con el uso de Visual Intelligence, que actualmente se abre al mantener pulsado el Control de Cámara. Claro que esto se podría solucionar eliminando el atajo de dicha función, considerando que también se puede lanzar desde la app de cámara.
Si el iPhone Duo se puede tomar como precedente, Apple ha optado por lanzarlo sin botón de acción, pero sí con Control de Cámara. Por supuesto que esto puede ser una mera decisión de diseño acotada al factor de forma del móvil, y no un indicio de que la compañía realmente desea deshacerse de la tecla. Después de todo, el costado donde reside este comando en los iPhone convencionales es el que tiene la bisagra en el plegable. Ya veremos qué sucede. Estaremos atentos a cualquier novedad.

articles.title: “Does Meta think we can’t read?” Meta abandons sketchy commercial terms update.
articles.text:
After weeks of backlash—and a failed attempt to quell it—Meta has indefinitely delayed plans to update its commercial terms and require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.
“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect,” a Meta spokesperson told Reuters.
Soon after Meta notified business account holders of the upcoming changes, legal experts warned Nieman Lab that the vague language could allow the company to ignore scraping preferences specified in robots.txt files and exhaustively crawl vast amounts of off-Facebook content for AI training. Since virtually every news publisher has a Facebook page, Nieman Lab sounded the alarm that Meta could potentially avoid millions in licensing fees if the TOS update happened as planned.
Ars broke down the changes after Meta announced them, noting that businesses—including news publishers involved in drawn-out legal battles over unwanted AI scraping—had no way to opt out. To keep a business Facebook page, they had to allow Meta to crawl any linked external sites. The terms even required publishers to create test credentials so Meta’s bots could reliably bypass paywalls.
Meta faced global scrutiny
The changes were initially supposed to take effect on October 30. But Meta pushed that date back to November 20 amid pushback from Facebook users, courts, and regulators around the world. Courts in Brazil and Norway issued preliminary injunctions blocking the terms after organizations in those countries promptly filed lawsuits, Nieman Lab reported.
The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority also opened a formal investigation into whether Meta was exploiting a dominant position to seize valuable AI training data. In a LinkedIn post, Theo Bamber, chief executive of the UK’s News Media Association, pointed to “the continued arrogance of this company to think everyone will just be OK with its actions” as “staggering.”

articles.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
articles.text:
OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.
OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.
Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.
OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

articles.title: Amazon ne fait pas l'impasse sur le Black Friday : voici les 8 bons plans tech à saisir — Frandroid
articles.text:
Amazon ne rentrera véritablement dans la course du Black Friday que dans quelques jours, mais avec des concurrents français déjà bien lancés, le géant américain n’a pas d’autre choix que de baisser ses prix, voire de s’aligner, pour ne pas rater de ventes.
Huit offres ont actuellement retenu notre attention, en passant par du smartphone haut de gamme de chez Google et Apple, jusqu’à du TV Neo Qled de Samsung à très bon prix ou encore une montre Garmin pas chère. Même les Joy Con 2 de la Switch 2 sont à prix réduit.
Les meilleures offres du Black Friday sur Amazon
- Nothing Phone (3) à 498 euros au lieu de 849 euros
- iPhone 18 Pro à 1 331,10 euros au lieu de 1 479 euros
- Google Pixel 11 à 799 euros au lieu de 999 euros
- iPhone 17 Pro Max à 1 249 euros au lieu de 1 479 euros
- iPhone Air à 989 euros au lieu de 1 229 euros
- Samsung 55QN80F à 579 euros au lieu de 799 euros
- Garmin Instinct E à 190,51 euros au lieu de 249,99 euros
- Joy-Con 2 (bleu & jaune) à 69,99 euros au lieu de 89,99 euros
Nothing Phone (3)
Le Nothing Phone (3) est le premier smartphone haut de gamme de Nothing, celui que la marque présente comme son premier flagship. Un modèle encore très séduisant grâce à son interface soignée, ses performances solides et son identité visuelle unique. Noté 8/10, ce modèle est chaudement recommandé, surtout maintenant qu’il est à moins de 500 euros.
Les atouts du Nothing Phone (3)
- Le design atypique et le système Glyph
- Des performances maîtrisées et suffisantes
- Un trio de capteurs de 50 Mpx efficace
Le Nothing Phone (3) avec 256 Go de stockage était affiché à 849 euros à son lancement. Aujourd’hui, il est en promotion à 498 euros sur Amazon.
iPhone 18 Pro
L’iPhone 18 Pro s’installe cette année sans iPhone 18 standard à ses côtés. Cet iPhone, c’est l’année de la maturité. Il n’a plus de gros défaut : la chauffe, la charge lente, l’autonomie, le mode photo Pro absent, tout ce qu’on reprochait aux Pro depuis l’iPhone X a été réglé.
Les forces de l’iPhone 18 Pro
- Un capteur principal ƒ/1,48, parmi les plus lumineux sur iPhone
- La puce Apple A20 Pro gravée en 2 nm avec chambre à vapeur
- Un écran OLED 6,3 pouces, 3 000 nits en extérieur, ProMotion 120 Hz
Au prix de lancement de 1 479 euros, l’iPhone 18 Pro 256 Go était déjà un investissement conséquent. Grâce au coupon affiché sur le site d’Amazon, il descend à 1 331 euros. Le Pro Max 256 Go suit le même mouvement, disponible pour 1 466 euros au lieu de 1 629 euros si vous préférez le grand format.
Google Pixel 11
Le Pixel 11 est l’entrée de catalogue de la nouvelle génération premium de Google, et il ne faut pas le snober. Son écran OLED de 6,3 pouces monte jusqu’à 3 000 nits, ce qui le rend lisible dans toutes les conditions, et le Tensor G6 gère sans sourciller les fonctions IA qui font la signature de la gamme : transcription automatique des messages vocaux, traduction en temps réel, Capture magique. Le téléobjectif 5x grimpe jusqu’à 30x en zoom numérique, avec des résultats franchement convaincants.
Les points forts du Google Pixel 11
- Téléobjectif 5x avec zoom numérique jusqu’à 30x
- Écran OLED jusqu’à 3 000 nits
- 7 ans de mises à jour Android garantis
Le Google Pixel 11 est habituellement affiché à 999 euros. Pour le Black Friday, Amazon le propose à 799 euros, soit 200 euros d’économie.
iPhone 17 Pro Max
L’iPhone 17 Pro Max était le modèle le plus haut de gamme d’Apple en 2025. La puce A19 Pro gravée en 3 nm signe d’excellentes performances sur iOS, et la gestion thermique a été entièrement revue grâce à une chambre à vapeur qui fait son travail. Côté photo, il aligne trois capteurs de 48 mégapixels à l’arrière et inaugure un capteur selfie carré qui permet de cadrer en paysage sans tourner le téléphone. Il sait aussi filmer avec les caméras avant et arrière en même temps (Dual Capture). L’autonomie progresse aussi nettement, avec jusqu’à 37 heures de lecture vidéo annoncées par Apple, contre 33 heures pour le 16 Pro Max.
Les points forts de l’iPhone 17 Pro Max
- Puce A19 Pro toujours très rapide, même si l’A20 Pro des iPhone 18 Pro lui a succédé
- Capteur selfie carré pour cadrer en paysage sans tourner le téléphone
- Autonomie en nette progression par rapport au 16 Pro Max
L’iPhone 17 Pro Max est affiché à 1 479 euros en temps normal. Amazon le propose en ce moment à 1 249 euros, soit 230 euros de remise.
iPhone Air
L’iPhone Air est une expérience à part. Avec ses 5,64 mm d’épaisseur et ses 165 grammes, c’est sans doute l’iPhone le plus agréable à tenir en main jamais conçu, cadre en titane et Ceramic Shield compris. La puce A19 Pro est là, l’écran OLED de 6,5 pouces monte très haut en luminosité, et le châssis encaisse sans broncher. Bon, ce n’est pas parfait : une seule journée d’autonomie au mieux, un seul objectif photo, un seul haut-parleur de qualité franchement décevante, et de l’USB 2.0 à ce tarif, c’est difficile à avaler.
Les points forts de l’iPhone Air
- 5,64 mm d’épaisseur, parmi les smartphones les plus fins du marché
- Prise en main légère et châssis titane très robuste
- Écran OLED 6,5 pouces très lumineux
L’iPhone Air (256 Go) a été lancé à 1 229 euros. Pour le Black Friday, Amazon affiche le prix à 989 euros, soit 240 euros de moins.
Samsung 55QN80F
Le Samsung 55QN80F occupe le milieu de gamme Neo QLED de Samsung, et c’est clairement là que le constructeur coréen fait le meilleur travail. La technologie Mini LED avec rétroéclairage Quantum Matrix Core sur toute la dalle donne des contrastes propres et des couleurs Quantum Dot bien calibrées. Le processeur NQ4 AI Gen2 embarque des fonctions d’interaction avec l’intelligence artificielle, et l’interface Tizen reste l’une des plus fluides du marché. Pour jouer, la dalle monte jusqu’à 144 Hz et le TV aligne quatre ports HDMI 2.1, de quoi le placer parmi les bons candidats face aux meilleurs TV gaming.
Les points forts du Samsung 55QN80F
- Rétroéclairage Mini LED Quantum Matrix Core pleine surface
- Dalle 144 Hz avec 4 ports HDMI
- Interface Tizen fluide et fonctions IA intégrées
Le Samsung 55QN80F est habituellement proposé à 799 euros. Amazon le descend à 579 euros pour le Black Friday, soit 220 euros d’économie.
Garmin Instinct E
La Garmin Instinct E ouvre la gamme Instinct : pas d’écran AMOLED, pas de recharge solaire, mais l’essentiel de ce qui fait la réputation Garmin. Le boîtier en polymère renforcé répond à la norme militaire MIL-STD-810G, l’étanchéité monte à 10 ATM, et l’écran MIP reste lisible en plein soleil sans effort. Le GPS multi-constellation est précis, le suivi de l’activité et du sommeil font le taf au quotidien, et l’autonomie annoncée atteint 16 jours en mode montre connectée sur la version 45 mm.
Les points forts de la Garmin Instinct E
- Boîtier MIL-STD-810G et étanchéité 10 ATM
- GPS multi-constellation précis en extérieur
- Jusqu’à 16 jours d’autonomie en mode connecté (version 45 mm)
La Garmin Instinct E est habituellement vendue 249,99 euros. Elle passe à 190,51 euros chez Amazon pour le Black Friday, soit près de 60 euros de remise.
Joy-Con 2 (bleu & jaune)
Bon, si vous avez une Nintendo Switch 2, vous savez que les Joy-Con 2 sont clairement une évolution par rapport à la première génération. Fini les rails grinçants : la fixation est désormais magnétique, avec un bouton d’éjection pour les retirer proprement. Chaque manette embarque un capteur optique qui lui permet de fonctionner comme une souris sur une surface plane, une vraie nouveauté pour certains jeux compatibles.
Les points forts des Joy-Con 2 (bleu & jaune)
- Fixation magnétique, retrait en un bouton
- Mode souris intégré via capteur optique
- Autonomie d’environ 20 heures
Habituellement affichés à 89,99 euros, les Joy-Con 2 (bleu & jaune) sont disponibles à 69,99 euros chez Amazon pendant le Black Friday, soit 20 euros de moins.
Black Friday 2026 : pour ne rien rater des meilleures offres Tech
Le Black Friday n’est plus qu’un week-end de bonnes affaires, mais tout un mois de promotions. On peut même parler de Black Month. Même AliExpress a déjà lancé ses offres du 11.11. Quoi qu’il en soit, c’est un bon moment pour faire ses achats de fin d’année et nous allons vous aider à trouver la pépite Tech qu’il vous faut.
