articles.title: How OPay’s past shows how it will react after pulling IPO
articles.text:
OPay’s rise to one of Nigeria’s largest fintechs came after a series of regulatory hurdles. Now, the latest—an inquiry from Chinese regulators—led it to withdraw its $304 million New York listing on October 30. How the company handled the earlier hurdles best guides what it might do now.
Last week, as OPay’s executives rang the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange, it was supposed to symbolise the final step in the company’s long journey from a small mobile money operator in Nigeria to a global fintech.
Instead, it was another in a long series of hurdles the fintech has endured as the company suspended the listing after a regulatory inquiry from China, its founder Zhou Yahui’s home country.
Since Opera, the browser company owned by a consortium led by Zhou, acquired a controlling stake in Paycom, a mobile-money operator, in 2018, a mix of luck, almost endless capital, and a willingness to start afresh has created a fintech with 50 million users.
A hyperfocus on payments after it ditched its super app play meant OPay was prepared when Nigeria’s 2023 cash crisis broke commercial banks’ apps, and it emerged alongside other fintechs as a trusted digital payment option. Then it turned profitable in 2025 after rapid growth in its lending business.
External events and policy decisions beyond its control have shaped almost every phase of the company’s journey. To pass this latest hurdle, the company will need to revisit its previous attempts that have brought it success.
How OPay got here
In 2018, a Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) capital rule set a ₦2 billion ($1.4 million) minimum capital for mobile money operators, which made institutions that could not meet the requirements cheap to buy. Paycom was one of those institutions. By July, OPay, with Opera’s backing, launched mobile payments in Nigeria, built on an agent banking model that reached unbanked people. The agent network remains part of its moat.
It also sold OKash, its lending product, to Opera for $9.5 million in December 2018. This sale would be important later, as lending grew to OPay’s largest revenue driver.
By May 2019, it launched ORide, a motorcycle-hailing business in Lagos, that brought visibility and app downloads. Other verticals, like OFood, a food delivery service, and OBus, a bus-sharing service, deepened the company’s relationship with the country’s informal sector.
By July 2019, OPay had raised $50 million from investors like Sequoia China, Source Code Capital, and Meituan-Dianping in the largest Nigerian startup round of 2019, until it raised a $120 million Series B round in November. Most of its investors were Chinese platform builders that helped push the super-app playbook that became successful in Asian markets.
By the end of 2019, OPay claimed to have over 140,000 agents and over $10m in daily transaction volume. Its revenue was $16.7 million for the 2019 financial year—almost 20x growth. It lost $71.5 million that year, with almost half, $36 million, going to scaling ORide.
This was the peak of OPay’s blitzscaling era, where it threw a lot of capital into creating a super app that served Nigerians at different points in their daily lives. This super app approach drew users to its payment service. By launching different verticals that Nigerians interacted with at various points, the idea was that it would create stickiness with OPay, the long-term play.
The super app falls apart
In January 2020, OPay got its first reputational shock when Hindenburg Research, the investigative short-seller publication, published a report that alleged Opera, its parent company, was targeting Nigeria’s poor population with predatory loans as its browser margins disappeared and it pursued revenue growth.
The report showed how Opera launched a series of short-term lending businesses—OKash, OPesa, OPay, and CashBean—in Kenya, Nigeria, and India that violated major Google Play Store short-term lending policies by providing an inaccurate description of its loan businesses.
OPay responded by denying the allegations and taking the lending product off its app.
While it was recovering from the shock of the Hindenburg report, a February ban on commercial motorcycles and tricycles in Lagos State, its biggest state in Nigeria, effectively ended ORide, its most visible product and biggest customer acquirer. It sold some bikes and transferred others to OExpress, a delivery product that was soon shut down. In April 2020, Yahui Zhou, OPay’s founder, officially resigned as Chairman of Beijing Kunlun to become full-time CEO of OPay, a move that showed how OPay’s decision-making power did not reside in its biggest market, Nigeria.
While its super app play was falling apart, OPay told TechCabal at the time that it was having its best year ever, claiming 5 million users and over 60% of mobile money transactions in Nigeria. This would be the moment that birthed today’s OPay, as the company focused on becoming a payments and agent-banking company.
By the end of the year, Opera reported that OPay’s monthly transaction value was over $2 billion, a 4.5x growth.
Unicorn status
When OPay raised $400 million in an August 2021 funding round led by SoftBank Vision Fund, the venture capital arm of Japanese conglomerate SoftBank, it achieved a $2 billion valuation, becoming Africa’s third-largest startup worth over $1 billion. It is still the single-largest investment round secured by an African-based startup.
It also hired Olu Akanmu, a former executive director for retail banking at FCMB, a Nigerian commercial bank, as President and co-CEO of OPay Nigeria. It also acquired a microfinance bank licence from the CBN, allowing it to give out loans, which a mobile money licence does not.
Then, by December 2022, OPay got its single biggest gift when the CBN released redesigned naira notes and set an expiry date for the new ones at the end of January 2023. Cash, the backbone of Nigeria’s economy, became scarce, and the apps of several commercial banks failed.
OPay and other fintechs like PalmPay and Moniepoint benefited from this policy as customers opened accounts and began transacting with them because they worked while banks failed, and their agent networks brought banking to doorsteps.
Akanmu, OPay’s former co-CEO, stepped down in January 2024 after almost two years at the company due to a clash of vision between the former banker and the rest of the company’s leadership based outside Nigeria.
Reckoning
By the second half of 2023, OPay had become a mainstay in the fabric of Nigerian life. By October 2023, OPay was the country’s most-downloaded app. But with scale comes regulatory oversight.
Nigeria’s Data Protection Commission (NDPC) investigated OPay over claims that it opened accounts for people without their consent, which the company denied after an internal investigation. No outcome has been made public after NDPC’s investigation.
OPay’s next interaction with regulators was not that smooth. In April 2024, TechCabal broke the news that the CBN barred OPay from opening accounts for new customers. That ban lasted for six weeks, and the fintech, among other fintechs, had to block P2P crypto transfers, verify physical addresses for all account tiers, and update facial verification.
Then, the CBN fined OPay ₦1 billion ($742,991) in the second quarter of 2024 after a routine CBN audit of the fintech sector revealed compliance issues.
It did not end there. An August 2025 CBN circular ordered every PoS terminal to be geo-tagged within 60 days and locked to within 10 metres of the merchant’s registered address, directly limiting OPay’s agent network business. That same month, the CBN capped PoS agents’ daily cash-outs at ₦1.2 million ($930) and individual customers’ at ₦100,000 ($70), another shock to its agent network.
These policy shocks might have shuttered the growth of most businesses, but OPay weathered these storms and drew 88% of its $536 million revenue from Nigeria.
OPay’s road to the shuttered IPO
On February 12, OPay confidentially submitted a draft registration statement, which became public only in October. In April, Opera, which holds 8.6% of OPay, told investors in a securities filing that it saw an 85% chance of an OPay listing within two years.
Opera was confident because OPay had made a sharp turnaround after losing $50.8 million in 2024. The following year, it made a $72.5 million profit on $536.3 million in revenue, up 161%, as new loans grew 285% to $938.3 million.
On May 1, Bloomberg reported that OPay had hired Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and JPMorgan to prepare a U.S. listing that could value it at about $4 billion, double the $2 billion SoftBank’s Vision Fund 2 set in 2021. With these backers, news about OPay’s IPO picked up pace, and what initially sounded like a pipe dream quickly got credibility.
OPay made its filing public on October 9. It showed first-half 2026 revenue of $467.1 million, up 136.5%, and net income of $90.9 million. Lending, at $236.1 million, had overtaken payments as its biggest business, and Nigeria supplied 89.5% of revenue.
The filing listed the risks that came with OPay’s listing: rising provisions for credit losses as lending grew, heavy dependence on Nigeria, and an Indonesian lending arm that OPay controls through contractual arrangements Indonesia does not expressly recognise.
However, one risk it dismissed in its IPO prospectus came back to prevent its listing. In the prospectus, OPay said it was not required to obtain approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) or complete its filing procedures under China’s 2023 overseas listing rules.
But, according to Bloomberg, a Chinese regulatory inquiry prompted the Nigeria-focused payments company to halt its IPO just hours after setting the price. OPay said it was confident the inquiry would be resolved satisfactorily “in the near future.”
The redemption deadline gives OPay until the end of 2027 to try again, about 14 months. To scale its second IPO attempt, the company will need to revisit how well it bounced back from inquiries by Nigerian policymakers.

articles.title: La plus vendue des citadines électriques de BYD perd une roue arrière en pleine route, les automobilistes commencent à se poser des questions sur la qualité des voitures chinoises
articles.text:
La plus vendue des citadines électriques de BYD perd une roue arrière en pleine route, les automobilistes commencent à se poser des questions sur la qualité des voitures chinoises
La plus vendue des citadines électriques de BYD est dans la tourmente. En cause, un propriétaire qui a perdu sa roue arrière en pleine route. Depuis, le débat sur la qualité des voitures chinoises bat son plein en ligne.
L’histoire se déroule à Jakarta et concerne la BYD Atto 1. Pour rappel, il s’agit de sa citadine électrique la plus vendue du constructeur, appelée Seagull en Chine et Dolphin Surf chez nous avec un prix de départ de 19 990 €. Ce sont 529 537 exemplaires qui furent écoulés en 2025.
La qualité des voitures électriques chinois fait débat
Ceci étant dit, pour en revenir à notre histoire, le conducteur se trouvait donc sur la route à Jakarta quand sa BYD heurte un séparateur en béton. Après entre un et deux kilomètres, plusieurs bruits métalliques se font entendre et la roue arrière droite se détache. Les images ont rapidement circulé sur les réseaux sociaux en Indonésie et la qualité des voitures électriques chinoises est désormais au centre des discussions.
BYD Indonesia a réagi par la voix de Luther Panjaitan, son responsable des relations publiques et gouvernementales. Il explique que les premières informations évoquent bien le choc violent contre le séparateur et qu’une inspection complète du véhicule est en cours.
	
Il y a encore eu un incident similaire hier. Ça ne fait pas peur de se dire qu'à grande vitesse, il suffit de toucher un petit nid-de-poule pour qu'une roue se détache ?
Mais cela ne calme pas les débats en ligne. La vidéo de l’événement qui circule sur les réseaux sociaux indonésiens s’accompagne d’une formule pour le moins explicite : "La mauvaise qualité des voitures électriques chinoises, c’est une constante."
Cet épisode arrive d’autant plus au mauvais moment que BYD a fait face à plusieurs rappels récemment. La Seagull elle-même l’a vécu en avril 2024 avec un correctif logiciel pour 16 666 exemplaires. En octobre 2025, ce sont plus de 115 000 Tang et Yuan Pro qui ont été rappelées pour des défauts de conception et des risques liés à la batterie.
	
Malheureusement, cela révèle la mauvaise qualité des voitures chinoises commercialisées auprès des consommateurs de notre pays
Plus récemment, en septembre 2026, BYD a rappelé 183 211 Qin et Tang à cause d’un défaut de fabrication sur une pièce de la pédale de frein.
La voiture concernée est une citadine très populaire
La vidéo virale en Indonésie ne fait que renforcer les critiques autour de la qualité des voitures électriques chinoises alors que récemment, Huawei a aussi subi une mauvaise publicité suite à un test qui montrait la piètre qualité des pédales de frein de son véhicule.
Et puis le fait qu’il s’agisse d’une Seagull amplifie la portée de cet événement puisque c’est la plus vendue des citadines électriques de BYD. La BYD Seagull est un modèle très populaire dans le monde et forcément, de potentiels intéressés pourraient être refroidis.
Rappelons que cette BYD Seagull est disponible en France pour s’attaquer directement aux Renault 5 E-Tech et Citroën ë-C3 sur le marché des petites électriques.
Suivez toute l'actualité des Numériques sur Google Actualités et sur la chaîne WhatsApp des Numériques
Envie de faire encore plus d'économies ? Découvrez nos codes promo sélectionnés pour vous.

articles.title: Identity as an Architectural Concern: Enterprise IAM Beyond Authentication
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Decide how identity will shape your data model during the initial design. A security review at the end can catch a missing check or a bad scope, but it can't restructure a schema that was never built to explain who had access and when.
- Once your access questions are about ownership and validity, a graph fits better than a role table. In our role tables, "who owns this account" required a chain of joins. In Neo4j, it's one traversal.
- About eighty thousand people own our service accounts. Keeping those owners engaged through job changes and departures is most of the governance work, because an account whose owner has moved on is a credential nobody is watching.
- When revocation travels over an event stream, it's eventually consistent. Know your worst-case staleness, cap it with a maximum cache age, and tell your security team what it is.
- Merging attestation, rotation, and vaulting into one workflow cut time-to-revoke from about three days to under one.
After the Login
For a single application, identity is mostly a vendor decision. You pick an identity provider, wire up SSO, validate tokens at the edge, and move on with the features. For one application and one team, that's the right call. It stops being enough as the organization grows. Login keeps working fine. Everything after that gets difficult: who approved a given access and whether it should still exist when an auditor asks about it months later.
This article draws on building and operating an identity and access management platform in regulated financial services, where a wrong entitlement becomes an audit finding. My argument is that at enterprise scale, identity has to be treated as part of the architecture. Teams that add it late tend to find it conflicts with decisions they've already locked in. I'll assume you have experience shipping OAuth 2.0 or SSO. What follows covers the design problems that appear once many services, and many owners, are involved.
Identity as an Architectural Concern
Identity belongs in architecture discussions because it constrains decisions that look unrelated. The data model is where this shows up first. Once you have to explain and audit access, "who can touch this resource" needs to be a relationship you can query with history, because auditors ask what was true six months ago as well as what is true today. Service boundaries and event flows raise their own problems; each gets its own section below.
Regulation adds another constraint. Here's a useful test: Could you answer "Who had access to this system on 14 March?" from your data model alone, without grepping logs across several tools? If not, an audit wasn't part of the design.
A security review can catch a missing check or a misconfigured scope, but it can't retrofit a schema that was never built to answer that question. The cheapest way to pass that test is to record every grant, revocation, and attestation as an event with a timestamp and an actor from the start. Then the auditor's question is one query against the event log.
Where Flat RBAC Breaks Down
The Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) model is used by default and is usually sufficient. It strains when your questions shift from "Does this user have this role?" to how things relate to each other. Our entities are people, the service accounts they own, and the accesses those accounts hold. The questions we kept asking were: "Who owns this account?", "Is this access still valid?", and "What does this person control?"
All three are relationship questions. Ownership is a relationship. An access has a validity window and an attestation history attached to it. A person who leaves or changes roles pulls a set of owned accounts along behind them. In a role table, you rebuild each of those links with joins every time you ask. In a graph, each link is an edge and the query walks them.
That's why our backend models these relationships in Neo4j, queried through GraphQL. GraphQL fits because a query's nesting mirrors the traversal: this account, then its owner, and then its access. A caller asks for exactly the slice of the graph it needs, from an account down to its valid accesses. Nobody handwrites traversal logic or over-fetches a large object and filters it in memory. Figure 1 shows the shape of the underlying model.
Figure 1. Ownership-and-access graph modeled in Neo4j, showing how flat RBAC breaks down when access needs expiration and nuance. (Image source: created by the author.)
Before the query, here is the model it runs against. There are three kinds of nodes: Person, ServiceAccount, and Resource. There are two associations between them. First, a person OWNS a service account, while second, a service account HAS_ACCESS to a resource. The association, HAS_ACCESS, possesses some properties such as expiration, the date for when the access will be no longer valid, and lastAttested, which displays the last date when the access was attested by the owner. Validity is an attribute of the edge rather than of any node since it refers to the particular combination of the account and resource nodes.
This query, as shown below, poses a question we frequently ask ourselves: Who is the owner of this account and which of its accesses are currently valid? Looking through the query from the top, the first MATCH gets the account based on its ID and follows the OWNS relationship until it reaches the owner. The next OPTIONAL MATCH follows the HAS_ACCESS relationship towards each of the resources, and the WHERE clause appended to it filters out any access where the expiry date has expired. Because it is an OPTIONAL MATCH, an account having no accesses left will yield its owner anyway. Finally, the RETURN clause yields the owner’s name along with all the accesses left with their resources, expiry dates, and last attested date in a single array.
Neo4J Cypher Query
// Who owns this account, and which of its accesses are still valid today?
MATCH (p:Person)-[:OWNS]->(a:ServiceAccount {id: $accountId})
OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[g:HAS_ACCESS]->(r:Resource)
WHERE g.expires >= date()
RETURN p.name        AS owner,
       collect({
         resource: r.name,
         expires:  g.expires,
         lastAttested: g.lastAttested
       })              AS validAccesses
Written as SQL against role tables, the same question needs every link lined up by hand:
-- Who owns this account, and which accesses are still valid today?
SELECT owner.name, res.name, g.expires, g.last_attested
FROM service_account acct
JOIN account_owner ao   ON ao.account_id = acct.id
JOIN person owner       ON owner.id = ao.person_id
LEFT JOIN account_grant g
       ON g.account_id = acct.id
      AND g.expires >= CURRENT_DATE
LEFT JOIN resource res  ON res.id = g.resource_id
WHERE acct.id = :accountId;
Even here, it's easy to get it wrong. Put the expiry check in the WHERE clause instead of the join, and accounts with no valid grants vanish from the result, owner and all. The query works, but it still leaves three problems out of view. Ownership is a single join in this example, but ownership can be delegated, and once it can, that join becomes a walk up a chain of unknown length. In the graph, the same chain is a variable-length path in one pattern. The expiry check also has to be repeated in every query that touches grants. Any query that leaves it out returns access that should have been removed. In the graph, the check sits inside the traversal, so a consumer can't skip it by accident. Finally, when a person leaves, the accounts they own aren't in front of you, and you have to go looking for them. In the graph they're one hop away, because "owns" is an edge. Both queries are simplified from what we run in production.
But Neo4j has inherent costs. It's one more datastore to operate, and traversal performance depends heavily on how you model things. A badly shaped graph can be slower than the join it replaced. It was still worth it for us, because ownership and validity are things we traverse constantly. The flat version pushes the hard part onto whoever writes the next query.
Service Accounts: Eighty Thousand Owners, Three Tools
Comparing everything in the platform, the service accounts took the most governance work. Every service account is owned by a real person: Roughly eighty thousand people review, rotate, and vault the accounts they own. An account’s safety depends mostly on that owner: whether they're still engaged and whether they've changed teams or left the company. An account whose owner has moved on is exactly the stale, over-privileged credential that nobody notices until it's misused.
Before the rebuild, the three things an owner had to do (attestation, rotation, and vaulting) lived in three separate tools. An owner had to remember which tool did what. That's a small annoyance for someone who does it daily. For someone who does it twice a year, or who inherited an account when a colleague left, it's a real failure mode.
The rebuild put all three owner requirements into a single workflow, so an owner sees one screen with what they own and what's due. Getting there took more than wiring screens together. Each tool had been built with its own assumptions about schedules and ownership, and once they shared a workflow, those assumptions had to be reconciled. Figure 2 shows the revocation workflow before and after the consolidation: Three separate tools, with revocation taking about three days, became one unified workflow that revokes in under a day.
Figure 2. Revocation workflow before and after tool consolidation. (Image source: created by author.)
Integrating a Vault We Didn't Own
In enterprise identity work, the risky integrations are usually the ones where your system depends on a system you don't govern. For us, that was vaulting. We already handled attestation and rotation well before the rebuild. We had written that code ourselves, so we knew how it failed. Vaulting ran in a separate tool, owned by another team, on infrastructure we couldn't change. Folding it into our workflow meant a critical control now depended on their release schedule and their outages.
The hard part was deciding what our workflow should believe when their API didn't answer, or answered slowly, or answered after our call had already timed out. Those are not edge cases when you're doing this for tens of thousands of owners. They happen every day, somewhere. So we made the integration "fail closed". If the vault was unreachable, the workflow didn't report the step as complete, and an owner was never told a credential was vaulted when it wasn't. That sounds obvious on paper. In practice it meant our side couldn't treat "we sent the request" as success. We had to confirm the vault's own state, reconcile it against ours, and treat any gap between the two as something our side resolves.
Propagating Identity Across Service Boundaries
If every service makes its own access decisions, authorization logic ends up scattered across dozens of codebases, where nobody can audit it. When a rule changes, you hunt for it through every service that has implemented its own version, and you can miss one. What works is letting identity context travel across boundaries while the decision stays in a dedicated policy decision point. Identity propagates through scoped claims using OAuth 2.0 token exchange, so a service acting for a caller gets a narrowed token instead of reusing a broad one.
The controller asks, and the policy decision point decides as shown in the following code snippet:
Java Code
// Authorization delegated to a policy layer, not hard-coded in controllers.
// Illustrative Spring Security style; exact API varies by version.
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http, PolicyDecisionPoint pdp) throws Exception {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .anyRequest().access((authentication, context) -> {
            AccessRequest req = AccessRequest.from(authentication.get(), context.getRequest());
            return new AuthorizationDecision(pdp.permits(req));
        })
    );
return http.build();
}
The controller never sees the rules, so changing a rule requires changing the PDP and nothing else.
Across a service hop, the incoming token is exchanged for a scoped one before the downstream call:
Java Code
// Narrow the caller's token to just what the downstream call needs,
// via OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693). Illustrative.
TokenExchangeRequest exchange = TokenExchangeRequest.builder()
    .subjectToken(incomingAccessToken)
    .audience("downstream-service")
    .scope("accounts:read")           // scoped down, not the caller's full grant
    .build();
String downstreamToken = tokenExchangeClient.exchange(exchange).accessToken();
The token for each hop records its audience and scope, so the audit log shows what every call was for.
Revocation Over Kafka
Entitlement changes propagate as events using Kafka. A grant, a revocation, or a change of ownership becomes a message that interested services consume. That's a sensible design for a distributed system and it indicates revocation is eventually consistent. Access stops once consumers process the event and invalidate any cached decisions, which happens some time after the revocation is recorded. That gap should be measured and capped before anyone describes revocation to a security stakeholder.
A consumer handling a revocation invalidates the cached decision, so the next check re-resolves from the source of truth:
Java Code
// Kafka consumer: an entitlement revocation invalidates the cached decision.
// Illustrative; run against your own broker and cache.
@KafkaListener(topics = "entitlement-events", groupId = "authz-cache")
public void onEntitlementEvent(EntitlementEvent event) {
    if (event.type() == REVOKED) {
        decisionCache.invalidate(event.accountId(), event.resourceId());
        auditLog.record(event);   // the revocation is itself an audited fact
    }
}
Events can be lost, so the cache also has a time limit. A cached decision is served only while it's younger than a maximum age. After that, it's re-resolved from the source of truth whether or not an event arrived. That maximum age is the worst case scenario for a dropped event. Before we relied on the design, I simulated the consumer and cache to confirm that a missed event never kept access live past it.
Choosing the maximum age involves a real trade-off. A short maximum age causes stale access to expire quickly, which is what security wants, but every expiry sends another check back to the source of truth. At our volume that load isn't free. A long maximum age is easy on the system and worse for revocation, because a dropped event has longer to matter. You pick a number you can live with on both sides, then state it plainly: A lost event leaves access live for at most that long. That's a sentence a security team can plan around.
The cache window was the small part, though. The larger delay was procedural. Before the rebuild, fully revoking access took around three days, most of the time being spent on steps a person had to complete in separate tools. With a single workflow, access revocation takes under a day.
When This Is Overkill
For a single app with a few roles and one team, you can skip all of this. Flat RBAC in your primary database is the right choice, and Neo4j, Kafka, and a policy layer would be over-engineering you'll regret maintaining. The threshold is organizational: many services making access decisions, service accounts that outnumber and outlive the people minding them, ownership that has to be re-verified, and an audit obligation with teeth. Here's how I would weigh each piece:
| Component | Worth It When | Skip It When | 
| Graph database | You traverse ownership and validity constantly | Whether a user holds a role is all you need to ask | 
| Event stream for entitlements | Access changes must reach many services, and you can state the staleness bound | A handful of services read access from one database | 
| Central policy layer | Authorization logic would otherwise spread across many codebases | One app owns all of its own rules | 
What's Next
Authorization is moving out of individual services and into policy engines that can be tested on their own. For service accounts, the zero-trust version of this is continuous verification: an account re-proves its entitlements on a schedule instead of keeping them by default. Our service account rebuild was a manual version of the same idea, because attestation is reverification with a human in the loop. The interesting question is how much of that human step can be made automatic without losing the accountability that a named owner provides.

articles.title: Ottawa earmarks $176 million to establish online super regulator | BetaKit
articles.text:
An online “super regulator” that was first announced by Ottawa this summer is beginning to take shape after the federal government announced millions in budget spending to support its creation.
The news: Thursday’s federal budget includes $176.3 million over five years to establish the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada (DSDPCC). The commission will be charged with overseeing private-sector privacy regulation under Bill C-36 and implementing the Safe Social Media Act, which is intended to hold social media and chatbot platforms accountable for online harms.
From the source: The DSDPCC has been described by AI Minister Evan Solomon as “a regulator with teeth.” It would have the ability to impose rules and transparency requirements on companies operating social media or AI chatbots, issue binding orders, compel audits, and fine companies who break those rules up to $10 million, or three percent of their global revenue, whichever is higher.
More on #Budget2026
The context: Initially pitched as the Canadian Digital Safety Commission, the DSDPCC was first unveiled in June when the Government of Canada announced its Safe Social Media Act, and later expanded upon when Ottawa proposed changes to the country’s existing privacy laws. Under Bill C-26, which has yet to be passed into law, the DSDPCC would oversee private-sector privacy regulation, taking those responsibilities away from Canada’s existing Office of the Privacy Commissioner.
The budget was sparse on details as to what the rollout of the commission would look like, or benchmarks for when it might come into effect, but said that funding to establish it would begin being deployed during this year and into next year. Previously, the feds said it could take as long as 18 months to get the commission up and running.
Final thought: The legislation Ottawa’s new super regulator is tasked with overseeing and implementing has drawn criticism from some in the tech community, academia, and elsewhere over its broad mandate, its ability to deliver on goals around age-verification and online safety for youth, and its potential to increase digital surveillance and infringe on privacy rights.
Feature image courtesy Evan Solomon via LinkedIn.

articles.title: In Other News: Trezor Implant, LLMJacking Bills Hit $1M, SAP Flaws Weaponized Within Days
articles.text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.
This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.
Here are this week’s highlights:
Anthropic adds security center, admin controls to Claude Enterprise
Anthropic has rolled out additional security and administration capabilities for Claude Enterprise, including a security center (in beta) that checks an organization’s Claude configuration for chat, Cowork and Claude Code against settings Anthropic recommends. Inference hooks, now generally available, route prompts and tool calls to an organization’s existing data loss prevention and security tools for inspection, while a centralized console (also in beta) lets companies handle single sign-on, SCIM and other settings across all their Claude organizations from one place.
Fake OpenAI and SpaceX event invites phish Microsoft and Google accounts
Push Security has documented a phishing campaign built around fake registration pages for OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic events, which dangle rewards such as three months of ChatGPT Pro or Grok Heavy to get marketing employees to sign in with their work accounts. The Microsoft option launches a device code phishing flow run through the Kali365 phishing-as-a-service platform. Push links the operator, with medium-high confidence, to earlier fake Zoom event pages and says the campaign relies on Google and Zapier short links, Cloudflare challenges and domains swapped out every few weeks to avoid detection.
Chainalysis breach also exposed password hashes and tokens
Chainalysis has widened its breach disclosure, saying it discovered on November 2 that names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all its users had been exposed, after initially reporting that only non-sensitive data was accessed. The company has since taken several products offline, including its KYT transaction monitoring service after detecting abnormal activity, and is reaching out to customers whose KYT accounts show signs of unauthorized access.
Google hands Agent Substrate, gVisor to CNCF for sandboxing AI agents
Google is donating Agent Substrate, an open source orchestration layer on top of Kubernetes for running large numbers of isolated AI agent sessions, and gVisor, its open source application kernel, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) as Sandbox projects. When an agent goes idle, Agent Substrate saves its state to storage and can bring it back in under 500 milliseconds. gVisor handles system calls in user space so that untrusted, AI-generated code doesn’t interact directly with the host kernel. According to Google, placing both projects under the CNCF gives the community a shared, vendor-neutral base for agent infrastructure that can run on any Kubernetes cluster meeting conformance standards.
‘Hello’ messages hide Chinese-language attack framework targeting Flowise
Era researchers have detailed Greeter, a Chinese-language exploitation framework that bombarded Flowise honeypots with thousands of chat messages reading only “hello” while abusing an old code injection flaw (CVE-2024-58351) to execute commands. The framework mapped the host, queried cloud metadata services, searched for SSH keys and other credentials, tried to set up persistence, and tested whether it could run payloads from memory. Era counted 4,372 Flowise instances exposed online, and of those whose version it could identify, 703 lacked authentication and 46 appeared to share the vulnerable setup used in its honeypots.
LLM Mixers turn hijacked enterprise AI access into underground business
Mandiant says it investigated several LLMJacking cases this year in which attackers took over companies’ access to AI models, generating fraudulent bills of more than $100,000 in a day and as much as $1 million in total at some organizations. Initial access mainly came from stolen or exposed cloud credentials and API keys, and in one intrusion the attackers exploited a LiteLLM vulnerability (CVE-2026-40217) to upgrade ordinary keys to full admin credentials. Google Threat Intelligence Group also found hijacked access being sold through so-called LLM Mixers, including the Jet Night token routing service, which it believes uses stolen keys to offer unlimited plans with claimed frontier model access for around $60 a month.
CryptoBilis-sold Trezor allegedly fitted with seed-stealing implant
Trezor is telling customers who bought its hardware wallets from CryptoBilis since March 2026 to transfer their funds to a freshly created wallet with a new seed, after a buyer reported finding an implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 purchased from the former Southeast Asian reseller, which also sold Ledger devices that were found to have been tampered with. According to the report, which Trezor has not yet verified, an added circuit board fitted with a cellular module and antenna captures the recovery phrase displayed on screen and transmits it over a mobile network whenever the device is connected. No stolen funds have been reported.
Harvard alumni and donor data from 2025 breach added to HIBP
Have I Been Pwned has loaded roughly 851,000 unique email addresses from Harvard University’s November 2025 breach, an incident subsequently tied to a ShinyHunters extortion bid. The records come from Harvard’s alumni and fundraising systems and contain detailed profiles of donors, alumni and parents, as well as some faculty, staff and students, including names, contact details, birth dates and places, employers, ethnicities, marital statuses and donation histories.
SAP exploitation window shrinks to days as ransomware interest grows
Onapsis and Recorded Future report that for SAP vulnerabilities patched in 2025 and 2026, the median gap between a security note’s release and the first verified exploitation or public proof-of-concept was one to three days, down from 489 days for flaws patched in 2021. Ransomware and extortion groups showing up in SAP-related content grew from 8 in 2023 to 26 in 2025, and SAP CVEs with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation or public proof-of-concept code doubled from 9 to 18 between the end of 2023 and mid-2026. The study, drawing on over 1.2 million threat intelligence events, also tracked underground listings for SAP access priced from $500 to $30,000.
Synology flaw patched in 2024 now exploited in ransomware attacks
Synology warns that attackers are abusing a vulnerability fixed in December 2024 to hit devices still running outdated DSM releases, with the goal of encrypting data and extorting victims. The company has not identified the specific flaw beyond pointing to its Synology-SA-24:20 advisory. Synology recommends that anyone on a vulnerable release update DSM right away and turn on automatic updates.
Alleged Nomad Bridge exploiter appears in US court after extradition
Alexander Gurevich, a 49-year-old Israeli national now known as Alexander Block, appeared in a US court for the first time on October 30, a day after Israel extradited him to face charges that he exploited the Nomad Bridge smart contract in August 2022 to take virtual currency worth roughly $2.89 million. According to the indictment, he swapped the stolen WBTC and WETH for other cryptocurrencies and spread them across multiple addresses to obscure their origin. The money laundering charge alone carries a maximum of 20 years in prison.
Related: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak

articles.title: Physicl raises $10M to make the digital world real enough for robots | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Alex de Vigan’s last business got swamped by the rise of generative AI, but now he’s betting the tech that team had built, a platform for creating tempting product renderings for e-commerce, can be re-purposed to make robots more useful.
His new venture, Physicl, has raised $10 million in seed funding led by Inovia Capital to help world model designers and robot builders solve thorny training problems with more realistic simulations.
Founder and CEO de Vigan spent the last decade building nfinite, which made it easy for brands and retailers to create 3D models of their goods and display them online. The arrival of transformer-based AI models led that company to focus more on generative imagery, but de Vigan saw a new purpose for his team and the tech stack they’d built to faithfully render 3D environments.
“What we were super unique about doing in 3D, AI was going to replace, but something was missing in AI: its ability to understand, interact, and manipulate space and objects,” de Vigan says.
Researchers developing physical AI models to make robots more capable of tasks like handling diverse, small objects have been frustrated by the returns of training them on video, and the expense of gathering data through remote operations.
Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult. De Vigan believes that the pipeline his previous company built to “transform unstructured, incomplete, heterogeneous real-world information into a high-fidelity physical representation… with correct geometry, materials, and physics” can now be used to make physical AI models more effective.
Physicl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits. There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise.
In particular, Physicl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases. The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects. It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems. For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow.
SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week. SpAItial’s tool generates 3D simulations from 2D imagery, and to do that effectively, its CEO and founder Matthias Niessner said they needed to train on the kind of high-fidelity synthetic data Physicl offers.
However, Physicl wants to be more than a data provider; it sees itself as the tooling for ongoing synthetic data generation. “What we created 10 years ago, without knowing it, was basically an agentic workflow to transform unstructured information into high-fidelity 3D,” de Vigan said. He imagines customers bringing trillions of images or millions of hours of lidar capture data to feed into his platform and turn them into high-quality 3D representations that can be used to generate billions of permutations to train their models.
“The real challenge is, you have to curate the data by hand, and this is a very long cycle,” Niessner, also a professor of robotics at the Technical University of Munich, told TechCrunch. “To us what seems very attractive is you can just do this on the fly […] You’re running Claude, and it checks, ‘Oh, I need more data of this in my training,’ and then it auto generates that data, depending on the training state. That, to me, is super exciting, and this is exactly what Physicl is offering.”

articles.title: Wisconsin reports measles death of a baby, first death in over 35 years
articles.text:
An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the first measles death in the state since 1990, officials reported Thursday. The death comes amid an outbreak in the Badger State that has stricken over 430 people across 13 counties this year.
“Any death of a child is a tragedy, and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” Wisconsin Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. “Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.”
The baby’s death is the third measles fatality nationally just this week, following the death of a New York child reported on Monday and another death in Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday. The Pennsylvania death was of an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County; the state health department did not provide additional details, such as the age of the person. The state’s explosive, ongoing measles outbreak has led to 1,467 cases so far this year.
In all, there have been nine reported measles deaths this year in the US, eight of which have been confirmed by state officials. The deaths include the baby’s death in Wisconsin, the child’s death in New York, and seven deaths (six confirmed) in Pennsylvania, including two babies, a healthy teen, and several adults with underlying health conditions.
National context
As of November 5, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting 5,182 measles cases in the US this year across 47 states and jurisdictions. The CDC is reporting four measles deaths, though it’s unclear which of the reported deaths the CDC has counted.
The national case and death tallies are the highest recorded since 1991, though the reported cases likely represent a significant undercount of actual cases. As Wisconsin health officials noted in the announcement of the baby’s death, “Not everyone who becomes ill seeks medical care or gets tested, which means cases may go unreported.” This is particularly true given that large outbreaks, including the one ongoing in Pennsylvania, have struck in tight-knit religious communities that are less likely to seek conventional medical care.

articles.title: Paraguay president steps down after digital bank Ueno collapses with 3 million customers inside
articles.text:
Facepalm: Paraguay's central bank has seized Ueno Bank after examiners looking at the digital lender's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending and expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets. Once those errors were corrected, Ueno's capital fell to less than half the legal minimum, and the bank's app, cards and transfers went dark as its branches locked their doors. About 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people, were cut off from the savings, payments and benefits they handled through the bank.
The warning signs went back months. ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper, reported in June that central bank inspectors found a pattern of risky insider lending. Ueno had lent large sums to owner-linked companies beyond legal limits and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.
Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud. They allege that some of the money lent to related companies was diverted to other businesses in the group. On Thursday, a judge ordered six executives jailed pending trial, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, and put two others under house arrest. All eight had turned themselves in after arrest warrants were issued.
Gustale's lawyer, José Fernández Zacur, argued that senior executives relied on staff for lending decisions. "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan," he told local media.
Ueno grew quickly. It was a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company and won its banking license in 2023. In less than five years, it went from an obscure lender to a household name that claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Generous cash-back offers on groceries brought in users. The bank also opened more than 70 locations, sponsored the national soccer team and put its name on the country's main stadium. That logo has since been removed.
The bank also held a large share of public money. As of last month, Ueno reported about $800 million in public deposits, roughly a quarter of its total. That included money from the state pension and health fund and from the operators of Paraguay's hydroelectric dams.
Those deposits are at the center of the political fight. Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo, the former president of Ueno's predecessor, Financiera Ueno, to run the central bank that supervised the lender. Earlier this week, the central bank chief resigned at Peña's request. Peña also had ties to Grupo Vázquez, which owned Ueno until March 2025. He says he sold his stake in the group that month and had no improper role in the bank's affairs. As recently as last month, he called concerns about Ueno a smear campaign.
 – Santiago Peña (@SantiPenap) November 5, 2026
Opposition lawmakers accuse Peña of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and helping shield the bank from scrutiny. He denies wrongdoing and says the matter is a regulatory issue for the courts. His own Colorado Party turned on him anyway. Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes backed impeachment and said the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money."
In a video posted to X, Peña said he was stepping down for "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions." He also apologized. "I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
Peña said he would still appear before the Senate to "exercise my right to a defense." Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation, which would let Vice President Pedro Alliana take office without a Senate trial. Opposition senators are still pushing for one. They argue that a resignation would keep Peña eligible to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution. Alliana has distanced himself from Peña and put his own presidential ambitions on hold until the crisis is resolved.
The crisis has hit the economy as well. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the dollar on Thursday, bringing its loss for the week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data. The Labor Ministry estimates about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and related businesses have been affected. Outside the Labor Ministry, young employees still in Ueno uniforms burned their credit cards and demanded severance and unpaid wages.
Peña urged a fast fix for the customers still locked out. "Clarifying the facts and resolving the payments are obligations that must advance at the same time," he said.

articles.title: IPVanish clears a third independent audit, reinforcing its no-logs credentials for the second year in a row
articles.text:
IPVanish clears a third independent audit, reinforcing its no-logs credentials for the second year in a row
- Schellman Compliance’s latest audit of IPVanish has confirmed no traffic, metadata, or session logging
- The audit is the third since 2022, and marks the second audit since IPVanish committed to annual audits
- It follows IPVanish’s recent RAM-only server rollout and expansion to a 150-location network
IPVanish has announced the results of its third independent no-logs audit, and once again its privacy claims have a clean bill of health.
The audit was completed by Schellman Compliance, a leading provider of attestation services, on September 25, 2026.
Following two previous third-party audits in 2022 and 2025, the review is the latest in what's become an annual tradition for the VPN provider: inviting an outside firm to poke holes in its no-logs policy.
According to the results shared, the policy is accurate and fully aligned with IPVanish’s public privacy commitments – with its zero-logs promise strictly enforced across the company’s global server network.
Proof, not promises
The evaluation was comprehensive. Schellman’s auditors were given unrestricted access to IPVanish’s systems, configurations, and teams.
Interviews were conducted with engineering and operations staff, and company workflows were reviewed alongside infrastructure, internal documentation, and the administrative procedures governing the VPN app itself.
They also ran test traffic exercises – simulating real-world scenarios and watching closely for any evidence of VPN logging, including DNS queries, VPN metadata, and server responses.
The conclusion: no records of browsing traffic, session history, or connection metadata are collected or stored on active servers. Further, any real-time systems used to detect network abuse operate purely in memory, leaving nothing behind.
The auditors also checked IPVanish’s internal safeguards, confirming that any changes to how its servers work need sign-off from multiple people. This makes it much harder for logging to be quietly switched back on.
“A no-logs policy is only as credible as the evidence behind it,” said Subbu Sthanu, General Manager, Consumer Cybersecurity at IPVanish.
“People shouldn’t have to rely on promises when it comes to their privacy. By committing to annual independent audits of our no-logs policy, we’re making transparency and accountability an ongoing practice, not a one-time exercise.”
Customers who want to dig deeper can download the full report themselves via the Security Reports page in the My IPVanish account portal.
Part of a bigger picture
The audit doesn’t arrive in isolation. IPVanish has spent the past year restructuring its plans – Essential, Complete, and Advanced – around a suite of security extras, while growing a server network that now spans more than 150 locations.
Meanwhile, the company is midway through migrating its infrastructure to RAM-only servers, which wipe all data on every reboot and eliminate the possibility of storage-based logging; it has pledged to complete that transition by 2027.
Taken together, the picture is of a provider treating privacy less as a marketing slogan and more as something baked into how it operates.
In a market where rivals like NordVPN and ExpressVPN have made repeat audits their own baseline, the third-party stamp of approval is now a must-have rather than a nice-to-have. IPVanish seems intent on keeping up.
Mark is a Tech Security Writer for TechRadar and has been published on Comparitech and IGN. He graduated with a degree in English and Journalism from the University of Lincoln and spent several years teaching English as a foreign language in Spain. The Facebook-Cambridge Analytica data scandal sparked Mark’s interest in online privacy, leading him to write hundreds of articles on VPNs, antivirus software, password managers, and other cybersecurity topics. He recently completed the Google Cybersecurity Certificate, and when he's not studying for the CompTIA Security+ exam, Mark can be found agonizing over his fantasy football team selections, watching the Detroit Lions, and battling bugs and bots in Helldivers 2.

The device that arrived at my building belongs to Tau Robotics, a local startup. Its long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but the technology isn’t quite there yet. For now, humans pilot the robots remotely, watching them work through onboard cameras.

Generative AI models depend on stacks of specialized memory chips. To meet soaring demand, Samsung is building a vast new semiconductor manufacturing campus in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
I visited the sprawling campus south of Seoul, where three fabs already operate around the clock, a fourth is coming online, and thousands of workers are racing to build a fifth.

articles.title: Tu iPhone podría estar cambiando algunas palabras cuando escribes sin que lo notes
articles.text:
La función de autocompletado es una de las características más útiles que nos han entregado los móviles. Millones de personas dependen de la escritura predictiva para redactar mensajes más rápido, pero una investigación reveló que el iPhone está limitando algunas palabras. Un investigador descubrió que el teclado de iOS evita algunas palabras y expresiones a la hora de autocompletar, lo que obliga a escribirlas de forma manual.
Según Reuters, Apple mantiene una lista gris dentro de iOS conformada por miles de términos y frases en distintos idiomas. Cuando escribes en el teclado del iPhone, el sistema de autocompletado evita sugerirlas, incluso cuando deslizas el dedo para hacer el swipe typing. La lista lleva activa desde hace unos años, con términos que se van añadiendo a partir de lo que ocurre en el mundo.
En una publicación de web Swipeblocked, que recopila las palabras "prohibidas" para el autocompletado del iPhone, el investigador Derik Kauffman explica que estas listas se encuentran dentro de los datos lingüísticos de iOS. Algunas vienen integradas en el sistema y otras se descargan mediante los paquetes de lenguaje que Apple distribuye a los dispositivos.
Entre las palabras y frases no permitidas por el autocompletado del iPhone se encuentran "inmigrante ilegal", "gibraltar español" o "anticatolicismo". Existen otras expresiones e insultos que se usan en España, México y otros países de América Latina. El listado incluye 6.123 entradas en múltiples idiomas, siendo el inglés el que predomina con 4.513, mientras que en español solo hay 288 frases.
Cómo funciona el bloqueo de palabras en el iPhone
De acuerdo con Kauffman, cuando el teclado del iPhone va a mostrar una sugerencia, autocompletado o resultado de escritura por deslizamiento, siempre realiza una comprobación previa. El sistema toma la secuencia de palabras candidata y verifica si está incluida en una lista de bloqueo interna. Si la coincidencia existe, la sugerencia se descarta y no se muestra al usuario.
En términos más técnicos, el teclado convierte cada palabra en un identificador numérico, luego agrupa esos identificadores en una secuencia de entre 2 y 6 palabras para calcular una huella digital de 32 bits usando el algoritmo hashword(). Posteriormente, busca la secuencia en una tabla hash y, si coincide con una entrada no permitida, la marca como bloqueada eliminando la sugerencia.
El investigador explica que este mecanismo se usa para predicciones y sugerencias del teclado, autocompletado y escritura por deslizamiento, o QuickPath, como se conoce en el iPhone. Aunque las palabras están bloqueadas y no se sugieren, iOS nunca impedirá que los usuarios las escriban manualmente. Otro detalle es que el autocompletado podría usar una palabra parecida para generar la frase.
Apple también usa un diccionario para etiquetar las palabras individuales como vulgares, ofensivas o sensibles. Las vulgares no se recomiendan hasta que hayas escrito la palabra de forma manual tres veces. Las ofensivas, que incluyen insultos, nunca se sugieren, por muy a menudo que las uses. Por último, las sensibles nunca se ofrecen como predicción o autocompletado, y algunas de ellas se omiten cuando deslizas el dedo para escribir.
La tecnológica no ha confirmado la existencia de esta lista, pero dijo que las sugerencias predictivas están diseñadas para evitar recomendaciones que puedan resultar ofensivas o inapropiadas.

articles.title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
articles.text:
China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.
China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips.
Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.
The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

articles.title: Nintendo’s latest Zelda remake already circulating online as a Switch 2 ROM — OpenAI-assisted software jailbreak, new game dumper let pirates share game for free, immediately following release
articles.text:
Nintendo’s latest Zelda remake already circulating online as a Switch 2 ROM — OpenAI-assisted software jailbreak, new game dumper let pirates share game for free, immediately following release
Nintendo's new Zelda remake has barely launched, but hackers have already found a way to extract its game files and circulate copies online
Nintendo’s remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has reportedly been dumped the same day it launched on the Switch 2. The game launched today, but ONE jailbreak says copies of the original 1.0.0 release and its 1.1.1 update are already circulating outside Nintendo's official distribution channels. The update reportedly weighs 23 GB.
The leak is not entirely surprising. Physical copies had already started turning up at buyers' homes several days before the release date. Footage of the game was already appearing online by Nov. 1. Those early cartridges gave hackers access to the remake before most players could get their hands on it, with some gamers sharing videos of themselves playing the game on social media. 
However, the game still remains far from playable on PC, with emulators struggling to render its graphics correctly. Some users encountered washed-out visuals or black screens, while others saw terrain bleeding through objects or could not get past the title screen.
Notably, the game is identified by title ID 0400486024DEC000, with its report naming two tools involved in extracting the files: ‘ns2jb and OunceCake’. The first is a software jailbreak developed by security researcher Sammy ‘pepsipu’ Hajhamid.
Last month, Hajhamid explained how he managed to get code running on Nintendo's latest console without installing a modchip, and also described what the exploit does: "This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2."
That opens up several possibilities for homebrew developers and researchers as well as pirates, but ns2jb has limitations. It is a tethered jailbreak, meaning it has to be activated again after the console restarts. The exploit also does not provide unrestricted kernel access. The same extraction method has reportedly been used with two other games: Deltarune Chapters 1-4 and Mario Kart World.
This is not the first time hackers have found a way into Nintendo's hardware. Just a day after Switch 2 went on sale in June 2025, an exploit that allowed hackers to run custom code on the system popped up, although it did not provide root access or a full jailbreak. Cartridge-based backups have also caused headaches. In August this year, we reported that Nintendo had targeted more than 400 GitHub repositories, with 401 repos removed following seven Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) notices. Several Yuzu forks were among the affected projects.
Nintendo has not publicly commented on the Ocarina of Time dump or the nsj2b exploit yet. However, SmileBASIC 4, the application used to launch the jailbreak, has disappeared from the Nintendo eShop following the exploit’s disclosure.
