articles.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
In Part 1, you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server.
The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools:
| What Part 1 does | Why it stops scaling | What Part 2 does instead | 
| The agent holds each MCP server’s runtime ARN and calls it directly | N agents against M servers is a wiring matrix, and every new tool touches every agent that needs it | Agents reach one Gateway endpoint, and the Gateway holds the target registry | 
| The agent’s role holds the token-exchange permission and reads the provider’s secret | Every agent that acts for users gets a credential path to every resource it might reach | The Gateway redeems the grant, and the agent’s role holds no token-exchange or secret permissions | 
| Each MCP server carries the same groups check in its own code | The same rule, copied into thousands of servers, drifts and can’t be audited or changed in one place | One default-deny Cedar policy set, evaluated at the Gateway before tools run | 
In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant.
What changes from Part 1
The Okta configuration, the AgentCore Identity credential provider, and the MCP servers from Part 1 stay as they are. Figure 1 shows the architecture with the additions.
- The user signs in, and the backend for frontend (BFF) exchanges the ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) issued to the task agent, agent A, as in Part 1.
- The BFF invokes agent A on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG.
- Agent A forwards the ID-JAG to its Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer accepts only agent A’s ID-JAGs.
- Policy in AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies for each tool listing and each tool call, before the Gateway invokes a target.
- For calls that Cedar permits, the Gateway has AgentCore Identity redeem the ID-JAG for each target at Okta’s custom authorization server through the Part 1 credential provider. A call that Cedar denies doesn’t redeem the ID-JAG.
- The MCP server checks the user’s groups and scope, as in Part 1, and records each decision as an authz.check span.
- Every hop emits OpenTelemetry spans to AgentCore Observability, which CloudWatch Transaction Search collects, and Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge.
The reporting agent, agent B, runs on Amazon EKS and follows the same path through its own Gateway.
Prerequisites
In addition to the Part 1 solution, you need the following:
| Prerequisite | Needed for | 
| eksctl, kubectl, and Docker | The second agent on Amazon EKS | 
| Okta Log Streaming | Okta’s System Log in CloudWatch | 
| AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions | AgentCore Gateways and policy engines, Amazon EKS clusters, CloudWatch log groups, and Amazon EventBridge rules | 
The additions take about 90 minutes. The EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus nodes and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode management fee, and the AgentCore features charge for what you use. See Amazon EKS pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.
As in Part 1, the base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain on GitHub, and you can build the Part 2 additions on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.
Create a Gateway that accepts the ID-JAG
The Gateway’s inbound authorizer works like the runtime authorizer from Part 1. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, its audience is the custom authorization server, and allowedClients pins it to one agent:
Figure 2 shows the resulting inbound authorizer.
Each MCP server becomes a Gateway target whose outbound authorization uses TOKEN_EXCHANGE through the Part 1 credential provider, so the Gateway performs the second exchange:
Figure 3 shows a target configured this way.
Three details matter here. First, as in Part 1, the target’s scopes must equal the ID-JAG’s. Second, give each target a static tool schema (listingMode set to DEFAULT with an inline mcpToolSchema), so the tool names your Cedar policies reference are fixed when you write them. In our tests, policies that name tools also couldn’t attach to dynamically listed targets. Third, the Gateway pages tools/list by target, so your client must follow the pagination cursor, or tools from later targets disappear. AgentCore Identity keeps the token from the Gateway’s exchange, so one single-use ID-JAG serves every tool call in a session. In our tests, it also opened a second session within its 5-minute life.
Because a credential provider authenticates as one Okta agent, give each agent its own Gateway and provider. Sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain takes a different route, in which a Gateway interceptor performs both exchanges itself.
Bind tools to agents with Cedar
Attach a Policy in AgentCore engine to the Gateway in ENFORCE mode, and write permit-only policies. Cedar exposes JWT claims as tags. A policy that reads a missing tag errors and is skipped. A skipped permit grants nothing, so default deny holds, but a skipped forbid blocks nothing. Guard each tag with hasTag:
The scope tag holds the ID-JAG’s space-separated scope claim, so the four conditions match xaa:write only as a whole entry. A scope such as xaa:write-admin doesn’t match. A matching policy, written the same way, permits the read tools with xaa:read. Check that every policy is ACTIVE before you attach the engine: an engine whose policies failed to create leaves the Gateway denying every call. Cedar binds tools to the agent and its delegated scope, and the MCP server still decides each user’s authority from the groups claim, as in Part 1.
Point the agent at the Gateway
Agent A now forwards its inbound ID-JAG to the Gateway instead of calling AgentCore Identity itself:
Remove the Part 1 AgentCore Identity statements from the agent’s execution role. That’s the only change to the role, which now holds no token-exchange or secret permissions, because the Gateway’s role holds the permission to exchange tokens. Keep allowedClients on the runtime’s authorizer.
Run a second agent on Amazon EKS
Our second agent, a reporting agent, runs the same code on Amazon EKS with its own Okta registration. Its resource connection allows only xaa:read, and it has its own Gateway and credential provider. EKS Pod Identity gives the pod an IAM role that can invoke models and write its own logs and traces, and nothing else. The AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK exports its traces. The agents-on-eks sample shows the Pod Identity setup.
Outside AgentCore runtime, no authorizer sits in front of the pod, so the agent validates the ID-JAG before a model call. It checks the signature, issuer, audience, token type oauth-id-jag+jwt, expiry, and that client_id is its own. If you kept the Part 1 agent check in the MCP servers, add agent B’s client ID to REGISTERED_AGENTS. Two settings tripped us up. The EKS Auto Mode general-purpose node pool runs only amd64, so build multi-architecture images. And the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, binds to localhost unless you set DOCKER_CONTAINER=true.
Trace every decision with AgentCore Observability
The spans in this section are AgentCore Observability, the component in Figure 1 that sits between the agents and CloudWatch. Runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Policy emit OpenTelemetry spans for each hop without code changes, after you turn on Transaction Search and trace delivery. Your own services add theirs with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). CloudWatch Transaction Search collects them, the AgentCore console reads them as agent traces, and Amazon CloudWatch Omni reads the same spans as traces.default, which is what lets one query put them beside Okta’s events.
One tool call therefore produces this chain of spans, each naming the control that made a decision:
| Span | Emitted by | What it records | 
| AgentCore.Gateway.InboundAuth | Gateway | Whether the inbound ID-JAG was issued to this agent | 
| AgentCore.Policy.AuthorizeAction | Policy | The Cedar decision for this tool | 
| AgentCore.Identity.GetWorkloadAccessToken | Identity | Binding the agent’s workload identity to the user | 
| AgentCore.Identity.GetResourceOauth2Token | Identity | Redeeming the ID-JAG at Okta for a scoped access token | 
| AgentCore.Gateway.InvokeTool | Gateway | The tool call and its outcome | 
| authz.check | The MCP server (ADOT) | The user’s groups, the agent, the decision, and the reason | 
Okta’s System Log is the one record AWS can’t emit, so you bring it in. Figure 4 shows both paths meeting in Omni.
To set it up:
- Turn on CloudWatch Transaction Search, turn on trace delivery for each Gateway (see this sample script), and add ADOT to the BFF and the MCP servers. The task manager writes each decision, the user, and the agent onto an authz.check span.
- In Okta, add a Log Stream for Amazon EventBridge. Okta delivers each event to a partner event bus in your account, and a rule writes it to a CloudWatch Logs log group. In our tests, events arrived about 1 second after Okta published them. Each ID-JAG grant event names the agent as the actor, the user as a target, and the granted scopes and resource connection.
- Set up an Omni space in the account and AWS Region, add the Okta log group to the CloudWatch Dataset integration, and save a view, view.xaa_authz_decisions, over the authz.check spans.
One query then joins each ID-JAG grant to the decisions it led to:
For Alice, the result shows Okta granting the task agent xaa:read xaa:write for her, then the MCP server denying her create_task 16.7 seconds later and allowing list_tasks after that, as Figure 5 shows.
Each request is also one trace, from the BFF through the agent, the Gateway’s identity and policy checks, and the MCP server’s decision, as Figure 6 shows. Omni marks the trace as a fault because the agent’s create_task call returned the denial.
Two instrumentation details matter. ADOT finds the Region and signs its exports through botocore, so add botocore to services that lack it. Until we did, our MCP servers exported no spans. And ADOT’s agent mode turns off instrumentation for HTTP client libraries such as requests and urllib3 by default, so set OTEL_PYTHON_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS in your BFF to override that default with a list that leaves out the BFF’s HTTP client (requests, in ours), or its trace context won’t reach the agent.
Validate the results
We ran each check through both Gateways with the users from Part 1. Each session listed the tools, then called list_tasks, create_task, and an employee lookup:
| Caller and path | Tools listed | create_task | Reads | 
| Alice, agent A, Gateway A | 6 | Denied by the MCP server: requires xaa-writers | Allowed | 
| Bob, agent A, Gateway A | 6 | Created | Allowed | 
| Carol, agent A, Gateway A | 6 | Denied by the MCP server: no groups claim | Allowed | 
| Bob, agent B, Gateway B | 4: Cedar hid the write tools | Refused by the Gateway: “No policy applies to the request (denied by default)” | Allowed | 
Through the deployed agents, the results matched: agent A denied Alice and Carol and created Bob’s task, and agent B told Bob it had no tool to create tasks. The same user got different authority through different agents, and Okta decided it.
These requests stopped at the front door:
| Request | Response | 
| Agent B’s ID-JAG at Gateway A, or agent A’s at Gateway B | HTTP 403, MCP error -32002 insufficient_scope | 
| An Okta access token instead of an ID-JAG | HTTP 403, the same error | 
| No token | HTTP 401, “Missing Bearer token” | 
| Agent A’s ID-JAG sent to agent B on EKS | Refused in 98 milliseconds, before a model call: “issued to a different agent” | 
The Gateway returns the same generic error for a wrong agent and for the wrong token type, so check your configuration against the token’s client_id and aud when you see it.
The Gateway’s identity and policy work is small next to the tool itself. Medians and 90th percentiles from 24 hours of Gateway A spans in Omni:
| Span | p50 | p90 | 
| Gateway.InboundAuth | 34 ms | 69 ms | 
| Identity.Authorize | 25 ms | 60 ms | 
| Identity.GetWorkloadAccessToken | 48 ms | 94 ms | 
| Identity.GetResourceOauth2Token | 70 ms | 439 ms | 
| Policy.AuthorizeAction (Cedar, per call) | 47 ms | 56 ms | 
| Policy.PartiallyAuthorizeActions (Cedar, per tool listing) | 65 ms | 75 ms | 
| Gateway.TargetInvocation (the MCP server on AgentCore runtime) | 5,565 ms | 6,273 ms | 
The identity and policy spans for one tool call sum to about 0.2 seconds at their medians, and the MCP server’s own authz.check span took under 1 millisecond. Gateway B showed the same pattern, with GetResourceOauth2Token at 408 milliseconds at the median.
Cross App Access or per-user consent
XAA applies where the target application’s authorization server accepts an ID-JAG. There, your Okta administrator decides which agent may act for which users, users see no consent prompt, and Okta evaluates policy each time a token is requested. Applications with their own authorization servers, such as GitHub, rely on each user’s own OAuth consent instead. Figure 7 compares the two, as we measured them.
We deployed the AWS sample 07-consent-portal-auth-code-flow-targets beside our stack, with Okta signing users in to an AgentCore Identity consent portal and a GitHub target on its own Gateway. Alice connected a GitHub test account through the portal, and Bob never connected one. The post Manage end-user OAuth consent for AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore describes this lane in full. Here’s what we observed:
| Action | Next GitHub tool call | 
| Alice consented in the portal | Returned her GitHub identity | 
| Bob, who never consented | MCP error -32042 with an AgentCore authorization URL | 
| Alice suspended in Okta, earlier token reused | Still worked: the Gateway checks the inbound token’s signature and expiry, and that token lived 1 hour | 
| Alice suspended, new sign-in | Refused | 
| Alice unsuspended | Worked with no new consent | 
| Alice’s grant disconnected through the consent portal’s API | Not connected, then -32042 again | 
The two lanes revoke differently. In XAA, Okta’s controls stop the next ID-JAG mint, and issued tokens expire within about 5 minutes. In the consent lane, Okta controls only sign-in: the stored grant outlived the suspension and stayed until we disconnected it. Choose per target application, not once for the enterprise.
Where this pattern applies
In media and entertainment, the fleet arrives quickly. A studio or streaming or games organization has agents for production tracking, title and asset metadata, rights and localization, and viewer or player support, each sitting in front of a different system with its own authorization model and its own auditors. The question isn’t whether one agent can be governed. It’s whether the hundredth one is governed the same way, and whether an administrator can still answer which agents reach which systems for which users.
Nothing here is specific to that industry. The agent is an identity in your IdP, the target is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and the Gateway is where authorization is decided. Teams in financial services, healthcare, and the public sector put different resources behind the same front door and get the same audit trail.
What’s next: observability and evaluations
This post uses AgentCore Observability for one purpose: to prove that each allow and deny traces back to a control. There’s more in it than that, and it’s a body of work in its own right. The spans already carry the model and tool latency behind every governance decision, Transaction Search can alert on a spike in denials, and AgentCore evaluations can score an agent’s behavior against your own criteria, online for live traffic or on demand over a chosen set of spans. A later post takes that up: what to measure on a governed agent, which evaluators catch an agent that reports success after a refused tool call, and how to run both without turning your traces into your largest bill.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the Part 2 resources, then follow the cleanup steps in Part 1:
- Delete the Amazon EKS cluster (eksctl delete cluster) and its Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository.
- Delete the Gateways and their targets, then the Policy in AgentCore engines, and then agent B’s credential provider.
- Delete the CloudWatch Omni space and domain, the Dataset integration, the Amazon EventBridge rule and partner event bus, and the CloudWatch log groups.
- If you deployed sample 07, follow its cleanup steps.
- Delete the IAM roles and policies you created.
- In Okta, delete the log stream, and deactivate and delete agent B and its linked app.
Conclusion
In this post, you moved the Part 1 solution from a topology that suits a few agents and tools to one that holds up across many. The Gateway became the single front door and redeemed Okta’s grant, so the agents held no tool credentials. Cedar policies evaluated by Policy in AgentCore replaced the check copied into each server. A second agent on Amazon EKS joined under its own Okta identity. And AgentCore Observability, with Okta’s System Log beside it in CloudWatch Omni, traced each allow and deny back to the agent, the user, and the control that decided it. The governance mechanism didn’t change, which is the point: only the topology around it did.
To get started, explore the AgentCore samples and Okta’s Cross App Access documentation. For plain token exchange through a Gateway, read Implement on-behalf-of token exchange for multi-tenant agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

articles.title: VeloDB’s Nitin Waghulde on why AI agents break down after the demo
articles.text:
VeloDB
View Brand Publisher
VeloDB’s Nitin Waghulde on why AI agents break down after the demo
At TechSparks 2026, VeloDB’s Regional Director for APAC explained why AI agents that work in pilots struggle in production, and why the fix often lies in the database underneath them.
AI agents tend to look good in a pilot. The scope is narrow, the data is controlled, and the questions are predictable. Production is different, and that gap is where many projects stall.
Gartner predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls. For Nitin Waghulde, Regional Director, APAC at VeloDB, a large part of the problem sits below the model, in the data layer.
In a keynote titled ‘AI agents at scale: Surviving beyond the demo’, Nitin explained how AI agents use data differently from people, what they need to work reliably at scale, and how companies are redesigning their data infrastructure to support them.
Nitin started his session with an example. In a traditional system, a business manager who wanted last year’s sales figure would run a ready-made report and get the number in one lookup.
Ask an AI agent why sales dropped over the last three quarters, and the work changes. The agent pulls order records from the ERP and CRM systems, scans support tickets and chats to check whether major customers have escalated problems, and reads sales team reports on territory dynamics. If its reasoning is incomplete, it goes back for more.
“What used to be completed in one simple lookup or one simple query, now you’re taking hundreds of lookups for the same thing,” he said.
AI is now a customer of your data
In the past, people and reports were the main consumers of business data, and systems were built around fixed reports with clear boundaries.
Now, Nitin said, AI has become a new customer of that data, and it behaves very differently.
Agents run around the clock, ask many questions at once, and work in an iterative loop: ask, think, search, and retry until they can answer. Their questions are also unscripted. That puts a heavy, unpredictable load on the data layer.
The challenge grows because business data lives in several places at once: transactional records, chat memory, documents, dashboards and pre-built reports, and vector stores for meaning-based search. An agent has to search all of them and combine the results before it can answer.
Each extra trip to the data adds cost. If the data is stale, the answer is wrong. Nitin compared it to driving with an inaccurate traffic map. And when data comes from many sources, it becomes harder to know where an answer came from, which creates a trust problem.
He likened it to sending someone to five filing cabinets to collect pieces of paper. By the time the person returns from the fifth cabinet, the information from the first may already be out of date.
What production agents need
Nitin outlined four requirements for agents to move from pilot to production.
- Access to every data type: Agents need numbers from structured records, text from documents, and meaning from unstructured sources.
- Scale: A single query may now need to scan petabytes of data, not the few terabytes that systems were once designed for. Also, the platform should support concurrency at scale to support iterative querying for data-hungry agents
- Freshness: Agents can only act correctly on current information. If an agent processing a refund cannot see the latest transaction record, it has to wait. Every change, including updates and deletions, needs to be visible to the agent immediately, without waiting for a nightly batch job.
- A record of every interaction: Every AI interaction leaves a trail. These logs are growing faster than business data itself, and they feed back into decision-making.
VeloDB’s answer is a single engine that handles all of these needs. The company was founded in 2023 by the original creators of Apache Doris, an open-source real-time analytics database that became a top-level Apache Software Foundation project in June 2022. According to VeloDB, Apache Doris has more than 14,000 GitHub stars and 700 contributors, and is used by over 5,000 enterprises worldwide.
To cut down the back-and-forth trips that slow agents down, VeloDB supports hybrid queries. A single query can combine SQL, vector search, and text search, running deterministic and probabilistic searches in parallel. The result is one unified source of truth instead of scattered data.
What it looks like at scale
Nitin shared two examples of companies running this architecture in production.
The first was one of the largest crypto exchanges, with more than 120 million users, which he did not name. The exchange makes transaction data available to AI agents that retail investors can query, for example to see what positions large traders are taking on an asset. He said its agents handle about 33,000 conversations with a tail latency of around 3 milliseconds, running round the clock.
The second was MiniMax, a Chinese AI company that listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in January 2026 and says it serves 212 million users in more than 200 countries. MiniMax rebuilt its logging system on Apache Doris after moving away from Grafana Loki, because logs had become a valuable source of intelligence worth keeping and querying.
Nitin said MiniMax ingests data at 10 Gbps and can query about 10 petabytes in under two seconds, at 70% lower cost. VeloDB has separately reported that the Doris-based system now supports logs across all of MiniMax’s business lines at petabyte scale with over 99.9% availability.
The same challenges apply to early-stage startups building agents, Nitin added. VeloDB works with fintech startups that face the same scaling problems as MiniMax or the crypto exchange, just at an earlier stage.
His closing point was that agents will always ask hundreds of questions, so the infrastructure has to make each one cheap, fast, and current.
For Nitin, scaling AI agents is less about finding a better model and more about giving agents real-time, trustworthy data from a single source. Companies that get the data layer right, he argued, can make decisions faster, reduce costs, and move their agents from pilot to production with confidence.

articles.title: Durante años Ueno Bank pareció conquistar las finanzas de Paraguay. Ahora ha reavivado el fantasma del "corralito"
articles.text:
Ueno Bank ha pasado de ser el sueño financiero más ambicioso de Paraguay a protagonizar su mayor pesadilla. La historia de semejante cambio puede resumirse en tres cifras. En un tiempo récord (de 2023 a 2026) la entidad elevó su cartera de 500.000 clientes a más de tres millones, una cifra asombrosa en un país de 6,5 millones de habitantes. El problema es que esa expansión acelerada quedó empañada el martes, cuando el Banco Central intervino la entidad al comprobar que no alcanza el mínimo de solvencia exigido.
Ahora el país tiene a miles de familias sin acceso a sus cuentas… Y ve cómo resuena una palabra maldita: corralito.
¿Qué ha pasado? Que Paraguay vive una crisis financiera y política con epicentro en Ueno Bank, un banco esencial en el tejido económico del país. Desde el martes la entidad está intervenida por orden del Banco Central (BCP), lo que significa que millones de clientes han visto cómo se congelaban sus ahorros. Lo mismo le ocurre al Estado con fondos públicos que suman cientos de millones.
¿El motivo? Los activos y pasivos se han quedado suspendidas mientras el BCP aclara la situación del banco y, lo más importante, cómo de cubiertas están sus obligaciones. Los propios usuarios no tardaron en comprobar que no podían operar de forma normal en los cajeros y la banca online.
🇵🇾 La gente en Paraguay protesta después de que su dinero se desvanezca en el aire de un día para el otro Ueno Bank, que tenía el dinero del 70% de la población, fue cerrado por el gobierno por problemas financieros La gente perdió sus ahorros de toda la vida e incluso el gobierno perdió el dinero de jubilación guardado en el banco para los ancianos El gobierno ahora promete reembolsar algo de dinero y se vive una incertidumbre total
— Pato Bonato (@patobonato) November 5, 2026
¿Tan grave es? No se trata solo de que Ueno tenga más de tres millones de clientes en la nación (“dos de cada tres paraguayos eligen Ueno Bank”, presume la entidad en su web), es que también mantiene importantes vínculos empresariales, políticos e institucionales. Eso explica que desde el martes haya dimitido el responsable del regulador bancario, Carlos Carvallo, o que el mismísimo presidente del país, Santiago Peña, haya renunciado al cargo, si bien el Congreso no aprobó su salida y ha activado un juicio político contra él.
En los últimos días se han publicado también noticias que apuntan a que el Estado tiene depositados 850 millones de dólares en el banco. Entre los fondos públicos que administra se incluirían además alrededor de 355 millones de dólares del Instituto de Previsión Social (IPS), el organismo que se encarga de administrar el Seguro Social de Paraguay.
¿Qué es Ueno Bank? Durante años, una historia de éxito empresarial rutilante. Desde el martes, el epicentro de un seísmo político y social en Paraguay. Aunque la entidad se transformó en un banco en 2023, cuando obtuvo la licencia del BCP para operar como tal, sus orígenes se remontan mucho más atrás, a mediados de los 70. Como financiera, su actividad se centró en pequeños comerciantes y un perfil de cliente al que le costaba acceder a la banca tradicional.
Con el tiempo, la firma captó el interés de Grupo Vázquez, un importante holding que la adquirió en 2021. Dos años después se incorporó al sistema financiero y en 2024 se consolidó con la absorción de Visión Banco. Desde entonces ha crecido hasta convertirse en un gigante con más de tres millones de clientes en el país que gestiona, según sus estimaciones, tres millones de transacciones al día.
Esas cifras se han repetido hasta la saciedad esta semana, igual que se han repasado también los vínculos de Ueno con importantes figuras de Paraguay: Santiago Peña fue accionista de Ueno Holding, aunque vendió su participación en 2025; y antes de asumir la presidencia del BCP en 2023 el propio Carlos Carvallo fue directivo de Financiera Ueno.
Comunicado sobre el inicio de pagos de garantía a los depositantes de ueno bank S.A. Enlaces habilitados: https://t.co/Gc9LL253Bq https://t.co/FBmqbFSJOp https://t.co/dA3ZvWzza5 https://t.co/w4M2wYO3Lc
— Banco Central del Paraguay (@BCP_PY) November 5, 2026
¿Por qué está intervenido? Para entenderlo hay que remontarse al martes, cuando el BCP emitió un comunicado en el que informaba del “inicio del procedimiento de resolución del banco Ueno”. La nota no ahondaba en detalles, pero deslizaba un argumento clave: la decisión se adoptó “tras constatarse una insuficiencia en su índice de solvencia por debajo del 50% del mínimo requerido”. “La medida busca atender su situación de manera ordenada, proteger a los depositantes y preservar la estabilidad del sistema financiero”, añadía.
La misma madrugada del martes la aplicación de Ueno Bank emitía un mensaje en el que explicaba que no podía mostrar los saldos. Solo unas horas después empezaron a reunirse frente a la sede central de la entidad y decenas de sucursales personas empeñadas en retirar fondos. Así lo relata El País, que habló con una peluquera que insistía en que necesitaba dinero para comprar medicinas para su hijo.
¿No ha dicho nada más el BCP? Sí. Para calmar los ánimos Liana Caballero, miembro del directorio del BCP, aclaró qué había ocurrido: “Procedimos al cierre de la entidad, por lo tanto ni la aplicación ni las tarjetas ni ningún servicio de la entidad está activa a partir de la fecha”. También recordó que el fondo de garantías cubre el equivalente a hasta 75 salarios mínimos mensuales “por persona física o jurídica en cada entidad financiera”. Eso equivale a 37.700 dólares.
¿Y ahora, qué? Es la gran incógnita. Más allá de la tormenta política e institucional que ha desatado, Ueno Bank es el banco de miles de familias y concentra 850 millones de dólares en depósitos públicos, incluidos varios cientos del IPS. La entidad financiera también gestiona las pensiones de decenas de miles de jubilados. Esa relevancia explica que en los últimos días haya ciudadanos que han salido a la calle para protestar por la caída de la entidad, preguntar cómo se ha llegado a la situación actual y demandar soluciones.
“Seamos claros sobre lo que ocurrió. Un banco perteneciente a un solo conglomerado empresarial terminó concentrando los ahorros de la mayoría de los adultos del país, además de cientos de millones de dólares de fondos de pensiones”, comenta en la BBC Orkun Saka, del City St George's. Aunque el BCP ya había advertido sobre los “préstamos excesivos” a empresas ligados a sus propietarios, el experto recuerda que “aún así siguieron llegando fondos públicos”. “Esto no es simplemente la historia de un banco mal gestionado”.
Por lo pronto, se ha detenido a varios directivos de la entidad y hay casi una treintena de imputados. El foco ahora está puesto en la gestión del esquema financiero, la concesión de créditos y su efecto en la solvencia del banco.

articles.title: It's almost 2027, and the FAA is finally replacing the floppy disks used by US air traffic control
articles.text:
Better late than never It's almost 2027, and the US Federal Aviation Administration has just announced it will replace the floppy disks still used by many US air traffic control systems. The upgrade won't be complete until the end of 2028, almost 20 years after most floppy disk manufacturing ended.
At more than 400 sites, the FAA still uses floppy disks in four systems to upload data to aging information displays that controllers consult for weather conditions, airport status, and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs).
One of these is the Information Display System 4, or IDS-4, which was deployed in the early 1990s and runs on a Microsoft platform that is no longer supported. These systems provide operational information controllers need to manage traffic.
 – Secretary Sean Duffy (@SecDuffy) November 5, 2026
Many US air traffic control facilities still rely on legacy systems tied to infrastructure built in the 1990s. These systems have undergone extensive safety testing and must remain operational around the clock. Replacing that technology is a difficult and expensive undertaking, requiring new systems that meet strict safety and security standards and can be introduced without disrupting operations.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted a message on X yesterday confirming the modernization of the facilities. "Floppy disks from the 1980s: OUT 21st century tech: IN," he wrote.
The new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) will replace the four 1980s-era systems. It consolidates operational information into a shared platform, including weather impacts, equipment disruptions, flight alerts, restricted-airspace schedules, and pilot weather reports. The FAA says it will improve information distribution and reduce repairs and workarounds associated with older equipment.
The FAA wants E-IDS installed at 435 facilities by the end of 2028. Five sites have already replaced their floppy disk-based systems: Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport, Greater Rochester International Airport, and data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City.
In 2023, an FAA assessment found that over a third of the nation's air traffic control systems were unsustainable, and some were starting to fail.
It was reported last year that several FAA sites were still running Windows 95. The FAA also uses decades-old Compaq computers that are so out of date that replacement parts have to be bought from eBay. Another legacy technology still in use is paper flight strips, the pieces of cardstock on which key details of a single flight – such as call sign, aircraft type, and altitude – are printed or handwritten.
"We're moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement.
A lack of funding has long been one of the issues preventing air traffic control modernization. The FAA is now using $12.5 billion in funding provided by President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill to replace the archaic systems.

articles.title: Clap de fin pour le Tesla Cybertruck : chronique d’un échec industriel annoncé
articles.text:
Il devait redéfinir le marché automobile américain et faire passer les Ford F-150 pour des reliques du passé. Le Tesla Cybertruck restera finalement dans les livres d’histoire comme l’un des plus spectaculaires dérapages industriels modernes.
Elon Musk a annoncé, le 6 novembre 2026, sur X (ex-Twitter) la fin de production du pick-up à la Gigafactory d’Austin vers la mi-2027. Tesla veut utiliser l’espace libéré pour produire davantage de Cybercab, son robotaxi sans volant ni pédales, fabriqué également à Austin et qui a commencé à transporter des clients payants dans la ville depuis septembre.
Du mirage à moins de 40 000 dollars au gouffre à six chiffres
Dévoilé en grande pompe fin 2019, le Cybertruck est resté dans les mémoires pour les couacs de sa présentation (vitres brisées et grandes promesses). Tesla annonçait alors une version de base à 39 900 dollars (environ 35 800 €), un tarif dont le pick-up ne s’est jamais approché.
Après de nombreux retards dans son développement et son industrialisation, la facture a rapidement dérapé : les premiers clients de la série Foundation ont dû débourser plus de 100 000 dollars (environ 89 700 €). L’autonomie a fondu, elle aussi. Tesla promettait jusqu’à 500 miles (environ 800 km), alors que la version Premium vendue aujourd’hui affiche 325 miles (environ 523 km) selon le cycle américain EPA.
Surtout, l’équation économique était viciée dès l’origine. En s’entêtant à concevoir une carrosserie en tôle d’acier inoxydable laminée à froid, Tesla s’est enfermé dans des coûts fixes bien trop élevés qui n’avaient de sens qu’avec des volumes de production importants. Tesla avait prévu la ligne du Cybertruck au Texas pour 250 000 exemplaires par an.
Or, les réservations à 100 dollars, remboursables, ne se sont jamais traduites en commandes réelles. Elon Musk en revendiquait plus d’un million en octobre 2023, et des estimations indépendantes en comptaient près de deux millions.
Il restera le plus gros flop de Tesla
Tesla ne publie pas ses ventes modèle par modèle, mais Kelley Blue Book estime à environ 70 000 les Cybertruck vendus aux États-Unis depuis 2024. La demande s’est tarie dès que le premier cercle des inconditionnels de la marque et des influenceurs a été servi. Coincé par son poids et ses arêtes coupantes, le Cybertruck n’a jamais pu être homologué en Europe ni sur les grands marchés mondiaux, réduisant son terrain de jeu à la seule Amérique du Nord, où les professionnels et les utilisateurs de pick-up traditionnels l’ont largement délaissé, notamment en raison de ses limites à l’usage.
Sur les neuf premiers mois de 2026, Cox Automotive estime à 11 586 le nombre de Cybertruck vendus aux États-Unis, dont 4 323 au troisième trimestre. À ce rythme, Tesla en écoule environ 15 000 par an, soit seize fois moins que ce que la ligne d’Austin devait produire.
Pour achever le spectacle avec un joli coup de cynisme commercial, Tesla avait, la veille de l’annonce, gelé les commandes de la version d’accès Dual Motor et relevé les prix des versions restantes. La Premium AWD, désormais la moins chère, passe de 84 990 à 92 490 dollars (environ 83 000 €), soit 8,8 % de plus, et le Cyberbeast grimpe à 102 490 dollars (environ 91 900 €). C’est la deuxième hausse en moins de trois mois, après celle d’août. Une technique classique pour presser le citron des derniers acheteurs, avant de tirer le rideau.
Pour les propriétaires, Elon Musk s’est voulu rassurant en répondant à un internaute sur X : la flotte de Cybertruck « sera là pour longtemps ». Il n’a en revanche rien précisé sur la durée de vente des stocks, ni sur les pièces détachées et l’entretien, un point sensible pour un véhicule aux panneaux de carrosserie uniques.
En voulant imposer un délire de science-fiction plutôt qu’un outil de travail rationnel, Tesla a gaspillé des milliards de dollars et des années d’ingénierie qui auraient été infiniment plus utiles pour renouveler les Model 3 et Model Y ou lancer une compacte populaire à 25 000 euros. Ses avancées techniques (l’architecture électrique en 48 volts, la direction sans liaison mécanique dite steer-by-wire) serviront aux futurs modèles. Wes Morrill, l’ingénieur en chef du projet, assure d’ailleurs que le Cybertruck « survit à travers le Cybercab ». Commercialement, en revanche, le mastodonte en inox restera un caprice d’ingénieur devenu trop lourd à porter.

articles.title: Vault Fork OpenBao Adds External Keys and Quantum-Ready TLS
articles.text:
OpenBao has released version 2.7, adding read scaling for PostgreSQL-backed deployments, support for external hardware security module (HSM) and key management service (KMS) keys, and post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. The release also introduces control groups for human review of sensitive operations and new headers intended to keep requests consistent across load-balanced OpenBao nodes.
OpenBao began as a community fork of HashiCorp Vault after HashiCorp changed Vault's licence from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License in 2023. The project is now governed under the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation and is distributed under MPL 2.0, an Open Source Initiative-approved licence. Its stated aim is to provide a secrets manager under open governance rather than control by a single vendor.
The fork was both ideological and commercial. Some users objected to the loss of an OSI-approved licence and to the possibility that a vendor could change the terms governing infrastructure they had already adopted. Others saw a practical opportunity: Vault had placed capabilities such as namespaces, HSM integration and advanced scalability behind enterprise licences, while an open fork could make comparable functionality available without those restrictions. The move followed the wider pattern that produced OpenTofu from Terraform and Valkey from Redis.
OpenBao has developed well beyond a simple continuation of Vault Community Edition. Since the fork, the project has added namespaces for multi-tenant isolation, plugin-based auto-unseal integrations, and read scalability for its integrated Raft storage backend. Version 2.7 extends that scaling work to PostgreSQL, allowing standby OpenBao instances using that backend to serve reads in a similar way to Raft-based deployments.
Alex Scheel announced the release for the OpenBao project, writing that it adds "PostgreSQL horizontal scalability, External HSM and KMS-Backed Keys support, and Post-Quantum Cryptography". He also noted that the release arrived after a shorter development cycle than the previous one and included "many substantial features and several major security patches".
"We are thrilled to announce the availability of OpenBao v2.7, adding PostgreSQL horizontal scalability, External HSM and KMS-Backed Keys support, and Post-Quantum Cryptography!" Alex Scheel
The external keys feature lets the PKI and Transit secrets engines use key material held in an HSM or KMS rather than storing it inside OpenBao. Support is delivered through third-party plugins, building on the auto-unseal plugin work in the previous release. This should appeal to organisations that must keep root certification authority keys or other high-value material under hardware control.
The post-quantum work adds ML-DSA and ML-KEM to TLS listeners, certificate authentication, PKI and Transit. Operators can therefore use post-quantum signatures and key exchange in relevant parts of the platform. The change does not by itself make a deployment quantum-safe: clients, certificate authorities and surrounding systems must also support the chosen algorithms. It does, however, give OpenBao users a route to begin testing hybrid and post-quantum configurations.
"Despite a shorter turnaround than from v2.5.x to v2.6.x, we were excited to see many substantial features and several major security patches land within this release." Alex Scheel
Control groups add an approval workflow to OpenBao. A new control_group stanza in an ACL policy can require a second party to review access to specified paths. This is aimed at high-risk operations where a single authenticated identity should not be able to act alone.
The release also includes breaking changes. The separate HSM distribution has been discontinued because the PKCS#11 plugin is now externalised. Vendor-specific built-in auto-unseal mechanisms for Alibaba Cloud, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud have also moved to plugins. Kerberos, LDAP and RADIUS authentication, along with the LDAP secrets engine, have moved into the openbao-plugins repository. The file storage backend has been removed; the project had never recommended it for production because it lacks high availability and transactions.
Luca Berton, who interviewed Scheel at Open Source Summit Europe, wrote that external keys allow operators to "run your PKI root backed by an HSM" with key material comparable to Vault Enterprise managed keys. He also highlighted the importance of post-quantum support before government transitions expected around 2030, citing the risk that encrypted traffic recorded today could be decrypted in the future.
Commercial support is also becoming part of the OpenBao ecosystem. ControlPlane launched ControlPlane Enterprise for OpenBao in March, offering security hardening, supply-chain assurance, rapid CVE remediation, optional FIPS 140-3 compliance support and 24/7 technical support. That offering illustrates how an open-source project can remain freely licensed while vendors compete on operational assurance. ControlPlane positions the product as a supported path for organisations that want OpenBao's licence and governance model but still need enterprise-style operational commitments. Its materials also contrast OpenBao's MPL 2.0 licence with Vault's BSL 1.1 licence and note that OpenBao retains API compatibility with Vault for many use cases.
Secrets management being a foundational dependency has been covered in InfoQ recently. We previously reported on Vault 2.0 and IBM's support model following its acquisition of HashiCorp, as well as on the broader pattern of community forks preserving open standards after vendor licence changes. OpenBao's progress suggests that the fork is becoming a credible alternative rather than merely a protest project.
OpenBao version 2.8 is expected to focus more on security and stability, with likely improvements to authentication. For teams evaluating a migration, the immediate questions are less about individual features than about operational maturity: plugin lifecycle management, PostgreSQL high-availability configuration, post-quantum client compatibility and the availability of support for production incidents.

articles.title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
articles.text:
I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.
I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.
I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.
Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.
But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.
With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.
But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.
The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.
When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)
You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.
In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.
The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.
Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.
But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.
Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.

articles.title: When code is cheap, trust is not: Inside the AI-era engineering roundtable
articles.text:
When code is cheap, trust is not: Inside the AI-era engineering roundtable
In a closed-door roundtable, leaders from logistics, healthcare, telecom, fintech, and e-commerce discussed where to automate, where to keep humans in charge, and why observability can no longer be an afterthought.
AI has made writing code faster than ever, but the harder question for engineering leaders is what happens after the code is written. At a roundtable on operating engineering in the AI era, leaders from logistics, food tech, healthcare, telecom, fintech, ecommerce and higher education compared notes on scaling with AI without losing reliability, security or control. The shared view was that speed is no longer the hard part. Governing it is.
The roundtable, moderated by Ipshita Basu, brought together Manjunath Nakshathri, Head of Engineering, Mojro; Shobhit Suman, CPO, HungerBox; Pavan Kumar A T, CTO, Digii (DigiiCampus); Pranjal Nadhani, Co-founder and CTO, Cautio; Kenil Paul, VP, Technology and Solutions, 6D Technologies; Rimjhim Agrawal, Co-founder and CTO, BrainSightAI; Dhruv Rastogi, Chief AI Officer, MediAssist; Chandrakesh Pandey, Senior Vice President of Technology, Niyo Solutions Inc.; Achal Sharma, CTO, TechnoSport; Sunil Kumar, Director Engineering, Meesho; and Anshul Sharma, Director Engineering, Scaler.
The session was hosted by groundcover and Data Signals in partnership with YourStory, and was led on the host side by Paul Trebe, Head of Sales and Partnership, groundcover, and Satish Dange, Founder, Data Signals.
Where the bottleneck has moved
Participants agreed that AI has compressed build time, but the pressure has shifted downstream. When agents generate large volumes of code, the questions become who reviews it, who tests it and who monitors dozens of deployments a day. Several leaders said their teams now spend more time on design, context and governance than on writing components. Agents are only as effective as the context they receive, and few organizations yet have repository knowledge, documentation and templates in a form an agent can reliably use.
Drawing the line on autonomy
The room converged on a progressive approach. Reversible, read-only work, such as fetching data or generating reports, can go to agents with little friction. Irreversible actions, such as deleting data or running database updates, stay behind human review. Blast radius matters as much as reversibility. If a wrong call could affect end users or production systems, a person makes it.
One of the participants described a ‘four eyes’ model in which AI does the maker work of reading and analyzing, deterministic rules deliver clear yes or no outcomes, and a human signs off. Another speaker described risk scoring based on severity and occurrence, which focuses human review on medium and high criticality items. Others drew the line by specialization, letting engineers use agents freely in their own domain while production ownership stays with people who can debug at 2 AM.
That scenario also surfaced in a hopeful form. Instead of waking an engineer, an agent can investigate an incident and hand over a report by morning, leaving the decision with a human. Trust, participants said, will build gradually, much as it did with online payments, and the line will keep moving.
Accountability and the skills question
Accountability drew firm agreement: it cannot be delegated to a model. Leaders remain answerable for what agents do. AI works as an intelligence multiplier, one participant noted, which means mistakes are amplified as quickly as good decisions.
Skill erosion sparked livelier debate. Some saw a shift in skills, much as calculators changed arithmetic. Others, particularly in healthcare, worried about losing the expertise needed to judge AI output at all. One practical answer was to decide deliberately where AI drafts and where humans do.
Data control as a design decision
For telecom and healthcare leaders, data control is settled at design time. Models cannot simply run in a public cloud when regulators, tenancy separation, and residency rules apply, and one mistake can bring heavy penalties. Others stressed governance from the first stage, covering what data is ingested, what is used for training versus inference, and how it is masked or de-identified. Concerns about intellectual property and bias also led to a call to vet AI tools as rigorously as new hires.
Observability for an agentic world
Observability ran through every topic. Teams described tracing agent inputs, decisions, and handoffs so they can see why an agent acted as it did and correct it. One ecommerce team learned the cost of underinvesting: a ranking change left every dashboard green while business impact surfaced days later, and the root cause analysis took more than a week. It has since built a change ledger, lineage, a system graph, and a debugging agent that proposes ranked hypotheses.
The observability view was that it can no longer sit apart from development. Paul Trebe put it plainly: “You can no longer decouple observability from development.” Agents need context-rich data to act well, he noted, and the agents themselves must be monitored, since AI traces can run to 500,000 lines that only other agents can realistically parse.
What comes next
No one claimed a finished playbook. Open questions remain on measuring agent reliability and return on investment, protecting data and IP, and keeping engineers sharp enough to challenge what AI produces.
Still, the conversation pointed to a common direction. Give developers room to move fast, but build the guardrails first. Keep humans in charge of irreversible and high-impact calls, and widen automation as trust is earned. Several participants argued that standing still is not an option, since competitors will not wait. The real test of the AI era is less about how quickly teams can build and more about how confidently they can run what they have built.

articles.title: Los directores financieros asumen la gestión de la inteligencia artificial como nueva responsabilidad corporativa
articles.text:
Los directores financieros (CFO) están ante una transformación sin precedentes: a las responsabilidades tradicionales de supervisión contable y control presupuestario se suma ahora la gestión de la inteligencia artificial como herramienta de trabajo y como área de rendición de cuentas corporativa. Un nuevo informe de Salesforce, elaborado a partir de una encuesta doble ciego a 865 líderes financieros de tres continentes, documenta cómo la función del CFO se ha ampliado en el último año y cómo la IA —incluyendo los agentes autónomos— está en el centro de ese cambio.
Casi tres cuartas partes de los responsables financieros reconocen que el alcance de su rol creció durante 2026. La gestión del uso y la expansión de la inteligencia artificial es la razón más mencionada, por encima de cualquier otro factor consultado en la encuesta, incluida la propia complejidad de los ingresos. Al mismo tiempo, el 65 % de los equipos financieros gestiona ahora múltiples modelos de ingresos, y el 71 % vende a través de más canales que hace un año.
“A los responsables financieros se les pide que hagan más: no solo informar sobre los resultados financieros, sino también ampliar hacia nuevos modelos de negocio, habilitar más canales de distribución y desarrollar una estrategia de IA para su empresa. Lo que llama la atención es que muchos están recurriendo a la IA, no porque sea la última tecnología de moda, sino porque necesitan una forma de gestionar la complejidad sin tener que aumentar la plantilla. La oportunidad es significativa, pero también lo es el riesgo. Los responsables financieros necesitan una IA en la que puedan confiar, gestionar y que se vincule directamente a los resultados empresariales de los que son responsables”, afirmó Sam Chung, Chief Customer Officer de Agentforce Revenue Management.
La mitad de los líderes financieros encuestados afirma ser el principal responsable de las decisiones en materia de estrategia de IA dentro de su empresa. Esto representa un nuevo tipo de competencia: el departamento de finanzas ya no se limita a informar sobre el negocio. Cada vez más, ayuda a determinar cómo la empresa adopta la IA, dónde genera valor y cómo se debe medir ese retorno.
Para los CFO, esto implica que la gobernanza de la IA dejó de ser una cuestión exclusivamente tecnológica para convertirse en una financiera. Las decisiones que antes recaían principalmente en el área de tecnología —dónde implementar la IA, a qué datos puede acceder, qué controles aplicar y cómo medir el impacto— ahora también involucran al departamento financiero, dado que tienen implicaciones directas sobre el control y la auditoría.
El 71% de los CFO ya vende a través de más canales que hace un año
La ampliación del rol del director financiero ocurre en un entorno empresarial cada vez más difícil de analizar y proyectar. El 71 % de los líderes financieros afirma que su empresa vende a través de más canales que hace 12 meses. Si bien las ventas directas siguen representando la mayor parte de los ingresos, el autoservicio en línea, las ventas indirectas o a través de socios, las redes sociales y las aplicaciones móviles contribuyen de manera creciente a la combinación de canales.
Los modelos de ingresos también se diversifican. Aunque los equipos financieros se centraban tradicionalmente en las ventas únicas, el 65 % ya realiza un seguimiento de transacciones en más de un modelo: suscripciones, servicios profesionales, modelos basados en consumo e híbridos conviven dentro de un mismo balance. En otras palabras, los equipos financieros no solo dan seguimiento a más transacciones, sino que gestionan más formas de generar, fijar el precio, facturar, cobrar y reconocer esos ingresos.
Más canales de venta fragmentan los datos y complican la conciliación financiera
Contar con más canales y formas de venta puede significar más formas en que los datos de ingresos se fragmentan. Una transacción puede comenzar en un canal, involucrar a un socio u otra acción de venta y, finalmente, requerir una conciliación entre múltiples sistemas antes de que el departamento financiero tenga una visión completa del negocio. Esa fragmentación operativa es uno de los principales desafíos que los CFO identifican en la encuesta.
Los modelos basados en consumo añaden otra capa de complejidad. Casi 9 de cada 10 líderes financieros afirman que su empresa planea incorporar más productos de este tipo en el futuro. A diferencia de una transacción única —en la que el evento financiero es relativamente sencillo—, los ingresos basados en consumo dependen de lo que el cliente utilice realmente a lo largo del tiempo. Esto exige que los equipos financieros concilien datos de uso con contratos, reglas de precios, registros de facturación y reconocimiento de ingresos, a menudo en sistemas que no fueron diseñados para funcionar juntos de manera fluida.
El trabajo manual todavía representa al menos el 20% de los flujos de trabajo financieros
Cuanto más complejo se vuelve el ciclo de vida de los ingresos, más costoso resulta el trabajo manual. Aproximadamente 7 de cada 10 líderes financieros (67 %) afirman que su equipo aún ejecuta al menos uno de cada cinco flujos de trabajo de forma manual, con frecuencia mediante hojas de cálculo —un trabajo que consume horas significativas cada semana y genera riesgos operacionales—. Frente a ese diagnóstico, los propios líderes estiman que existe margen para automatizar hasta el 40 % del trabajo de sus equipos, siempre que cuenten con la infraestructura adecuada y el apoyo necesario.
La oportunidad que abre esa brecha es precisamente la que está impulsando la adopción de herramientas de inteligencia artificial en el área financiera. El trabajo manual no solo es ineficiente: también es una fuente de error en contextos donde la precisión de los datos afecta directamente la toma de decisiones estratégicas y la información reportada a directorios e inversores.
El 90% de los CFO que usa IA reporta un retorno de inversión positivo
Entre los líderes financieros que ya utilizan inteligencia artificial, el 90 % reporta un retorno de inversión (ROI) positivo. Entre quienes emplean específicamente agentes de inteligencia artificial, más del 90 % reporta beneficios en ahorro de tiempo, productividad, reducción de costos y precisión en las proyecciones, y aproximadamente la mitad califica esos beneficios como significativos.
Muchos de estos resultados se observan en tareas de alto volumen basadas en reglas que, históricamente, han requerido intervención manual. PwC informa que la IA agéntica ya está reduciendo hasta en un 80 % el tiempo que tarda una factura en pasar de recibida a liquidada, entre otras tareas del ciclo financiero. Además de permitir que los equipos aborden el trabajo existente con mayor rapidez, la IA también amplía su capacidad analítica: simular rápidamente cómo un cambio en los precios o en la combinación de canales afectaría las proyecciones es una tarea que antes demandaba días y ahora puede completarse en minutos.
La seguridad y la gobernanza frenan una adopción más amplia de la IA
Los beneficios documentados no han eliminado los obstáculos. Casi la mitad de los líderes financieros (46 %) señala la seguridad como el principal freno para ampliar el uso de la IA, seguida por las preocupaciones sobre gobernanza e integración con los sistemas existentes, con un 42 %. Para los CFO, estos no son conceptos abstractos: se trata de controles concretos, auditabilidad, acceso a los datos y rendición de cuentas ante accionistas y reguladores.
Del mismo modo, muchos líderes identifican la limitada experiencia interna en la materia como una barrera relevante —una brecha notable para una función a la que, al mismo tiempo, se le pide que encabece la estrategia de IA de toda la compañía—. El costo de implementación también figura entre los obstáculos mencionados, aunque en menor proporción que los factores de seguridad y gobernanza.
Los CFO gestionan la IA de la empresa mientras la usan para mantenerse al día
“Las decisiones sobre IA ya no llegan al departamento de finanzas como solicitudes de presupuesto, sino como preguntas sobre riesgo, control y rendición de cuentas. El director financiero ha pasado de simplemente aprobar la IA a ser responsable de ella”, señaló Chung. Esa doble responsabilidad resume el nuevo rol que documenta el informe de Salesforce: los líderes financieros deben gestionar la implementación de la IA en toda la empresa y, al mismo tiempo, apoyarse en ella para manejar una complejidad operativa para la que sus propios equipos aún no se han modernizado por completo.
Los datos recogidos entre el 4 y el 15 de mayo de 2026 —mediante una encuesta doble ciego a 865 directores financieros, directores de contabilidad, vicepresidentes ejecutivos de finanzas y vicepresidentes de finanzas de Francia, Alemania, Japón, el Reino Unido y los Estados Unidos— sugieren que los CFO están abordando ambas tareas con una visión clara del valor para el negocio. La IA ya genera beneficios para la mayoría de los líderes financieros que la utilizan, con margen para ampliar su impacto. El informe completo sobre las prioridades de los directores financieros está disponible en el sitio de Salesforce.

articles.title: Perseverance acaba de descubrir algo en el polvo de Marte que complica mucho nuestras posibilidades de colonizarlo
articles.text:
Mucha gente no sabe que cuando el rover Perseverance partió rumbo a Marte, llevaba con él varios fragmentos de trajes de astronautas del tamaño de un pequeño sello cada uno. El objetivo era, una vez en el planeta rojo, exponerlos a sus condiciones ambientales, y comprobar qué tan bien las soportaba cada tejido. Sobre todo, había interés en analizar el polvo del regolito, ya que se sabe que en la Luna está compuesto por partículas afiladas, muy irritantes y abrasivas, tanto para la piel como para las mucosas. Por suerte, se ha comprobado que las partículas de polvo marciano son mucho más redondeadas. Pero ahí terminan las buenas noticias.
De cascos a guantes. En total, Perseverance cargaba con cinco muestras de tejidos de trajes de astronautas. Estas incluían un trozo de visera de casco de policarbonato; un fragmento de un material resistente a cortes, llamado Vectran, que se usa para confeccionar guantes; dos tipos de teflón, que tienen propiedades antiadherentes repelentes al polvo; y un material comúnmente utilizado para trajes espaciales, llamado Ortho-Fabric. Este último consta de varias capas. como el Nomex, un material que se encuentra en los trajes de bomberos por ser resistente al fuego; el Gore-Tex, que es impermeable pero transpirable; y el Kevlar, un material que se usa en chalecos antibalas por su gran resistencia. Se trata de tejidos muy útiles en la Tierra, ¿pero protegen frente a las inclemencias marcianas?
Perseverance se pone en modo científico. Las muestras de tejido iban montadas en el blanco de calibración de SHERLOC, un instrumento del brazo robótico del rover. Una vez expuestas al exterior, se usó el espectrómetro de rayos X (PIXL) del rover para analizar la composición de las partículas adheridas a cada muestra. Así, se vio que las partículas de polvo son muy redondeadas, porque han sido moldeadas por el viento, pero que su composición y su tamaño sí pueden ser muy peligrosos.
Demasiado pequeñas y tóxicas. Algunas partículas de polvo son tan sumamente pequeñas que podrían inhalarse y pasar al torrente sanguíneo, desde el cual serían capaces incluso de atravesar la barrera hematoencefálica y llegar al cerebro. Este sería solo uno de los órganos que podrían ser dañados por el regolito. Y es que su composición tampoco es muy esperanzadora, pues incluye sustancias como el azufre, el hierro, los percloratos y otros compuestos tóxicos. Los percloratos, de hecho, se encuentran entre los principales culpables de que Marte sea un lugar tan inhóspito.
La electricidad estática manda. Según los análisis realizados por Perseverance, la electricidad estática parece decidir qué tamaño de grano se adhiere a qué superficie. Los granos se cargan eléctricamente al chocar en el aire, por lo que pueden ser atraídos por los tejidos con carga contraria, como un imán. Sin embargo, cada material atrae granos de tamaños distintos. Se vio que las partículas más finas aguantaron pegadas durante años de conducción y perforaciones y que los polímeros orgánicos, como el teflón, son los que más fácilmente recogen el polvo fino.
Posibles soluciones. Detectar el problema es importante para ir pensando en posibles soluciones de cara a futuras colonizaciones al planeta rojo. Los científicos que han analizado los resultados de Perseverance creen que podría ser útil el uso de chorros de nitrógeno líquido, como en un lavadero de coches, o incluso la fabricación de trajes autolimpiables para los astronautas. Debe hacerse todo lo posible para que cuando vuelvan a la seguridad de sus naves y se quiten las escafandras no haya ninguna partícula peligrosa adherida a sus trajes.
Elon Musk llegó a hablar de pisar Marte por primera vez en 2028. Posiblemente la fecha no vaya muy bien encaminada, teniendo en cuenta que para entonces, como mucho, habremos vuelto a la Luna. De hecho, se dice que, después, ha hablado informalmente de la década de 2030. Aun así, es importante ir buscando medidas de protección. En este tipo de situaciones, la improvisación es una mala decisión.

articles.title: Six palettes de cartes graphiques Nvidia d’une valeur de 10 millions d'euros disparaissent après avoir été confiées à un faux transporteur qui a disparu avec son camion
articles.text:
Six palettes de cartes graphiques Nvidia d’une valeur de 10 millions d'euros disparaissent après avoir été confiées à un faux transporteur qui a disparu avec son camion
Ce sont six palettes de cartes graphiques d’une valeur de 11,4 millions de dollars qui ont été dérobées, soit environ 10,2 millions d’euros. Elles ont été confiées à un camion en Californie qui se faisait passer pour un transporteur alimentaire.
Rien d’étonnant lorsque l’on sait que les cartes graphiques Nvidia valent une petite fortune et sont très prisées par les voleurs face à leur rareté. Ici, ce sont donc six palettes qui ont disparu pour une énorme valeur de plusieurs millions de dollars.
Un camion chargé de Nvidia se volatiliste dans la nature
La cargaison a été confiée à un transporteur alimentaire avec comme mission de rejoindre Fort Worth au Texas. Mais ces conducteurs ont tout simplement disparu avec l’intégralité des cartes graphiques. La police d’Oakland enquête sur ce vol. Si personne ne s’est douté de rien, c’est que le camion avait bien le logo alimentaire qui était attendu.
Les enquêteurs ont perdu la trace de la cargaison dans le comté de San Bernardino après plusieurs très longs arrêts. À l’heure actuelle, aucun suspect n’a été appréhendé, la cargaison est toujours dans la nature. La valeur du chargement suffit à expliquer pourquoi la cargaison a pu attirer des voleurs puisque chaque palette représente environ la somme de 1,9 million de dollars, soit environ 1,7 million d’euros.
Olaf Groth, professeur à l’école de commerce Haas de l’université de Californie à Berkeley, résume tout l’intérêt de ce vol : "Si une puce coûte environ 550 000 $ aux États-Unis, soit environ 490 000 €, elle peut dépasser le million de dollars à l’étranger, soit environ 890 000 €."
Olaf Groth parle aussi d’un risque en termes de sécurité nationale puisqu’on ne sait pas où ces cartes graphiques atterriront. On pense notamment à la Chine qui n’a pas le droit d’utiliser du matériel étatsunien dédié à l’IA, dont des cartes graphiques Nvidia. La situation est telle qu’un marché parallèle a même vu le jour, largement toléré par les autorités chinoises.
Les GPU Nvidia sont une cible de choix
Et il ne s’agit pas d’une affaire isolée. CargoNet a recensé 677 vols de fret organisés aux États-Unis et au Canada pour une perte d’environ 304,6 millions de dollars, soit environ 271,3 millions d’euros, le double par rapport à un an auparavant. Le nombre d’affaires a toutefois baissé de 26 %. Mais les conséquences restent les mêmes : les pertes ont doublé.
Keith Lewis, vice-président des opérations chez CargoNet, explique : "C’est comme voler des lingots d’or pur. C’est beaucoup plus simple que de braquer une banque." Si l’on remonte à l’année dernière, du matériel Nvidia a notamment été volé autour de Fremont et Union City pour plus de 7,5 millions de dollars, soit environ 6,7 millions d’euros.
En septembre dernier, des voleurs ont aussi emporté deux remorques avec des logos Nvidia dessus en Californie. Mais malheureusement pour eux, les véhicules ne transportaient que 18 tonnes de sable. Au-delà des États-Unis, deux palettes de GeForce RTX 5090 d’une valeur proche de 440 000 € ont disparu à l’aéroport international de São Paulo au Brésil.
Depuis, la police soupçonne trois employés de l’aéroport, plus exactement deux caristes qui auraient sorti les palettes d’un entrepôt et un troisième qui aurait facilité leur passage dans les contrôles. C’est le mois dernier qu’une RTX 5090 de cette cargaison est apparue sur une plateforme de vente en ligne pour 32 000 R$, soit environ 5 300 €. C’est son numéro de série qui a permis de découvrir qu’elle était rattachée au lot volé.
