articles.title: MacBook Neo 2 : Apple verrait les choses en grand pour éviter une nouvelle rupture de stock
articles.text:
Nous le savons, le MacBook Neo a connu un succès pour le moins retentissant. En l’espace de trois semaines après sa sortie, ce sont pas moins de 1,1 million d’unités qui ont été expédiées, et la demande n’a ensuite pas vraiment faibli. Il aura fallu un certain temps pour que les stocks parviennent à suivre la demande. L’entreprise à la pomme semble avoir retenu certaines leçons de cet épisode triomphal et elle ne compte pas réitérer la même erreur pour la seconde génération de son MacBook Neo.
Apple veut éviter une nouvelle rupture de stock pour son prochain MacBook Neo
Même si Apple ne l’a pas encore confirmé, il semble maintenant acté qu’un nouveau MacBook Neo est en préparation. L’information provient d’ailleurs du toujours très bien informé Mark Gurman, journaliste chez Bloomberg, qui précise que la sortie de l’appareil aurait lieu « pour le premier semestre de l’année prochaine ». En réalité, Apple a tout intérêt à miser sur ce Mac dont la première génération s’est vendue à plus de 8 millions d’exemplaires à travers le monde.
Mais l’entreprise à la pomme prévoirait un stock au lancement bien plus important. En effet, selon le célèbre leaker Lanzuk, la production du MacBook Neo de seconde génération serait doublée par rapport à celle de la première génération. Du moins, lors de son lancement. Apple prévoirait ainsi de produire 16 millions d’unités rien que pour le premier semestre 2027. À titre de comparaison, le MacBook Neo de première génération avait été produit à 8 millions d’exemplaires pour son lancement.
Qu’attendre du MacBook Neo de seconde génération ?
Autant le dire tout de suite, Apple n’a communiqué aucune information à ce sujet. En revanche, Mark Gurman est venu rapporter quelques informations : le prochain MacBook Neo serait doté de 12 Go de RAM et d’une puce A19 Pro, soit celle que l’on retrouve dans les iPhone 17 Pro, Pro Max et Air. Pour rappel, le MacBook Neo de première génération intègre 8 Go de mémoire vive et une puce d’iPhone 16 Pro, l’entreprise à la pomme ayant pris l’habitude de recycler certaines des puces qu’elle produit. À noter également que des rumeurs annoncent de nouveaux coloris, ce qui serait logique pour ce type de produit.
Il reste maintenant la question épineuse du prix. Le succès du MacBook de première génération tient en partie au prix attractif qu’il avait affiché lors de son lancement : 699 euros. En juin dernier, l’appareil avait déjà connu une hausse de tarif de 100 euros. Par conséquent, qu’en sera-t-il d’un MacBook Neo de deuxième génération, doté de davantage de mémoire vive et d’une puce plus performante ? Un modèle vendu à plus de 1 000 euros ne risquerait-il pas de dénaturer ce qui a fait en partie le succès de son prédécesseur ? Une chose est sûre : la crise mondiale de la mémoire ne risque pas de s’estomper de sitôt.

articles.title: DigiCert Data Breach Impacts Business Customer Information
articles.text:
DigiCert has disclosed a data breach impacting its business customers’ contact information, including names and email addresses.
The incident involved an internal business system used for archiving customer information, which was moved to a different network segment in February 2025, inadvertently becoming exposed to the internet.
Attackers abused a self-registration feature in the system’s account manager, built for other purposes and not requiring MFA, to create a read-only account that had access to archived data between June 27 and July 2.
DigiCert blocked the unauthorized account on July 2, and determined in October that the account was used to access archived customer contact information, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.
In some cases, driver’s licenses, passports, utility bills, and other documents containing a name and address that its customers provided were also compromised.
“The access could not write records, act as a validation approver, or issue certificates,” DigiCert says. “The CA systems operate on their own secure network segments and were not affected by this external access.”
According to the company, the incident was initially investigated and remediated as an account-creation event. On October 12, however, it started suspecting that the unauthorized account may have accessed archived data, and launched an investigation.
Since mid-October, the company also implemented additional monitoring and alerting, verified or removed remaining non-DigiCert accounts, reset passwords for all business system users, deactivated the feature that enabled users to self-register, and verified the ownership of the business system and the enforcement of permission policies.
DigiCert did not say how many customers might have been affected. SecurityWeek has emailed the company for information on the matter and will update this article if it responds.

articles.title: Could potential AI clones of GTA VI force a quicker official port?
articles.text:
Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC’s DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU, we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator.
Obbe Vermeij hasn’t worked at Rockstar since 2009, but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun, he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game’s 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release.
“So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console,” Vermeij said. “So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn’t really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better.”
Those sales caused Rockstar to pivot hard toward the console side of the business, with oft-delayed PC ports of its major games only hitting many months or even many years after their console counterparts. It’s a trend that Rockstar has stuck with even as many formerly console-focused game publishers have started treating the PC as an equally relevant platform and as the line between PCs and consoles itself has gotten much fuzzier in recent years.

articles.title: Gelsinger-backed Nagare Labs’ capacitorless Z2RAM promises SRAM speed with DRAM density — latest published cell retains data for over 300 seconds at 85°C, but further figures are projected
articles.text:
Gelsinger-backed Nagare Labs’ capacitorless Z2RAM promises SRAM speed with DRAM density — latest published cell retains data for over 300 seconds at 85°C, but further figures are projected
Its founders’ papers take hot retention from 0.1 to over 300 seconds, but stop at 85°C.
A Pat Gelsinger-backed Georgia Tech spinout, Nagare Labs, says its Z2RAM can put SRAM-speed memory, at DRAM density, directly on top of AI chips. The founders’ own papers show a fast-improving cell that, tested up to 85 degrees Celsius, holds data for over 300 seconds. Gen 1 is projected to have 5x SRAM density with six stacked layers, 14x DRAM speed, and 3x less read energy than SRAM.
AI chips require a lot of bandwidth, and it has been challenging to get sufficient yields of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to feed them. Even when manufacturers can get it, some reportedly plan to settle for fewer layers for yield reasons, and heat is another. Heat is also why Samsung’s zHBM, which stacks DRAM directly on the processor, is planned at only about four layers.
Alternatives include high-bandwidth flash, still in development, which stacks NAND like HBM and would sit beside the GPU, or SRAM stacked directly on the die, which is less dense and more expensive for the capacity, but also faster. DRAM, which is more capacious, can sit on top of the compute, but heat limits how hard the logic underneath can run.
That limit is already shaping chipmakers’ design path for stacked memory. Micron’s vHBM plans, for example, include heat-spreading structures. With HBM stacked on a logic die, and DRAM needing to be kept at or below 95 degrees Celsius, the logic’s heat output is capped at 220 W/cm², or 300 W/cm² with better thermal vias, according to a 2025 simulation by co-founder Shimeng Yu’s group. Nagare Labs says peak compute has grown 70% a year over the past three decades, against 20% for memory bandwidth.
The company describes its Z2RAM as “Two transistors and a shield. No capacitor,” where a write transistor places a charge on a storage node and the shield blocks noisy neighbors. The read transistor can sense without draining. In a gain cell like this, the read transistor’s gate capacitance holds the charge, so reads are non-destructive and the cell avoids DRAM’s write-back. Nagare aims for well under a picojoule per bit.
Nagare builds Z2RAM by depositing its layers on top of the accelerator and patterning them “together on one die,” much as 3D NAND flash scales by adding layers. There’s no interposer and no bonds between the memory layers, which is part of the secret sauce. One lithography exposure covers several layers at once, and standard 300 mm tools with DUV do the job, with no EUV required. The current roadmap is aiming at over 100 layers with “hundreds of thousands” of vertical connections.
Retaining data at higher temperatures is the challenge, and one the founders have probed repeatedly with their testing. A 2020 paper from co-founder Suman Datta’s group, on a tungsten-doped indium oxide two-transistor cell, had retention of 1 second at 25 degrees Celsius and just 300 milliseconds at 85°C. An update in 2025, which has Datta as a co-author, adds a third transistor and removes the gate overlap from its transistors, managing over 1,000 seconds at 25°C, up from 200 seconds with overlapped ones. It also simulated a GPU L2 at twice SRAM’s capacity but in the same area with 75–80% lower energy-delay-area product, a combined score that multiplies energy, delay and area.
Six months later, both founders showed a “folded asymmetric boosted” three-transistor cell that held data for over 300 seconds at 85°C, as compared to only 100 milliseconds for a conventional three-transistor design. That’s still below the roughly 95°C that Nagare says DRAM must stay under, so neither the founders’ published cells nor Z2RAM have shown retention above that line yet. The boosted cell is also “refresh-free,” which means data in the GPU’s last-level cache, profiled from AI workloads, doesn’t have time to decay before it is overwritten.
| What the founders’ papers measured and simulated, and what Nagare projects |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Figure | Value | Measured, simulated or projected | Conditions | Source | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2020 two-transistor cell, retention | 1 s; 300 ms | Measured | 25°C; 85°C | Datta’s group, IEDM 2020 | 
| 2025 three-transistor cell (self-aligned), retention | More than 1,000 s | Measured | 25°C | Georgia Tech, IEDM 2025 | 
| Conventional three-transistor cell, retention | 0.1 s | Measured | 85°C, to a 100 mV decay | Georgia Tech, VLSI 2026 | 
| Boosted three-transistor cell, retention | More than 300 s | Measured | 85°C, to a 100 mV decay | Georgia Tech, VLSI 2026 | 
| Write pulse | 10 ns | Measured | Two-transistor cell | Georgia Tech, IEDM 2025 | 
| Read delay | 2.6 ns | Simulated | 7nm design, 128×128 array | Georgia Tech, VLSI 2026 | 
| Cell area | 0.0168 µm² | Projected | 7nm design rules | Georgia Tech, VLSI 2026 | 
| Bit density | 5.7× that of 7nm SRAM | Simulated | Four tiers, 256MB, same area | Yu’s group, IEEE Trans. Computers 2026 | 
| GPU L2 energy-delay-area product | 75–80% lower than SRAM | Simulated | Twice the capacity in the same area | Georgia Tech, IEDM 2025 | 
| Logic power under stacked DRAM | 220 W/cm² (300 W/cm² with better thermal vias) | Simulated | DRAM kept at 95°C or below | Yu’s group, JxCDC 2025 | 
| Nagare Gen 1 density | 5× SRAM | Projected | Six layers, vs. 2nm HD SRAM | Nagare Labs | 
| Nagare Gen 1 speed | 14× faster than DRAM | Projected | Gen 1 | Nagare Labs | 
| Nagare Gen 1 read energy | 3× less than SRAM | Projected | Gen 1 | Nagare Labs | 
Physical space is also limited for this application, and the founders project their boosted cell at 0.0168 µm² at 7nm, compared with 0.0199 µm² for a high-density SRAM cell on TSMC’s 3nm (N3) process. A separate study from Yu’s group found that a four-tier, 256MB cache of two-transistor gain cells at 7nm could reach 5.7x the bit density of 7nm SRAM in the same area, in simulation. However, the return on investment falls off past seven or eight tiers because masks scale with layers. Nagare Labs’ claim of single lithography would potentially bypass this limitation.
That has not yet been proven, and nothing published yet shows it. “Where we are is literally lab prototypes,” Datta told The Register, adding that sampling of Z2RAM tiles is targeted within four years and production shipments, if they arrive, within the next decade. Yu told the outlet that no standard yet exists for integrating this kind of memory with an accelerator, which means Nagare might have to come up with the interface itself. Datta also mentioned reliability to the outlet, as single-electron effects can shift a cell’s threshold enough to upset the stored bit. It also remains to be seen if the tested three-transistor cells work sufficiently well as a two-transistor, single-shield product.
Even if Nagare clears those hurdles, a more important one lingers: It currently has no fab. The plan to scale depends on getting partners for fabrication as well as packaging. Nagare is reportedly looking for an R&D fab partner so it can scale beyond the university clean room. Perhaps the most similar type of memory-on-compute shipping today, and the one Datta cited to the outlet as a model for working with chipmakers, is AMD’s 3D V-Cache.
Z2RAM isn’t the first capacitorless memory to promise a 5x improvement over SRAM in density; it follows in the footsteps of Innovative Silicon’s Z-RAM from 20 years ago, a technology AMD licensed, though it was not pursued. A Georgia Tech paper due at IEDM in December covers a different device, a one-transistor, one-ferroelectric-transistor cell, aimed at the same gap between SRAM latency and DRAM density.
Gelsinger, previously CEO of Intel, which started as a memory company, phased out Optane, a low-latency non-volatile memory, in favor of CXL. Optane sought to bridge the gap between slower non-volatile storage, such as HDDs and standard SSDs, and DRAM. Now he sits on Nagare’s board, and Playground Global, where he is a general partner, led the startup’s $5 million round as Nagare searches for a solution to a different but related problem.
Nagare declined to share measured retention, latency, or energy figures. The founders’ boosted cell already holds data at 85°C longer than a cache needs, but until a fab-built, multi-layer Z2RAM stack is measured, retention above 95°C included, its headline numbers remain projections.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Massive wants to help small businesses turn Google searches into customers
articles.text:
For four years, Segun Olaiya worked in local search engine optimisation (SEO) in the United States, helping large operations, including AT&T and businesses in San Diego and Texas, improve their visibility in online searches.
But he observed that marketing technology largely catered to organisations with multiple locations, leaving smaller businesses overlooked.
“Most of this kind of industry, which is marketing technology, is usually focused around big organisations that have multiple locations across cities and states that want to be as visible as possible. But small businesses are not always really paid attention to,” Olaiya told TechCabal in an interview.
He began helping small business owners manually optimise their Google Business Profiles. Some reported receiving more calls from customers who found them through organic search rather than paid advertisements. “They were like, ‘Oh, now I get more calls,’” he recalled.
“Maybe I can actually just make this into a proper thing and then automate it,” Olaiya said.
That idea led to Massive in 2026, an AI-powered local SEO platform that helps businesses like restaurants, clinics, salons and home-service providers improve their visibility on Google. It combines automated optimisation with human account managers who monitor search rankings and review business profiles.
Why being on Google is not enough
Being listed on Google does not guarantee a business will appear prominently when potential customers search for its services. Google says local search results are mainly based on three factors: relevance, distance, and prominence.
Relevance measures how closely a business profile matches a search; distance considers how far the business is from the person searching. Prominence reflects how well-known it is online, including through customer reviews and links from other websites.
Olaiya says businesses can improve their visibility by ensuring their Google Business Profiles accurately describe their services, keeping their business information consistent across online platforms, and encouraging customers to leave reviews.
For many Nigerian microenterprises, establishing an online presence remains a challenge. A 2024 Research ICT Africa report, based on a survey of 718 Nigerian microenterprises, found that only 13% used the internet for business activities. Just 0.3% had their own websites, while 6.7% had a social media presence. The report also found that 37% lacked the digital skills to use the internet productively for their businesses.
Yet online search can be an important source of customers. A study commissioned by Google and conducted by Public First found that, on average, businesses surveyed in Nigeria reported that around 11% to 20% of their new customers found them through Google Search. The survey covered 140 business leaders from small, medium, and large online businesses.
For business owners already occupied with running their operations, keeping their online profiles competitive adds another responsibility. Olaiya says Google’s frequent changes to its local search priorities make it difficult for businesses to know what to update or improve.
“Typically, the problem is that Google usually changes the rules. More often than not, they usually change what they really care about,” he said.
He said many business owners lack the time to keep up with these changes and work out how to improve their visibility, so some outsource the task to specialists to focus on running their businesses.
He believes this makes services like Massive more appealing to businesses that would rather focus on their daily operations.
How Massive manages local search for businesses
Massive’s process begins with a free visibility scan on its website, TryMassive.ai. Business owners enter their business name and a search term potential customers might use, such as “barber near me.” The platform then generates a map showing where the business appears in Google Maps search results across the surrounding area.
Olaiya said the scan simulates searches from 49 points around a business by default, showing how its ranking changes depending on where a potential customer is searching.
He said the system uses Google data to estimate what someone searching from each location would see.
“The Massive system goes and simulates that search across, by default, 49 points in the city,” he said. “We simulate it as if somebody physically went to that physical location and then opened their phones and they search for that keyword.”
Businesses looking to assess a wider area can increase the number of points to 81 or 100. Massive also calculates an average ranking across the locations, giving business owners an overview of their visibility in the area.
Those who want to improve their rankings can subscribe to the platform and book a 30-minute call with a member of Massive’s team. During the call, an account manager reviews their existing results and business profile, discusses their goals and explains the changes Massive recommends. Olaiya describes the arrangement as a “done-for-you experience”, adding that “we literally do everything for you”.
The platform uses AI to analyse business profiles and identify areas for improvement. It reviews a business’s existing description and recommends changes that could help Google better understand its services and the customers it wants to reach.
“Once a business is imported to Massive, the system itself automatically reviews the existing description and then recommends the proper description,” Olaiya said.
Massive also checks for inconsistencies in a business’s online information, such as differences between the descriptions on its website and social media pages. For businesses without websites, Olaiya said the platform can automatically generate one using their business information and update it as changes are made. It also recommends changes to ensure that the business presents consistent information across its online platforms.
Some tasks run automatically without requiring the business owner or an account manager to intervene. When a customer leaves a Google review, Massive analyses it, considers the business’s services and communication style, and drafts a response. Olaiya said the system can then publish the response directly on Google without the business owner having to log in and reply.
However, account managers remain involved in reviewing recommendations and handling issues that require human judgement. Olaiya said some businesses upload images or other content that Google may not accept. When the system flags such material, an account manager can contact the business owner, explain the problem, and advise them on what to change.
“We believe that a person should talk to another person instead of us just running a system that AI is talking to the person,” he said.
Massive runs visibility scans every two weeks to track changes in a business’s rankings. If rankings do not improve after two weeks, Olaiya said the team changes its strategy. Subsequent scans can also reveal declines, allowing the team to identify changes that may have affected a business’s position and reverse them where necessary.
Olaiya said that after three to four months of optimisation, once a business’s profile is stable, the system becomes largely autonomous and continues monitoring its visibility with less direct intervention from the team.
Who Massive is building for
Massive targets businesses whose customers need to find them in a particular location. Olaiya identified four main categories.
The first is businesses with physical outlets, including restaurants, gyms, salons, spas, and law firms. The second is service-area businesses, such as electricians and lawn-care companies, which travel to customers rather than operate from a fixed location. The third is multi-location businesses that want customers searching for their services to find the outlet closest to them. The fourth is new businesses entering an established market and trying to attract local customers alongside existing competitors.
Olaiya said businesses in less populated areas could have an advantage because they face fewer competitors and can serve a wider area.
“For places that are not very dense, the businesses there who happen to find Massive, for example, are at a good advantage because they have fewer competitors and they can cover even a bigger area,” he said.
However, not every business needs local SEO. Olaiya said Massive is not designed for online-only businesses, software companies, newsrooms or blogs whose customers do not need to find a physical location or service provider nearby.
Massive earns revenue through monthly and annual subscriptions. Its website lists the service at ₦18,000 ($13.37) a month per business location, or ₦216,000 ($160.47) for a year. The subscription includes profile optimisation, weekly Google Business Profile updates, review management, map-rank tracking and a dedicated account manager. Businesses can also try the full service free for 14 days before subscribing. Olaiya said the company has more than 20 active customers.
Olaiya said many small businesses rely on social media to reach customers without fully exploring how Google Search can help them attract new ones. He
sees educating business owners about local SEO as an important part of growing Massive’s customer base.
“One of the things that can drive the product is to educate business owners to say, ‘ You need this,” he said. “We are currently bootstrapping, and it is quite limiting how far we can go in terms of reaching out to the business owners. But we are on it.”
Building Massive’s next phase
Massive is entering a market with established international platforms offering similar local SEO and location-marketing services. Olaiya identified Polish platform Localo, San Diego-based SOCi, a]nd New York-headquartered Yext as competitors.
He said Massive is cheaper than competitors outside Africa, which he believes allows it to serve African businesses and small businesses in other markets. Massive’s published monthly price is lower than Localo’s $49 Single Business plan, which falls to $39 per month with annual billing.
However, the two platforms offer different service models. Localo provides software tools for businesses to manage their own Google Business Profiles. Massive offers a done-for-you service with an account manager. SOCi and Yext do not display comparable prices on their enterprise pricing pages, instead directing prospective customers to request customised information or a demo.
However, the company still has to convince business owners that local search visibility is worth paying for and expand its reach beyond its current customer base. Olaiya said he wants Massive to demonstrate its value through the business decisions customers make after improving their visibility.
“Over the next year, I need to have at least 100 businesses who can attest to the fact that Massive has helped them expand their businesses,” he said.
For him, that would mean more than businesses appearing higher in Google Maps results. He wants customers to use the visibility insights to make decisions such as opening another outlet or moving into a new area. He said such expansion would show that Massive had made a significant impact on their businesses.

articles.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end.
In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch.
Solution overview
Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime.
Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this:
- The user signs in to the web front end, a backend for frontend (BFF), with OpenID Connect through the agent’s linked Okta app.
- For each request, the BFF exchanges the user’s ID token for an ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server, authenticated as the agent (RFC 8693 token exchange). Okta checks that the agent is active, that the user is assigned to it, and that an administrator connected it to the target authorization server for the requested scopes. The ID-JAG is single-use and expires in 5 minutes.
- The BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG as its bearer token. The runtime’s JWT authorizer accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent.
- The runtime gets a workload access token from AgentCore Identity that binds the agent’s workload identity to the user, and passes it to the agent code. This workload access token is an AWS-internal binding token: neither Okta nor the resource sees it, so it isn’t one of the three tokens.
- The agent asks AgentCore Identity for an access token. AgentCore Identity redeems the ID-JAG at the resource’s Okta custom authorization server with the JWT authorization grant (RFC 7523), authenticated as the agent. Okta returns a 5-minute access token that names both the user and the agent and carries the user’s groups.
- The agent calls the MCP servers with that token. The task manager checks that a registered agent obtained it, and that the user’s group and scope allow the tool.
Figure 2 shows the same request as a sequence, with the check that each party makes.
Prerequisites
To follow along, you need the following:
| Prerequisite | What we used | 
| An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock | US West (Oregon) | 
| An Okta org with Cross App Access for AI agents and API Access Management (custom authorization servers) | An Okta Integrator Free Plan org | 
| Python, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), boto3, the AgentCore CLI, and the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Python 3.11, AWS CLI version 2, boto3 1.43, AgentCore CLI 0.31.1, and AgentCore Python SDK 1.24.1 | 
| AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions | Permission to create AgentCore resources and IAM roles | 
The walkthrough takes about 1 hour. AgentCore charges for what you use. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.
The base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, and you can build the solution in this post on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.
Register the agent in Okta
Okta needs an authorization server for the resource, the agent, a connection between them, and a policy that admits the agent’s grant. Do all of these steps in the Okta Admin Console: registering the agent creates its linked app, so you don’t need an app integration wizard.
- Create a custom authorization server for the resource application with the audience api://task-manager and the custom scopes xaa:read and xaa:write. Request only the resource’s custom scopes: Okta rejects an ID-JAG request that includes OpenID Connect scopes such as openid or profile (invalid_scope), so a request needs at least one custom scope and no OpenID Connect scopes.
- Add a groups claim to its access tokens, filtered to groups that start with xaa-. This claim carries each user’s authority to the tools.
- In the Admin Console, go to Directory > AI Agents, choose Register AI agent and then Register manually, optionally assign an owner, and create a linked OpenID Connect app. On Client registration, choose Client secret, generate a secret, and then activate the agent. The agent and the app share one client ID, and that app must sign your users in: an ID token from another app fails the exchange with “the client application is not registered for delegation to this agent.”
- On the agent’s Resource connections tab, connect it to the authorization server, limited to the scopes it needs, as Figure 3 shows.
- Add an access policy rule to the custom authorization server that allows the agent’s JWT Bearer grant, with a 5-minute access token lifetime. Without the grant type, the second exchange fails with no_matching_policy, and the lifetime bounds how long a revoked delegation keeps working.
- Assign the users or groups who might act through the agent. They sign in through the linked app, so give it an app sign-in policy that admits them with the authenticators they’ve enrolled. In our sandbox org, the linked app had its own policy with a rule for the test group. For real users, apply your organization’s policy, including multifactor authentication.
Okta’s Cross App Access guide covers the console steps, and the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain scripts the authorization server and its JWT bearer policy. The BFF then requests the ID-JAG, authenticated as the agent:
The AWS sample 06-okta-xaa sends the same request in Python (agent/xaa_client.py). The BFF authenticates as the agent, so store the agent’s client secret in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in code or configuration files.
Set up AgentCore Identity
AgentCore Identity holds three things for this solution, and your agent code doesn’t see the client secret or call Okta’s token endpoint:
| Part of AgentCore Identity | What it holds | Who creates it | 
| Workload identity | The agent’s identity on AWS, bound to the signed-in user for each request | AgentCore runtime, for each agent runtime | 
| OAuth2 credential provider | The agent’s Okta client ID and secret, and the grant to use | You, once per Okta agent | 
| Token vault | The access tokens the provider obtains | AgentCore Identity | 
Create the credential provider
The credential provider performs the second exchange. Point it at the custom authorization server, authenticate it as the AI agent, and set the on-behalf-of grant to JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT, which AgentCore Identity sends as jwt-bearer with the ID-JAG as the assertion:
Okta binds both exchanges to the client named in the ID-JAG, so each Okta agent needs its own provider: when we redeemed one agent’s ID-JAG as another, Okta refused with “The ‘client_id’ in the JWT Bearer Grant must match the ‘client_id’ used to authenticate the client.” AgentCore Identity keeps the secret in a service-managed AWS Secrets Manager secret, which you rotate with update-oauth2-credential-provider. If your team already manages the client secret in Secrets Manager, you can reference that secret’s ARN instead. AgentCore Identity reads the client secret from it, so you can rotate the secret without updating the provider (see Reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secrets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity). To avoid a shared secret, authenticate with a private key instead. See Authenticate with Private Key JWT using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. Figure 4 shows the provider in the AgentCore console.
Use the workload identity that AgentCore runtime manages
AgentCore runtime creates and manages a workload identity for each agent runtime. When a request passes the runtime’s JWT authorizer, the runtime gets a workload access token for that workload identity and the inbound token’s issuer and subject, and passes it to your code. AgentCore Identity then uses the ID-JAG behind it as the assertion for the exchange.
The AgentCore Python SDK keeps the workload access token in BedrockAgentCoreContext, not in the request headers that your entrypoint receives. Our first version looked for it in the headers, found nothing, and fell back to its own GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT call with a second workload identity, on all 21 requests we checked. Read it from the context instead:
AgentCore Identity keeps the access token in its token vault for the rest of the request. Across 10 requests, the agent’s first call redeemed the ID-JAG in about half a second (see the latency table in Validate the results), and the second, for the other MCP server, returned the same token in a median of 58 milliseconds without redeeming the single-use ID-JAG again. A new ID-JAG for the same user got a new token, so each request reflects Okta’s latest decision. The sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain reads the workload access token the same way (agent/agent.py).
Scope the agent’s role to its workload identity and provider
AgentCore Identity doesn’t bind workload identities to credential providers in the same account. The agent’s IAM role does, so scope it to the agent’s own workload identity and provider, and to that provider’s secret:
Take the workload identity’s name from workloadIdentityDetails in GetAgentRuntime, and the provider’s ARN from credentialProviderArn: the segment is oauth2credentialprovider, and with the hyphenated form every call failed with AccessDeniedException. The role needs no GetWorkloadAccessToken permission, because the runtime gets that token, not the agent. Our tests passed with only these two statements.
Deploy the agent on AgentCore runtime
Configure the agent runtime’s inbound authorizer to accept only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, and its audience is the resource’s custom authorization server. In agentcore.json:
allowedClients matches the client_id claim that an ID-JAG carries. Without it, the runtime admitted another agent’s ID-JAG with HTTP 200 and the request failed later, at the exchange. With it, the runtime refused that token with HTTP 401.
Besides the policy from the previous section, the execution role needs bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream. It needs no bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime permission for the MCP servers: each runs on AgentCore runtime behind its own JWT authorizer, with the custom authorization server as issuer and api://task-manager as audience, so the agent calls it with the Okta access token as a bearer token, not with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4).
Enforce each user’s authority in the MCP server
The resource connection sets the scopes for every user of an agent, so all three test users received xaa:read xaa:write, and per-user authority travels in the groups claim instead: Alice’s token carried xaa-readers, Bob’s xaa-writers, and Carol’s had none.
The task manager checks two things: it accepts only tokens a registered agent obtained, and it allows a write only when the group and the scope are both present:
Both checks close gaps we found: a write check that allowed tokens without a groups claim let Carol, who belongs to neither group, create tasks, and before _require_agent a plain token-exchange token, issued to a service app with no act claim, created a task for Bob. The server can read the claims without verifying the token again only because the runtime’s JWT authorizer already verified it. A server without that authorizer in front of it must check the signature, issuer, audience, and expiry itself, as the Part 2 agent on Amazon EKS does.
Validate the results
We ran every check against the deployed solution. Alice, Bob, and Carol each asked the agent to create a task and then list the project’s tasks:
| Caller | create_task | list_tasks | 
| Alice | Denied: requires membership in xaa-writers | Allowed | 
| Bob | Created | Allowed | 
| Carol | Denied: no groups claim | Allowed | 
| Bob, then Alice right after him | Created for Bob, then denied for Alice: no authority carried over | Allowed | 
These requests stopped before tools ran:
| Request | Stopped by | Response | 
| Agent B’s ID-JAG sent to the task agent | The runtime’s JWT authorizer | 401: “Claim ‘client_id’ value mismatch with configuration.” | 
| An ID-JAG held for 245 seconds | The runtime’s JWT authorizer | 401: “Ineffectual token, will expire within the next minute” | 
| A malformed bearer token | The runtime’s JWT authorizer | 403: “Failed to parse token” | 
| One ID-JAG redeemed twice | Okta’s custom authorization server | 400: “The id-jag was already used.” | 
| A narrower scope at the second exchange | Okta’s custom authorization server | 400: “The scope parameter must exactly match the scopes in the id-jag.” | 
| A scope outside the connection | Okta’s org authorization server | 400 invalid_scope | 
| A plain token exchange token at the MCP server | The MCP server | Denied: only tokens that a registered AI agent obtained | 
The token that AgentCore Identity returned matched one we redeemed directly at Okta, claim for claim: sub was the user, cid and act named the agent, scp held the connection’s scopes, groups held the user’s groups, and it lived 300 seconds.
AgentCore Identity adds about 0.6 seconds to a request that takes about 30 seconds end to end, most of it model and tool calls. Medians of five runs from our test client:
| Call | Median | 
| Sign-in, scripted (authorization code flow) | 1,205 ms | 
| ID token to ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server | 216 ms | 
| GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT | 135 ms | 
| GetResourceOauth2Token, including Okta’s JWT bearer grant | 508 ms | 
Govern agents in operation
Okta evaluates the agent, the user, and the connection when it mints an ID-JAG. We measured what each administrator action does to the next request and to issued tokens:
| Admin action in Okta | New requests | Tokens already issued | 
| Delete the agent’s resource connection | Refused immediately ( invalid_target) | Work until they expire, up to 5 minutes | 
| Remove the user’s assignment | Refused within about 1 second, even with an ID token the user already held | Up to 5 minutes | 
| Deactivate the agent | Refused after Okta runs the operation, which our test org queued for 86 minutes | Up to 5 minutes | 
Actions on one agent left the other working. Okta doesn’t re-check the user when an ID-JAG is redeemed: its custom authorization server issued an access token 3 seconds after we removed a user, for an ID-JAG minted before the removal. Okta’s System Log records each grant with the agent as the actor, and Part 2 streams those events into CloudWatch.
Best practices for the delegation chain
Six practices came out of these measurements, each one a property of the chain rather than a preference:
| Practice | What we measured | 
| Mint a fresh ID-JAG for each request | An ID-JAG is single-use and lives 300 seconds. The runtime refuses one with under 60 seconds left, so 225 seconds worked, 245 didn’t | 
| Carry per-user authority in the groups claim, and request one scope set per request | Okta sets scopes from the resource connection, so all three users got the same scopes, and the second exchange must request exactly the ID-JAG’s | 
| Pin the agent at the runtime, and check act and cid in the tool | allowedClients matches the client_id claim an ID-JAG carries. Okta access tokens carry cid instead | 
| Reproduce a failed exchange directly against Okta | Through AgentCore Identity, a scope mismatch and a wrong client both surface as “Token exchange failed with HTTP status 400” | 
| Grant the agent’s role read access to the provider’s secret | GetResourceOauth2Token failed until the role could read it | 
| Keep lifetimes short, and use the resource connection as your kill switch | Deleting the connection took effect immediately. Deactivating the agent sat in Okta’s beta AI agent API queue for 86 minutes, with no cancel | 
Cross App Access compared with plain token exchange
Plain RFC 8693 token exchange also carries the user’s identity downstream. We compared it with XAA against the same Okta authorization server and user:
| Behavior we observed | Plain token exchange | Cross App Access | 
| Agent identity in the token | No act claim | act names the agent | 
| Scopes | Widened: Alice’s own token had xaa:read, and the exchange returned xaa:read xaa:write | The scopes the administrator approved | 
| Exchange rule limited to xaa-writers | Alice still received a token | Alice denied | 
| User unassigned, earlier token reused | Still exchanged | Refused | 
| What administrators see | A service app with a grant type | The agent, its connections, and the agent in each log event | 
These results reflect our Okta configuration. Okta’s guide shows an act claim for exchanged tokens, which we didn’t receive. Plain token exchange carried the user’s identity, but not the user’s authority.
Where this pattern applies
We work with media and entertainment companies, and this is where we met the problem first. A studio or streaming or games organization runs agents against production tracking, title and asset metadata, rights and localization, and viewer or player support. Each system has its own authorization model and its own auditors, and a user’s authority differs by title, territory, or release window, so “which agent might act for which user in which system” has to be answered before an agent ships.
Nothing in the chain is specific to that industry: the agent is an identity in your IdP, the target is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and the user’s authority rides in a claim. Financial services, healthcare, and public sector teams put different resources behind the same controls.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created:
- Delete the AWS CloudFormation stacks that the AgentCore CLI created for the agent and the two MCP servers.
- Delete the credential provider with aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-oauth2-credential-provider --name okta-xaa-obo, and any workload identity you created yourself with delete-workload-identity.
- Delete the IAM policies you added to the execution roles.
- In Okta, deactivate and delete the AI agent and its linked app, and remove the resource connection, the authorization server’s policy rule, scopes, and claim, and the test users and groups.
Conclusion
In this post, you used Okta Cross App Access to decide which agent might act for which user, and AgentCore Identity to carry out each decision. The runtime admitted only the agent’s own ID-JAGs, the credential provider redeemed each one with a secret the agent didn’t hold, the token vault reused the result within a request, and the MCP server enforced each user’s authority from the groups claim.
This design keeps the exchange in the agent’s role and repeats the authorization check in every MCP server. See Part 2 of this series to learn why its design moves both behind one AgentCore Gateway with Cedar policies, adds a second agent on Amazon EKS, and joins the Okta System Log with AgentCore traces in CloudWatch.
To get started, explore the AgentCore samples and Okta’s Cross App Access documentation. For the API details, see On-behalf-of token exchange in the AgentCore Developer Guide.

articles.title: « Être une femme, ça aide » : Sophie Adenot raconte comment son corps a vécu l'espace (en vidéo)
articles.text:
Lors d’une conférence de presse organisée par l’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA) ce lundi 2 novembre 2026, à laquelle Numerama assistait, l’astronaute française Sophie Adenot est revenue sur les effets de la microgravité sur son organisme.
L’astronaute de l’ESA a amerri le 8 octobre 2026 au large de la Californie, avec le reste de l’équipage Crew-12, au terme de sa mission à bord de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS). Au total, elle a vécu 237 jours dans l’espace (un record européen pour un vol unique). Elle a ensuite passé 3 semaines en réadaptation au Centre des astronautes européens de Cologne, en Allemagne, avant cette conférence de presse au siège parisien de l’ESA.
Elle a surtout décrit un corps qui s’est bien adapté à la vie en orbite, loin de l’image d’un organisme uniquement malmené par l’apesanteur. Pour en savoir plus sur son témoignage, vous pouvez regarder notre vidéo complète sur YouTube.
« Être dans l’espace pour le corps féminin, c’est quand même la panacée », selon Sophie Adenot
Sophie Adenot livre un témoignage qu’on entend rarement, le métier d’astronaute étant encore majoritairement exercé par des hommes : selon elle, le corps féminin se sent particulièrement bien dans l’ISS. Elle explique que les variations hormonales et biologiques régulières préparent en quelque sorte les femmes aux changements profonds d’environnement. Le cycle menstruel ou les grossesses habitueraient peut-être le corps à réagir à des stress extérieurs, avance-t-elle prudemment.
L’astronaute dresse un bilan enthousiaste de son séjour en orbite, où elle dit n’avoir ressenti ni jambes lourdes ni ballonnements. Selon elle, cette capacité d’adaptation du corps féminin rend l’arrivée en microgravité beaucoup plus douce. « Le corps féminin, il a l’habitude de s’adapter et de réagir à des stress extérieurs. »
Sophie Adenot compare volontiers ce voyage en orbite à son expérience de la maternité, deux moments qu’elle qualifie d’intimement « transformateurs ». Devenir mère lui a permis d’aborder sa mission spatiale avec un grand apaisement et une authenticité renforcée. Cette sérénité l’accompagne aujourd’hui, alors que sa mission court officiellement jusqu’en avril 2027 : même de retour sur Terre, Sophie Adenot a tout un protocole à respecter.
Le défi physique des scaphandres inadaptés
Tout n’est pas simple pour autant. Les sorties extravéhiculaires, notamment, sont physiquement très éprouvantes. Sophie Adenot le sait bien, elle qui s’est aventurée trois fois hors de l’ISS en 14 jours, pour un total de 19 heures et 42 minutes passées dans le vide. La Française n’a pas caché l’exigence extrême de ces opérations, confiant récemment que rien que de tenir un stylo est douloureux après cet effort.
Pour tenir le choc, l’entraînement physique est indispensable, d’autant que le scaphandre actuel est, de son propre aveu, mal adapté à la morphologie féminine. « Pour l’instant, on a un scaphandre qui est pas vraiment adapté à la morphologie féminine, mais ce n’est pas grave, c’est pas impossible d’y arriver non plus. » Pour compenser l’ergonomie rigide des combinaisons spatiales actuelles, l’astronaute a dû redoubler d’efforts en amont : « C’est aussi pour ça que j’ai fait autant de sport, pour avoir des gros biceps ! »
Au-delà de la performance physique et scientifique, Sophie Adenot revendique une approche décomplexée et globale de son identité, refusant de s’enfermer dans un rôle unique : « Ce qui compte, c’est d’être authentique. Je suis une femme, je suis une maman, je suis une astronaute, je suis une pilote, je suis une machine quand je suis sur la machine de muscu… C’est important de pouvoir honorer toutes ces facettes et de les accepter. »
Alors que les futurs scaphandres sont déjà en développement pour les missions lunaires du programme Artemis, le témoignage de l’astronaute française rappelle que ces combinaisons devront aussi convenir aux femmes. La question reste sensible pour la Nasa, qui n’a retenu aucune femme dans l’équipage d’Artemis III, mission prévue en 2027, tout en promettant d’envoyer la première femme sur la Lune dans le cadre du programme.

articles.title: Noch Super-Nintendo-Spiele im Schrank? Dann ist dieses Gadget für euch
articles.text:
Ohne alte Konsole und Kabelsalat: So bringst du deine originalen SNES-Module auf moderne Bildschirme
So eine Retro-Spielesammlung kann auch ziemlich lästig sein. Nur mit teils umständlichen Stecksystemen oder kostspieligen Konvertern lassen sich die alten Konsolen noch an moderne Fernseher oder Monitore anschließen. Und dann stehen die klobigen Kisten auch gerne mal im Weg herum – wenn sie denn noch funktionieren.
Wer aber dennoch den Charme von alten Cartridges mag, womöglich sogar noch ein paar Spiele für das Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) herumliegen hat, sollte einen Blick auf den SN Operator von Epilogue werfen. Der kann sogar deutlich mehr, als nur alte SNES-Games abzuspielen.
Alte Spiele auf modernen Rechnern
Bereits seit 2021 bietet Epilogue mit dem GB Operator eine Möglichkeit an, physische Spiele für Gameboy und Gameboy Advance auf Windows, macOS oder Linux zu spielen. Die Cartridges werden in das Gadget gesteckt, das wiederum per USB-C mit einem Rechner verbunden ist. Steuern könnt ihr die Games dann mit einem angeschlossenen Controller, oder einer Tastatur.
Doch das Gadget hat viele weitere nützliche Features, die auch im SN Operator enthalten sind. So könnt ihr etwa die Speicherstände eurer physischen SNES-Spiele (sowohl NTSC als auch PAL) digitalisieren und auf dem PC oder Mac speichern. Denn eine Schwachstelle der alten Cartridges sind oft die Batterien, die für die Sicherung der Speicherstände nötig sind.
Besonders für Sammler dürfte es interessant sein, dass der SN Operator auch gefälschte Spiele erkennen kann. Es kann schließlich immer wieder vorkommen, dass ihr gebrauchte Spiele auf einem Flohmarkt oder auf Ebay kauft – und gar nicht merkt, dass es sich nicht um Originale handelt. Schon der GB Operator hat eine Genauigkeit von 98,7 Prozent beim Erkennen von Fälschungen versprochen.
SNES-Spiele mit Achievements
Eine weitere Funktion spricht derweil Gamer an, die Statistiken mögen, oder Wert auf kompetitives Spielen legen. Durch eine Integration der Online-Plattform Retroachievements ist es möglich, Achievements für eure physischen SNES-Spiele zu erhalten, Bestzeiten mit Freunden zu vergleichen oder euren Fortschritt festzuhalten – so wie es auf modernen Systemen längst der Fall ist.
Solltet ihr zudem zu den wenigen Personen gehören, die die Light Gun Super Scope oder die SNES Mouse besitzen, hat der SN Operator auch dafür eine Lösung. So könnt ihr einfach eure normale Maus für diese Steuerungsmethoden nutzen.
Der SN Operator kostet 71,39 US-Dollar, umgerechnet um die 62 Euro. Hinzu kommen etwa 10 Euro Versandkosten nach Deutschland.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 30.12.2025 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
articles.text:
SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth.
As part of its plans to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, SpaceX has inked a deal with Qualcomm, which will deploy its cellular technology across tens of thousands of 5G cell sites starting in 2027. SpaceX is also reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile, potentially allowing it to launch Starlink Mobile through the service. Another report suggests SpaceX may tap into 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out its network.
SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry. Tim Höttges, the CEO of T-Mobile’s parent company Deutsche Telekom, said he takes SpaceX’s plans “super serious” but that it could cost Musk more than $200 billion to pull off.
Follow along for the latest updates on Starlink’s major mobile carrier ambitions.
- Pinned SpaceX’s ambitious, pricey gamble to replace AT&T and Verizon Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier. Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.” Read Article >
- What will it take for SpaceX to launch its “major” mobile network? Bloomberg has a breakdown of how Starlink Mobile will operate — and what SpaceX still needs to do to get its hybrid 5G network up and running.
- SpaceX is working with Qualcomm to build its Starlink Mobile 5G network SpaceX is teaming up with Qualcomm to build out its nationwide mobile network. Under the multi-year deal, SpaceX will bring Qualcomm’s Dragonwing technology to “tens of thousands” of 5G cell sites across the US, with the first deployments set for 2027. The news of the partnership comes as part of SpaceX’s push to make Starlink Mobile a “major” carrier in the US, competing directly with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The Elon Musk-owned company has already snapped up a swath of spectrum, while recent reports suggested that SpaceX was exploring an acquisition of Boost Mobile. Read Article >
- SpaceX could buy Boost Mobile as part of its big mobile carrier plans SpaceX has discussed a deal with Boost Mobile to launch its own service through the budget-friendly carrier, according to a report from The Washington Post. The deal, which comes as SpaceX aims to make Starlink a “major” mobile carrier, reportedly involves the Elon Musk-owned company acquiring Boost Mobile or accessing its network. Musk discussed the potential agreement with Charlie Ergen, chairman of Boost Mobile parent company EchoStar, last month, as reported by The Washington Post. Boost Mobile’s network is currently powered by T-Mobile and AT&T, meaning SpaceX may need permission from the two carriers to launch its service. Read Article >
- SpaceX’s mobile carrier push reportedly involves tapping into 80,000 cell sites SpaceX plans to access at least 80,000 cell sites as part of efforts to compete directly with Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T, according to a report from Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that SpaceX is in talks with Crown Castle Inc., one of the nation’s largest cell tower owners. The move would give SpaceX access to half of the 158,500 cell towers currently operational in the US, according to Reuters. When asked about a potential partnership with SpaceX, Amazon, or other satellite services during an earnings call on Wednesday, Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant said, “I don’t think I want to get into customer-specific detail, but you can assume that we’re talking to all parties.” SpaceX plans to pair a network of cell towers with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites. Read Article >
- SpaceX announces plan to become a ‘major mobile carrier’ SpaceX has acquired a portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses — a move the company says “will pave the way” for its Starlink Mobile service to become a “major” US carrier. When the Federal Communications Commission signs off on the deal, SpaceX says it will deploy its new architecture that combines its satellite-to-mobile constellation with a terrestrial mobile network, directly competing with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The licenses include up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, which SpaceX says will allow Starlink Mobile’s signal to penetrate through walls and buildings. SpaceX previously acquired 2GHz spectrum from EchoStar as part of efforts to bolster its direct-to-device service. Read Article >
- SpaceX is coming for T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon SpaceX is preparing to build a terrestrial mobile network to “acquire quite a few” of the customers now subscribed to T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The message to compete head-to-head with the US carriers was delivered by SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and CEO Elon Musk during the Q&A section of the company’s first earnings call. “The spectrum that we purchased from EchoStar does have terrestrial components, so we definitely intend to build out the terrestrial component,” said Shotwell. “You will have not only the capacity from the satellites themselves, but you will have a buildout of the terrestrial, basically the hardware and systems necessary to make a true mobile service exactly what you want it to be.” Read Article >

articles.title: 'Gen Z uses AI the way their grandparents smoked': Students say they feel pressured to use AI, and many would ban it if they could
articles.text:
'Gen Z uses AI the way their grandparents smoked': Students say they feel pressured to use AI, and many would ban it if they could
Students are too dependent on AI
- 96% of college students now use AI, but half of them would ban it tomorrow
- Heavy users are more likely to feel schoolwork would become harder without it
- They're worried about cognitive decline, but more so about AI's environmental damage
New research has likened the relationship between Gen Z and AI use to that of previous generations with smoking cigarettes, characterizing it as widespread adoption, awareness of the negative consequences and a reluctance to give it up.
The study from Fizz found nearly all (96%) college students now use AI, but more than half (56%) would permanently ban the technology.
But although one in two would support banning AI, Fizz shows just how reliant students have become on it, with the proportion of learners believing their work would become much harder rising significantly among frequent AI users.
Students have become reliant on AI despite its potential consequences
"The heaviest users are hooked," Fizz declared, noting that 68% of students who use AI multiple times a day believe schoolwork would become harder without AI. This proportion falls to 59% among daily users, 42% among weekly users, 22% among users who use AI just a few times a month, and 9% among those who use it less than once monthly.
Fizz also warns that the effects have having a much broader reach than just homework, with 43% of heavy users agreeing preparing for their career would also be harder without AI. Two in five even worry their daily lives would be more difficult.
This could be because students still recognize that traditional skills and qualities are still in big demand – 27% put communication and people skills as their priority, indirectly implying that their AI use could actually be harming those.
A staggering majority (86%) of daily AI users admit to having used it for something they would previously have discussed with another person, like career or life advice (51%), personal problems (48%) and even deciding how to reply to a message (45%).

The report claims that nearly half of the heaviest AI users feel under pressure to use the technology because they fear falling behind in the employment market, despite acknowledging that it could also be harming their ability to succeed in employment.
But it might not be entirely their fault, because nearly two-thirds (64%) of the surveyed students said they feel at least some pressure from teachers or educational institutions to adopt AI.
They may be addicted, but they want it gone
As many as one in two (56%) students said they would ban AI tomorrow if they could, hinting at a broad recognition that it's impacting much more than just their education.
But cognitive decline and dependence (28%) actually came in second place, behind worries of environmental damage (35%).
It could just be that many students' dependence has now made them unable to give up AI, even though they have worries about its negative impacts.
"They reach for it when they're anxious or alone... And almost nobody believes it's actually making them better," the paper concludes. "Silicon Valley believes it handed Gen Z a superpower. Gen Z would hand it back tomorrow, as long as everyone else did too."

articles.title: Deepinder Goyal hits back at doctors, defends wearable device Temple
articles.text:
Deepinder Goyal hits back at doctors, defends wearable device Temple
In a post on X, Goyal said $30 million was invested in building the device, of which he put in $20 million of his personal money.
Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Describing Temple as “an ambitious project”, Goyal gave a detailed explanation on what the team is building.
“The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. And we will,” he wrote on Friday. He also later added that the first 10,000 orders will not have to pay a subscription to use Temple.
Criticising the doctors, he said, "All my emotion last night was directed at a few influencer doctors, who are more influencers than doctors. They did not read our research in detail, and spread twisted facts to call something new a scam. They get views by piling on us."
The open debate started on Thursday when Goyal took to X to defend the device. He said, “First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple.”
He also said the device features a 14-day no-question return policy. “If the product doesn't work, it fails out of the gate and the company dies before recovering a tenth of its R&D," he said.
Goyal is currently Vice Chairman and Non-Executive Director of Eternal (parent company of Zomato). He is also the founder of healthtech wearable startup Temple and LAT Aerospace.
In the post, Goyal highlighted that $30 million was invested in building the device, including $20 million of his personal money.
Calling this his purpose, he said it's not about the money. “I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck.”
Goyal argued that most wearable companies start with internal studies. He referred to Whoop which shipped its fitness band in 2015 but the first published validation happened a few years later. He also added that Temple had a higher standard. "Pre-prints are a step prior to peer reviewed publications, and they are coming up."
Reposing confidence in the product, he said, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.”
Moreover, he added that this device is a fitness tracker, and wellness device, not a medical device. “If at some point, we clinically validate any of our metrics, we will let you know.”
However, some doctors were not convinced by Goyal’s response.
Responding to Goyal's claim on showing scientific evidence, an X user, who goes by the handle TheLiverdoc, said the Apple Watch Series 11 and Fitbit Sense had shown clinical evidence before launch. Similarly, Samsung Galaxy Watch8 and Watch9 also passed FDA trials prior to release.
"Meanwhile, the Oura Ring 4 and Whoop 4.0 launched as wellness trackers backed by peer-reviewed sleep studies."
On X, Dr Rishabh Jain responded saying Goyal shared financial and personal sacrifices but no scientific evidence. "Stop calling legitimate scientific scrutiny 'rage'. You have responded to questions about medical accuracy with investment figures, return policies, personal reputation, and promises of future studies. None of these constitutes scientific validation.”
Criticising the return policy he said, "Subjective satisfaction cannot establish medical accuracy.”
Dr Jain further said that doctors are not against innovation. However the evidence needs to show it. "If Temple delivers what it promises, doctors will be among its biggest supporters."
He also said that science is not a popularity contest, and criticism is not “rage".
Dr Jain also asked for data that can be reviewed by independent researchers.
Temple is a wearable device that tracks blood flow and oxygenation inside the brain. Goyal has not disclosed the price of the device.
In May this year, Goyal announced that the first 100 devices were ready to ship to select founding users and was aimed at athletes, scientists, doctors, founders, creators, and others who could provide feedback on the device. Pre-orders for Temple officially opened in India earlier this month.
In February this year, Temple raised $54 million in its first funding round from friends and family investors, at a valuation of about $190 million.

articles.title: Cómo recuperar fotos eliminadas del celular: paso a paso para rescatar las imágenes en Android, iPhone y Google Fotos
articles.text:
Eliminar una fotografía por error puede convertirse en un problema cuando se trata de un recuerdo importante o de una imagen que no está guardada en otro dispositivo. Sin embargo, antes de recurrir a aplicaciones de recuperación o pagar por programas especializados, existe una alternativa gratuita: revisar la papelera del celular o del servicio de almacenamiento donde estaba guardado el archivo.
Tanto Android como iPhone cuentan con herramientas para recuperar fotografías eliminadas recientemente. Google Fotos, por ejemplo, conserva temporalmente las imágenes borradas y permite restaurarlas desde el teléfono o una computadora. Apple también ofrece una función similar dentro de su aplicación Fotos.
El tiempo disponible para recuperar los archivos depende del servicio utilizado. En Google Fotos, los elementos respaldados permanecen en la papelera durante 60 días, mientras que aquellos que no tienen copia de seguridad se conservan durante 30 días. En el iPhone, las fotografías eliminadas permanecen disponibles durante 30 días antes de borrarse definitivamente.
Por eso, si una imagen desapareció de la galería, conviene revisar estas opciones cuanto antes.
Cómo recuperar fotos borradas en Android con Google Fotos
Google Fotos es una de las herramientas más utilizadas para almacenar imágenes y vídeos en teléfonos Android. La aplicación incorpora una papelera que permite recuperar archivos eliminados mientras permanezcan dentro del periodo de conservación.
Para restaurar una fotografía, sigue estos pasos:
- Abre la aplicación Google Fotos en el celular.
- Pulsa la opción Colecciones, ubicada en la parte inferior de la pantalla.
- Ingresa en el apartado Papelera.
- Busca la fotografía o el vídeo que deseas recuperar.
- Mantén presionado el archivo seleccionado.
- Pulsa Restaurar.
Una vez completado el procedimiento, la imagen volverá a aparecer en la biblioteca de Google Fotos y, cuando corresponda, en los álbumes donde estaba guardada.
Es importante comprobar si la fotografía tiene una copia de seguridad, ya que el tiempo de permanencia en la papelera cambia según esta condición. Si el archivo fue eliminado definitivamente o la papelera fue vaciada, no será posible recuperarlo mediante esta herramienta.
Cómo recuperar fotos eliminadas en un iPhone
Los teléfonos de Apple también cuentan con una función para rescatar imágenes borradas por accidente. La aplicación Fotos incorpora un álbum llamado Eliminado recientemente, donde permanecen las fotografías y los vídeos durante 30 días.
Para utilizar esta opción:
- Abre la aplicación Fotos del iPhone.
- Ingresa en Colecciones.
- Desplázate hasta el apartado Utilidades.
- Selecciona Eliminado recientemente o Eliminados, según la versión de iOS.
- Desbloquea el álbum mediante Face ID, Touch ID o el código del dispositivo.
- Selecciona la fotografía que deseas recuperar.
- Pulsa Recuperar.
También es posible seleccionar varias imágenes para restaurarlas al mismo tiempo. Después de confirmar la operación, los archivos volverán a aparecer en la fototeca.
Si la fotografía ya superó los 30 días o fue eliminada manualmente de este álbum, Apple no ofrece una opción para restaurarla desde la aplicación Fotos.
Cómo recuperar fotos borradas de Google Fotos desde una computadora
Otra alternativa consiste en utilizar una computadora para acceder a la papelera de Google Fotos. Este procedimiento puede ser útil cuando el usuario perdió su teléfono, cambió de dispositivo o no puede ingresar a la aplicación móvil.
Para hacerlo, es necesario seguir estos pasos:
- Ingresa a la página web de Google Fotos.
- Inicia sesión con la misma cuenta de Google utilizada en el celular.
- Abre el apartado Papelera.
- Localiza la fotografía que deseas recuperar.
- Selecciona el archivo y pulsa Restaurar.
La imagen volverá a estar disponible en la biblioteca de esa cuenta. Si el usuario tiene varias direcciones de correo electrónico, también conviene revisar cada una, porque algunas fotografías pueden estar almacenadas en una cuenta diferente.
¿Es posible recuperar fotos eliminadas definitivamente?
No existe una herramienta gratuita que garantice recuperar cualquier fotografía borrada de manera permanente. Cuando un archivo desaparece de la papelera de Google Fotos o del álbum de eliminados del iPhone, las opciones de restauración de esos servicios dejan de estar disponibles.
En estos casos, todavía es posible comprobar si existe una copia en otros lugares, como una computadora, un disco externo, una tarjeta de memoria o algún servicio de almacenamiento en la nube.
También hay aplicaciones de terceros que prometen recuperar imágenes eliminadas, pero sus resultados dependen del dispositivo, del tipo de almacenamiento y de las condiciones en las que se borró el archivo. Algunas, además, solicitan permisos para acceder a información personal o exigen un pago antes de mostrar los resultados.
Por eso, conviene desconfiar de los programas que aseguran recuperar el 100 % de las fotografías. La alternativa más segura es revisar primero las papeleras de Android, iPhone y Google Fotos, y mantener copias de seguridad para evitar perder imágenes importantes en el futuro.

articles.title: D-Link warns of multiple zero-days in DGS-3130 Series switches
articles.text:
D-Link shared mitigation measures for multiple unpatched security flaws affecting DGS-3130 series managed Gigabit stackable switches.
These switch models provide multi-gigabit uplinks, allowing enterprise network administrators to eliminate data bottlenecks, and are designed primarily for small-to-medium businesses (SMBs) and metro Ethernet deployments.
While D-Link didn't share details on these flaws and has yet to publicly disclose the CVE IDs for easier tracking, it said Spectrum Community Solutions network engineer Giresh Kumar Enugu found the bugs in the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) authentication, access control, and information handling.
Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service disruptions and device resets.
The zero-days affect multiple DGS-3130-30TS firmware versions, and the company is still investigating the impact on other D-Link switching platforms and firmware security mechanisms (including SSH service security configuration, safeguards underlying operating-system credentials, and handles firmware encryption/embedded cryptographic keys).
"The reported vulnerabilities involve the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) and certain components of the device's firmware security architecture," D-Link said.
"According to the security researcher, successful exploitation of certain vulnerabilities may allow an attacker with access to the affected network to obtain sensitive device information, perform unauthorized administrative operations, modify device configuration, or disrupt network services."
Until it releases new firmware to address these flaws, D-Link asked admins to disable DDP to remove the primary known attack vector, remove unnecessary or default SNMP community strings, and restrict SSH, web UI, and SNMP accessibility solely to isolated management networks and designated admin hosts.
D-Link also advised admins to maintain offline switch configuration backups and track device logs for unexpected configuration changes, unprompted reboots, or factory resets.
In September, D-Link warned customers of a maximum-severity zero-day (tracked as CVE-2026-86296) with a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit and no patch, affecting legacy DIR-822A dual-band Wi-Fi routers.
