Les aspirateurs balais, traîneaux, nettoyeurs de sol et aspirateur robot Dyson profitent actuellement de belles réductions grâce au code promo exclusif LESNUMS10. Plusieurs modèles sont concernés parmi lesquels le V12 Detect Slim, le Cinetic Big Ball Mult Floor 2, le V8 Cyclone et le Spot+Scrub AI.
Le Black Friday est l'occasion de prendre soin de son logement en renouvelant certains équipements du quotidien. Et si vous envisagiez de jeter votre dévolu sur un appareil Dyson, c'est peut-être le bon moment pour regarder les offres de plus près. En effet, le fabricant propose une offre de réduction réservée aux lecteurs des Numériques via le code promotionnel LESNUMS10.
Ce dernier, à utiliser directement sur le site internet de la boutique officielle de la marque jusqu'au 30 novembre, offre jusqu'à 10 % de remise supplémentaire sur de nombreux produits dont le Dyson V12 Detect Slim, le Dyson V8 Cyclone, le Dyson Cinetic Big Ball Absolute 2 et le Dyson Spot+Scrub AI. Une belle occasion de s'offrir un appareil Dyson à prix réduit sans attendre les prochaines démarques.
Dyson V12 Detect Slim Absolute
Points forts
- Estimation de l'autonomie à la minute près.
- Efficace sur tous types de sols.
- Filtration parfaite.
- Entretien simplissime.
Points faibles
- Emplacement du bouton marche/arrêt.
- Autonomie encore trop juste.
Proposé à 379 euros, l'aspirateur balai Dyson V12 Detect Slim reprend une bonne partie de la recette du V11 tout en misant sur un format plus léger et compact. Efficace en aspiration sur tous les types de sols, il assure également une filtration exemplaire ainsi qu'un entretien particulièrement simple. Son poids contenu améliore également le confort d'utilisation.
Dyson Cinetic Big Ball Absolute 2
Points forts
- Entretien quasiment inexistant.
- Vidange très simple.
- Maniable.
- Compact.
- Livré avec une pléthore d'accessoires.
- Bonnes performances d'aspiration sur tous les sols.
Points faibles
- Bruyant.
- Collecteur assez petit.
Le Dyson Cinetic Big Ball Absolute 2 mise sur une conception éprouvée pour offrir une aspiration efficace au quotidien. Cet aspirateur-traîneau sans sac se distingue notamment par sa technologie Cinetic qui permet d'éviter d'avoir à laver ou remplacer les filtres. Une fonctionnalité qui simplifie considérablement son entretien.
S'il inclut un collecteur assez modeste, ce modèle assure de solides performances d'aspiration et se révèle particulièrement pratique à utiliser sur la durée. Une solution intéressante pour celles et ceux qui préfèrent un aspirateur-traîneau classique aux modèles balais, d'autant qu'il est livré avec de nombreux accessoires.
Dyson V8 Cyclone
Points forts
- Belles performances d'aspiration.
- Entretien facile.
- Relativement discret, aussi bien visuellement qu'acoustiquement.
Points faibles
- Autonomie trop faible à la puissance turbo.
- Extraction de la brosse pénible.
- Manque d'astuces pratiques (pas d'indicateur d'autonomie, de rampe de leds…).
Avec le V8 Cyclone, Dyson propose un aspirateur-balai qui va à l'essentiel sans négliger l'efficacité. Son moteur assure un nettoyage soigné sur les différents revêtements, tandis que sa conception facilite le passage d'une pièce à l'autre et le nettoyage des zones difficiles d'accès. On apprécie également la simplicité de son entretien et sa filtration efficace qui retient les poussières dans le collecteur.
Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai
Points forts
- Navigation efficace.
- Opérations d'entretien simples.
- Filtre HEPA qui ne s'encrasse pas trop vite.
- Collecteur de la base sans sac.
Points faibles
- App moins riche que la concurrence.
- Encore un peu tendre avec certaines taches.
- Aire de stationnement toujours sale.
L'aspirateur robot Dyson Spot+Scrub AI combine aspiration et lavage pour simplifier l'entretien quotidien des sols. Il effectue les deux actions en un seul passage, repère automatiquement les saletés grâce à sa caméra intelligente et les frotte à l'aide de son rouleau motorisé.
L'appareil navigue facilement dans la maison, contourne les obstacles sur son chemin et nettoie chaque recoin. De plus, sa station de vidange sans sac jetable évite l'achat régulier de consommables. C'est une solution pratique pour garder des sols propres sans devoir passer l'aspirateur ni la serpillière soi-même.

articles.title: La pantalla sin recortes del iPhone 20 aniversario se complica porque el iPhone Duo muestra el precio de esconder la cámara
articles.text:
Para celebrar el décimo aniversario del iPhone en 2017, Apple lanzó un iPhone X que eliminó el botón 'Home' y dio paso a la pantalla de esquina a esquina. para el vigésimo aniversario el año que viene, los rumores y filtraciones apuntan a otro rediseño importante, con un iPhone 20, iPhone XX o como termine llamándose que llevará al límite esa promesa de "frontal todo pantalla". El problema es que habría que recortar en la calidad de la cámara selfie.
Y el iPhone Duo ya nos ha demostrado el precio de dichos recortes.
La filtración hasta ahora. Antes de nada, y como siempre decimos, se trata de una filtración, por lo que es posible que las cosas cambien. De hecho, lo que nos demuestra la última información es que uno de esos planes y objetivos de hacer un iPhone con un frontal totalmente limpio ya habría cambiado. Hasta ahora, lo que sabíamos apuntaba en esta dirección:
- Pantalla curvada por los cuatro lados con una curva suave, no los bordes pronunciados que Samsung usó durante años en algunos modelos de Galaxy.
- Marcos y traseras también curvados para mejorar el agarre, pero con menos metal que los modelos actuales.
- Trasera de cristal.
- Botones que serían hápticos para respetar ese diseño casi de "cápsula".
- Pantalla frontal sin Isla Dinámica y con todos los sistemas de Face ID y cámara frontal bajo el panel. Esto es lo que está en disputa.
Compromiso. Con el iPhone 18 Pro, Apple ya ha empezado a probar el esconder sistemas críticos de Face ID bajo el panel, pero también ha usado el iPhone Duo como banco de pruebas. La cámara de la pantalla interior está bajo el panel y, como vimos tanto en el análisis como en numerosas pruebas que han ido apareciendo estos días, la calidad deja bastante que desear.
Las cámaras bajo el panel no son algo nuevo y, de hecho, la compañía ZTE lleva generaciones probándolo en móviles como los Nubia. Visualmente son imponentes porque ese frontal totalmente limpio mola muchísimo, pero si te gusta hacerte selfies, tendrás que pasar por el aro de una calidad muy, muy justita. Ese compromiso en un móvil que no apunta a ser barato y, además, de una compañía como Apple que no quiere crisis reputacionales es algo que los de la manzana no estarían dispuestos a asumir.
A medias. Eso nos ha llevado a la última filtración que recoge 9to5Mac. No se sabe si la Isla Dinámica tendrá el mismo tamaño en el iPhone 20, pero sí que estará presente de un modo u otro porque se pueden esconder los elementos de Face ID, pero no la cámara si se quiere mantener la calidad fotográfica.
El resto del plan de diseño como ese cambio de material o la presencia de bordes curvados y una pantalla que se fundiría con ellos se mantendría, pero el frontal no sería tan "limpio" como se habría buscado en un principio. Simplemente, la tecnología aún no está lista.
Otra opción sería, directamente, volver al botón de desbloqueo capacitivo. Sería extremadamente raro para un iPhone "normal" dar un paso atrás de esa manera, ya que Face ID no sólo es cómodo, sino que se ha convertido en un estándar de seguridad del iPhone, pero en el caso de un modelo conmemorativo como el que se plantea, sería una posibilidad. El propio iPhone Duo carece de Face ID y apuesta por el botón lateral.
Camino por recorrer. De la manera que sea, ya decimos que es pronto y que todo esto se basa en filtraciones que beben de la producción inicial del modelo y de lo que comenta Mark Gurman. No tenemos nombre comercial, no sabemos si finalmente meterán los elementos de la Isla Dinámica bajo el panel o el salto en precio.
Pero en cuestión de horas hemos pasado de anticipar un iPhone todo pantalla de verdad... a un modelo que seguirá manteniendo las líneas de diseño de esas filtraciones, pero que no nos librará del recorte en la parte superior central. Una opción sería meter todo Face ID bajo el panel y dejar un único orificio en la parte superior para la cámara como hacen todas las demás marcas. Y no sé yo si Apple recurrirá a eso.

articles.title: GitHub Actions Lockfiles Reach GA to Secure Workflow Dependencies
articles.text:
GitHub has made workflow dependency lockfiles for GitHub Actions generally available on October 28, 2026, two weeks after the feature entered public preview. Workflows can maintain clear tag and branch references. The runner executes the specific commits listed in the .github/workflows/actions.lock file, even if those references change later. The feature is available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. The GA release includes the capabilities from the preview.
The change targets a long-standing weakness in how Actions resolves dependencies. A reference like actions/checkout@v4 or a branch name can change. This means a hacked action can add bad code to a pipeline without altering the repository using it. Teams can pin to full commit SHAs, but this reduces readability. It also leaves transitive dependencies, like those from composite actions, unpinned. Lockfiles address both gaps by recording commits for direct and transitive dependencies.
Tooling comes through the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI, hosted in the gh-actions-lock repository, which generates and maintains the lockfile. Adoption follows the workflow. Once a workflow is onboarded, every dependency needs a lockfile entry. The Actions runtime then runs the recorded commit, no matter where the tag or branch points. This lets teams migrate incrementally rather than converting an entire organization at once. The extension has a verification mode. It checks if the lockfile is up to date without changing any files. This way, it can act as a CI gate to spot differences between workflow files and the lockfile.
Dependabot integration addresses the usual cost of pinning, which is stale pins. When Dependabot opens a version update for an action in an onboarded workflow, it also updates the matching lockfile entry. Both changes appear in the same pull request, so the workflow reference and locked commit stay in sync. GitHub says this works without additional configuration. For governance, enterprise, organization, and repository admins can enable a "Require lockfile" policy. This policy helps enforce adoption at the relevant scope.
GitHub is explicit about the limits of the mechanism. A lockfile guarantees that runs use the commits you locked, but it does not determine whether those commits are safe, and the announcement advises reviewing dependencies before locking them. The security value therefore depends on the review that happens when an entry is created or updated. In practice, the Dependabot pull request becomes the review point, and teams that auto-merge those updates will carry any malicious change straight into the lockfile.
The release arrives as GitHub tightens other Actions defaults. A November 2 changelog entry announced that pull_request_target will be blocked by default starting December 2, another change aimed at limiting how untrusted code reaches privileged workflow contexts.
For teams evaluating adoption, setup instructions are in the GitHub Docs page on workflow dependency lockfiles. A reasonable starting point is to onboard a few high-privilege workflows, such as release or deployment pipelines, add the staleness check to CI, and confirm that Dependabot's combined pull requests fit existing review practices before enabling the enterprise-wide policy.
Competing platforms have not announced a native equivalent so far. GitLab's pipeline security guidance advises users to manually pin includes and components to commit SHAs. Users should also pin images to digests. After the March 2026 supply chain incidents, GitLab introduced open-source pipeline execution policies. These policies focus on blocking known attack patterns instead of creating a dependency manifest. Microsoft's Zero Trust guidance for Azure Pipelines also suggests using SHA pinning. It advises limiting Marketplace extensions too.
CircleCI orbs use a central semantic-versioning registry instead of commit hashes. This approach keeps the registry immutable. Teams on these platforms often use cross-platform tools. For example, they might use pinner to pin tags to SHAs and add a CI verification step. They may also rely on scanners like ActionSieve to flag unpinned references.
These tools pin the reference written in the pipeline file but do not resolve transitive dependencies, which is the gap GitHub's lockfile design addresses. As with GitHub's feature, none of them judges whether a pinned dependency is trustworthy, so the review step that precedes locking remains the control that matters.

articles.title: OpenAI Says New GPT-6 Cyber Model Hunts Flaws Without Crossing the Line
articles.text:
OpenAI on Thursday unveiled GPT-6 Cyber, a security model the company says is far more capable than its predecessor and more disciplined about respecting the limits researchers set for it.
On ExploitGym, which checks whether an AI can exploit a given flaw in a remote target, the new model achieved 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber.
OpenAI rated GPT-6 Cyber as Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, above the High designation given to GPT-5.6 Cyber.
In one alignment test, the model received an exploitation task alongside supporting services that were intentionally easy to hack but off-limits. Without deployment safety prompts, it refrained from exploiting them in 99.93% of cases, compared to 94.49% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. With the safety prompts, it never targeted the decoy services.
“This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately,” OpenAI said.
OpenAI researchers pointed the model at the Linux kernel, where it reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and built functional privilege escalation exploits for 948. GPT-5.6 Sol, tested with the same tooling, produced 166.
OpenAI has reported 304 critical issues to maintainers with proposed fixes.
In Firefox, the model documented 81 new flaws that Mozilla deemed high severity, backing each with evidence and reproducible tests. Mozilla has begun rolling out patches.
New protections include monitoring that checks whether the model’s actions line up with what a user is permitted to do, and safeguards meant to stop OpenAI’s models from aiding efforts to compromise industrial controls and other safety-critical systems.
OpenAI refined these safeguards using feedback from industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos, which tested Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab.
“The skill floor is dropping for the reconnaissance and vulnerability research needed before an attack,” said Dragos chief AI officer Rob T. Lee.
Access is currently limited to select approved customers of Daybreak Red, the part of OpenAI’s Daybreak program aimed at advanced exploit work and authorized testing. They can use GPT-6 Cyber through the API and Codex.
OpenAI plans to gradually open the model to all Daybreak Red customers, who are also getting GPT-5.6 Cyber. A dedicated Daybreak Red group for approved critical infrastructure defenders will permit sanctioned testing of critical systems.

articles.title: The Best GPU for Budget PCs: CPU/GPU Scaling Tested
articles.text:
If you're looking to upgrade the graphics card in a budget or older PC, buying a faster GPU doesn't necessarily mean you'll get better gaming performance. In fact, our testing shows that a Radeon RX 9060 XT can actually outperform the more powerful GeForce RTX 5070 when paired with a slower processor. It sounds counterintuitive, but there's a good reason for it.
Recently, we revisited Nvidia's CPU driver overhead issue and found that it can still be a problem for GeForce RTX 50 series GPUs. In that test, we compared the RTX 5070 Ti and Radeon RX 9070 XT using the Ryzen 5 5600, which admittedly is quite a slow CPU to pair with such expensive modern graphics cards.
However, as we've found in previous testing, this is an architectural issue that can affect GeForce GPUs beyond the RTX 5070 Ti. Logically, then, we should see similar behavior with something like the RTX 5060. But as they say, seeing is believing. Perhaps that's why some people dismissed our findings as a complete non-issue that wasn't worth investigating.
So this time, we're looking at more modest hardware configurations, focusing on the GeForce RTX 5060 and Radeon RX 9060 XT. We've also included the RTX 5070 to see how a more powerful GPU scales with slower processors.
It's entirely conceivable that those shopping for an RTX 5060 or RX 9060 XT have an older or lower-end PC, and right now isn't a great time to upgrade to the latest platforms using DDR5 memory.
One of the most popular budget CPUs of the last few years has been the Ryzen 5 5500, much to our frustration. It's a particularly poor choice, but at around $90, it seems buyers just can't resist.
We suspect most buyers see the Ryzen 5 5600 selling for around $150 and assume the $90 Ryzen 5 5500 is almost the same thing, just a bit slower. A 40% saving certainly sounds appealing. Unfortunately, despite the similar names, they're wildly different products.
AMD Ryzen 5 5600 vs. Ryzen 5 5500
|  | Ryzen 5 5600 | Ryzen 5 5500 | 
|---|---|---|
| Price (MSRP) | $200 | $160 | 
| Release Date | Apr 4, 2022 |  | 
| Cores / Threads | 6 / 12 |  | 
| Base Clock | 3.5 GHz | 3.6 GHz | 
| Boost Clock | 4.4 GHz | 4.2 GHz | 
| L3 Cache [Total] | 32 MB | 16 MB | 
| Box Cooler | AMD Wraith Stealth |  | 
| Chiplets | 1 x CCD, 1 x I/OD | N/A (monolithic) | 
| Core Config | 1 x 6 |  | 
| TDP | 65 W |  | 
Whatever the reason, the Ryzen 5 5500 has been selling like hotcakes for years, so there are plenty of them out there. That alone makes it worth including in our testing.
We have a good range of CPUs that should provide some interesting scaling data. The focus here is primarily on CPU performance, so this isn't an exhaustive CPU/GPU scaling benchmark across multiple resolutions. Instead, we're concentrating on 1080p testing to expose CPU limitations.
Then again, you could argue, and some certainly do, that 8GB GPUs like the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT are 1080p products anyway. We don't want to get too bogged down in the basics of CPU testing (again), so let's jump straight into the benchmark graphs.
Test System Specs
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D AMD Ryzen 7 7600 | MSI MAG X870E Tomahawk Max [BIOS 7E59v5A32] G.Skill Trident Z5 RGB 32GB DDR5-6000 CL30-38-38-96 | 
|  | AMD Ryzen 5 5600 AMD Ryzen 5 5500 | MSI MPG X570S Carbon MAX WiFi [BIOS 7D52v1D1] G.Skill Trident Z Neo RGB 32GB DDR4-3600 CL14-15-15-35 | 
| Graphics Card | GeForce RTX 5070, RTX 5060 & Radeon RX 9060 XT 8GB |  | 
| Power Supply | Kolink Regulator Gold ATX 3.0 1200W |  | 
| Storage | TeamGroup T-Force Cardea A440 M.2 PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD 4TB |  | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 26H2 |  | 
| Display Driver | Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver 621.01, AMD Radeon Adrenalin 26.10.2 WHQL |  | 
Benchmarks
War Thunder
Starting with War Thunder, it's clear that the RTX 5070 is substantially faster than the RX 9060 XT, as you'd expect. When paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, it was 35% faster on average, while even the standard RTX 5060 led the budget Radeon GPU by a 10% margin. Still, using the High Quality preset at 1080p, all three GPUs managed to push over 400 fps with the 9800X3D.
But when we step down to the Ryzen 5 7600, performance becomes much more CPU-limited, with all three GPUs delivering similar results. The RX 9060 XT was slightly faster than the RTX 5060, but Nvidia's additional CPU overhead isn't hurting the GeForce GPUs too much in this example.
Similar results were seen with the Ryzen 5 5600, but once we drop down to the 5500, the RX 9060 XT starts to enjoy a small performance advantage, beating the RTX 5060 by 8% and even the RTX 5070 by 5%.
So when heavily CPU-limited, the Radeon GPU does perform better, though only slightly in this example.
Marvel Rivals
The Marvel Rivals results are far more interesting. First, with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, we see that the RTX 5070 is massively faster than the RX 9060 XT, offering 42% more performance. However, the Radeon GPU manages to edge out the RTX 5060 by a slim 6% margin.
When we retest using the Ryzen 5 7600, not much changes between the RX 9060 XT and RTX 5060. In fact, the margin narrows slightly in favor of the GeForce GPU. However, the much faster RTX 5070 becomes considerably more CPU-limited, shrinking its lead over the Radeon GPU to just 23%.
Then, as we move to AM4 with the Ryzen 5 5600, the RX 9060 XT extends its lead over the RTX 5060 to 7%, while the increasingly CPU-limited RTX 5070 is now just 7% faster than the Radeon.
Up to this point, the data looks like a typical CPU bottleneck, but that starts to change with the Ryzen 5 5500. Using this low-end processor, the RX 9060 XT is now 20% faster than the RTX 5060 and, remarkably, 17% faster than the RTX 5070.
This unusual result highlights the impact of Nvidia's additional CPU overhead. Despite being a much faster GPU under normal circumstances, the RTX 5070 actually falls behind the budget Radeon when paired with a sufficiently slow processor.
Space Marine 2
Nvidia's CPU overhead issue is even more noticeable in Space Marine 2. When testing with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, everything looks pretty normal. The RTX 5070 is by far the fastest GPU tested, rendering 127 fps, making it 21% faster than the RTX 5060 and 31% faster than the RX 9060 XT.
But that all changes with the Ryzen 5 7600. Performance immediately becomes CPU-limited, and the RX 9060 XT is now 6% faster than the RTX 5060 when comparing average frame rates, and 10% faster for the 1% lows. It even manages to beat the RTX 5070.
As we continue to reduce CPU performance, those margins only grow. With the Ryzen 5 5600, the RX 9060 XT is now 15% faster than the RTX 5060, or nearly 20% faster when comparing 1% lows.
But we're not done yet. With the lowly Ryzen 5 5500, the margin balloons to 32%, with a 37% improvement in 1% lows. The RTX 5070 fares slightly better than the 5060, but even so, the RX 9060 XT is still 25% faster.
Hitman World of Assassination
Hitman World of Assassination also proved highly CPU-sensitive. With the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the RTX 5070 averaged 245 fps, with 1% lows of 128 fps. This represented a 33% advantage over the RX 9060 XT, which averaged 184 fps, while the RTX 5060 managed 181 fps.
Moving to the Ryzen 5 7600 saw the RTX 5070's average frame rate drop by 44% to just 136 fps, with 1% lows falling to 74 fps. Interestingly, the RX 9060 XT pulled slightly ahead at 138 fps, while also delivering stronger 1% lows of 77 fps.
This trend continued with the Ryzen 5 5600 and 5500, where the Radeon averaged 124 and 106 fps, respectively, outperforming the RTX 5070 by approximately 7-8% in both cases.
Battlefield 6
Battlefield 6 also revealed substantial CPU bottlenecks with the Ryzen 5 processors. Starting with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the RTX 5070 averaged an impressive 251 fps, making it 44% faster than the RTX 5060 and 48% faster than the RX 9060 XT.
However, moving to the Ryzen 5 7600 saw that advantage disappear almost entirely, with all three GPUs averaging between 167 and 169 fps. The 1% lows were noticeably better with the Radeon GPU, though.
Similar results were seen with the Ryzen 5 5600, where the RX 9060 XT edged ahead at 156 fps, compared to 151 fps for the RTX 5070.
Interestingly, with the Ryzen 5 5500, both GeForce GPUs delivered identical results, averaging 126 fps with 1% lows of 97 fps.
The RX 9060 XT, however, was noticeably faster, averaging 143 fps with 1% lows of 111 fps. That made it 13% faster in average frame rates and 14% faster for the 1% lows, another clear example of how Nvidia's additional CPU overhead can become a disadvantage when paired with a slower processor.
Horizon Zero Dawn
Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered gives us some interesting results that don't really highlight Nvidia's CPU overhead issue. Instead, they expose a VRAM-related problem, but only for the RTX 5060, despite both the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT having just 8GB of VRAM.
The problem for the RTX 5060 is that it features just a PCIe x8 interface, whereas the RX 9060 XT gets the full x16 bandwidth, effectively doubling the available bandwidth for transfers between the GPU and system memory. As a result, the Radeon was 27% faster with the 9800X3D, or a massive 47% faster when comparing 1% lows. That's despite the RTX 5070 beating the Radeon GPU by a 40% margin.
Dropping down to the Ryzen 5 7600 limits the RX 9060 XT more than the RTX 5060, though we're still using the same PCIe 5.0 interface and DDR5 memory.
But when we switch to the Ryzen 5 5600, we're now limited to PCIe 4.0 and DDR4 memory, and this cripples the RTX 5060. The result is particularly poor 1% lows, with the RX 9060 XT delivering up to 61% better performance.
Things get even worse for the budget GeForce GPU with the Ryzen 5 5500, which limits us to PCIe 3.0. Now the RX 9060 XT is more than twice as fast. The RTX 5060 was effectively unusable here, suffering constant stuttering and occasional pauses as data was transferred between video memory and system memory over the severely bandwidth-constrained PCIe connection.
Gears of War: E-Day
Gears of War: E-Day delivered some surprisingly consistent results, particularly with the Radeon RX 9060 XT. Regardless of whether it was paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Ryzen 5 7600, or Ryzen 5 5600, the Radeon averaged exactly 72 fps, dropping only slightly to 70 fps with the Ryzen 5 5500.
The RTX 5070 was considerably faster with the higher-end processors, averaging 97 fps with the 9800X3D and 96 fps with the Ryzen 5 7600.
However, its performance dropped to 79 fps with the Ryzen 5 5600 before falling to just 67 fps with the Ryzen 5 5500. This allowed the RX 9060 XT to pull ahead while also delivering stronger 1% lows of 53 fps compared with 45 fps, an 18% improvement. The Radeon also delivered 36% better 1% lows than the RTX 5060.
The RTX 5060 generally trailed both GPUs, although its results remained relatively consistent. Overall, the Radeon showed very little sensitivity to processor performance, while the RTX 5070 benefited noticeably from faster CPUs, as you'd expect at 1080p.
Hogwarts Legacy
Hogwarts Legacy showed some of the biggest performance differences between the processors, particularly with the RTX 5070. Paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the 12GB GeForce GPU averaged an impressive 133 fps, comfortably ahead of the RX 9060 XT at 103 fps and RTX 5060 at 99 fps.
However, things changed considerably with the Ryzen 5 7600, where the RTX 5070 dropped to just 76 fps. Interestingly, the RX 9060 XT managed 91 fps, giving it a comfortable 20% performance advantage despite being the slower GPU with the 9800X3D.
The Radeon maintained this lead with the Ryzen 5 5600, averaging 76 fps compared with 68 fps for the RTX 5070. That's a 12% performance advantage over the higher-end RTX 5070 and 17% over the RTX 5060.
Then, with the Ryzen 5 5500, both GeForce cards managed just 60 fps, while the Radeon delivered 73 fps alongside stronger 1% lows of 44 fps, making it up to 26% faster. Again, this strange data is entirely a result of Nvidia CPU overhead issue.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4
Modern Warfare 4 produced some interesting results, particularly for the Radeon RX 9060 XT. With the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the RTX 5070 comfortably led the pack, averaging 237 fps, followed by the RX 9060 XT at 195 fps and RTX 5060 at 173 fps.
The RTX 5070 maintained its lead with the Ryzen 5 7600, although the gap narrowed to just 16 fps as performance became much more CPU-limited.
Things became more interesting with the Ryzen 5 5600, where the RX 9060 XT actually pulled ahead, averaging 187 fps compared with 175 fps for the RTX 5070. It also delivered noticeably stronger 1% lows at 133 fps, making it up to 16% faster.
This trend continued with the Ryzen 5 5500, where the RX 9060 XT averaged 167 fps, comfortably ahead of both GeForce GPUs. But it was the 1% lows that really stood out, with the Radeon delivering at least 31% better performance.
Overall, the RX 9060 XT proved remarkably consistent across the different processors, while the GeForce GPUs suffered much larger performance losses as CPU performance decreased.
Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl
Finally, we have Stalker 2, and once again, the results are quite interesting. The RTX 5070 comfortably led when paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, averaging 120 fps compared with 86 fps for the RTX 5060 and 82 fps for the RX 9060 XT. So we're looking at a massive 46% advantage over the Radeon GPU.
Moving down to the Ryzen 5 7600, the RTX 5070 maintained a reasonable advantage at 102 fps, although the gap between all three graphics cards narrowed considerably with the Ryzen 5 5600. Here, they delivered between 75 and 78 fps, which looks very much like a typical CPU bottleneck.
However, when we reduce CPU performance further, the RX 9060 XT actually manages to pull ahead with the Ryzen 5 5500, averaging 73 fps compared with just 65 fps for the RTX 5070. It also delivers noticeably stronger 1% lows at 61 fps compared with 52 fps.
That's a 17% improvement in 1% lows and a 12% advantage in average frame rates. Once again, we're seeing a situation where Nvidia's additional CPU overhead allows the budget Radeon to outperform a considerably more powerful GeForce GPU.
10-Game Average
Looking at the 10-game average data, the results paint a pretty clear picture. First, as you'd expect, when not CPU-limited, the RTX 5070 is much faster than the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT, offering 36-39% more performance when paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D.
That margin is eroded to 16% over the RTX 5060 when paired with the Ryzen 5 7600, and just 7% when compared with the RX 9060 XT. This is what you'd expect to see, though, and the data is particularly relevant for those trying to maximize frame rates.
In games like Counter-Strike, Apex Legends, Valorant, and Fortnite, your CPU is often more important than your GPU, within reason, of course.
Something we noticed when comparing the Ryzen 5 7600 results with those of the 9800X3D is that the RX 9060 XT went from being just 2% faster than the RTX 5060 with the higher-end CPU to 8% faster with the Ryzen 5 processor. We also saw an even larger improvement in 1% lows.
This trend continued with the Ryzen 5 5600, where the RX 9060 XT was able to match the RTX 5070, making it up to 17% faster than the RTX 5060.
Then, with the Ryzen 5 5500, we run headfirst into Nvidia's CPU overhead issue. As we've said many times in the past, this really is a problem budget gamers need to be aware of.
Using this low-end processor, the RX 9060 XT was 36% faster than the RTX 5060 when comparing 1% lows, and 24% faster in average frame rates. That said, some of these results were skewed by the RTX 5060's limited PCIe bandwidth. However, even when comparing against the RTX 5070, we still find that the RX 9060 XT was 12% faster on average, or 14% faster when comparing 1% lows.
What We Learned: Older CPUs Change the GPU Equation
The main takeaway from all of this is that if you have a lower-end CPU that you're not ready to upgrade, you're generally better off pairing it with a Radeon GPU, such as the RX 9060 XT. It didn't take much of a reduction in CPU performance before the margins started to grow significantly in the Radeon GPU's favor.
For a typical GPU review, we'd normally aim to eliminate as many system limitations as possible, which means testing with a flagship processor such as the Ryzen 7 9800X3D. For the most part, this really is the best way to approach GPU testing, especially when comparing higher-end products like the RTX 5070.
Still, with the 9800X3D, we found the RX 9060 XT to be just 2% faster than the RTX 5060. That margin grew to 8% with the Ryzen 5 7600, which admittedly doesn't change a huge amount, but it does make the Radeon GPU more appealing.
Then, with the Ryzen 5 5600, the margin grew to 12%, a more statistically significant difference. Finally, with the Ryzen 5 5500, we were looking at a complete blowout, with the RX 9060 XT pulling ahead by a massive 24% margin. Again, though, some of that advantage was due to the 5500 being limited to PCIe 3.0.
It's worth noting that the Ryzen 5 5500 is roughly equivalent to the Ryzen 5 3600 in terms of performance, so it's not much slower than something like the Ryzen 7 3700X. This means AM4 owners with processors offering similar or lower performance will likely see better gaming results with a Radeon GPU, especially in scenarios where you're trying to maximize frame rates.
We should also clarify that this has nothing to do with AMD's Smart Access Memory technology, which is essentially Resizable BAR. That PCIe feature is unrelated to the behavior we're seeing here. Similar performance margins can also be observed when testing Intel CPUs of roughly equivalent performance.
We've seen some people claim that Nvidia's CPU overhead issue doesn't affect Intel processors. That's completely untrue, and we demonstrated this years ago. If you have an Intel CPU that delivers gaming performance similar to the Ryzen 5 5500, you're going to see comparable margins between the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT.
As for why we didn't include any Intel CPUs in this article, the reasons are simple: AMD has been crushing Intel in the retail CPU market for a while now, with Ryzen processors heavily outselling their Intel counterparts. As a result, a large portion of our audience is using Ryzen processors, so we're focusing on the hardware most relevant to those readers. Ideally, we would include even more data and Intel CPUs, but as it stands, adding more CPU models to the graphs would only clutter the results, making the data harder to digest without providing much additional insight.
Time is also a real factor. Each game required 36 benchmark passes to gather the data, and with 10 games, that's 360 benchmark passes in total. Adding more CPUs would only increase that workload, and as we've explained, without offering much additional value.
Bottom line, if you have an older system and want to upgrade its graphics card, a Radeon GPU is generally the better investment if your goal is to maximize frame rates. In some games, you could be looking at 20-30% better performance.

articles.title: It's a weird time to buy a laptop, but the new MacBook Pro doesn't skimp on quality
articles.text:
Let’s get that out there right away, because for a lot of people, it will be the only thing that matters. As with so many things in life, though, you get what you pay for. There’s no questioning the quality of the laptop’s display or most of its other hardware components.
But should you buy it? Well, that’s a complicated question in 2026.
We’re in a time of great uncertainty when it comes to buying a computer. Prices are at levels we’ve not seen in recent history, and they may well keep climbing. Meanwhile, users paying close attention to the early developments in both local and agentic artificial intelligence are asking an important question: “What will computing even look like in a few years, and what does that mean for the computer I should buy today?”
Apple’s new MacBook Pro sits at the intersection of all of this uncertainty. In multiple ways, it’s also straddling different worlds.
It arrives amid a changing of the guard in Apple’s leadership, potentially raising questions about the future direction of Apple’s ecosystem. It’s a mass-market consumer product, but configuring it with enough RAM and storage to make it feel future-proof pushes its price into territory mostly only well-funded businesses can afford. It’s firmly rooted in the computing paradigms of the past 20 years, but it shows early signs of flirtation with new AI workflows. It’s a conventional Apple laptop in most ways, but it also has a touchscreen—something that would never have happened in a prior Apple era.
It’s an outstanding, high-quality product, but whether it’s something you should buy depends on you—what you’re doing right now, what you’ll be doing in the future, and what you value.
Specifications and performance
For most of the specs we look at, Apple isn’t claiming any difference here. The new MacBook Pro promises 24 hours of battery life (though you’d have to use it in a conservative way to achieve that), it has the same ports (three Thunderbolt, one HDMI, one SDXC, and MagSafe), and it has the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity.
And like its immediate predecessor, it offers the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options. Running synthetic benchmarks, we found no meaningful difference at all compared to when we ran the same tests on the previous model, so we won’t spend time discussing their performance today. We’ve covered both thoroughly in prior reviews, and you can read up there if you’d like.
The chips are more than fast enough for normal workflows for the foreseeable future, including most 3D work. AI inference is the main area where they may be less future-proof. To be clear, they’re strong enough for now, but the field is evolving rapidly, and there’s reason to expect significant improvements in future chips on this front.
According to Bloomberg, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip that was introduced earlier this year to focus its attention on a significant rework for the M7 due in 2027. “The M7 line is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing,” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote. The line would emphasize memory bandwidth, which matters for fast, efficient AI inference.
Even without Bloomberg’s report, I’d expect Apple to prioritize those areas in its next high-end chip refresh. That’s partly because there’s another tea leaf to read here: Apple made just such an update with the A20 Pro, which debuted in its latest iPhones several weeks ago. That update brought a substantially improved Neural Engine and a significant increase in memory bandwidth. We also found that the A20 Pro delivered improved 3D graphics performance in some cases.
Similar improvements could come to Macs, meaning it might be worth waiting another year if you’re focused on AI workflows or even 3D applications—especially given the high cost of these machines. That’s part of what makes this such an uncertain time to buy a laptop. We’re in a moment when these companies are revisiting the architecture of these chips because of these new workflows, and we don’t know what the end result is yet.
A monster of a display
Here’s one thing that’s not at all uncertain: The display on the MacBook Pro is the best I have ever used in a laptop. If the display is your primary concern, this is a big moment.
Apple calls it a “tandem OLED display,” meaning a panel with two emissive layers. This approach helps achieve a higher peak brightness, but perhaps more importantly, it can reduce the risk of burn-in. Most of the time, the display won’t need both layers running at full power. Instead, they can share the load and run at a reduced current, helping extend the panel’s lifespan.
The new display can achieve up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness on HDR highlights, but it’s rated for 1,000 nits of sustained brightness. In general, I like the way Apple handles HDR for this at the OS level, too.
This photo doesn’t do the screen justice, but at least you can see the proportions and design here. (It’s the 16-inch model.)
Credit:
Samuel Aoxn
This photo doesn’t do the screen justice, but at least you can see the proportions and design here. (It’s the 16-inch model.)
Credit:
Samuel Aoxn
The brightness matters for HDR content, sure, but what really makes OLED stand out is per-pixel illumination—meaning each pixel can turn on or off independently. That allows for absolute black levels and very strong contrast. The MiniLED display in the previous MacBook Pro offered good contrast for an LCD display, but OLED has a fundamental advantage here, and it shows.
As you’d expect, the screen offers native support for both P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts. It also has a variable refresh rate from 10 to 120 Hz, just like many of Apple’s other products. As before, the MacBook Pro comes in roughly 14-inch (3,024×1,986 pixels) and 16-inch (3,472×2,226 pixels) variants. There’s also a nano-texture glass option to fight glare, though that will set you back another $150.
It’s one of the most impressive displays I’ve used in any device, and it’s certainly the best I’ve ever used on a laptop. The colors are vibrant, the contrast is outstanding, the blacks are inky, and it can get very bright when it needs to—not just with highlights but full-screen brightness as well. And on the whole, it’s extremely precise. Uniformity appears basically flawless. It’s what you’d expect from an ultra-high-end TV or reference monitor, not a laptop or computer screen, and it’s genuinely striking.
We’ll see about longevity, but OLED has come a long way in recent years, and my first impressions are that Apple has made all the right choices here.
I find myself trying to find something negative to say about the MacBook Pro’s screen to avoid sounding too effusive, but I can’t think of anything substantive. The best I can do is complain that Apple’s proprietary “PROLED XDR” label is silly and eye-roll-inducing.
Branding aside, the screen is the main reason to pay extra for this model.
Design
With its lid closed, the new MacBook Pro looks identical to its predecessor. The dimensions are largely the same. It’s slightly thinner, but you’d have to check the spec sheet or handle them side by side to notice.
Pick it up, though, and you’ll find that it’s noticeably lighter than the last model, by about half a pound. It’s not in a totally different weight class, but you can notice the change, and it’s a nice improvement. The reduction is partly due to the display technology switch; it’s easier to make a light OLED screen than a light MiniLED one.
Open the MacBook Pro and turn it on, and you’ll see one of a few other notable differences, depending on whether you’re behind or in front of it. From behind, you’ll see the Apple logo on the lid now lights up, as it did on MacBooks of yore. It’s arguably a little tacky, but it’s also neat and nostalgic. I don’t hate it.
The glow returns!
Credit:
Samuel Axon
The glow returns!
Credit:
Samuel Axon
From the front, you might notice that the already barely there bezels are even more barely there, though that’s subtle. More likely, you’ll see that the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by a cutout just like the Dynamic Island Apple introduced on the iPhone.
A comparatively sensible camera cutout
When I reviewed the first iPhone with a Dynamic Island, I was largely positive about it. No, it’s not ideal to have a cutout on the screen, but Apple has handled it as intelligently as possible, and I would even go so far as to say it has turned what should be an albatross into an attractive feature.
Thanks to the OLED display, it’s possible to make any of the pixels around the camera cutout just as black as it is. Apple has designed live activities, the volume bar, and more to appear as if they are expanding out of and around, and contracting back into, this little dot. It remains ingenious.
When the Dynamic Island first arrived on the iPhone, it helped unify several previously disparate approaches to displaying notifications in iOS, making it especially useful. This time, it doesn’t solve as many problems, but it’s an improvement over the dead weight of the notch. It also helps that the MacBook Pro’s much larger screen means the cutout takes up a small share of the screen’s real estate.
The Dynamic Island on the MacBook Pro.
Samuel Axon
The Dynamic Island on the MacBook Pro.
Samuel Axon
Full-screen apps cut off just below the Dynamic Island by default, just like with the notch before.
Samuel Axon
Full-screen apps cut off just below the Dynamic Island by default, just like with the notch before.
Samuel Axon
The Dynamic Island on the MacBook Pro.
Samuel Axon
Full-screen apps cut off just below the Dynamic Island by default, just like with the notch before.
Samuel Axon
The Dynamic Island works the same with full-screen apps as the notch did. By default, the top of the viewport ends just below the Dynamic Island, so it just looks like there’s a taller top bezel, and it doesn’t cut into the application interface. The menu bar, clock, and other system elements still occupy the space above the application (set against a totally black background) when you move the cursor up there.
I tested a few fullscreen games with it, like World of Warcraft and Cyberpunk 2077. Some behaved by default like the default fullscreen app behavior I just described, but others tried to occupy the whole thing, making the cutout visible. Vitally, every video app I tried avoided the cutout in fullscreen.
This isn’t something to upgrade for, of course. But on the whole, I think it’s an improvement over what we had before.
The most touchable MacBook Pro ever
Apple has finally added a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. I say “finally” because the possibility has floated around for about two decades. Steve Jobs was famously opposed to the idea; there’s even video of him explaining why he thought it would make for a poor user experience.
A couple of years ago, reliable reports emerged that Apple was moving forward with the idea regardless. When I first heard about it, I imagined what could be a really exciting implementation: a convertible laptop that would let you use it in a tablet-like mode, with Apple Pencil support for drawing and writing.
As a game developer, I imagined quickly sketching 2D game maps with an Apple Pencil, using a local AI model to convert them into 3D geometry, and then switching to a laptop configuration to start testing and coding. I also imagined using it like an iPad to more comfortably watch movies on a flight.
That’s not what we got, though. The laptop has the same form factor as the previous MacBook Pro model—no tablet mode or Pencil support. Instead, it just lets you reach up from the keyboard and trackpad to touch the screen. That feels like a missed opportunity.
Some creative apps have implemented touch features that might justify the touchscreen functionality if you use them a lot. For example, you can play the on-screen virtual piano keys on Logic Pro with multiple fingers, which could be nicer than clicking on them. I imagine many people already have workflows built around other approaches, though.
If you were specifically waiting for a touchscreen on your MacBook Pro, this seems like as good an implementation as you could hope for without turning the laptop into a convertible. Apple has put real care into it. For example, it has re-engineered the hinge so the screen is not particularly wobbly when you touch it. It’s fast, accurate, and responsive. It supports multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom or swiping with three fingers to switch desktop spaces.
There’s one use case I find compelling as a developer. Testing iPhone and iPad apps in the Simulator has always been a minor hassle because of the difference in input methods. You either have to approximate only a subset of the interactions available to users with a trackpad and mouse or connect an iPhone or iPad to test them that way. A touchscreen could provide a more elegant way to test such apps in Xcode, Unity, or whatever else you might use.
Unfortunately, some of the UI elements in macOS are too small for my large fingers, so I have to tap very carefully. I also keep forgetting the touchscreen is even there for hours at a time and go back to my normal habits, partly because there’s nothing you can do at the OS level that you can’t do just as easily with trackpad gestures. And as Jobs predicted all those years ago, my arm got tired while I was using it.
For me, it feels faster, easier, more comfortable, and more natural to use the keyboard and trackpad 100 percent of the time, but I admittedly have decades of muscle memory and habits built around them. There’s apparently a generation coming up with the same kind of familiarity with touch interfaces, so this feature may appeal to them. Plus, touchscreen laptops have been a thing on Windows forever, and some people seem to want to buy them, though I never quite got why without an added tablet configuration.
It’s unlikely to account for a big portion of the device’s cost compared with the rest of the OLED panel, memory, storage, and so on. So, my own bafflement aside, I’m not unhappy it’s here. I imagine it will serve those who want it well enough.
The same excellent workstation—if you can afford it
As noted earlier, whether this laptop is worthy of a recommendation depends on you and how you use your machine. That’s always been the case, but it seems more so here.
If you’re a creative professional or a display enthusiast who wants the best laptop screen you’ve likely ever seen, you won’t be disappointed if you shell out for it. And hey, maybe you can show me your workflow and prove me wrong about the touchscreen!
If you’re just looking for a great laptop with strong performance for everyday use, consider the non-OLED, non-touchscreen model that’s still in Apple’s lineup—or even a MacBook Air, which compromises relatively little for most users. And there is, of course, the entire world of Windows and Linux laptops.
If you’re a developer—especially one working at the frontier of AI workflows—well, that’s where things get tricky. Will waiting be worthwhile? So much about how those workflows will evolve and what they’ll demand from your hardware is still so up in the air that I can’t make a confident recommendation. (For what it’s worth, I fit best in this category, and I’m still holding onto my M1 Max machine, though my resolve is wavering.)
All that said, in most ways, this is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve reviewed again and again for the past few years. Touch adds a feature aimed at a particular niche, or perhaps it’s there to roll out the welcome mat for a newer generation. The display is a more substantial update and makes a compelling case for upgrading, especially if you’re coming from an older, pre-MiniLED laptop.
But this is an expensive machine. The configuration I reviewed here (16-inch, M5 Max, 128 GB of RAM, 2 TB SSD) retails for a whopping $7,399, though you could at least shave $1,600 off that by going to a more typical-for-most-people 64 GB. (The cheapest configuration starts at $2,899.)
For the vast majority of buyers, the pre-OLED version that’s still in Apple’s lineup or another MacBook altogether will offer more bang for your buck. If you’re the kind of person who wants OLED or a touchscreen, though, you probably know that already. Based on my time with the new MacBook Pro, both features deliver on their promises, even if the latter isn’t as ambitious as some of us had hoped.
The good
Outstanding display that offers notably better and more accurate image quality while modestly reducing the weight of the device
The M5 Pro and M5 Max are still plenty fast for the majority of users
Strong build quality, solid port selection, and everything else we had positive to say about the last MacBook Pro, too
The bad
For certain workflows, the M5 Pro and M5 Max are already a few months old in an environment where things are moving very quickly
The RAM and SSD price crunch is real, and these prices are a formidable barrier for most people
Samuel Axon is the editorial lead for tech and gaming coverage at Ars Technica. He covers physical and generative AI, large language models, software development, gaming, entertainment, and mixed reality. He has been writing about gaming and technology for nearly two decades at Engadget, PC World, Mashable, Vice, Polygon, Wired, and others. He previously ran a marketing and PR agency in the gaming industry, led editorial for the TV network CBS, and worked on social media marketing strategy for Samsung Mobile at the creative agency SPCSHP. He also is an independent software and game developer for iOS, Windows, and other platforms, and he is a graduate of DePaul University, where he studied interactive media and software development.
Hollywood video engineer here. What's important for the displays we use is that they are reference displays; they meet the intended spec (normally within <1 CIE ΔE2000), and are calibrated to both make sure they do, and to know that they do.
You could say the same about music recording studios: Why bother working with massively expensive, "perfect" speakers in a pristine acoustic environment, where nobody will be listening to the music this way?
It comes down to, there is no "representative" mediocre consumer display that would be worth working on: What's out there in the world varies massively by the monitor's technology, age, price level, and viewing (or listening) environment.
A few mastering studios that could afford it, have put together rooms full of various consumer displays to do what you said: Look at the same content (in an identical environment!) to gauge what do contemporary TV's do to it. It's expensive (yes, even for Hollywood facilities), it's a moving target, and eventually it doesn't tell you a ton. There is a spec of what color on TV's should look like (ITU Rec.709, SMPTE ST 2084, etc.), and it's the TV companies' job to work off it.
And a colorist who's in a room with a director setting the look of a show, can't sit every day staring at 10 screens and playing guessing games. Similarly, audio monitor have a "flat" reference response curve that doesn't represent any common, bass-loving consumer headphones.
That said, the colorist or audio mixer's job includes understanding what consumer tech is like out there, and for example, they may absolutely consider that not everyone has an OLED TV when dialing in the dark shadows. And yes, colorists and producers watch the shows at home on their consumer TV, and they better be happy with the results!
FYI High-end consumer TV's can be very close to the pro monitors. For TV / streaming content, what's often in the room is a reference monitor (e.g. Sony BVM-HX310) and a consumer "client monitor", which may be an off-the-shelf consumer TV like an LG G5 (albeit professionally and carefully calibrated).

articles.title: Q&A: How hackers turned up the heat on Europe’s fridges | BetaKit
articles.text:
European supermarkets have been targeted by costly cyberattacks to grocery stores, and even blood banks, that tamper with the temperatures of commercial fridges and freezers.
Jeff Shirley is the founder and CEO of Rivercity Innovations, a Saskatoon-based tech company founded in 2017 that uses low-powered sensors to monitor data like temperature, GPS positioning, moisture, and humidity—meaning it will alert a company if its fridges have experienced a drastic temperature change. Rivercity offers its systems in seven countries, and says it’s been receiving calls from European customers since the hacks.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporter Jesse Cole sat down with Shirley to chat about what happened in Europe, and whether Canadian Internet-of-Things devices, from fridges to HVAC systems, should be considered at risk.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Why does a fridge need to be connected to the internet in the first place?
Think of a grocery chain with hundreds of stores. You’re not going to send out a technician to every single case at every single store every day to adjust settings and controls. So, experts remote in and simultaneously monitor.
Those pieces of equipment are also not as simple as a house fridge. Sometimes they have different temperature zones. Ice cream is usually -25°C, whereas frozen pizzas might be at -18°C. That all ties into energy management and planning for predictive maintenance.
It’s not just a refrigerator: it’s a very complex, multi-million-dollar coolant system managing its energy to protect the environment and keep your food safe at the right level, and making sure that glass door doesn’t frost up every time you open it. It’s extremely complex.
Can you tell us what happened with these high-profile hacks?
These cooler systems—think your supermarket, your grocery store—they have very big refrigeration freezer systems. These have mechanical rooms that run coolant and power to them. Those coolant systems are monitored by companies and are controlled through a control system. The service companies remote into those systems to check the cooling, the performance, and ensure all of the temperatures are right.
What has happened in Europe is that a vendor had some hardware that required patches. If businesses didn’t patch it, people could see those systems if they were publicly on the internet, through the channels that the remote service companies would use.
Those people attempted to hack the systems and succeeded. They changed the settings, just like if you’re in your house; they increased the thermostat and said, “let’s go to 50°C,” and the system said, “OK, because you’re the service company.”
Freezers, by design, have to run defrost cycles. Sometimes, every eight hours or so, it’ll run up to like -5°C to burn off the frost from the humidity in the store condensing on the glass. Those defrost cycles were leveraged by the hackers to go to 50°C and stay there. Overnight, all the frozen pizzas thawed, all the meat thawed, all the ice cream melted, and you come into the store at 7 a.m. and you have puddles and ruined product.
Which, I imagine, is worth tens of millions of dollars across a chain.
Hundreds of millions of euros were lost in the first wave about three weeks ago, and in the last wave, more countries were hit by similar hacks.
The damage is immediate. The only thing that mitigates it is third-party monitoring, because these coolers are wired to behave like this. They’re not unusual settings for somebody to say, “I want you to be warmer temporarily.”
I don’t believe it was nefarious because there’s no malware that we’re hearing about. Nobody’s saying, “pay me in Bitcoin.” It seems to be across the platform of wired control systems, and I expect it will extend to more countries.
So you need third-party monitoring. Our business—that’s what we do. We’ve been getting calls.
Tell me how that third-party monitoring works.
Think about your local Co-op or IGA. The big grocery stores have wired control systems. They’re physically wired in the building. They’re very expensive and very complex. A smaller company is not going to put a $100,000 wired monitoring system in there. What River City does is monitor the coolers and the freezers. [Editor’s note: It does so using battery power and Long-Range, Wide-Area Network, rather than Wi-Fi.] We alert the staff if the freezer isn’t normal. We send out those alerts as a triage, kind of like a weather warning on your cell phone about tornadoes coming.
Here in Canada, this has been good for our business, but my heart goes out to these companies.
It’s also not just about the hacks. Whether it’s a hack or a forest fire or a flood season, businesses lose their power. So having the ability to get those alerts, to go back and validate that food, is still good.
We have a very awesome client in British Columbia. Do you remember the forest fires in the Okanagan Valley this summer? The power went out; they knew they were going to be down for more than a day. So they decided to donate that food to the first responders in the community, so that client of ours went in, sent the semi-trucks in with permission from the perimeter border guards, and brought that food out to the first responders. Doesn’t that sound better than it’s all melted and on the floor in the morning?
You mentioned these vulnerabilities are stemming from unpatched software. How vulnerable are we in Canada?
There are five or six major players in wired control systems worldwide. In Canada, three or four are very active. They have their own security teams, their own departments. They will advise the grocery chain that this hardware needs to be updated. If the chain has updated it, problem solved.
It’s no different whether it’s a computer or a refrigeration system. You can think of this as a very complex IT nightmare. There will be big chains doing due diligence right now, asking, “are we vulnerable? Have we patched it?” And if they haven’t, just imagine having 1,200 stores with 100 coolers each, and you need to update the control systems in those stores, which might be a complex circuit board and computer and management system. And every store has its latest versions and updates, which might not all be aligned.
Absolutely, it’s going to be our priority for Canadian brands. I think yes, we’re vulnerable, but Canada is a very developed country. We’re on top of things
Do you think this signals anything concerning about the broader Internet-of-Things ecosystem when it comes to cybersecurity risks?
The moral of the story is you can’t run a large enterprise business with IoT-connected devices for the public if you’re not going to put in best practices for security. Use a VPN. Use firewall rules. Use dedicated ports. Use two-factor authentication. Change your passwords to be complex. Change your passwords every 60 days. Who would have thought that the refrigeration control panel needed the default password changed?
It’s a major problem. The Internet of Things is more than just grocery stores.
Commercial properties have a remotely managed central HVAC system. Say somebody hacks a commercial building and turns everybody to 50°C? My advice is to get some safety nets in place.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by JC Gellidon.

articles.title: « Ils nous ont licenciés, on reconstruit leurs logiciels », avec l’IA, un mouvement s’attaque aux abonnements SaaS
articles.text:
Sous la bannière d'un mouvement de développeurs licenciés, une initiative entend reconstruire des logiciels professionnels vendus par abonnement. Pour y parvenir, elle s'appuie sur des agents IA et du code open source. Une première version candidate vient d'être publiée, mais elle n'est pas encore prête pour la production.
Un abonnement pour gérer ses clients, un autre pour connecter les utilisateurs à une application, un troisième pour organiser le travail d'équipe… Les dépenses logicielles peuvent rapidement s'accumuler, particulièrement lorsque les tarifs dépendent du nombre d'utilisateurs.
Et si l'intelligence artificielle permettait de reconstruire une partie de ces outils plutôt que de continuer à les louer ? C'est le pari d'OccupySaaS, une initiative apparue en octobre 2026, dont le slogan annonce la couleur : « Ils nous ont licenciés. Nous reconstruisons leurs SaaS. »
Une révolte contre les abonnements, avec l'IA comme arme
Le nom OccupySaaS fait référence à Occupy Wall Street, le mouvement de contestation des inégalités né en 2011. Ici, la contestation passe… par GitHub. L'initiative se présente comme un mouvement d'ingénieurs victimes des licenciements dans l'industrie technologique.
Son objectif est de proposer des alternatives gratuites, open source et auto-hébergeables à des logiciels professionnels payants, notamment ceux qui facturent chaque utilisateur supplémentaire et rendent difficile le passage à une solution concurrente.
Deux projets ont démarré à la mi-octobre. Le premier, ZeroAuthy, cherche à reproduire Auth0, un service permettant notamment de gérer la connexion et l'identification des utilisateurs d'applications. Le second, SalesCompel, vise Salesforce, une plateforme destinée à la gestion des clients et des activités commerciales.
Cette semaine, ZeroAuthy a franchi une étape avec la publication d'une première version candidate, téléchargeable pour plusieurs plateformes. Les deux projets sont distribués sous licence Apache 2.0, qui autorise leur utilisation, leur modification et leur redistribution, y compris commerciale.
Mais derrière l'ambition de réunir une communauté d'ingénieurs, les dépôts GitHub racontent pour l'instant une histoire plus modeste, et peut-être plus étonnante.
Selon une analyse des contributions arrêtée au 4 novembre, ZeroAuthy totalisait 836 commits en 22 jours, dont 770 attribués à un compte humain et 66 à un compte associé à Claude. Mais l'implication de l'IA est bien plus importante : 535 commits, soit près des deux tiers, mentionnent un modèle Claude d'Anthropic comme co-auteur. Cette mention étant facultative, la participation réelle des agents pourrait être plus étendue.
Sur SalesCompel, les contributions recensées provenaient du même compte humain. Cela n'exclut pas l'intervention d'autres personnes en dehors des dépôts, mais ne permet pas vraiment pour l'heure de parler d'un vaste collectif de développeurs.
Des centaines de milliers de lignes de code, mais encore beaucoup à prouver
La vitesse de développement est impressionnante. En trois semaines, ZeroAuthy a accumulé environ 151 500 lignes de code Go hors tests et code généré, auxquelles s'ajoutent 124 700 lignes de tests, selon la même analyse. Le nombre de commits cosignés confirme une participation importante de l'IA, sans permettre de mesurer précisément la part de code qu'elle a produite.
La méthode revendiquée par OccupySaaS repose sur une approche dite clean room, ou réimplémentation en salle blanche. L'idée consiste à repartir de documentations publiques et de standards ouverts pour reconstruire un logiciel sans reprendre son code propriétaire.
L'objectif n'est pas simplement de produire un programme ressemblant à l'original, mais de permettre aux applications existantes de fonctionner sans modification. Pour vérifier cette compatibilité, les projets utilisent notamment les bibliothèques de développement publiques des éditeurs concernés et les font communiquer avec leurs propres serveurs.
ZeroAuthy a d'ailleurs obtenu une certification de l'OpenID Foundation pour trois profils du protocole OpenID Connect : Basic OP, Config OP et Form Post OP. C'est un résultat vérifié extérieurement, même s'il ne garantit ni la sécurité globale du logiciel ni sa compatibilité avec toutes les fonctionnalités d'Auth0.
La méthode elle-même pose question. En principe, une réimplémentation en salle blanche repose sur deux équipes distinctes : l’une étudie le logiciel original et rédige une description de son fonctionnement, l’autre écrit le code à partir de cette seule description, sans jamais avoir vu l’original. Cette séparation permet de prouver, en cas de litige, que rien n’a été copié. Le document de politique de ZeroAuthy applique cette règle, y compris aux agents IA. Celui de SalesCompel, en revanche, autorise une même personne, ou une même session d’agent, à observer Salesforce puis à programmer son équivalent. Le second projet se prive ainsi de la principale protection juridique qu’offre la méthode.
- Méthodes de connexion variées
- SDK et documentation fournis
- Contrôles de sécurité intégrés
À cela s'ajoute la question des données ayant servi à entraîner les modèles IA, qui peuvent comprendre du code protégé. Cette situation ne rend pas automatiquement une réimplémentation illégale, mais les précautions affichées ne suffisent pas à exclure tout litige.
Surtout, les logiciels restent incomplets. ZeroAuthy ne prend pas encore en charge certaines fonctionnalités avancées, notamment les clés d'accès (passkeys), SAML ou les annuaires d'entreprise. SalesCompel se trouve à un stade beaucoup plus précoce. Aucun des deux n'est recommandé pour un déploiement général en production. Et puis, supprimer les frais de licence n'élimine pas les coûts d'hébergement, de maintenance, de sécurité ou d'assistance technique, sans compter que l'usage intensif d'agents peut aussi générer des frais importants. 
En bref, OccupySaaS ne signe pas la fin des abonnements logiciels. Mais le projet illustre un paradoxe savoureux : l’IA, que l’industrie présente comme un moyen de faire plus avec moins d’ingénieurs, pourrait aussi permettre à ces mêmes ingénieurs de concurrencer leurs anciens employeurs.

articles.title: Una simple nota de 'gracias' de Angelina Jolie ha llevado a la Generación X y a la Generación Z a debatir si su escritura es legible
articles.text:
Una sencilla nota de agradecimiento de Angelina Jolie terminó convirtiéndose en un pequeño rompecabezas para miles de usuarios en redes sociales. Así, todo empezó en 2023 durante el rodaje de Maria, ya que la intérprete dejó una nota para el personal del hotel Aldemar Olympian Village de Grecia.
Tres años después, la fotografía ha vuelto a circular y la conversación se está centrando en su peculiar caligrafía. Así, mientras algunos aseguran que pueden leerla sin dificultad, otros dicen que solo consiguen distinguir unas pocas palabras. Si quieres saber lo que dice, resulta que el mensaje agradece la estancia en el establecimiento y explica que el equipo de la película disfrutó de su paso por allí, pero descifrarlo fue más complicado de lo esperado.
Como recoge BuzzFeed, algunas personas comparan los trazos con la letra de un médico, pero otras consideran que el problema está en la falta de costumbre de leer textos manuscritos. Por ello, la discusión terminó enfrentando opiniones sobre las habilidades de distintas generaciones.
La escritura cursiva ha ido perdiendo espacio frente a los teclados
El debate tiene un precedente interesante en Estados Unidos, país en el que la enseñanza de la escritura cursiva perdió presencia después de que los estándares educativos Common Core (publicados en 2010) dejaran de incluirla entre sus requisitos. Como ejemplo, la historiadora Drew Gilpin Faust relató en un artículo publicado en The Atlantic que casi dos tercios de los estudiantes de uno de sus seminarios eran incapaces de leer ese tipo de letra.
Una experiencia así no representa a toda una generación, pero sí muestra cómo están cambiando algunas habilidades. La popularización de los ordenadores, las tabletas y los teléfonos móviles han reducido muchas situaciones en las que necesitamos escribir a mano. Por suerte, eso no significa que la caligrafía haya desaparecido de las escuelas y varios estadounidenses han recuperado su enseñanza obligatoria en los últimos años.
Lo que demuestra la nota de Jolie es que algo tan cotidiano como interpretar una carta manuscrita puede variar dependiendo de nuestra educación y nuestras costumbres.

articles.title: Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck in 2027 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, according to CEO Elon Musk, who said on X that the company will use the factory space to build more two-seater Cybercab robotaxis.
The decision to wind down the futuristic, steel-clad EV comes after just a few short years of underwhelming sales. When Musk handed over the first few Cybertrucks in late 2023, he predicted Tesla would sell around 250,000 per year. It was supposed to be such a cornerstone of Tesla’s future that, before construction began, the company talked about its Texas factory as the “Cybertruck factory.” But Tesla has instead sold just tens of thousands — total — over the last three years.
Tesla is killing off the Cybertruck at a moment when it is trying to become an AI- and robotics-focused company. A big part of that is its robotaxi ambitions.
The company has spent the last two months putting Cybercabs on the streets in its hometown of Austin, Texas. With no major incidents to date, the company has said it plans to expand the Cybercabs operations to other cities, starting with Dallas later this month. (Tesla also operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUVs in Austin, Houston, and Dallas, as well as three cities in Florida.)
This is the third product Tesla has discontinued in order to fuel those greater ambitions. Earlier this year, the company decided to end production of the Model S sedan and Model X SUV and instead use the factory space dedicated to those vehicles to make Optimus humanoid robots.
First announced in 2019, the Cybertruck was a product that Musk had long obsessed over.
“Probably my personal favorite for the next product is the pickup truck, and we are going to just do an amazing pickup truck,” he said on one of Tesla’s earnings calls that year.
Musk promised the Cybertruck would be radical, inspired by the designs of cyberpunk sci-fi stories like “Blade Runner.” While that certainly bore out in the design, the company overpromised on the basics of the Cybertruck from the jump. During the now-infamous reveal event in 2019, when head designer Franz von Holzhausen cracked the Cybertruck’s windows with steel balls, Tesla said the EV was supposed to start at under $40,000 and have up to 500 miles of range. It achieved neither of those figures.
Instead, the truck was delayed for two years, in part because of the COVID-19 pandemic. When it finally did hit the market in late 2023, Tesla handed over the first few Cybertrucks to customers in a short, somewhat odd for Tesla event (by the company’s own standards, at least), which saw a poorly-lit Musk standing in a truck bed promising the truck was “the finest in apocalyptic equipment” fit for “late civilization vibes.” The base price had inflated to around $60,000, and the top-end range had shrunk by over 100 miles.
The truck has struggled on the market ever since. The polarizing design never seemed to sit well with buyers, especially at a higher-than-expected price. Then, during its first full year of sales in 2024, Musk became a major financial backer of Donald Trump, which turned the instantly recognizable Cybertruck into a target for protesters. That continued into 2025 as Musk led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, which fired thousands of federal workers.
