articles.title: TSMC podría comenzar a fabricar RAM, pero no te ilusiones con que baje de precio
articles.text:
Con una crisis de memoria RAM que aún no habría mostrado su peor cara, la industria de los semiconductores busca alternativas para tratar de cubrir la brutal demanda impulsada por la inteligencia artificial. En este contexto, TSMC, el principal fabricante de chips del mundo, podría comenzar a fabricar módulos DRAM.
Según reporta The Information, TSMC analiza ingresar a la producción en masa de memoria 3D RAM por pedido de NVIDIA, su cliente más importante. Todavía no se sabe si la firma taiwanesa realmente dará el paso hacia el citado segmento, pero el solo hecho de que lo estudie es una señal interesante de cara al futuro.
En la actualidad, los principales proveedores de memoria RAM avanzada para servidores de inteligencia artificial son Samsung, SK Hynix y Micron. La demanda de sus clientes es tan grande que las tres están al límite de sus capacidades. Recientemente, Samsung informó que ya tiene vendida toda su producción de memoria de alto ancho de banda para 2027. Micron, en tanto, abandonó la fabricación de memoria para consumidores y se enfocó en el segmento dedicado a los servidores de IA generativa.
Así las cosas, TSMC podría ingresar en el mercado de la RAM para convertirse en otro proveedor de gran escala para las principales tecnológicas del mundo. Hsu Kuo-chin, vicepresidente de empaquetado avanzado de la compañía taiwanesa, estaría liderando esta iniciativa. No obstante, aún se desconoce si realmente se concretará.
TSMC analiza comenzar a fabricar memoria RAM avanzada
Al parecer, las opciones que baraja TSMC en el presunto plan de expandirse al campo de la memoria RAM avanzada son dos. Por un lado, montar sus propias fábricas dedicadas a la producción de este tipo de componentes para NVIDIA y otros de sus clientes más importantes. Por el otro, comprar alguna planta de semiconductores ya existente y adaptarla a la fabricación de 3D RAM.
Es posible que la primera opción sea mucho más lenta y costosa que la segunda, aunque por cómo viene la cosa la crisis de la RAM no se acabará de la noche a la mañana. Samsung espera que la escasez se agrave en 2027 debido a los altísimos niveles de demanda para centros de datos de inteligencia artificial. La empresa coreana incluso vaticina que las consecuencias de la situación actual se extiendan al menos hasta 2028.
Eso sí, si TSMC realmente comienza a producir memoria, no esperes una bajada de precios en la RAM para consumo general. NVIDIA le habría pedido a los taiwaneses que comiencen a fabricar módulos 3D RAM, que tienen celdas de memoria que se apilan en vertical y que se usan principalmente en servidores, superordenadores y centros de datos de IA. Así que esta estrategia no va a cambiar el panorama complejo que hoy afrontan los consumidores.

articles.title: Llega la primera movilización europea contra los centros de datos: “No queremos ser el patio trasero de nadie”
articles.text:
Llega la primera movilización europea contra los centros de datos: “No queremos ser el patio trasero de nadie”
España es uno de los 15 países en los que hay convocados este sábado diversos actos para exigir una moratoria en la construcción de estas infraestructuras
Este sábado hay convocadas movilizaciones en 15 países europeos para solicitar una moratoria en la construcción de centros de datos, esas instalaciones repletas de servidores y procesadores sin los que no funcionaría internet y que han florecido en los últimos años de la mano de la irrupción comercial de la inteligencia artificial (IA). España aglutina 22 de las 90 acciones de protesta previstas, que se desarrollarán en ciudades como Barcelona, Madrid, Sevilla y Pamplona. Es la primera iniciativa de este tipo coordinada a escala europea.
“Pedimos una moratoria inmediata sobre la construcción de nuevos centros de datos a gran escala a nivel local, nacional y europeo”, resume Aurora Gómez, de 43 años y nacida en Ballesteros de Calatrava, Ciudad Real. Esta psicóloga es la fundadora del colectivo Tu Nube Seca Mi Río y coordinadora de los eventos organizados en España. “Los gobiernos, la UE y las grandes empresas tecnológicas están avanzando a toda velocidad con la construcción de estas instalaciones. Exigimos que se detenga de inmediato este proceso, que se lleve a cabo un análisis exhaustivo de las repercusiones medioambientales, democráticas y sociales, y que se establezcan marcos claros para decidir si deben construirse centros de datos a gran escala y en qué condiciones”, apunta.
Países como Irlanda, Países Bajos o Singapur ya han puesto en marcha moratorias de este tipo. En EE UU, que concentra la mitad de los centros de datos del mundo, la carta blanca otorgada a la industria por el presidente Trump ha provocado la reacción de los votantes en las elecciones de medio mandato. Los analistas creen que el deseo de imponer una moratoria y ordenar el crecimiento del sector explica parte del impulso que ha permitido al Partido Demócrata arrollar en los comicios, asegurándose el control del Senado y la Cámara de Representantes, aunque también hay republicanos que comparten esa inquietud.
La resistencia ante estas infraestructuras es poliédrica. Sus externalidades negativas son variadas: consumen mucha energía, hasta el punto de subir la factura de la luz en algunas regiones; generan poco empleo, más allá del necesario para construirlos; necesitan agua, hacen un ruido constante, acaparan y modifican mucho territorio y se sabe también que pueden generar problemas para la salud de los vecinos.
Gómez no quiere ver todo eso en España. “En Irlanda, los centros de datos suponen ya más del 30% de la demanda estatal de electricidad, según la operadora Eirgrid. En Latinoamérica han exacerbado sequías. No queremos ser el patio trasero de nadie, queremos juntarnos en las plazas públicas y defender nuestra agua, clima y territorios”, sentencia. La vertiente internacional del movimiento es, en su opinión, esencial para su crecimiento. Alemania, Austria, Bélgica, Dinamarca, Finlandia, Francia, Irlanda, Italia, Países Bajos, Polonia y Reino Unido participan también en la movilización.
“Llevamos un año pensando en esta campaña, y entendiendo que las movilizaciones de estos días son solo un punto de partida. Cada país tiene unas características diversas, desde el tiempo que llevan implantados los centros de datos hasta la situación política, el estado de sus resistencias o los impactos que más preocupan. Hemos buscado una coordinación plural, donde desde la parte europea se aporten la idea central de moratoria y las comunidades puedan adaptar las demandas específicas y los formatos de acción que mejor encajen”, explica.
En España hay convocadas para este sábado 22 movilizaciones de naturaleza muy diversa. “Por ejemplo, habrá manifestaciones más clásicas en Zaragoza, y paseos reivindicativos en Madrid. Pero también bicicletadas alrededor de los centros de datos, medir la distancia del centro de datos a su vivienda, grupos que se juntan a hacer peticiones públicas de transparencia, recitales de poesía o lecturas de fanzines. Cada comunidad elige la manera de protestar que mejor le encaje, que a la vez sirva de punto de encuentro y debate”, señala Gómez.
Aunque en países como EE UU el debate en torno a los centros de datos ha entrado de lleno en la conversación pública o incluso en la campaña electoral, en España todavía no estamos en ese momento. Con todo, Gómez detecta un creciente interés en el asunto, acaso alimentado por la animadversión que despiertan los dueños de las grandes tecnológicas. “En los cuatro años que Tu Nube Seca Mi Río lleva como colectivo hemos visto una sensibilidad creciente respecto a los impactos de los centros de datos y una mayor preocupación de los europeos respecto a este tema, como refleja una encuesta que hicimos hace un año”, indica. “La gente en lo rural se está levantando contra los centros de datos, y en las ciudades cada vez están más preocupados por los impactos de la IA. Ambas son dos caras de la misma moneda, y es ese hermanamiento entre las luchas rurales y de ciudad lo que puede dar todo el impulso que necesitamos para parar un problema tan grande”.

articles.title: If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world
articles.text:
If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world
At TechSparks 2026, the Founder and President of TDK Ventures said Indian deeptech founders should plan for international markets from the start, and use the country’s tough operating conditions to develop capabilities that customers elsewhere would value.
For years, India’s best scientists left for the US. Now they are staying, and more of them are choosing startups over corporate labs. For Nicolas Sauvage, Founder and President of TDK Ventures, those two shifts are the biggest changes in Indian deeptech over the past five to 10 years.
“The best talent starts to go into the startups in deeptech, and they try things that they would not have tried 10 years or even five years ago,” Sauvage said in a fireside chat with Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, at TechSparks 2026.
TDK Ventures is the corporate venture capital arm of Japanese electronics company TDK Corporation. Set up in Silicon Valley in 2019, it opened its Bengaluru innovation hub in 2023, its first office outside the US. India is its second largest market by number of investments, Sauvage said.
The ecosystem he is betting on is growing. India is home to more than 4,200 deeptech startups, which raised $2.3 billion in 2025, up 37% from the year before, according to a Nasscom–Zinnov report.
During the session titled ‘Global by design: What Indian deeptech needs to become globally iconic’, he laid out what Indian founders need to get right to build companies that compete globally, from picking a first customer and the right investors to planning for scale before it becomes expensive to do so.
Where India has the right to win
Speaking on investing in SpaceTech, Sauvage named the US, China, and India as the three countries where he would consider investing as a VC. Space is one area where he believes India has a clear advantage, built on decades of institutional investment through the Indian Space Research Organisation. The government’s space promotion agency, IN-SPACe, projects that India’s space economy will grow from $8.4 billion to $44 billion by 2033, raising its share of the global market from 2% to 8%.
TDK Ventures co-led a $20.5 million Series A in Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Ethereal Exploration Guild (The Guild), which is developing a fully reusable medium-lift launch vehicle.
Sauvage also pointed to a shift in AI. The conversation, he said, has moved from tokens and compute to electrons and gigawatts, which means everything involved in delivering power to chips now matters. TDK Ventures invested in C2i Semiconductors, a Bengaluru startup founded in 2024 by former Texas Instruments engineers that builds power management technology for AI data centres. Germany’s Infineon Technologies announced the acquisition of C2i in August 2026 and completed it in October, about two years after the startup was founded.
Beyond individual sectors, Sauvage credited a cultural trait: jugaad, or resourcefulness under constraint.
“Think about the entrepreneurship journey. It means going from an idea with massive constraints and creating something that’s valuable and does a job. That sounds like jugaad to me,” he said.
That resourcefulness shows up in the numbers, he added. Capital efficiency among Indian portfolio companies is world class. “I’m from Europe, but don’t talk about Europe when we think about capital efficiency,” he said.
Let the first market shape the product
When asked what founders building from India for the world should think about first, Sauvage pointed to Exponent Energy. Founded in 2020 by former Ather Energy executives Arun Vinayak and Sanjay Byalal, the company offers 15-minute fast charging. In June 2026, TDK Ventures co-led a Rs 200 crore ($21.1 million) round in Exponent, taking the company’s total funding since 2020 to $65.7 million.
Exponent’s long-term goal was megawatt-scale fast charging for intercity buses. It could not start there. Instead, it began by supplying battery management systems (BMS) to three-wheeler makers, a fragmented market with more than 70 manufacturers at the time.
“There was no way a German startup would convince BMW to take their solution. No way a US startup would convince General Motors to take their BMS solution,” Sauvage said.
India’s fragmented market let Exponent deploy across many manufacturers in Bengaluru and beyond, giving it a base to build from.
Founders need superpowers, and so do their investors
Sauvage described founders as superheroes. Each needs a superpower: something they know or can do that no one else can. That is what draws investors in. But, like any superhero film, there are many battles before the end, and founders need allies.
“You want to make sure that the investors you pick as an entrepreneur bring the right superpower at the right time,” he said.
Corporate VCs can bring a go-to-market channel, an early anchor customer, a hard-to-access supplier, or help reducing scientific risk, depending on who they are. He urged founders to choose investors based on what they add that the cap table does not already have.
For TDK Ventures, that means drawing on TDK’s work in energy, sensing, passive components, and power supplies. Sauvage said electric motorcycle maker Ultraviolette now gets components typically reserved for TDK’s largest customers, while TDK is working with The Guild on future component requirements and roadmaps.
Alongside seeking venture-capital financial returns, he said, TDK Ventures looks for ways TDK’s capabilities, or “superpowers”, can accelerate and de-risk a founder’s journey towards building a globally significant company.
First principles over trade-offs
Sauvage traced several portfolio wins back to first-principles thinking. TDK Ventures invested in AI chip company Groq in 2020. During an interview with founder Jonathan Ross before investing, Sauvage noticed that every answer, from setting company values to hiring, firing, and designing the compiler, came back to first principles.
That approach produced a chip architecture designed around the compiler, which allowed for fully predictable, low-latency inference. Sauvage said he was convinced inference was the future before the ChatGPT moment, when he estimated the market for inference alone at more than $60 billion. In December 2025, NVIDIA signed a non-exclusive licensing deal for Groq’s technology, reportedly worth about $20 billion, and hired Ross and several members of his team.
He applied the same lens to engineering decisions that look like trade-offs. Ultraviolette, he said, uses first-principles engineering to pursue improvements in performance, weight and cost together. The company now sells its bikes in Germany, France, Switzerland, the UK, and other European markets, bringing its products into markets served by established manufacturers such as BMW. Ultraviolette recently raised $85 million in a round led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures.
Patience and impatience at the same time
Deeptech founders, Sauvage said, need both. “Overnight success takes 10 years,” he said, noting that Groq took 10 years and SpaceX took 17. At the same time, founders need urgency and a sense of contribution to society.
Before investing, he looks for four things: a founder with a superpower, a category-defining product, a large enough market, and evidence the company can win one customer and then the next while staying capital-efficient. Markets worth $1 billion to $2 billion can be too small for the venture returns TDK Ventures seeks, he said, because the firm looks for each investment to have the potential to return the entire fund.
He cited SPAN, a Silicon Valley company led by Indian-origin founder Arch Rao. SPAN began by redesigning the home electrical panel, a product largely unchanged for a century.
As AI infrastructure demand surged, SPAN extended its power-management technology into distributed compute through partnerships, which Sauvage said changed the company’s trajectory.
Longer cycles also explain why India needs more corporate investors now, he argued. Using a roughly four-year journey to success in SaaS and fintech as an illustration, Sauvage described an ecosystem that can recycle entrepreneurial experience about 2.5 times a decade, as founders and employees carry what they have learned into new companies. A ten-year deeptech journey allows only one such cycle over the same period. Networks of repeat founders and alumni-founded businesses, like those associated with PayPal and SpaceX, therefore take longer to develop. Corporate investors can help bridge that gap with technical expertise, suppliers and customer relationships.
“I want global companies, corporates, and their corporate VCs to know this is the time to invest in India for deeptech,” he said.
Build for scale before it gets expensive
Sauvage emphasised thinking about scale and international expansion early, because shortcuts taken to win the first market in India can become expensive to reverse later.
When TDK Ventures met Ultraviolette, the team was already deliberate about Europe while focused on winning in India first, with customers riding its bikes as far as the Himalayas.
His advice to founders: find what is specific to India that a global customer would trust. India’s wide temperature range, for example, could favour energy storage that performs across extremes, such as sodium-ion or thermal batteries.
“Try to think about what makes you being in India a proof point that because you’re successful in India, you will win everywhere,” he said.
For Sauvage, India’s deeptech opportunity rests on more than talent. The founders most likely to build iconic companies are those who treat India as a starting point rather than a boundary, pick investors who fill specific gaps, and design for international markets before shortcuts become costly to undo. It is a long game that demands patience and impatience at once, and in his view, the moment for global capital to back it in India has arrived.

articles.title: MetaMask says recent attack didn't affect wallet infrastructure
articles.text:
Cryptocurrency wallet provider MetaMask said a recent security incident has not affected MetaMask wallets or its wallet infrastructure.
The MetaMask non-custodial crypto wallet (developed by blockchain software company Consensys) lets users store and manage assets on the Ethereum network and compatible blockchains.
MetaMask revealed on September 30 that it was investigating an "ongoing infrastructure security incident" and exited affected validators (Ethereum network nodes responsible for proposing blocks, verifying crypto transactions, and maintaining Ethereum blockchain security) within non-custodial staking operations.
While the company shared almost no details at the time and redirected BleepingComputer to the public statement when asked what part of its infrastructure was affected, in a Thursday update it said that a threat actor gained access to systems used to store recipient addresses and diverted some execution-layer staking rewards.
"The issue was identified and addressed on the same day, and approximately 0.385 ETH in rewards was diverted. These rewards are separate from customers' staked ETH," MetaMask said. "We have found no evidence that customers' staked principal or withdrawal keys were compromised, and the affected systems have been secured."
It also added that the attack did not compromise MetaMask users' Secret Recovery Phrases or private keys and that it was working with affected customers to refund the lost rewards.
"Some customers have experienced temporary withdrawal delays as a result of the precautionary validator exits. The process may also have resulted in missed staking rewards while validators were exiting or awaiting reactivation. We are working directly with affected customers and partners to address any outstanding impact," MetaMask noted.
"MetaMask wallet users do not need to take any action as a result of this incident. Customers whose staking arrangements were affected should follow any guidance provided directly by MetaMask or their staking provider."
Last month, Ledger also asked Asian resellers and distributors to halt wallet sales and remove products from shelves while it was investigating multiple hardware implant incidents.
More recently, crypto exchange Binance confirmed that North Korean hackers stole $6.34 billion after compromising its wallet infrastructure by tricking an employee into installing malware in a fake job interview.

articles.title: « Aucune interaction n’est nécessaire » : une faille critique met en danger votre smartphone Android, faites vite la mise à jour
articles.text:
Google vient de déployer le correctif de sécurité de novembre pour Android. La mise à jour corrige 216 failles de sécurité, dont 23 jugées critiques. Parmi elles, une brèche particulièrement dangereuse permet de prendre le contrôle d’un smartphone à distance, sans le moindre clic de la part de la victime.
À lire aussi : 1,3 million de boîtiers TV Android piratés – Google démantèle un botnet chinois, installé dès l’usine par un fabricant
Une faille dans le cœur d’Android
La défaillance se trouve dans le Framework, l’un des composants centraux d’Android. Comme l’explique Google dans son bulletin de sécurité, « la plus grave de ces vulnérabilités est une faille de sécurité critique dans le composant Framework qui pourrait conduire à une exécution de code à distance sans qu’aucun privilège d’exécution supplémentaire ne soit nécessaire ». En fait, « aucune interaction de l’utilisateur n’est nécessaire pour l’exploiter », prévient le géant de Mountain View.
La faille se situe plus précisément dans le code chargé de créer les aperçus des photos et des vidéos, comme les miniatures affichées dans une galerie. En exploitant la faille, un pirate pourrait exécuter du code malveillant sur le smartphone sans que son propriétaire n’ouvre un lien ou ne télécharge quoi que ce soit. Toutes les versions d’Android sont concernées, d’Android 14 à Android 17.
Pour l’instant, rien ne prouve que des cybercriminels aient exploité la vulnérabilité pour lancer des attaques. Néanmoins, les cyberattaques reposant sur la faille ne devraient pas tarder à pointer le bout de leur nez. Conformément aux habitudes de Google; le code source des correctifs est rendu public 48 heures après le bulletin. Des pirates pourraient alors l’analyser pour comprendre comment exploiter la brèche. C’est pourquoi il est urgent de mettre à jour votre smartphone.
40 % des smartphones laissés de côté
Malheureusement, tous les smartphones Android ne recevront pas les correctifs adéquats. D’après les données de distribution d’Android, plus de 40 % des appareils actifs tournent encore sous Android 13 ou une version plus ancienne. Ces versions, considérées comme obsolètes, ne reçoivent plus de mises à jour de sécurité de la part de Google. Les smartphones concernés se retrouvent donc à la merci des cybercriminels. Si votre smartphone n’est pas obsolète, l’arrivée de la mise à jour dépend du fabricant, qui doit adapter le correctif à sa surcouche. Certains constructeurs réagissent vite et lancent le déploiement en quelques jours, d’autres en plusieurs semaines.
Pour savoir si votre téléphone est à jour, ouvrez l’application Paramètres, puis rendez-vous dans À propos du téléphone et Version d’Android. Consultez ensuite la date de la mise à jour de sécurité Android. Si elle affiche le 1er novembre 2026 ou une date plus récente, vous êtes bien protégé contre la faille critique. Si une mise à jour est disponible, installez-la sans attendre. Si votre smartphone n’en reçoit plus depuis bien longtemps, on vous encourage à envisager l’achat d’un nouveau smartphone.

articles.title: Installés sur les ponts, ces nouveaux radars mobiles à intelligence artificielle traquent la position de vos mains pour détecter le téléphone au volant
articles.text:
Des radars mobiles pour sanctionner le téléphone au volant, une nouveauté allemande qui pourrait séduire la France ?
Après plus d’un an de test, l’Allemagne déploie dans tout le pays des radars mobiles équipés d’intelligence artificielle pour verbaliser les automobilistes utilisant leur téléphone au volant.
Se servir de son téléphone au volant est un danger connu de tous, mais rares sont les automobilistes pouvant affirmer ne l’avoir jamais fait. En Allemagne, l’ADAC, principale association d’automobilistes du pays, estime d’ailleurs à 400 000 le nombre d’infractions de ce type relevées chaque année par les forces de l’ordre et les radars. Pour endiguer ce phénomène, le gouvernement fédéral va déployer dans tout le pays le système néerlandais MonoCam, testé depuis mars 2025 dans le Land de Rhénanie-Palatinat.
Une détection par intelligence artificielle depuis les ponts et des amendes moins sévères qu’en France
Pour fonctionner efficacement, les radars mobiles MonoCam sont installés par les forces de l’ordre sur des ponts, au-dessus de la voie contrôlée. Leur caméra, orientée selon un angle oblique, vise directement l’habitacle pendant que l’intelligence artificielle analyse les images en direct. Entraînée à reconnaître différentes positions des mains, elle détermine si le conducteur tient son smartphone.
Lorsqu’une infraction potentielle est repérée, l’appareil prend automatiquement une photo. La décision finale de l’amende revient toutefois à un agent habilité, qui vérifie le cliché avant de valider la contravention.
Fait inhabituel pour l’Allemagne, où chaque région décide d’ordinaire au cas par cas, ce dispositif est généralisé à l’échelle nationale. Une mesure exceptionnelle qui répond à une urgence statistique, le ministre fédéral des Transports, Steffen Bilger, rappelant que “plus d’un millier d’accidents surviennent chaque année à cause de l’utilisation d’appareils électroniques, comme les téléphones portables, au volant et ce chiffre est en constante augmentation”. Selon l’ADAC, lire un SMS durant deux secondes équivaut à parcourir 30 mètres à l’aveugle à 50 km/h, et près de 72 mètres à 130 km/h sur autoroute.
Côté sanctions, le barème allemand prévoit une amende de base de 100 € assortie du retrait d’un point, pouvant grimper à 150 €, deux points en moins et un mois de suspension si le conducteur a mis la vie d’autrui en danger. Des peines qui demeurent moins lourdes qu’en France, où les radars ne détectent pas encore l’usage du smartphone. Dans l’Hexagone, l’infraction entraîne un retrait systématique de quatre points et 135 € d’amende.
Surtout, l’usage du téléphone au volant expose désormais partout en France à une suspension administrative immédiate du permis de conduire. D’une durée de 15 jours à six mois, cette sanction prononcée directement par le préfet, sans passer par un juge, a récemment été généralisée à l’ensemble des départements.

articles.title: McDonald's demandó por una herramienta de IA que recomienda precios a los franquiciados en EE. UU.
articles.text:
McDonald’s se enfrenta a una demanda en Estados Unidos por una herramienta de IA que lleva años utilizando para recomendar los precios de sus productos. Al parecer, el sistema analiza información sobre las ventas de cada establecimiento, su ubicación y los precios de la competencia, y tras eso calcula cuánto debería costar cada artículo del menú.
Sin embargo, un consumidor de Illinois considera que esta tecnología podría estar facilitando la coordinación de precios entre restaurantes que deberían competir de manera independiente aunque pertenecen a la misma cadena. La demanda, presentada el 2 de octubre por Michael Thomas, sostiene que McDonald’s utiliza datos comerciales que normalmente no compartirían unos franquiciados con otros, incluidos los resultados de ventas de cada local.
Según recoge Reuters, el denunciante acusa a la empresa de aprovechar esa información para recomendar precios que podrían reducir la competencia y, al mismo tiempo, encarecer los productos. Thomas, que suele comprar una hamburguesa con queso, patatas y un refresco, comenzó a cuestionarse el funcionamiento del sistema al toparse con diferencias de precios entre restaurantes cercanos.
McDonald’s asegura que la IA no decide los precios de sus restaurantes
La compañía ha rechazado las acusaciones y asegura que sus herramientas solo ofrecen recomendaciones que los franquiciados pueden aceptar o ignorar. En un comunicado publicado en su web, McDonald’s insiste en que no utiliza precios dinámicos y que la IA tampoco modifica de manera automática lo que paga cada cliente.
En este escenario, la empresa recuerda que cerca del 95 % de sus 14.000 restaurantes estadounidenses están gestionados por franquiciados, o lo que es lo mismo, responsables de establecer sus propias tarifas. El problema (según los demandantes) es que McDonald’s tendría suficiente influencia sobre esos establecimientos como para presionarlos a seguir las recomendaciones del sistema, y una investigación previa de Reuters ya había señalado que algunos franquiciados percibían esa presión. Sea como fuere, la compañía rechazó dicha interpretación.
Así, la demanda solicita que el procedimiento pueda representar a otros consumidores afectados y reclama una indemnización, pero todavía no existe una resolución judicial que determine si la herramienta ha servido realmente para coordinar precios.

articles.title: Bitcoin: cómo se ha movido en el mercado este día
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Valor de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
Mientras el debate se acalora cada día más sobre la conveniencia o no de su uso, bitcoin cotiza este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) en 75729.11 USD, lo que supone un cambio de -4.77% con respecto a las últimas 24 horas y una variación de 0.0% con referencia a su valor alcanzado en la última hora.
En cuanto a su capitalización de mercado, ha mantenido el puesto #1 entre las monedas digitales.
Bitcoin alcanza un nuevo récord y lidera el auge en el mercado de las criptomonedas
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: El primer sistema Mesh WiFi 8 del mundo ya es oficial: ASUS presenta el ZenWiFi BN12 con ambiciones de gama alta
articles.text:
La evolución de las redes domésticas inalámbricas sigue su curso y, tras la masificación del WiFi 7, la industria ya empieza a tantear el siguiente estándar. Asus ha anunciado el lanzamiento del Asus ZenWiFi BN12, un sistema de red mallada (Mesh) que se posiciona como la primera solución comercial del mundo basada en la tecnología WiFi 8.
Más allá de la cifra comercial de velocidad y de las especificaciones sobre el papel, este lanzamiento sirve para entender hacia dónde evoluciona la conectividad en el hogar hiperconectado: menos obsesión exclusiva con el pico de velociddad bruta y más énfasis en la estabilidad a media y larga distancia, la gestión del tráfico y la convivencia con decenas de dispositivos IoT. El Asus ZenWiFi BN12 ya está disponible en el mercado español con un precio de venta de 1.205,12 euros.
ASUS Zenwifi BN12, para módem Operador y ONT, WiFi 8, Blanco, 2 Unidades
¿Qué supone dar el salto al WiFi 8 en un sistema Mesh?
El ZenWiFi BN12 es un equipo de tres bandas capaz de alcanzar una velocidad combinada de hasta 19 Gbps. Sin embargo, la verdadera carta de presentación de este estándar no es solo que la cifra de pico sea alta, sino las tecnologías de transmisión que integra para solucionar los problemas clásicos de cobertura en casas grandes o con obstáculos arquitectónicos.
Cuenta con nuevas modulaciones y codificación (MCS) y modulación desigual (UEQM), diseñadas para mantener el tipo cuando la señal atraviesa tabiques o se encuentra a varios metros del nodo principal.
El acceso a canales no primarios (NPCA) y coordinación entre puntos de acceso permiten que los nodos se comuniquen entre sí de forma más limpia, reduciendo la congestión en entornos saturados de redes vecinas.
Además, este router incluye Smart AiMesh, una evolución del sistema de nodos de la marca que combina el mallado tradicional con las directrices del WiFi 8 para optimizar el enlace de retorno (backhaul). Según los datos facilitados por la marca, un pack de dos unidades está pensado para cubrir grandes superficies de hasta 7.000 metros cuadrados.
Gestión inteligente y control del tráfico
En una casa actual no solo importa la velocidad de bajada de la fibra, sino cómo se reparte el ancho de banda cuando varios miembros de la familia hacen videollamadas de trabajo, juegan online, descargan archivos pesados y manejan docenas de bombillas, enchufes o cámaras de vigilancia al mismo tiempo.
Para lidiar con esto, el equipo introduce el concepto de QoE (Calidad de Experiencia) adaptativa. A diferencia de las herramientas de QoS tradicionales (que suelen depender de reglas estáticas y prioridades predefinidas por el usuario), este sistema supervisa el tráfico en tiempo real y redistribuye los recursos dinámicamente según lo que demanden las aplicaciones en cada milisegundo.
Además, incluye la herramienta WiFi Insight, una utilidad orientada a visualizar el estado de la red en tiempo real, auditar interferencias de todo el espectro y consultar un registro histórico de 24 horas para detectar cuellos de botella o anomalías en la señal.
Conectividad física y seguridad
En el plano del hardware cableado, el sistema no escatima en puertos de alta velocidad, algo fundamental si se quiere aprovechar el backhaul por cable o conectar un NAS o un PC de alto rendimiento y cuenta con un amplio apartado de conectividad con:
- Dos puertos Ethernet de 10 Gbps (uno para WAM/LAN y otro dedicado a LAN).
- Tres puertos Ethernet de 2,5 Gbps (uno para WAN/LAN y dos para LAN).
- Un puerto USB-A a 5 Gbps.
Todo ello viene respaldado por el ecosistema de seguridad de la casa, que incluye la plataforma de protección AiProtection, opciones de navegación segura, controles parentales avanzados, DNS protegido y compatibilidad nativa con VPN.

articles.title: Optasia is betting bigger on microfinance a year after listing
articles.text:
One year after its R23.5 billion ($1.4 billion) debut on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), Africa’s biggest securities market, Optasia is growing faster than expected. But its biggest opportunity may lie beyond the airtime advances that built its business.
The pan-African-listed fintech generated $270 million in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% year on year, as it accelerated its shift towards microfinance. The business uses artificial intelligence (AI) and alternative data to extend credit to underserved consumers. It now wants more than 80% of its revenue to come from microfinance solutions.
Across the continent, millions earn money through informal businesses and gig work but remain excluded from conventional lending because they lack payslips, formal credit histories or assets to serve as collateral. Fintechs use mobile transaction histories, behavioural patterns and machine learning to assess these customers.
Optasia’s ambitions extend beyond consumer loans to merchant financing and working capital for small businesses. But widening access to credit also raises questions about affordability, responsible lending and over-indebtedness.
“The company started with airtime credit, and we did a fantastic job in that space. However, airtime credit is essentially a convenience product,” Salvador Anglada, its chief executive, told TechCabal in an interview on Thursday.
He said the company has shifted focus towards meeting the broader borrowing needs of consumers and small businesses overlooked by traditional lenders. Only 7% of adults in sub-Saharan Africa borrowed from mobile money providers in 2024, yet these providers accounted for nearly 60% of all formal borrowing in the region, according to the World Bank’s Global Findex Database 2025.
“Microfinance services represent a much broader opportunity. They reveal the extent of the demand among people who have never had access to financial services,” said Anglada.
Optasia built its business by allowing mobile subscribers to access airtime advances when they did not have enough money to top up their phones. Its platform has since evolved into a digital financial services business that enables telecommunications companies, banks and other partners to distribute credit.
Microfinance is now central to its growth strategy. In the first nine months of 2026, the segment contributed $194 million, about 72% of group revenue. Airtime credit contributed $75 million.
Anglada said demand came from consumers who need short-term financing and small businesses that struggle to secure conventional bank loans.
“Many small businesses cannot access financial services or loans because they lack the formal structures and documentation traditional lenders require,” he said. “We are building products to address these gaps.”
Anglada points to Pakistan as one of its strongest markets outside the continent, while Ghana, Uganda, Zambia and other West African markets are also recording increased demand.
Traditional lenders typically rely on payslips, credit histories, property ownership and other formal indicators to determine whether someone qualifies for a loan. These requirements can exclude people with irregular incomes who may still repay.
Optasia uses alternative data and machine learning to identify behavioural patterns to establish creditworthiness.
“What we do is identify what we call the signals of the market. These are signals that exist but are not necessarily formalised. We capture them through data and use them to develop features and identify patterns relating to individuals,” Anglada said.
He says the company has developed more than 100,000 features per person, selecting relevant combinations to build a picture of each customer’s behaviour and risk profile.
The objective, he explained, is not simply to determine whether someone qualifies for credit, but to establish how much they can borrow without defaulting and what they can realistically afford to repay.
Optasia’s expansion is taking place under public-market scrutiny. The company listed on the JSE in November 2025, in an initial public offering (IPO) that valued it at R23.5 billion ($1.4 billion).
Reflecting on its first year as a listed business, Anglada says its financial performance has exceeded expectations set at listing.
“Our first-half results in September showed growth of close to 60%. We have also issued a trading update this week covering the first nine months of the year, with revenue growth of approximately 45%,” he said.
He added that both growth and profitability were performing above the guidance provided at the time of the IPO.
Operating as a public company has also changed how Optasia manages its business. Anglada said it has strengthened its regulatory and compliance functions, introduced board committees, and expanded its investor relations capabilities.

articles.title: Edera's Object Capability Bounded Authority Promises to Isolate Credentials From AI Agent Workloads
articles.text:
Promising to secure autonomous AI agent workloads, Edera has launched Object Capability Bounded Authority, a security model that isolates autonomous AI workloads and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers from sensitive credentials. Led by Edera co-founder and distinguished engineer Ariadne Conill, known for her contributions to low-level open-source security, the technology tackles one of modern enterprise architecture's most urgent challenges by enforcing granular object capabilities directly at the hypervisor level, keeping AI agents strictly contained without handing them standard access credentials. The Object Capability Bounded Authority is a security model that isolates autonomous AI workloads and MCPl servers from sensitive credentials while enforcing granular access controls.
As organisations increasingly deploy autonomous coding agents and external tool integrations into production, they routinely expose sensitive API tokens, cloud keys, and administrative access credentials directly to execution environments that remain vulnerable to prompt injection and supply chain manipulation.
Bounded Authority's core architecture decouples the operational authority needed to perform a task from the underlying credentials required to execute it. Traditional container security relies heavily on boundary isolation combined with static secrets injected into environment variables or configuration files. If an LLM-driven agent is compromised, attackers can typically extract those tokens and pivot laterally across internal systems. Edera proposes addressing this with hypervisor-enforced object capabilities that restrict an agent to narrowly defined actions without placing secrets inside the workload itself. For instance, an AI coding assistant can be authorised to modify a single GitHub repository without a personal access token, ensuring any compromise remains strictly bounded to that context.
To achieve this granular isolation, several runtime components are integrated into its Agent Runtime framework. Credential-free API access is handled by capcurl, routing authorised requests through an isolated broker while keeping the underlying authentication material hidden from the agent. Similarly, capsudo manages scoped command execution, allowing workloads to run specific privileged commands without acquiring standing administrative privileges or root access. Workload identity is cryptographically verified using SPIFFE and SPIRE integrations, establishing mutual TLS connections and service identities without relying on long-lived static secrets.
These architectural mechanisms extend directly to Model Context Protocol servers, which frequently act as high-value targets by bridging large language models with enterprise tools and databases. By defining explicit object capabilities at the infrastructure layer, security teams can restrict an MCP server to specific external resources and commands, preventing unchecked access even if the host model behaves unexpectedly or encounters a prompt injection vulnerability. This approach complements hardware-enforced runtime isolation by shrinking the blast radius of potential compromises from environment-wide access down to discrete, task-specific actions.
Engineering teams evaluating autonomous agents often spend significant development effort building custom credential-handling middleware and ad hoc permission proxies. The Bounded Authority promises to shift this enforcement mechanism into the hypervisor and runtime layers, standardising how enterprise systems provision authority to non-deterministic software. Initial functionality, focused on scoped command execution and workload identity, was released, with credential-brokered API access and deep orchestrator integrations to follow as part of the broader Project Lunchbox initiative.

articles.title: Wie lange bekommt meine Fritzbox noch Updates? Diese Tabelle verrät es dir
articles.text:
Support bis 2033: Diese Tabelle zeigt, wie lange deine Fritzbox noch Updates bekommt
Fast jedes Update bringt neue Funktionen auf Router, Repeater und andere Geräte von Fritz. Die FritzOS-Version 8.4o bringt etwa einen DNS-Filter auf Fritzboxen, mit dem sich bestimmte Werbeanzeigen, etwa auf Smart-TVs, ausblenden lassen. Die nächste Aktualisierung, FritzOS 8.50, steht auch schon für mehrere Router bereit. Doch wie lange geht das noch so? Nicht nur Smartphone-Besitzer:innen wissen, dass es irgendwann ein Ende hat mit dem Software-Support.
Bei Routern kann der besonders schwer wiegen, wenn kritische Sicherheitslücken nicht mehr geschlossen werden. Schon mehr als einmal hat ein Hersteller in diesem Fall zur Entsorgung geraten. Allerdings lässt sich schwer vorhersagen, wann ein Router oder entsprechendes Zubehör keine Updates mehr bekommt. Fritz hat deswegen für seine Kund:innen eine Liste veröffentlicht, die genau das beantwortet.
Fritz mit Software-Support bis in die 2030er
Die gute Nachricht: Wer ein halbwegs aktuelles Modell besitzt, muss sich in naher Zukunft keine Sorgen machen, plötzlich ohne Software-Updates darzustehen. Viele aktuelle Modelle unterstützt Fritz bis Anfang 2033. Seid ihr mit eurem jeweiligen WLAN-Standard zufrieden, braucht ihr euch also noch mindestens fünf Jahre keine Gedanken um einen Router-Neukauf zu machen. Bei einigen wenigen Modellen läuft dieser Updatezeitraum am 1. Januar oder Oktober 2032 aus. Selbst das ist aber mehr als genug Zeit, um sich Gedanken über das nächste Modell zu machen. articles.title: US Agencies Urge Organizations to Harden Refrigeration Controllers
articles.text:
The US government is urging healthcare, chemical, food, and transportation organizations to harden their industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems.
Over the past weeks, threat actors have been hacking monitoring systems to tamper with fridges and freezers in supermarkets and blood banks across Europe, causing millions in losses.
Hundreds of supermarkets were hit on October 11, when the attackers turned the temperatures in fridges to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and set freezers to defrost, spoiling food and, in some cases, causing fires.
A second wave of attacks hit more than 100 supermarkets and a blood bank this week, but only supermarkets suffered losses. Quick action from staff prevented the compromise of blood products and samples, the French Blood Establishment (EFS) said.
Russian hacktivist groups such as Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance reportedly claimed hacking Danfoss, leading to speculation that they mounted the supermarket attacks. However, nothing has been confirmed, and Iranian hacktivists or state-sponsored hackers may also be responsible, BBC notes.
CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA, and DoT say they “are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.”
“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies note (PDF).
Hackers may exploit authentication bypasses, code injection, and weak configurations to access the management systems and tamper with refrigerator and cold storage systems’ temperature or cause denial-of-view conditions, the agencies say.
According to internet intelligence firm Censys, out of 6,695 internet-exposed refrigeration controllers identified on October 9, only 3,124 (or 47%) remain accessible from the web as of November 5.
The company’s analysis covers the widely used Copeland/Dixell XWEB and Danfoss StoreView controllers: XWEB exposure dropped 35% (3,708 to 2,420), while StoreView dropped 76% (3,004 to 708).
Per the US government’s recommendations, taking the control systems off the internet is the best action organizations can take to prevent attacks. If web access is necessary, these systems should be protected by a firewall or edge device.
Organizations should also isolate OT devices, restrict access to trusted identities, enforce strong password policies and phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, keep systems updated, maintain backups offsite, and enable logging and monitoring.

articles.title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Greenlight Financial resolves more than 90 percent of up to 4,000 security and risk cases each month without human intervention. Greenlight’s Luna uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, infrastructure for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale. Specifically, Greenlight uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to host Luna’s agent code. It uses AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to support its tiered multi-agent system. This avoids the need to build and operate these capabilities in-house. Luna triages dark web breach-card alerts, identity anomalies, and financial-risk events in seconds.
This post explains how Greenlight Financial built an autonomous security operations center (SOC) solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover its multi-tiered supervisor architecture, more than 30 specialized agents, episodic memory for continuous learning, and expansion from SOC use cases into financial risk triage. We share production metrics, infrastructure decisions, and patterns for building autonomous security operations in regulated industries.
What Greenlight needed to solve
Greenlight Financial provides financial products for families: debit cards, savings tools, and connected devices such as the Family Hub and Pet Tracker. The company processes sensitive financial data at scale under the same regulatory requirements as major banks.
Greenlight’s SOC receives 3,000–4,000 security and risk alerts per month from four primary vectors:
- Dark web breach cards – Card Network and internal threat intel flag Greenlight customer cards found on the dark web.
- Identity and access anomalies – Unusual login patterns, privilege escalations, and policy violations across Identity Provider (IdP) and internal systems.
- Infrastructure alerts – Signals from Signals from EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), Asset Inventory, and other observability tools.
- Financial risk events – Suspicious transaction patterns, compliance triggers, and fraud indicators from card processing systems.
Each alert demands cross-referencing multiple data sources before an analyst can render a verdict. A single dark web breach card notification requires checking whether the card is active, deduplicating against prior notifications, reviewing customer session data, and checking open support tickets. This workflow takes a human analyst 15-30 minutes per case. At 4,000 cases per month, that math breaks.
Greenlight needed a system that could:
- Triage and resolve routine cases autonomously at machine speed.
- Escalate complex cases with full context to human analysts.
- Learn from resolution patterns to improve accuracy over time.
- Operate within financial services compliance guardrails.
Architecture: Tiered multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Greenlight built Luna as a hierarchical multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture follows a tiered supervisor pattern that mirrors how human SOC teams operate. L1 handles volume, and L2 handles complexity.
Tier 1 supervisor: High-volume triage
Tier 1 supervisor uses an advanced language model available through Amazon Bedrock running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The runtime uses private subnets and direct code deployment through a ZIP file and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). It handles initial triage of incoming cases by orchestrating more than 30 specialized agents:
| Domain | What the agent does | 
| Identity and Access | Checks login history, MFA status, session anomalies | 
| Endpoint Detection | Pulls endpoint alerts, process trees, IOC matches | 
| Observability | Correlates infrastructure metrics with alert timing | 
| Asset Inventory | Maps affected assets, ownership, exposure surface | 
| Data Analytics | Queries historical patterns and baseline deviations | 
| Payment Processing | Verifies card status, transaction history, account state | 
| Customer Experience | Reviews customer session behavior around incident time | 
| Customer Support | Checks related open tickets, prior complaints | 
| Code and Repositories | Traces code changes correlated with alerts | 
| Project Tracking | Links incidents to recent deployments or known issues | 
| Threat Intelligence | Enriches IOCs with external threat context | 
| Automation (SOAR) | Executes approved remediation playbooks | 
The Tier 1 supervisor receives cases through two paths: Amazon API Gateway, which exposes the Luna Queue API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint, and Tines SOAR for automated alert ingestion. It determines which specialized agents to invoke based on alert type, synthesizes their findings, and renders a verdict. The median triage time for routine cases is single-digit seconds.
Tier 2 supervisor: Deep-dive investigation
Cases that exceed Tier 1’s confidence threshold escalate to a Tier 2 supervisor using an advanced foundation model on Amazon Bedrock with extended reasoning capabilities. This agent handles the 10 percent of cases that require multi-step reasoning:
- Re-investigates escalated cases with deeper cross-source correlation.
- Invokes specialized agents through boto3 with expanded context windows.
- Chains reasoning across 3–5 data sources to establish causality.
- Produces detailed investigation reports with evidence chains for human review.
The Tier 2 supervisor runs on a scheduled basis, using Amazon EventBridge rate triggers and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) queue completions to batch-process escalated cases, and on demand for urgent Tier 1-escalated cases.
Entry points for different personas
Different teams engage Luna in different ways, so the application exposes three entry points. These range from fully automated alert ingestion to interactive, on-demand investigation. Each entry point maps to a persona and how their work arrives:
- Tines SOAR – Primary volume driver. Automated alert ingestion feeds cases directly into Tier 1.
- Security, Risk, and ProdOps engineers – Direct API access for ad-hoc investigation requests.
- Claude Desktop extension – Chat-based interface for on-call engineers. An engineer opens the extension, describes what they want investigated, and Luna executes a deep-dive with full tool access.
Memory and learning: How Luna gets smarter over time
The memory layer is built on AgentCore memory. This layer is what separates Luna from a stateless triage tool. It supports pattern recognition, deduplication, and continuous accuracy improvement.
Episodic memory (30-day rolling window)
Stores recent events and resolution outcomes. When a new alert arrives, Luna checks: “Have I seen this pattern in the last 30 days? What was the verdict? Is this a known behavior that I should allowlist?”
Concrete example: A Greenlight infrastructure role generates a specific access pattern every Tuesday at 3 AM for scheduled maintenance. Without memory, Luna would flag this every week. With episodic memory, Luna learned after the first resolution that this pattern is expected and auto-allowlists it.
Long-term memory
Persists semantic preferences and resolution templates beyond the 30-day window:
- “This access pattern is expected because that’s the role’s purpose.”
- Greenlight’s historical case data shows “Cards from this specific dark web source have a 73 percent false-positive rate – prioritize deduplication.”
- Resolution templates for recurring case types that encode institutional knowledge.
Case-learnings pipeline
A dedicated pipeline feeds resolution outcomes back into the system:
- Ingestion – An AWS Lambda function captures every case resolution from Tines events.
- Learnings + Dedup – DynamoDB stores resolution patterns and deduplicates similar cases. When Luna resolves a case the same way three times, it records that as a confirmed pattern.
- Digest – A Lambda function processes new learnings into actionable context that supervisors consume at inference time.
- Feedback loop – Resolution learnings feed back into Tier 1, improving first-pass accuracy incrementally.
This pipeline drove Luna’s autonomous resolution rate from 83 percent (Tier 1 only) to more than 90 percent (Tier 1, Tier 2, and learnings).
Expanding from SOC into financial risk triage
Greenlight expanded Luna into financial risk assessment within two months of the SOC deployment. The architectural changes were minimal: new specialized agents and a risk-domain supervisor layered onto the existing infrastructure.
Dark web breach card workflow
When a Greenlight customer card appears on the dark web, Luna executes this workflow autonomously:
- Ingest – Threat intel providers (Mastercard, internal feeds) report compromised card numbers.
- Verify – Luna queries Galileo: Does this card belong to Greenlight? Is it currently active? What’s the recent transaction history?
- Deduplicate – DynamoDB check: Is this a repeat notification? Has this card already been remediated? Multiple providers often report the same breach.
- Cross-reference – Query Mixpanel for customer session anomalies, Zendesk for related tickets, and internal fraud scoring.
- Assess and act – Determine risk levels. Low risk: log and monitor. Medium risk: flag for review. High risk: escalate to human analysts with full evidence chain.
Greenlight receives hundreds of breach card notifications daily. Luna processes each in seconds. A human analyst doing the same work, logging into Galileo, checking DynamoDB, opening Mixpanel, searching Zendesk, takes 15-30 minutes per card.
Results
The following table tracks Greenlight’s security operations on the metrics that matter most to the SOC. It compares three stages: manual triage before Luna, Tier 1 automation, and the full Tier 1 and Tier 2 system.
| Metric | Before Luna | With Tier 1 | With Tier 1 and Tier 2 | 
| Autonomous resolution rate | 0% (all manual) | 83% | More than 90% | 
| Cases processed per month | 3,000-4,000 | 3,000-4,000 | 3,000-4,000 | 
| Median time-to-triage (routine) | 15-30 minutes | Seconds | Seconds | 
| Human analyst escalations | 100% of cases | 17% | <10% | 
| Cost avoidance | Baseline | Significant | Equivalent of multiple full-time employees | 
| Risk reduction | Baseline | Faster detection | Consistent 24/7 quality | 
Estimated analyst time avoided:
Based on Greenlight’s case volume and manual handling-time measurements, processing 4,000 cases at 15–30 minutes each would require approximately 1,000–2,000 analyst hours per month. Greenlight reports that Luna autonomously resolves more than 90 percent of these cases, avoiding an estimated 900–1,800 hours of routine manual work each month. Analysts can focus instead on cases that require human judgment.
The risk reduction comes from two factors: speed (seconds compared to minutes reduces the exposure window) and consistency (Luna applies the same triage logic at 3 AM on Saturday that it does at 10 AM on Tuesday, with no fatigue and no shortcuts).
Five lessons from building Luna
Building Luna and expanding it from security operations into financial risk surfaced five lessons for teams building multi-agent systems in regulated environments:
1. Start with a bounded domain, then expand horizontally
Greenlight started with security triage because the success criteria were clear: resolve the case correctly or escalate. After the pattern proved reliable at 83 percent resolution, expanding financial risk required adding new specialized agents and a risk-domain supervisor, not rebuilding the architecture.
2. Mirror your human team structure
The Tier 1/Tier 2 pattern maps directly to how SOC teams already operate. L1 analysts handle volume with playbooks. L2 analysts handle the complex cases with investigation skills. This made trust-building with the security team faster. They understood the model intuitively because it matched their own escalation logic.
3. Memory compounds in value
The episodic and long-term memory layer is what moved Luna from 83 percent to more than 90 percent. Each resolved case teaches Luna something: a new allowlisted pattern, a confirmed false positive source, a resolution template. After 6 months of operation, Luna has accumulated institutional knowledge that would take a new human analyst months to build.
4. Triage first, action later
In a regulated environment, Greenlight designed Luna to triage and recommend, not to take autonomous remediation actions without explicit policy approval. The risk expansion follows the same principle. Luna provides evidence supporting its recommendation. In this human-in-the-loop model, a human analyst or an approved automated policy authorizes and executes remediation. This separation satisfied Greenlight’s compliance requirements and built trust with the risk team.
5. Share specialized agents across domains
When Greenlight expanded into financial risk, they reused existing specialized agents (Datadog, Zendesk, Mixpanel) and added domain-specific ones (Galileo, fraud scoring). The same agent that checks Zendesk tickets for security cases also checks them for risk cases. This reduces maintenance overhead and helps keep consistency across domains.
Infrastructure stack
Luna runs entirely on managed AWS services. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the orchestration runtime, and the rest of the stack handles scheduling, messaging, state, secrets, and integration. The following table lists each service and its role in the infrastructure:
| Service | Role | 
| Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Multi-agent orchestration runtime. VPC deployment, private subnets, direct code through ZIP and S3 | 
| Amazon EventBridge | Scheduled rate-based triggers for Tier 2 deep-dive triage cycles | 
| Amazon SNS | Queue completions and notification routing between tiers | 
| Amazon DynamoDB | Learnings storage, case deduplication, resolution pattern persistence | 
| Amazon S3 | Agent packages and Terraform state management | 
| Amazon CloudWatch Logs | 30-day retention for audit trails and compliance evidence | 
| AWS Secrets Manager | External API credentials | 
| AWS Lambda | Ingestion, resolution post-processing, kickoff, and digest functions | 
| Amazon API Gateway | Luna Queue API and MCP endpoint for external integrations | 
What Greenlight is building next
Building on the security and risk foundation, Greenlight is extending Luna’s multi-agent pattern into new operational domains and tooling:
- Full risk domain coverage – Autonomous triage for financial and business risk cases (in progress, launched about one month ago).
- Product operations – Exploring AWS DevOps Agent for incident investigation, root-cause analysis, and mitigation guidance. Greenlight is also evaluating how Luna’s existing agents could support operational investigations where their capabilities overlap.
- Custom operational workflows – Exploring AWS DevOps Agent custom agents, skills, and Model Context Protocol integrations for repeatable operational workflows and access to Greenlight’s internal tools.
- AWS DevOps Agent and skills – Combining the UI and skills framework of AWS DevOps Agent for script execution workflows (90-second execution time limit).
- Well-Architected reviews – Exploring Model Context Protocol servers for automated infrastructure assessments against AWS best practices.
Conclusion
According to Greenlight’s production measurements, Luna autonomously resolves more than 90 percent of the company’s security and risk cases and processes up to 4,000 cases each month. Cases requiring additional judgment are escalated to human analysts. This human-in-the-loop approach allows Greenlight to automate routine triage while retaining control over remediation decisions.
Teams in other regulated industries can apply the same approach by starting with a bounded use case, defining clear escalation criteria, and adding specialized agents and memory as the system matures. After the initial pattern proves reliable, teams can extend it to related operational domains.
To learn more, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.

articles.title: Opinion: Canada needs a better definition of what makes a company Canadian | BetaKit
articles.text:
On Wednesday, non-partisan public policy institute The Canadian Shield Institute published a policy paper titled “Canadian Dupes: A Better Definition for Real Canadian Companies.” With the Institute’s permission, an edited excerpt from that paper appears below.
“We will be our own best customer,” Prime Minister Mark Carney declared in November 2025, when he announced plans to implement a Buy Canadian Policy as part of the federal budget. But how do you define a Canadian company?
Canada already has a heap of different definitions, and in the past year the government introduced two new policies that each include their own definition of a Canadian company.
“Only a few years ago, the idea of implementing a national Buy Canadian policy was seen as distasteful and parochial. Today, it seems like a natural response to rising trade tensions.”
However, these new procurement policies are among the weakest in terms of defining a Canadian company. The Buy Canadian Policy primarily concerns itself with Canadian supplier materials and whether a company is incorporated in Canada and paying taxes here. By this definition, Walmart Canada or Microsoft Canada would count as Canadian. The Defence Investment Agency relies on the Strategic Partnership Framework definition, which is 161 words long and broadly defines a Canadian company as any company operating in Canada.
The situation is a bit of a mess.
The solution is actually quite simple: For the purposes of public funding, procurement, and strategic industrial policy, the cleanest way to define a Canadian company is simply to start by defining what is clearly not a Canadian company.
We suggest a simple definition: A Canadian company is a Canadian-headquartered firm that is not majority-controlled by a foreign parent or foreign government.
The problem
Inevitably, any time we’re trying to establish a definition of which companies count as authentically Canadian, the government is engaging in a policy project motivated by some kind of economic nationalism.
The economic strategy of Canada’s governments over the past 50 years or more has generally been to prioritize trade, foreign investment, and economic integration. The Buy Canadian Policy, for example, gives a company’s bid a 10-percent discount if it is incorporated in Canada with business operations here—but, of course, that includes local subsidiaries of foreign multinationals.
What we see in this is a policy aiming to encourage as much economic activity as possible without imposing a binary “Canadian vs. foreign” distinction. This light-touch approach may have been fine for the 20th century, but it does not address the most important aspect of the 21st-century economy.
Consulting firm Ocean Tomo estimates that 92 percent of the value of the S&P 500 was derived from intangible assets in 2025, whereas in 1975, only 17 percent of the value of the S&P 500 came from intangibles. These intangible assets move frictionlessly across borders. Patented innovations developed through research and development in one place can be commercialized globally. Wealth creation in the digital economy comes more from ownership and rents that are extracted from intangible assets.
Canada’s fixation on jobs as a primary qualifier for Canadian-ness misses the real engine of economic growth in the 21st century. This decades-long trend has only been supercharged by the recent explosion of AI.
Canada’s light-touch approach is also rooted in a geopolitical time when deeper integration with global supply chains was seen as reciprocal and positive. Put simply: The old definitions are rooted in an economy that no longer exists, and Canada urgently needs a different approach.
The solution
We initially sought to develop some kind of “gold standard” definition for what makes an authentically Canadian firm. Ultimately, there are good arguments to be made that an expansive definition of a Canadian firm should account for multiple factors:
- ownership;
- control;
- headquarters; and
- intellectual property and intangible assets.
Each of these factors captures something real about where value resides. But taken together they create a definition that is harder to administer, easier to contest, and more vulnerable to edge cases. A company can maintain a substantive headquarters in Canada while still being ultimately directed from elsewhere; It can hold important intellectual property here while remaining accountable to a foreign parent.
On the other hand, a Canadian company may take on foreign capital without ceasing to be meaningfully Canadian in every practical sense. In fact, the majority of a venture-backed company’s equity may be owned by foreign investors, but if none of those investors is the majority owner, the company is still functionally Canadian.
That is why we recommend a narrower and more operational rule: foreign subsidiaries should not be treated as “Canadian” firms for preferential access to procurement, public funding, or industrial support when the policy goal is to scale homegrown firms.
A Canadian company is a Canadian-headquartered firm that is not majority-controlled by a foreign parent or foreign government. Paying taxes here should not be enough to establish that a firm should receive preferential treatment intended to build Canadian capacity.
How Canada can implement a fix
Over time, the federal and provincial governments should exclude Canadian subsidiaries of foreign multinationals in all areas of law and policy where we have an existing definition of a Canadian company.
There are some immediate priority areas that the government can get to work on right away. The clearest place to elevate the bar for a Canadian firm is the Defence Industrial Strategy. This strategy is explicitly focused on strengthening Canada; moreover, Canada’s trade agreements have specific carve-outs for national security matters. The same logic should extend to the Buy Canadian procurement policy. When firms are assessed for Canadian-ness, we should not rely only on address and incorporation.
“When firms are assessed for Canadian-ness, we should not rely only on address and incorporation.”
The same definition should govern access to major business supports and economic development tools. Programs explicitly meant to build Canadian capacity should be designed to ensure that public money doesn’t unintentionally subsidize branch plant activity or help foreign parents capture Canadian talent, IP, or tax-supported commercialization. That same principle is especially relevant for innovation supports such as the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax credit.
The provinces and territories should mirror this approach. A common operating definition would ensure firms do not face one test federally and another test provincially.
The world is rapidly changing, and Canada’s national economic and geopolitical strategies need to adjust. Only a few years ago, the idea of implementing a national “Buy Canadian” policy was seen as distasteful and parochial. Today, it seems like a natural response to rising trade tensions. In the realm of digital sovereignty, we are more vividly aware than ever before of the importance of engaging strategically in global trade.
Our proposed standard will not resolve every edge case. But it would end the more serious error Canada makes today: treating foreign subsidiaries as domestic firms for the purposes of building Canadian capacity. If Buy Canadian is meant to mean anything, it has to start there.
The opinions and analysis expressed in the above article are those of its author, and do not necessarily reflect the position of BetaKit or its editorial staff. It has been edited for clarity, length, and style.

- 7 dicas para fotografar a lua com seu celular
Calendário fases da Lua em novembro de 2026
- Lua Minguante: dia 1, às 17h30
- Lua Nova: dia 9, às 4h02
- Lua Crescente: dia 17, às 8h48
- Lua Cheia: dia 24, às 11h55
O que é o ciclo lunar?
Uma lunação ou ciclo lunar, como é chamado o intervalo de tempo entre luas novas, é sutilmente variável, com média de duração de 29,5 dias. Durante esse período, ela passa pelas quatro fases principais (nova, crescente, cheia e minguante), e cada uma se prolonga por aproximadamente sete dias.
Também existem as “interfases”: quarto crescente e crescente gibosa (entre as fases nova e cheia) e minguante gibosa e quarto minguante (entre a cheia e a minguante).
Entenda cada fase da Lua
Lua Nova
Na Lua Nova, o satélite se posiciona entre a Terra e o Sol. Isso faz com que o lado iluminado da Lua fique voltado para o Sol, enquanto o lado escuro fica voltado para nós. Por esse motivo, a Lua não é visível no céu noturno. Essa fase marca o início de um novo ciclo lunar e está relacionada ao recomeço e a novas possibilidades.
Lua Crescente
Depois da Lua Nova, surge a fase Crescente. Aos poucos, uma pequena faixa iluminada começa a aparecer no céu, aumentando noite após noite. No início, vemos apenas um fino arco de luz, mas com o passar dos dias a parte iluminada cresce até que metade da Lua esteja visível, momento chamado de Quarto Crescente. Essa fase simboliza crescimento, desenvolvimento e a construção de novos caminhos.
Lua Cheia
Na Lua Cheia, a Terra se encontra entre o Sol e a Lua. Isso permite que o lado lunar voltado para nós receba luz por completo, tornando-se totalmente visível e brilhante no céu. É o período de maior intensidade luminosa, quando a Lua nasce no horizonte exatamente no momento em que o Sol se põe. A Lua Cheia é associada à plenitude, ao auge de processos e à energia em seu ponto máximo.
Lua Minguante
Após a Lua Cheia, a luz da Lua começa a diminuir gradualmente. A cada noite, vemos menos da sua superfície iluminada. Quando apenas metade dela está visível, ocorre o Quarto Minguante, fase oposta ao Quarto Crescente. A Lua continua a perder luminosidade até chegar novamente à Lua Nova, reiniciando o ciclo. A fase Minguante simboliza reflexão, encerramento e preparação para novos começos.
Qual a fase da Lua hoje?
Hoje a Lua está na fase Minguante.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned by Congress over Chinese espionage concerns
articles.text:
Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.
“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.
The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.
Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
