articles.title: MacBook Pro with M6 review - brilliant combination of speed, performance and battery efficiency - Tech Guide
articles.text:
- RATING
The MacBook Pro continues to prove itself as the ultimate pro laptop for users who work hard and play hard. With the new M6 chip on board it adds even more power, performance and efficiency to your workflow.
Apple’s new MacBook Pro with M6 is a workhorse laptop that is now even more powerful and versatile with greater access to Siri AI and Apple Intelligence to really supercharge your workflows.
Tech Guide received the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 for our review. It is also available in a 16-inch version.
This is Apple’s annual upgrade of the MacBook Pro with its latest silicon. In this case the M6 which includes an advanced 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core and a 12-core GPU that offers up to 30 per cent faster graphics and up to 25 per cent faster AI workloads than the M5.
That’s a remarkable upgrade from last year’s device.
Customers tend to hold onto laptops for a lot longer than they do their smartphones so it could be several years between upgrades.
With that in mind you can imagine the improvement a customer will see with the MacBook Pro with M6 if they’re upgrading even from the M4 and other earlier laptops.
Apple released the MacBook Pro with M1 back in 2020 and that’s probably served users well since then.
So for those customers, upgrading to the MacBook Pro with M6 would be an absolute game changer.
For example, on-device AI on the new MacBook Pro with M6 is 13 times faster than on the M1.
Design-wise the MacBook Pro with M6 is identical to the previous model.
This is a move we applaud because the current design works.
The MacBook Pro is not that heavy (1.55kg) or too thick (1.55cm) and it’s still very easily portable.
It has a stunning 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display with 1,600 nits of peak HDR brightness and a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
Everything you view on the screen, including your videos and photos, looks amazing.
Same thing with the applications you’re working on or the content you’re creating.
You will never tire of the quality of this amazing display.
But one difference there is from last year’s model is the price.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 started, when it was released in 2025, at $2,499.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $3,199.
But you are getting a better computer that’s faster and more power efficient.
For our review we put it to the test with some video and photo editing which gave us instant results and renders.
Our go-to video editing application is Final Cut Pro and editing videos with the MacBook Pro with M6 is effortless.
And the biggest improvement is when it comes to exporting the video, which could be up to 10GB in size.
Before, it would take several minutes but with the MacBook Pro with M6 it took less than a minute.
Here are some other improvements you can expect with the MacBook Pro with M6:
– Up to 13x faster time to first token performance for LLM prompt processing compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
– Up to 11.7x faster render performance with ray tracing in Blender compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
– Up to 3.3x faster image-processing performance in Affinity compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.2x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
– Up to 2.5x faster project build performance when compiling code in Xcode compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
With this much performance and power at your back, the MacBook Pro with M6 is also an incredible gaming computer as well.
Another welcome addition to the MacBook Pro with M6 is Wi-Fi 7 – finally! Wi-Fi connectivity is now faster and up to speed with today’s mesh routers
It also has Bluetooth 6 on board.
It also has two Thunderbolt 4 ports on the left side and another Thunderbolt 4 port on the right. There’s also an HDMI port and a memory card slot, plus a headphone jack.
And it uses the same brilliant MagSafe charging connection.
Another top feature of the MacBook Pro with M6 is its battery life runs for up to 24 hours on a single charge.
That’s 14 hours more than Intel-based MacBook Pros.
And the MacBook Pro with M6 charges faster as well and can get to 50% in just 30 minutes with a higher-wattage USB-C power adapter like the 96W Power Adapter.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is available now and is priced from $3,199.
The 16-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is also available now and starts at $4,799.
VERDICT
The MacBook Pro continues to prove itself as the ultimate pro laptop for users who work hard and play hard. With the new M6 chip on board it adds even more power, performance and efficiency to your workflow.

articles.title: Black Friday : Darty fait -300 € sur ce home cinéma sans fil 4.2.1 Hisense conçu avec Devialet et noté 9/10 — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les barres de son classiques ont souvent du mal à restituer une véritable sensation d’immersion, surtout quand elles se résument à une barre et un caisson de basses. C’est là qu’Hisense propose une bonne alternative avec son système HT Saturn développé en collaboration avec Devialet qui repose sur quatre enceintes satellites sans fil, un caisson de basses et un boîtier central qui distribue le signal audio. Le tout développe une puissance totale de 720 W pour profiter des bandes-son Dolby Atmos et DTS sans passer par un système 5.1 filaire. Darty profite du Black Friday pour le faire passer de 799 euros à 499,99 euros, alors que le système coûtait 1 500 euros à sa sortie.
Les atouts du Hisense HT Saturn
- Un son 360 degrés avec seulement 4 enceintes
- La calibration Devialet est efficace
- La puissance totale de 720 W avec l’architecture 4.1.2
À sa sortie, le Hisense HT Saturn coûtait 1 500 euros. Récemment, Darty le proposait pour 799 euros, mais là vous pouvez l’acheter pour 499,99 euros pendant le Black Friday.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le Hisense HT Saturn. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un vrai home cinéma 4.1.2 sans les contraintes du câblage
Le principal intérêt du Hisense HT Saturn, c’est de proposer une véritable installation home cinéma sans les contraintes habituelles d’un ensemble multicanal. Il se compose de quatre enceintes satellites identiques, d’un caisson de basses et d’un petit boîtier central qui fait office de hub. Les satellites peuvent être posés sur un meuble ou fixés au mur grâce aux supports fournis. Ils font 122 x 196 x 122 mm et s’intègrent discrètement dans un salon. Le caisson de basses adopte lui aussi un format discret et le hub peut être caché derrière votre téléviseur.
Sous cette apparence minimaliste, on a une architecture 4.1.2 qui développe jusqu’à 720 W de puissance. Chaque satellite embarque trois haut-parleurs, dont un transducteur orienté vers le plafond pour reproduire les effets verticaux du Dolby Atmos et du DTS. Il profite du traitement acoustique de Devialet et de sa technologie RoomFitting Tuning pour ajuster automatiquement la restitution en fonction de l’acoustique de la pièce. Le caisson, lui, est alimenté par une amplification de 280 W RMS. Pour les branchements, le hub rassemble deux entrées HDMI 2.1 compatibles 4K, une sortie HDMI eARC, une entrée optique et un port USB pour les mises à jour. Le Bluetooth 5.3 permet de diffuser de la musique depuis un smartphone ou une tablette.
Un son immersif et puissant convaincant au global
Sur le terrain, et c’est souligné dans notre test, le Hisense HT Saturn nous avait particulièrement convaincus. Son atout principal, c’est sa capacité à créer une véritable bulle sonore, avec une spatialisation convaincante pour un système d’apparence si compacte. Les haut-parleurs orientés vers le plafond parviennent à donner une vraie sensation de hauteur aux effets sonores. Et le caisson apporte de vraies basses physiques qui ne masquent pas les dialogues, c’est un vrai tour de force. Le système est même convaincant pour les jeux vidéo, avec une localisation précise des pas et autres effets audio qui permettent de réagir au quart de tour.
Mais voilà, tout n’est pas parfait et malgré ses qualités, le Hisense HT Saturn montre ses limites dans la spatialisation latérale et la largeur de sa scène surround. Surtout quand on le compare à des systèmes plus ambitieux comme le Sony Bravia Theatre Quad. Le caisson manque un peu d’assise dans les grandes pièces, les voix manquent parfois un peu de chaleur et il n’y a pas de Wi-Fi, d’AirPlay, de Chromecast ou d’app mobile pour piloter l’ensemble. Il faut se contenter du Bluetooth et de la télécommande fournie. Mais malgré ces concessions et grâce à la baisse de prix, ça reste une solution intéressante pour retrouver les sensations d’une salle de cinéma à la maison.

articles.title: Airbnb prépare un agent de voyage IA pour planifier, réserver et gérer les imprévus
articles.text:
Airbnb veut vous accompagner dans la préparation d’un séjour, sa réservation et les problèmes rencontrés en cours de route grâce à un agent IA. Son déploiement doit commencer au premier semestre 2027, sans calendrier précisé pour la France.
Trouver un logement qui plaît à tout le monde, comparer les emplacements, vérifier les disponibilités : avant les vacances, il y a souvent quelques soirées de recherches. Airbnb veut simplifier ces étapes avec son propre agent IA, dont il vient de préciser le fonctionnement. L’idée est de vous aider à choisir et à réserver, puis de rester disponible lorsque le séjour ne se déroule pas comme prévu.
Une interface qui compose votre voyage avec des cartes, des photos et des comparatifs
Airbnb affirme ne pas croire qu’un chatbot classique soit la bonne manière de planifier un voyage. Le service décrit plutôt une interface construite autour de la demande du voyageur. L’agent puisera dans une bibliothèque de centaines d’éléments — cartes, photos, comparatifs, calendriers et itinéraires — pour les assembler en temps réel selon les besoins.
La plateforme défend ainsi une approche plus visuelle que celle d’un chatbot classique. Chercher une maison pour les vacances ne se résume pas à obtenir une adresse : on regarde les chambres, on vérifie la distance avec la plage et on envoie les favoris aux personnes qui partent avec nous. Airbnb veut conserver cette exploration, tout en aidant à trier les possibilités et à passer à la réservation.
Cette orientation prolonge la recherche en langage naturel et les comparaisons de logements présentées cet automne. L’agent doit aller plus loin en réunissant l’exploration, les décisions prises avec ses compagnons de voyage et les actions dans l’application.
Après la réservation, une aide pour les changements et les imprévus
Airbnb entend aussi accompagner les voyageurs pour modifier une réservation, résoudre un problème de paiement, obtenir de l’aide pour un remboursement ou réserver à nouveau. La plateforme évoque également l’accès à son assistance de sécurité disponible 24 heures sur 24.
C’est sur ce terrain qu’elle revendique un avantage face aux agents généralistes. Airbnb gère déjà la réservation, le paiement et le service client : son agent pourra s’appuyer sur cette intégration pour aider à résoudre un problème. Pour le voyageur, l’intérêt serait de pouvoir passer d’une question sur son séjour à une action sur sa réservation dans le même service.
Cette proximité ne garantit toutefois pas que l’outil pourra tout régler seul. Les conditions d’annulation et de remboursement resteront déterminantes, et Airbnb ne détaille pas encore les validations demandées avant une modification ou une nouvelle réservation.
Lors de la présentation des résultats, Brian Chesky a également annoncé vouloir multiplier les intégrations avec des partenaires. À terme, l’objectif est de permettre des réservations dans toutes les catégories du voyage depuis Airbnb, sans calendrier fixé pour cette extension.
Le premier déploiement de l’agent doit commencer au premier semestre 2027. Les pays, les langues et le périmètre exact des fonctions accessibles au lancement restent à préciser : les voyageurs français devront encore patienter pour savoir quand ils pourront lui confier la préparation de leurs vacances.
- Le plus grand choix de logements au monde
- Variété des hébergements proposés
- Système d'avis authentiques

articles.title: AI-powered cyberattacks put Indian fintechs on alert; Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
articles.text:
AI-powered cyberattacks put Indian fintechs on alert; Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
An advisory from the government body said the AI-assisted financial threat is still active and warns BFSI entities to treat it as an “immediate and continuing threat”.
Dear Reader,
Investor appetite for India’s B2C ecommerce sector appears to be cooling. Funding fell 33% to $1.6 billion across 356 rounds between January and November 3, 2026, compared with $2.4 billion across 621 rounds in the year-ago period, according to Tracxn. Late-stage and seed-stage funding declined 51% and 50%, respectively, while early-stage investments remained relatively stable, growing 3%.
While investors are becoming more cautious, the AI infrastructure boom is facing a different challenge: rising public concerns over its impact on local communities. OpenAI has pledged to pay the full electricity costs of data centres it owns and operates, while committing to greater transparency around construction plans and community consultations.
Meanwhile, India's cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has warned of AI-driven attacks targeting fintech firms and NBFCs, with hackers exploiting payment systems to siphon off funds.
Cybersecurity concerns are also surfacing across global financial services. Binance has revoked all API keys linked to third-party trading platform SignalPlus following a potential security issue reported by the company. The exchange said its own systems and user funds remain safe, and advised affected users to review their trading positions before reconnecting.
The risks extend beyond financial services. A cyberattack targeting refrigeration control systems at three sites operated by France's national blood service raised storage temperatures for plasma and other blood products. Monitoring systems detected the breach in time, allowing staff to move supplies before any products were compromised. Authorities are investigating the incident.
In today’s newsletter:
- CERT-In flags AI-driven attacks on NBFCs, fintech firms
- Saraniya Periasamy’s journey at Agnikul Cosmos
- Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
Here’s your trivia for today: What is a 'zero-day' vulnerability in cybersecurity? (Scroll down for the answer)
Artificial Intelligence
CERT-In flags AI-driven attacks on NBFCs, fintech firms
AI-powered cyberattacks targeting India’s financial services sector are escalating, prompting a fresh warning from CERT-In. The government cybersecurity agency has flagged a campaign called CRAFTY FALCON, which uses AI tools to target NBFCs, fintech companies and other financial institutions. The attacks have involved exploiting payment systems and stealing cryptocurrency assets.
Key takeaways:
- CERT-In has identified an active campaign called CRAFTY FALCON, which uses machine intelligence and AI-assisted tools to target financial institutions.
- Attackers have exploited merchant settlement APIs to move funds and stolen wallet keys to siphon cryptocurrency assets.
- The campaign has affected NBFCs, digital lending platforms, payment aggregators, fintech firms and crypto exchanges, with CERT-In warning that the threat remains active.
Inspiration
Saraniya Periasamy’s journey at Agnikul Cosmos
From joining a space-tech startup with no prior experience in the sector to leading the development of an orbital launch vehicle, Saraniya Periasamy’s journey has been anything but conventional. As Agnikul Cosmos’ fourth employee, she has played a key role in the company’s efforts to build indigenous rocket technology. Today, as Executive Vice President and Vehicle Director, she is helping steer the development of Agnibaan while encouraging more women to explore careers in space-tech.
Breaking barriers:
- Saraniya joined Agnikul Cosmos eight years ago as a Systems Engineer and went on to lead the development of its Agnibaan SOrTeD suborbital mission, which successfully flew in May 2024.
- She is now leading the development of Agnibaan, the company's orbital launch vehicle, with plans to demonstrate booster recovery and reuse, alongside exploring ways to repurpose its upper stage.
- Having transitioned from civil engineering and ocean technology into space, Saraniya believes self-doubt is often a bigger barrier for women than a lack of opportunities.
Ecommerce
Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
Shiprocket turned profitable in Q2 FY27, reporting a net profit of Rs 60 lakh against a loss of Rs 20.3 crore a year ago, while revenue grew 35% to Rs 673.6 crore. Its emerging business, led by Martech and omnichannel solutions, grew 61% during the quarter. The company also repaid Rs 242 crore in borrowings following its IPO, ending the first half debt-free.
News & updates
- Ambulance pricing: Blinkit Ambulance will charge Rs 2,500 for non-emergency transfers, while emergency services will continue to remain free. Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal said the move aims to discourage routine hospital visits and transfers from using emergency ambulances, keeping them available for critical cases.
- Ronaldo retires: Cristiano Ronaldo will retire from Portugal's national team after the November international break, ending a 23-year international career. He leaves as men's international football's record goalscorer with 146 goals in 234 appearances, having led Portugal to the Euro 2016 title and two Nations League victories.
What is a 'zero-day' vulnerability in cybersecurity?
Answer: A security flaw that attackers can exploit before a fix is available

articles.title: Tesla dejará de fabricar la Cybertruck en Texas para producir su robotaxi
articles.text:
Tesla dejará de fabricar la Cybertruck en su planta de Texas alrededor de la mitad de 2027 para hacer lugar a más unidades del Cybercab, su vehículo sin conductor. Lo anunció el director ejecutivo, Elon Musk, en una publicación en la red social X el 6 de noviembre.
“Tesla estará reduciendo gradualmente la producción de la Cybertruck en Gigafactory Texas alrededor de mediados del año próximo para dar espacio a una mayor producción del Cybercab”, escribió en la red social.
Musk no precisó si la camioneta dejará de fabricarse del todo o si su producción se trasladará a otra planta. La fábrica de Austin es la única instalación conocida que ensambla la Cybertruck y que cuenta con el equipo para sus componentes especiales, según The Verge.
Wes Morrill, ingeniero jefe del proyecto, publicó en X una frase que la BBC interpretó como señal de que el modelo se discontinúa: “La Cybertruck fue una increíble plataforma de desarrollo tecnológico y sigue viva a través del Cybercab”.
Una camioneta lejos de las metas de Musk
Ante un seguidor que lamentaba que el modelo se “discontinuara el próximo año”, Musk respondió “cierto” y añadió que la flota de Cybertruck “seguirá circulando durante mucho tiempo”, según la BBC.
Tesla no informa por separado las ventas de la Cybertruck. Las agrupa con los Model S y Model X en la categoría “otros vehículos”, que sumaron 8.295 entregas en el tercer trimestre de 2026, de un total de 486.532 vehículos, según Notebookcheck.
Estimaciones de terceros recogidas por ese medio indican que Tesla entregó 4.323 Cybertruck en Estados Unidos en ese período. The Verge señala que incluso las proyecciones más altas de analistas calculan unas 70.000 entregas desde 2023.
Esa cifra queda lejos de las 250.000 unidades anuales que Musk llegó a prever, según The Verge. La camioneta salió al mercado en 2023, con una carrocería de acero inoxidable de formas angulares.
Su precio también se alejó de lo prometido. Musk dijo ante analistas que debía fabricarse a un valor accesible, y el modelo terminó en USD 61.000 para las versiones más equipadas, según la BBC. En 2026, la versión Cyberbeast cuesta USD 102.000.
Retiros y fallas de calidad en tres años
El modelo acumuló retiros del mercado. En 2025, un llamado a revisión afectó a más de 46.000 camionetas por el riesgo de que se desprendiera una pieza del revestimiento, según la BBC. The Verge añade que hubo otros componentes defectuosos y accidentes fatales.
El Cybercab es el reemplazo en la planta. Es el robotaxi sin pedales con el que Tesla busca ampliar su red de transporte autónomo. Según Reuters, la empresa planea vender el Cybercab al público antes de que termine 2026. Ese plan enfrenta investigaciones de la agencia de seguridad vial de Estados Unidos porque el vehículo carece de controles manuales, algo que la regulación federal suele exigir. Tesla no ha dado más detalles sobre el cambio en la planta. Musk fijó el plazo del recorte de producción de la Cybertruck en Texas alrededor de la mitad de 2027.

articles.title: From Bok star to fintech founder: Habana’s life after rugby
articles.text:
When PHATHISANI MOYO watched Bryan Habana deliver a presentation in Cape Town, he was intrigued by the personal journey to fintech behind one of South Africa’s most celebrated rugby careers.
Eight years after retiring from professional rugby, Bryan Habana found himself facing an unfamiliar opponent: himself.
The former Springbok winger and 2007 World Cup winner had spent much of his adult life mastering a sport that made him one of South Africa’s most recognisable athletes. He had represented his country on the biggest stage, performed under immense pressure and built a career around the discipline required to compete at the highest level.
But when he stepped into the fintech boardroom, the skills that made him a rugby star did not automatically translate into business success.
“I didn’t know how to do a PowerPoint presentation. I didn’t know how to put a table into a spreadsheet or read a budget,” Habana recalled during a presentation at BPC’s innovation event in Cape Town on October 22.
For someone accustomed to operating at the highest level of professional sport, it was humbling. The man once expected to know exactly what to do on a rugby field was suddenly a beginner in an unfamiliar world.
Yet that discomfort marked the beginning of a different career. Habana moved from the rugby field to fintech, co-founding Paymenow, a company that helps employees access wages they have already earned before payday.
His second act is about more than finding something to do after rugby. It is about applying the qualities that made him successful on the field to a different challenge, and discovering a new way to make an impact.
Watching Habana deliver his presentation in Cape Town, I was struck by how candidly he spoke about this transition. His story resonated because it was not just about an athlete moving into business. It was about what happens when the identity that has defined much of your life no longer prepares you for what comes next.
That is a challenge many people face: professionals forced to change careers, entrepreneurs rebuilding after business failure, and anyone who has had to start again after a major life change. Sometimes the hardest part is accepting that you must become a beginner again.
Habana’s second act
For elite athletes, retirement can be a particularly difficult transition. The routine, competition, team environment, and public recognition that once structured everyday life can disappear almost overnight.
Habana’s rugby career had given him a clear framework. He had training sessions, match days, coaches, teammates, and measurable goals. Success was often visible through a try scored, a match won, a trophy lifted.
Business was different—new systems to understand, unfamiliar language, and decisions whose consequences were not always immediately apparent. Habana studied computer science early in his life, before rugby took over. His interest in technology never entirely disappeared, but understanding technology was not the same as knowing how to build a business.
The transition demanded humility. His reputation on the rugby field would not automatically make him competent in the boardroom.
Habana reflected on the challenge of adapting to a world that would not simply accommodate the person he had been. “The future doesn’t go with you,” he said.
It is a striking way to describe the end of a career. The future does not arrive carrying your old identity, routines, or achievements. You have to meet it on its own terms.
A problem worth solving
In 2019, Habana co-founded Paymenow with chief executive officer (CEO) Deon Nobrega, chief technology officer (CTO) Willem van Zyl and chief development officer Gerbrand Potgieter. He explained that the company was built around earned wage access, which lets employees access a portion of the wages they have already earned before their scheduled payday.
The idea addresses a familiar problem for many workers. Salaries may arrive monthly, but everyday expenses do not wait for the end of the month. Transport, food, school costs, and unexpected bills can create pressure long before payday.
For workers with limited savings or access to affordable credit, that gap can push them towards expensive short-term loans. The pressure is reflected in Nedbank’s 2024 Financial Health Monitor, which found that 10% of workers had turned to payday loans to manage financial stress, while 12% had borrowed from informal lenders. FinMark Trust’s research offers a broader picture: 75% of South Africans who borrowed in 2024 used credit to cover essentials such as food.
Paymenow aims to give employees more flexibility over money they have already earned. Its services also include financial education and other tools intended to help people make better decisions about their money.
The idea is rooted in how people live and earn. Financial inclusion is not simply about giving someone a digital account or access to an app. It requires understanding when people receive their income, how they spend it, and what happens when money runs short.
A worker who can access earned wages when an unexpected expense arises may have an alternative to borrowing at high interest. In a country where many households live close to the edge of their monthly budgets, that flexibility can matter.
For Habana, the company’s purpose goes beyond making wages available earlier. It is about helping people manage financial pressure and improve their financial wellbeing. As he put it, “We’ve got an audacious goal of wanting to release ten million employees from financial stress through financial technology.”
From an idea to a regional business
Paymenow’s growth suggests that the problem it set out to address extends beyond South Africa. The company expanded into Namibia and Zambia before entering Pakistan.
By 2026, it reported serving more than 750,000 employees across the four markets, with clients including major employers in retail, telecommunications, healthcare and hospitality. In May 2026, Paymenow announced a merger with PayCurve, a South African employee financial wellness company founded in 2020.
The merger combines Paymenow’s wage-access service with PayCurve’s tools for identifying employees experiencing financial difficulties and helping them manage debt, build savings and improve their financial habits. The combined business will operate under the Paymenow brand.
The move reflects a wider understanding of the problem. Giving workers access to wages they have already earned can ease pressure before payday, but lasting financial stability also requires help with debt and savings.
For Paymenow, the merger broadens its services beyond short-term cash-flow problems. Habana has argued that growth must not come at the expense of the company’s purpose. “You’ve also got to stick with your purpose-driven approach,” he said.
Lessons that travel from the field
Habana’s sporting career did not become irrelevant when he left rugby. It gave him lessons he could apply in a different environment.
Teamwork is one of the most obvious. Rugby is a collective game, even when an individual player becomes the face of a defining moment. One person may score a try, but several teammates’ work often makes it possible.
Business operates in much the same way. A founder may be visible to investors, customers and the public, but a company’s success depends on people with different skills working towards a common goal.
“You can get quite far on your own, but it takes a lot longer,” Habana said.
Preparation is another lesson. In sport, talent alone is rarely enough. Training and repetition allow athletes to perform when the pressure is greatest. In business, preparation helps people recognise and harness opportunities.
Habana also highlighted the importance of responding to failure rather than allowing it to define the journey.
“Fail fast, but live faster,” he said.
That requires a willingness to change. The approaches that worked in one environment may not work in another, particularly in technology, where products and customer expectations evolve.
“We have to unlearn in order to learn,” he said.
Habana said this meant accepting that he could not rely on past achievements to navigate a new profession. He had to ask questions, acknowledge what he did not know, and learn from people with different expertise.
A different kind of impact
Habana has said sport allowed him to inspire hope. For many South Africans, the Springboks represent more than a team. Their victories can create moments of shared pride in a country where sport holds a powerful place in the national imagination.
Fintech offers a different kind of opportunity. A product that works can make a difference repeatedly in the everyday lives of its users.
That does not mean earned wage access can solve the structural problems behind financial insecurity. It cannot replace fair wages, stable employment, or broader economic opportunity. But it can offer a practical alternative for workers who need greater control over when they access money they have already earned.
For Habana, fintech offers a different kind of impact from the one he experienced on the rugby field. “As a rugby player, I could inspire hope,” he said. “But at no point in my rugby journey did anyone tell me that, because of what I did, I had saved their life.”
That sense of purpose, he said, is what makes the work particularly meaningful. “With financial technology, we are able to make an impactful difference in people’s lives on a daily basis,” he added.
Some of Africa’s most relevant fintech ideas have emerged from understanding everyday problems and building services around them. Paymenow’s proposition starts with a simple observation: the timing of income and the timing of expenses do not always match.
Turning that insight into a sustainable business requires trust, affordability, and sound execution. But the need it addresses is real.
Becoming a better version
Perhaps the most compelling part of Habana’s transition was not his move from rugby to fintech, but the personal philosophy that has helped him navigate the transition.
He recalled advice from former Springbok captain John Smit, who encouraged him to ask himself a question when looking in the mirror at the end of each day: “Every night when you go to bed… is that person an improvement on the person you saw the day before?”
It is a simple question that strips away trophies, titles, and public recognition. It asks whether you are learning, improving, and becoming better at what you do.
For an athlete, that might mean refining a skill or becoming a better teammate. For a founder, it could mean listening more closely to customers, understanding the business, or making a difficult decision for its long-term health.
Starting again can feel like losing ground, particularly when the world still remembers who you used to be. Habana knows what it is like to move from being the person everyone expects to succeed to the one sitting in a boardroom trying to understand a spreadsheet.
At Paymenow, he has found a different field in which to test himself. The scoreboard has disappeared, but the work of learning, improving and making a difference continues.
Perhaps that is why John Smit’s question about the person in the mirror carries such weight. At the end of the day, Habana no longer has to measure himself by the tries he scores or the matches he wins. He can ask a different question: is the person looking back at him a little better than the one from yesterday?
For someone who has had to start again, that may be the real victory: not returning to who you were, but becoming someone you had not yet imagined.

articles.title: Me fui de viaje con el Vivo X500 Pro Max temiendo que sus cámaras me vinieran grandes. Ha sido el móvil que más he disfrutado
articles.text:
Cuando recibí para un viaje de trabajo un teléfono que no solo presume de montar uno de los sensores más capaces, sino que viene acompañado de dos teleconvertidores de hasta 400mm y una empuñadura, mi primer instinto fue de entusiasmo, pero también de respeto. Quienes llevamos años probando cámaras sabemos que las propuestas premium sitúan el listón tan alto que, a veces, da vértigo: mi temor no era a una app de cámara repleta de funciones, sino a cargar con semejante portento y no estar a la altura de lo que es capaz de ofrecer.
Aterricé en Tenerife con esa incertidumbre. Y encima, el análisis del Vivo X500 Pro Max que tan magníficamente ejecutó mi compañero Alex ya anticipaba que estaba ante uno de los referentes de este 2026. Temía que el móvil me exigiese un esfuerzo constante para no desperdiciar sus posibilidades; sin embargo, bastaron unas pocas horas para comprobar que la vanguardia no consiste en hacer más complejo el uso, sino en que todo fluya con absoluta naturalidad. Te cuento mi experiencia.
Menudo hardware
Mi primer contacto me confirmó que no estaba ante un móvil cualquiera: "pantallón" AMOLED de 6,85 pulgadas y unos marcos reducidos al mínimo que hacen que transmita una sensación en mano brutal. Pero en cuanto lo giré, su enorme módulo me recordó que su prioridad en diseño es la fotografía.
Y la hoja de especificaciones de las cámaras, intimida: sensor principal Sony LYTIA de 50 MP (1/1,28 pulgadas y f/1.57), un telefoto de 200 MP de 3,5 aumentos (1/1,4 pulgadas) y un ultra gran angular de 50 MP.
Pero el despliegue no se queda en este punto: su kit incluye dos teleconvertidores de 200 y 400 mm equivalentes y un grip con botón de disparo y palanquita para el zoom. Con semejante arsenal, mi duda era si sería capaz de sacarle partido o me limitaría a hacer las fotos de siempre con un dispositivo sobredimensionado.
No tardé mucho en encontrar la respuesta. Aunque la app de cámara ofrece un modo 'Pro' muy exhaustivo para intervenir, no hace falta usarlo para sacar provecho de estas cámaras. El modo predeterminado, junto a los perfiles de color de Zeiss, resuelven cualquier escena.
Este Vivo X500 Pro Max interpreta luces y sombras respetando texturas, con una nitidez envidiable, sin saturar los verdes de los jardines por lo que paseé ni convertir el cielo en una masa celeste. La verdad es que no hace falta calcular cada disparo, el móvil asume el trabajo pesado para que solo tuviese que concentrarme en el encuadre.
Ahora te invito a recorrer la maravillosa isla canaria con las fotos que fui sacando. Empezamos. Las primeras pruebas llegaron durante un paseo por el Jardín Botánico de Puerto de la Cruz. En un entorno dominado por árboles centenarios, lo primero que puse a prueba fue la coherencia entre el sensor principal y el ultra gran angular.
La primera comparativa en el mismo lugar demuestra un calibrado del color muy bueno: pasar de los 15 mm a los 24 mm no altera la temperatura de la vegetación ni genera deformaciones en las esquinas.
Al adentrarme en sus caminos quise comprobar cómo se comportaba la compresión al saltar de focal sobre un mismo elemento. En lugar de limitarse a recortar píxeles, la transición entre lentes me permitió aislar una plata del denso fondo con una profundidad que no necesitó de trucos de software.
La prueba para la saturación vino con estos macizos de flores rojas. Sí, la mayoría de móviles tiende a empastar los tonos brillantes, pero aquí, saltando de nuevo entre distancias focales, el proceso retiene cada pliegue de los pétalos, sin sobresaturar la imagen.
En planos cercanos, el tamaño de los sensores marca la diferencia. Al enfocar el fruto verde y los racimos oscuros, el desenfoque surge de manera óptica, sin ese halo de recorte que delata a los modo retrato.
Esa misma naturalidad me la encontré al fotografiar un nenúfar rosa abriéndose entre juncos. El Vivo X500 Pro Max supo discriminar bien la distancia del motivo, manteniendo la flor en foco mientras las hojas de delante quedan sutilmente difuminadas.
Para poner a prueba la velocidad de enfoque y la respuesta, busqué insectos en las flores. Con el teleconvertidor de 200 mm, lograr congelar a esta abeja no fue fácil, pero para estos casos hice uso del modo deportivo. La óptica luminosa y la obturación del modo dedicado casi le hace rendir como una macro, con muy buena nitidez incluso en las alas.
El jardín también me sirvió para seguir exprimiendo el teleconvertidor más corto en otras situaciones como este retrato. Al encuadrar a un compañero caminando de espaldas, el rango dinámico equilibró la luz natural que se filtraba con las zonas más oscuras del camino sin que aparezca ruido.
El resultado al encuadrar a una pareja que avanzaba a lo lejos por el camino me gustó mucho: la compresión acerca a los sujetos mientras las palmeras enmarcan la escena con un desenfoque progresivo que le da un aire cinematográfico. Sin esfuerzo, solo sosteniendo el móvil y disparando.
De regreso al hotel al caer la tarde, trasladé las pruebas a los interiores y la iluminación artificial. En el vestíbulo del hotel, disparé con su telefoto. El sensor estira la sensibilidad hasta un respetable ISO 4.444 para compensar la luz de un foco, pero retuvo las vetas del material sin empastar las zonas oscuras.
Esa misma solvencia mostró al apuntar hacia estos adornos colgantes. Aquí el ISO bajó a 1.541 y el telefoto supo captar los reflejos de cada pieza sin halos de luz ni destellos.
Durante la cena, puse a prueba la distancia mínima de enfoque del teleobjetivo. En lugar de usar la cámara principal, lo que hubiese proyectado la sombra del móvil, el 85 mm permite retroceder y captar esta torrija con un desenfoque cremoso. Y todo sea dicho, dándole todavía mejor pinta gracias al 'Modo Comida'.
La prueba más extrema del zoom de la noche la reservé para el balcón de la habitación. Con el teleconvertidor de 400 mm montado y a pulso, apunté hacia un edificio que apenas veía con mis ojos. Eso sí: para sostener una toma a 1/17 segundos en tal distancia focal, el móvil tuvo que forzar el ISO. Y sí, aunque se pierde nitidez fina, la estabilización logró salvar la escena sin trepidación. El procesado también hizo su trabajo.
La segunda jornada se cerró con el evento de presentación en Adeje. Situado en una de las últimas filas de asientos, el Vivo X500 Pro Max se bastó con el telefoto periscópico para encuadrar a los protagonistas; la cámara resolvió con soltura el contraste y los rostros.
Entre rocas volcánicas y estrellas
La subida al Parque Nacional del Teide supuso la primera gran prueba. La alta montaña impone un escenario duro: la luz del sol incide sobre las laderas, generando un contraste bonito —pero complicado— entre la roca calcinada y las sombras. Es el típico lugar donde un sensor justito acaba reventando las altas luces.
En la imponente formación de los Roques de García, el telefoto demostró por qué es la lente más versátil del conjunto. El sensor retuvo la escala del monumento natural y su textura rugosa bajo una luz durísima, con un cielo azul muy bien interpretado.
Aprovechando la escena en estos lugares amplios, enrosqué el teleconvertidor de 400 mm para localizar a un compañero que se había encaramado en la cima de un risco. La lente me permitió acercar al sujeto con tanta contundencia que se distingue con claridad el móvil en sus manos y su postura. Debo reconocer que no usé esta lente tanto, pues su focal es enorme y aprecio una leve pérdida de calidad respecto a la otra.
Cuando la tarde comenzó a caer sobre las Cañadas, la luz transformó el paisaje volcánico en un escenario dorado. Con el 200 mm montado, encuadré a una compañera de espaldas contemplando las laderas; la focal comprimió la perspectiva, desenfocando matorrales y resaltando los destellos del sol con una calidez que parece firmada por una óptica de cine.
Justo antes del ocaso, la atmósfera del Teide nos brindó una de esas estampas difíciles de olvidar: una imponente nube se formó sobre el cráter del volcán. Disparé con el 85 mm a baja sensibilidad para exponer hacia las altas luces del cielo. No solo captó los pliegues de la nube, sino que la silueta del Teide quedaba recortada en una sombra limpia.
Apurando los últimos minutos de luz, giré el objetivo hacia las laderas que descendían hacia el mar de nubes. Con el teleconvertidor de 200 mm, el sensor consiguió registrar ese degradado entre tonos anaranjados, amarillos y violeta sin banding. Precioso cómo se mezcla el relieve con la caída del sol.
Con la llegada de la noche cerrada tocaba la experiencia de observación del cielo. Y aquí conviene que sea honesto: la sesión de astrofotografía no fue una clase técnica con monturas ni largas esperas exponiendo. El reto fue más directo: apoyar el teléfono a pulso, apuntar hacia arriba y dejar que la cámara principal hiciese su trabajo. Forzando la sensibilidad con el modo 'paisajes y noche' en una exposición de 1,3 segundos, logré capturar la densidad del cielo estrellado.
En alta mar: cetáceos y retratos sobre las olas
La tercera jornada cambió de escenario al desplazarnos hasta Puerto Colón para embarcarnos en un catamarán. En el muelle, utilice el angular para captar la panorámica de la cubierta: el Vivo X500 Pro Max expuso con precisión tanto el suelo de madera como los asientos en sombra, la costa y los edificios iluminados por el sol matutino.
Una vez estábamos mar adentro, la cubierta fue un entorno exigente donde todo se sacude y el viento no ayuda. Apuntando hacia el mástil con el 85 mm periscópico, una toma de 1/373 segundos bastó para congelar las banderas. Vaya agilidad en el enfoque tiene este móvil.
Navegando cerca del litoral, el Vivo X500 Pro Max me permitió también capturar la violencia con la que el océano rompía contra la orilla. Enfocando hacia una cala de arena negra, inmortalizó la espuma con una textura casi palpable y un agua que invitaba a bañarse.
A bordo, la naturalidad pedía retratos sin previo aviso. Sentado en la borda, aproveché para encuadrar a otro compañero que descansaba mirando hacia el horizonte; el 85 mm lo aisló con mucha nitidez de las barandillas del barco y dejó la costa lejana en un suave bokeh que ordena la escena.
Pero EL momento fue al avistar los primeros grupos de calderones nadando junto a la embarcación. Con el teleconvertidor de 200 mm confié en la empuñadura para disparar sin tocar la pantalla. Con velocidades en torno a 1/2000s, el teléfono consiguió captar el instante exacto en el que el lomo y la aleta del cetáceo rompían la superficie marina.
Para cerrar la sesión en el agua, el 200 mm volvió a lucirse en el retrato de personas. Fijaos en los tonos de piel, la textura de la ropa y el pelo hebra por hebra...
Lo que no te cuentan de viajar con semejante equipo
Cerrar una entresemana con casi mil disparos en la galería deja claro que este Vivo X500 Pro Max es uno de los móviles enfocados en fotografía más versátiles y completos jamás fabricados, pero el rigor exige poner sobre la mesa ciertos compromisos que implica convivir con él.
El primer peaje es físico: peso y ergonomía. Cuando le quitaba la empuñadura y guardaba los objetivos, el teléfono sigue siendo muy contundente. El módulo es tan grande que el centro de gravedad queda desplazado hacia arriba, haciendo que el agarre a una mano sea difícil.
Sí, con el grip y los teleobjetivos pesa más todavía. Ahora bien, gracias al agarre que ofrece llevar el accesorio, termina pasando más por una cámara compacta que por un teléfono, y eso se agradece a la hora de tirar fotos.
Aun así, hay un detalle a tener en cuenta en situaciones donde prima la rapidez: cierto retardo en el obturador. Aunque el sistema de enfoque automático es inmediato, existe una fracción de segundo entre que presiono el disparador y la cámara captura la imagen, un desfase que en momentos puntuales e impredecibles puede costar la toma perfecta.
Fuera de esto, de poco más me puedo quejar. Es cierto que mientras en fotografía el Vivo X500 Pro Max es de matrícula de honor, en grabación de vídeo baja un escaloncito: la conmutación entre sensores presenta saltos y la estabilización mete alguna que otra trepidación en paneos rápidos. No tuve problemas con el calor bajo el sol tinerfeño, nunca noté que el chip le hiciese coger temperatura, supongo que la funda necesaria para los accesorios de fotografía ayuda.
Regresé de Tenerife con la galería llena de recuerdos y una conclusión clara. Llegué temiendo que este móvil me exigiese tanta pericia que empañase el viaje; vuelvo convencido de que la mejor tecnología es justo la que no exige nada. Tener en la mano semejante despliegue de ópticas y comprobar que responde a la primera sin pedir mucho conocimiento ni obligar a pelear con ajustes, es la prueba de que, a pesar de lo completo —y complejo en modos y variables— que es, no necesité ser ningún experto para domar las cámaras del Vivo X500 Pro Max. Al contrario, lo único que hice fue dejarme llevar y disfrutar de sus capacidades.

articles.title: Blue Origin says it is building a higher-performing rocket engine at 1/4 the cost
articles.text:
KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida—Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon.
With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.
“There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,” Dave Limp, chief executive officer of Blue Origin, said during the UP.Summit conference at the Shuttle Landing Facility in Florida.
Blue Origin has already begun test firing a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. Separately, the company also said it was developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket, GS3, to give it an extra kick.
A new Northstar
The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine, Limp said. It has half the number of parts and 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed.
Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 engine and eventually reach the point where each engine can be assembled in less than a day. The company is deep into development and testing of Northstar, having already begun a test-firing campaign.
“To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,” Limp said. “This is going to be a game-changer.”
The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn today has a thrust of 640,000 pounds, and Limp said Northstar will have a starting thrust of 715,000 pounds. Like the BE-4 engine, Northstar burns methane and liquid oxygen using an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and a single-shaft turbopump architecture.
Limp said the company will continue to manufacture the existing BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, which uses two of the engines to power its Vulcan rocket.

articles.title: OpenSSH Rushes Patches for ‘SSHole’ Authentication Bypass
articles.text:
OpenSSH has rolled out emergency patches for a high-severity authentication bypass that allows attackers to log in using very long passwords.
Dubbed SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), the security defect affects the OpenSSH server (sshd) on Linux distributions that use the musl libc implementation with the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) disabled.
A “misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash” allows attackers to access certain accounts using any password that has between 257 and 1,024 characters.
Some accounts, such as root, should never accept a password, but in Linux distributions such as Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, and others, they do, Wakefield security researcher Özgün Kültekin says.
According to OpenSSH developer Damien Miller, the flaw is not in sshd itself, but can be exploited via sshd. Fixes were included in OpenSSH 10.6p2.
“We are making this release as fast as possible (we learned of the problem yesterday) because we have recently observed multiple cases of rapid bug rediscovery by AI agents, sometimes within hours, and so now consider long embargo periods to be a dangerous practice that primarily benefits attackers,” Miller said.
On Thursday, Alpine Linux urged users to immediately apply the OpenSSH patches and restart sshd to replace the running daemon, or disable password logins and restart sshd.
“The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash,” Alpine Linux warns.
Since version 3.16, Alpine Linux uses “*” to secure the root account, and $5$ or $6$ in password hashes show whether the SHA-256 or SHA-512 crypt was used.
“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries,” Alpine Linux notes.
Affected Alpine Linux deployments run OpenSSH without PAM, have password authentication enabled, have an account with the password field “*” (such as root, a key-only user created with adduser without a password, the alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images, or a user coming from a directory service through musl-nscd), and have at least one local account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash.
“Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20),” Alpine Linux says.
“We haven’t seen any reports of exploitation yet, but the details are public, and the attack is simple, so I expect scanning to start within hours. Finding targets is very easy. Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22, and the real number is higher because Shodan doesn’t see everything. Only some of those run Alpine, but each attempt is a single connection, so an attacker can afford to try all of them,” Detectify co-founder and principal security researcher Fredrik Almroth said.
“We’d be extremely surprised if we didn’t see SSH brute-forcers attempting this by the weekend. It’s virtually free to try and an easy win if it works. If your organization is affected, update to the latest version where possible, and disable password-based authentication as a temporary mitigation if you can’t,” WatchTowr head of threat intelligence Jake Knott said.

articles.title: 'AMD was a lot of people's last hope, but looks like PC gaming is over': AMD's CEO says it's now a 'data center first' company — and gamers are giving up at this point
articles.text:
AMD CEO enrages gamers by saying it's now a 'data center first' company — and predicts PC sales will plummet by a 'double-digit percentage' in 2027
Lisa Su: 'I see AI and super intelligence becoming more and more essential to every aspect of our lives'
- AMD's CEO has said that it's a "data center first company"
- Lisa Su observed that: "I see AI and super intelligence becoming more and more essential to every aspect of our lives"
- The CEO predicted a double-digit fall in PC sales next year, and gamers aren't happy at all with what they see as an abandonment by Team Red
AMD's chief executive hasn't been making many friends in the PC gaming community this week, having offered up a telling admission, alongside an ominous sales prediction, all off the back of the firm's latest financial results.
In an interview with Brian Sozzi, who is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, Lisa Su made it clear that AMD is a company with a lot of resources to expand its supply and the "ability to help our customers", but sadly the customers in this case are data centers, not consumers.
Su then delivered a frank admission: "We are a data center first company."
AMD's CEO also again underlined that AI is very much the future, and that "over the horizon I see AI and super intelligence becoming more and more essential to every aspect of our lives."
On top of this, as OC3D spotted, during AMD's earnings call for Q3 2026 (which was all about bumper profits), Su said that "PC sell-through slowed late in the quarter as higher memory and component costs weighed on demand," while forecasting that next year wouldn't be a good one for desktop computers and laptops.
The CEO observed: "In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage."
In other words, an over 10% slump. The chief exec added this caveat: "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our Ryzen roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
That presumably refers to the launch of Zen 6 processors for consumers (and businesses), the next-gen Ryzen family, which is expected to arrive early in 2027 and should obviously stoke some interest.
Analysis: dark times for the PC
It's no surprise that AMD has 'followed the money', as the old saying goes, because this is how businesses work, and profits reign supreme. Data center GPUs are way more profitable than consumer models.
If we look at the amount of revenue that AMD raked in from its data center business in this latest quarter, it very nearly doubled year-on-year and was up 97% to $8.5 billion. That dwarfed client and gaming (Ryzen and Radeon, mostly consumer) revenue, which was $3.7 billion (down 8%).
Looking at the balance sheet, it's clear enough AMD is a data center-first company — but actually saying this out loud, in no uncertain terms, sends out further signals about where Team Red wants to be, along with all the messaging that AI is the future.
Is it any wonder that gamers feel bitter about this? Hardly. Back at the start of 2024, AMD's consumer revenue was actually more than data center, albeit only marginally, but still — that picture has shifted massively over the past couple of years.
And with the prices of consumer GPUs shooting up as graphics chip production is increasingly prioritizing AI accelerators for data centers, there's a lot of bad feeling for obvious reasons. Nvidia's graphics card business is the same story too, of course, and GPU price hikes have been getting out of hand in the past few months for GeForce and Radeon cards alike.
Given clear negative predictions about the PC market next year — with AMD joining in on that — and the company's equally clear unwillingness to do anything about that with its plentiful resources, consumers are looking at a dismal future. One in which I fear that GPU price hikes are going to follow in the footsteps of steep RAM and SSD inflation, which has become beyond painful at this stage. Many forecasts point to the RAM crisis getting worse in 2027, of course.
All of which means it's hardly surprising that there's a profound sense of disappointment in AMD on social media, given this fresh data center comment from Lisa Su.
One Redditor declared: "AMD was a lot of people's last hope, but looks like PC gaming is over."
Dramatic? Well, yes, it is, but nonetheless, every single metric, forecast, and piece of analysis is strongly suggesting 2027 will be a desperately bleak time for the PC, and I have a hard time disbelieving that this is the truth. I've recently written about GPU pricing and how Black Friday could be your last chance to get an upgrade at a relatively reasonable price, if you need one.
