articles.title: Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
articles.text:
A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court.
“Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge. “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.”
The bill sacrifices caution for speed
The sea change in Congress following the midterm elections could put the bill in an even more precarious position, giving Democrats a better shot at pushing for their priorities in the bill and potentially triggering a fight with President Donald Trump. Should it come up for a vote during the current lame-duck session or get kicked to next year, the bill will test whether Democrats and Republicans can actually get something done to address some of the biggest issues voters carried with them to the polls: rising energy costs and data centers encroaching on their communities.
“They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge.
Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release.
The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement.
The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans.
“Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control.”
If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels.
Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.”
The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review.
The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues.
The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits.
Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action.
“It will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out.”
They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.
“One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.”
Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release.
“I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge.
Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays.
“This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.
Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down.
BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions.
Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future. Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group. The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA.
One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure.
The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off.
Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site.
Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections.
The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge. They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

articles.title: La película de animación de 'John Wick' recibe la luz verde definitiva: Keanu Reeves volverá
articles.text:
La saga John Wick ya está lista para volver. En 2025 se estrenó Ballerina, el spin-off protagonizado por Ana de Armas que, por el momento, se ha convertido en la última entrega de la franquicia. Pero mientras los fans esperan con ansias novedades sobre una posible quinta entrega de la historia principal, ahora se ha hecho oficial un proyecto diferente. Uno en el que, en cualquier caso, Keanu Reeves volverá a interpretar a su legendario asesino.
Y es que, tal y como informa Deadline, ya está en marcha una película de animación de John Wick. Será una precuela de la primera entrega que se centrará en cómo el protagonista llevó a cabo aquella "Tarea Imposible". Es decir, la misión que tuvo que completar para poder liberarse de su compromiso con la Alta Mesa y así obtener el derecho a estar junto al amor de su vida, Helen.
Esta es una de las grandes historias que aún no hemos visto de John Wick, por lo que la noticia de la película animada se ha convertido en toda una alegría para los fans. Con el proyecto, la saga podrá indagar aún más en el pasado del personaje y en cómo llegó a ser libre. Al menos durante un tiempo. Con Keanu Reeves como protagonista y productor, Shannon Tindle ( Kubo y las dos Cuerdas Mágicas) será el director bajo un guion escrito por Ryan y Kaz Firpo (Eternals).
La precuela de John Wick
En realidad, el desarrollo de la película precuela de animación de John Wick llevaba ya mucho tiempo en desarrollo, aunque no ha sido hasta ahora cuando ha recibido la luz verde definitiva. "Se supone que será divertida. Algunas de las precuelas y secuelas que se ven en otras franquicias no están pensadas para serlo. Solo queremos divertirnos. Queremos divertirnos con el mundo de Wick, pero ya lo hemos cubierto por un extremo [con John Wick 4], así que volvamos atrás y usemos un medio diferente", confesaba meses atrás Chad Stahelski, el coceador del personaje y su universo.
"Con la animación podemos volvernos un poco más locos y chiflados", prometía a su vez. Es decir, si todo sigue según su visión, la precuela de John Wick va a ser un nuevo espectáculo de acción, sangre y gore con las mayores libertades que ofrece este formato respecto a la imagen real. Por ahora no hay fecha de estreno estimada, pero próximamente se revelarán más novedades.

articles.title: OpenAI entdeckt und schließt dank KI-Agenten 948 Sicherheitslücken im Linux-Kernel
articles.text:
Dank KI: OpenAI findet 948 Lücken im Linux-Kernel – und schließt sie auch gleich
KI-Agenten können dabei helfen, Sicherheitslücken zu entdecken. OpenAI reicht das aber nicht aus. Der Mutterkonzern von ChatGPT will eine Systematik kreieren, in der KI-Agenten nach dem Auffinden der Sicherheitslücken auch gleich Patches dafür entwickeln lassen.
KI-Agenten entdecken 948 Exploits im Linux-Kernel
Ein solcher Prototyp hat im Linux-Kernel 948 Exploits entdeckt und diese auch gleich geschlossen. OpenAI präsentierte diese Ergebnisse in einem Blogbeitrag. Darin hieß es: „Unser Prototyp identifizierte und analysierte 2.308 potenzielle Befunde im Linux-Kernel, reproduzierte dynamisch 1.724 Schwachstellen und erzeugte 948 Exploits zur lokalen Rechteausweitung (LPE).“
Diese 948 Lücken sollen es Angreifer:innen ermöglichen, auf anfälligen Systemen ihre Rechte auszuweiten und Root-Zugriff zu erlangen.
Zahl der entdeckten Sicherheitslücken ist dank KI immer größer geworden
Welche Linux-Distribution getestet wurde, verriet OpenAI nicht. Laut mehreren Medienberichten soll es sich um ein weitverbreitetes Desktopsystem handeln, das in der Standardkonfiguration vorlag. Dafür verkündete OpenAI, wie hoch die Kosten für das Aufspüren der Sicherheitslücken waren: Sie betrugen mehr als 1,3 Millionen US-Dollar, was etwas weniger als 1.300 Dollar pro Sicherheitslücke entspricht.
Die Zahl der entdeckten Sicherheitslücken ist dank der Hilfe von KI zuletzt immer größer geworden. Das bringt ein neues Problem mit sich: Die Software-Entwickler:innen schaffen es oft nicht, zügig die nötigen Patches bereitzustellen, da die Entwicklung dieser in vielen Fällen mit großem Aufwand verbunden ist und die Software-Entwickler:innen aufgrund der Vielzahl an entdeckten Lücken nicht so schnell hinterherkommen. Das wiederum kommt den Angreifer:innen entgegen, welche mehr Zeit haben, die Lücken auszunutzen, bevor die schützenden Patches verfügbar sind.
OpenAI hält automatisierte Patch-Erstellung für unverzichtbar
Deshalb versucht OpenAI, die Entwicklung solcher Patches bestmöglich mit der Hilfe von KI zu automatisieren. „Angesichts der Geschwindigkeit, mit der Frontier-Modelle Schwachstellen entdecken, halten wir die automatisierte Patch-Erstellung für unverzichtbar“, betonte der US-Konzern in dem Blogeintrag.
„Nur so lässt sich Software im erforderlichen Tempo absichern und das Zeitfenster für die Ausnutzung begrenzen. Wir glauben, dass KI-generierte Patches […] unter Anleitung von Fachleuten funktional korrekt, mit bestehenden Programmierstilen vereinbar und gegen Angriffsvarianten robust sein können.“ OpenAI möchte deshalb in diesem Bereich weiter forschen.

articles.title: Speed Up Image Generation with FLUX 3 Image Klein on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
When deploying diffusion models in design tools, image editors, and visual production workflows, developers must account for inference latency. Generating an image requires multiple sequential passes through a model with billions of parameters, and higher resolutions increase attention costs.
FLUX 3 Image Klein is an image editing and generation model from Black Forest Labs (BFL) trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. It offers Base and distilled checkpoints for different latency and fidelity requirements.
This tutorial shows how to configure FLUX 3 Image Klein in NVIDIA TensorRT LLM VisualGen to take advantage of fused kernels, multi-GPU parallelism, FP8/NVFP4 support, caching, and attention optimizations. It compares latency and changes in generated outputs across optimizations. In the reported 2048×2048 tests on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, combined optimizations delivered up to 3.46x faster text-to-image (T2I) and 4.45x faster image-to-image (I2I) generation for FLUX 3 Image Klein Base compared with uncompiled BF16 inference. The tutorial includes deployment instructions and YAML configurations for applying these optimizations to your workloads.
FLUX 3 inference with TensorRT LLM VisualGen
FLUX 3 Image Klein combines Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer (DiT) to refine image latents, and an autoencoder to decode latents into images and encode I2I reference inputs. Klein processes text, noisy target-image, and optional reference-image streams independently before combining them through joint attention.
TensorRT LLM VisualGen, a dedicated runtime within TensorRT LLM, supported BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 variants at launch. On an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU, NVFP4 delivered up to 1.62x faster T2I and 1.58x faster I2I generation than BF16. Figure 2 compares generation latency, while Figure 1 compares example outputs. The following sections use NVFP4 as the starting point for further optimization.
Figure 1 compares outputs at 2048×2048. The summarized T2I prompt describes a kitchen still life; the summarized I2I prompt requests changes to a space scene, including a red gas giant, a silver dragon, and an engraved plaque.
Figure 1. BF16 and NVFP4 outputs for T2I and I2I
With NVFP4 as the starting point, VisualGen optimizations turned to denoising, which dominates overall generation time on B200. Accelerating FLUX 3’s DiT is therefore the focus of the following sections.
Table 1 shows pipeline latency at 2048×2048 on one NVIDIA B200 GPU using NVFP4, VANILLA attention, and torch.compile. Results are averaged over 10 requests after two warmup requests. Base uses 50 denoising steps with a classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 steps without CFG.
| Task | Model | Text + preparation | Denoising | Decode + postprocess | Total | Denoising share | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T2I | Base | 47 ms | 14.24 s | 416 ms | 14.70 s | 96.8% | 
| T2I | Distilled | 24 ms | 2.28 s | 410 ms | 2.71 s | 84.0% | 
| I2I | Base | 468 ms | 39.40 s | 417 ms | 40.29 s | 97.8% | 
| I2I | Distilled | 407 ms | 6.65 s | 418 ms | 7.48 s | 89.0% | 
Optimizing FLUX 3 in TensorRT LLM VisualGen
TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates NVFP4 DiT inference with optimized general matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels and epilogue fusion, low-precision and sparse attention, caching, and multi-GPU execution. Unless otherwise noted, the following benchmarks use torch.compile and seed 0. Base uses 50 denoising steps and a CFG scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 denoising steps.
NVFP4 inference
VisualGen supports BFL’s prequantized NVFP4 DiT checkpoints for FLUX 3 Image Klein and FLUX 3 Image Klein Base. To use these checkpoints, set variant to nvfp4 in pipeline_config:
pipeline_config:
  variant: nvfp4
GEMM kernel optimization
TensorRT LLM VisualGen uses FlashInfer’s PrimsTS FP8/NVFP4 GEMM kernels, built with CUTLASS Primitives and Task Scheduling to accelerate quantized inference. Tuned for FLUX 3 tensor shapes and enabled by default, they combine optimized GEMMs with fused epilogues, including GEMM with SwiGLU and query, key, and value (QKV) projections with query/key normalization and rotary position embeddings (RoPE). See FlashInfer PR #5758 for more details.
At launch, the pinned NVFP4 PrimsTS kernels delivered 1.02–1.10x faster T2I generation on B200 than the autotuned TensorRT LLM NVFP4 GEMM implementation.
Quantized and sparse attention
Attention is a major bottleneck in high-resolution image generation. In the reported 2048×2048 NVFP4 T2I tests on B200, VANILLA BF16 attention accounted for approximately 60% of DiT GPU kernel time for both Base and distilled Klein. VisualGen supports two approaches to reducing this cost: quantized attention with cuDNN FP8 or VC-Attention FP8, and sparse attention with Sol-Attention. VC-Attention FP8 is a TensorRT LLM variant of the method described in the VC-Attention paper.
Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) measures perceptual differences between generated images. In the following comparisons, lower scores indicate greater similarity to the corresponding VANILLA baseline output.
Compared with VANILLA BF16 attention, cuDNN FP8 delivered generation speedups of 1.08x for Base and 1.09x for the 16-step distilled Klein. The corresponding LPIPS scores were 0.072 and 0.161. VC-Attention FP8 delivered speedups of 1.18x for Base and 1.16x for distilled Klein, with corresponding LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151.
Figure 4 compares FLUX 3 Image Klein Base NVFP4 outputs at 2048×2048 with CUDA Graphs enabled.
These measurements suggest using VC-Attention FP8 for quantized attention at 2048×2048 on B200. The tested configuration uses a repair budget of ρ=0.005 to select the fraction of tokens with the highest quantization error for residual correction. To use quantized attention, replace attention_config with one of the following configurations:
For cuDNN FP8:
attention_config:
  backend: CUDNN
  quant_attention_config:
    qk_dtype: fp8
    v_dtype: fp8
For VC-Attention FP8:
attention_config:
    backend: TRTLLM
    quant_attention_config:
        qk_dtype: fp8
        v_dtype: fp8
        vc_attention: true
        vc_repair_budget: 0.005
Figure 4. BF16, cuDNN FP8, and VC-Attention FP8 example outputs
Sol-Attention reduces DiT computation with sparsity controlled by τ. The reported tests use the PrimsTS-based general block-sparse attention kernel in TensorRT LLM. Configure Sol-Attention as follows:
attention_config:
  backend: TRTLLM
  sparse_attention_config:
    algorithm: sol_attn
    tau: 1.0
    disabled_until_timestep: 0.96
For NVFP4 FLUX 3 Image Klein Base at 2048×2048 on B200, Sol-Attention with τ=1.0 delivered 1.24x faster denoising plus autoencoder decoding than compiled dense VANILLA with 16 initial dense steps, or 1.30x with 12.
These measurements suggest using 16 initial dense steps to prioritize fidelity or 12 to prioritize speed. Higher τ reduced output quality with little additional speedup.
Figure 5 compares NVFP4 FLUX 3 Image Klein Base outputs at 2048×2048 with CUDA Graphs enabled and τ=1.0.
Figure 5. Dense attention and Sol-Attention outputs with 16 or 12 initial dense steps
Step caching
Cache-DiT reduces FLUX 3 Image Klein inference latency by reusing intermediate transformer outputs across denoising steps without retraining or modifying model weights. A residual-difference threshold controls when cached outputs are reused, so you can adjust the balance between inference speed and output quality. Configure Cache-DiT with your desired parameters:
cache_config:
  cache_backend: cache_dit
  Fn_compute_blocks: 1
  Bn_compute_blocks: 0
  max_warmup_steps: 4
  max_continuous_cached_steps: 3
  residual_diff_threshold: 0.24
At a threshold of 0.24, Cache-DiT nearly halved NVFP4 Base T2I latency at both tested resolutions, with smaller gains for the distilled Klein. At 1024×1024, speedups were 1.97x for Base and 1.26x for distilled Klein, with corresponding LPIPS scores of 0.038 and 0.036 against their respective uncached outputs. At 2048×2048, speedups were 1.94x for Base and 1.20x for distilled Klein (Figure 6).
Figure 6. Base and distilled Klein outputs with and without Cache-DiT
Multi-GPU inference
The VisualGen runtime in TensorRT LLM scales FLUX 3 Image Klein using classifier-free guidance (CFG) and Ulysses sequence parallelism. Base assigns positive/negative branches to separate GPU groups and partitions each branch’s sequence with Ulysses; distilled runs without CFG and uses Ulysses alone.
VisualGen handles sequence splitting, distributed attention, and output gathering. For eight-GPU NVFP4 Base inference, use the following configuration:
parallel_config:
    cfg_size: 2
    ulysses_size: 4
For the distilled model, set cfg_size: 1, ulysses_size: 8, and use the flux-3-image-klein checkpoint.
At 2048×2048, scaling from one to eight GPUs on an NVIDIA DGX B200 reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled. Denoising speedups were larger, at 6.01x for Base and 4.44x for distilled Klein, but roughly half of eight-GPU distilled generation time remained outside denoising, limiting end-to-end gains.
At smaller resolutions, CUDA Graphs complement parallelism by reducing kernel-launch overhead as work per GPU shrinks. In a separate 1024×1024 NVFP4 experiment on eight B200s with VANILLA attention, adding CUDA Graphs to compilation reduced Base latency from 1.823 to 0.809 seconds (2.25x, CFG across two GPU groups with Ulysses across four GPUs per group) and distilled latency from 0.791 to 0.366 seconds (2.16x, Ulysses across eight GPUs). Enable CUDA Graphs with the following configuration:
cuda_graph_config:
    enable: true
FLUX 3 end-to-end performance
At 2048×2048, Figure 8 compares end-to-end generation speedups across successive TensorRT LLM VisualGen optimization stages against uncompiled BF16 VANILLA inference.
On a single B200, compilation, NVFP4 with PrimsTS GEMMs, Sol-Attention, and Cache-DiT delivered a 3.46x generation speedup for T2I, reducing latency from 22.36 to 6.46 seconds, and a 4.45x speedup for I2I, reducing latency from 54.64 to 12.28 seconds. The 16-step distilled Klein achieved up to 2.34x end-to-end speedups.
On a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, compilation, NVFP4 with fused CuTe DSL kernels, and Cache-DiT delivered 1.73-3.25x generation speedups, extending the gains across both platforms. Figures 9 and 10 compare example outputs across optimization stages.
The examples in Figures 9 and 10 were generated on a single B200 GPU.
Figure 9. FLUX 3 Image Klein Base T2I outputs across optimization stages
The editing prompt requests a weathered appearance for the canoe while preserving its shape, position, and surrounding scene.
Figure 10. FLUX 3 Image Klein Base I2I outputs across optimization stages
To apply these optimizations to your own workloads, follow the runtime setup, inference commands, and YAML configurations in the following sections for offline generation or online serving.
Prerequisites
Start the prebuilt TensorRT LLM container with the following command. To build it from the feat/flux3-image-klein branch, follow the FLUX 3 deployment guide.
docker run --rm -it --ipc=host --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \
      --name tensorrt_llm \
      -e TLLM_FMHA_LIBS=+prims_ts \
      -e HF_TOKEN=<your_hf_token> \
      -v ~/.cache:/root/.cache:rw \
      nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:feat-flux3-image-klein-1.4.0a0.dev202610280436
TLLM_FMHA_LIBS=+prims_ts enables the PrimsTS attention kernels VC-Attention requires. The optimizations and results in this post focus on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs.
Get started with TensorRT LLM VisualGen
With the runtime environment ready, you can run FLUX 3 offline or serve it through an image generation endpoint. Use the sample YAML configurations in the following sections to apply the optimization settings used for the results reported earlier.
These examples do not expand prompts. If you use BFL’s prompt upsampler, run it separately before inference. Reported latencies exclude prompt upsampling.
Offline inference
Inside the container, run the FLUX 3 example:
cd /app/tensorrt_llm/examples/visual_gen
python models/flux3.py \
  --model black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \
  --visual_gen_args configs/flux3-images-1gpu.yaml \
  --prompt "A small robot tending a rooftop garden at sunrise" \
  --height 2048 --width 2048 --seed 0 \
  --output_path flux3.png
For NVFP4 on Blackwell, add --variant nvfp4; use --variant fp8r for row-wise FP8 or omit --variant for BF16. Select black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein for the distilled model. For editing, add an editing prompt and --image /path/to/reference.png; repeat --image for multiple references.
Online serving endpoint
From the same container directory, launch the OpenAI-compatible /v1/images/generations endpoint:
cd /app/tensorrt_llm/examples/visual_gen
trtllm-serve black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --visual_gen_args configs/flux3-images-1gpu.yaml
Once the server is ready, open a second terminal, enter the running container, and run the client:
docker exec -it tensorrt_llm bash
python examples/visual_gen/serve/sync_image_gen.py \
  --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1 \
  --model black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \
  --size 2048x2048 \
  --prompt "A small robot tending a rooftop garden at sunrise" \
  --output flux3-served.png
For NVFP4 serving, add pipeline_config: {variant: nvfp4} to the YAML before starting the server; use fp8r for FP8.
Optimized single-GPU deployment
For 2048×2048 inference on one B200, save the following as configs/flux3-nvfp4-vc-fp8-1gpu.yaml, which combines NVFP4 weights, torch.compile, and VC-Attention FP8.
pipeline_config:
  variant: nvfp4
torch_compile_config:
  enable: true
compilation_config:
  resolutions: [[2048, 2048]]
  num_frames: [1]
  modes: [t2i, i2i]
attention_config:
  backend: TRTLLM
  quant_attention_config:
    qk_dtype: fp8
    v_dtype: fp8
    vc_attention: true
    vc_repair_budget: 0.005
For Sol-Attention and Cache-DiT, copy this file to configs/flux3-nvfp4-sol-cache-1gpu.yaml, replace attention_config, and add cache_config:
pipeline_config:
  variant: nvfp4
torch_compile_config:
  enable: true
compilation_config:
  resolutions: [[2048, 2048]]
  num_frames: [1]
  modes: [t2i, i2i]
attention_config:
  backend: TRTLLM
  sparse_attention_config:
    algorithm: sol_attn
    tau: 1.0
    disabled_until_timestep: 0.96
cache_config:
  cache_backend: cache_dit
  Fn_compute_blocks: 1
  Bn_compute_blocks: 0
  max_warmup_steps: 4
  max_continuous_cached_steps: 3
  residual_diff_threshold: 0.24
The timestep cutoff of 0.96 keeps the first 12 denoising steps dense for 50-step FLUX 3 Image Klein Base and the first four steps dense for 16-step distilled Klein under the packaged α=6.93 schedule. For the 16-dense-step setting recommended above, set disabled_until_timestep: 0.94. The cutoff specifies a noise level rather than a number of steps. Remove cache_config to use Sol-Attention without Cache-DiT.
Set --visual_gen_args in the offline inference or serving commands to the path of your selected YAML file. Set the image size to 2048×2048 to match the performance examples.
Conclusion and next steps
TensorRT LLM VisualGen supports FLUX 3 Image Klein inference with configurable performance optimizations. NVFP4, fused kernels, compilation, multi-GPU execution, and CUDA Graphs accelerate execution; quantized and sparse attention and caching provide further latency reductions with measurable effects on output quality. Together, they deliver up to 3.46x faster T2I and 4.45x faster I2I generation using a single GPU on an NVIDIA DGX B200, compared with uncompiled BF16 VANILLA inference.
Get started:
- Run the end-to-end FLUX 3 example
- Explore the TensorRT LLM VisualGen runtime and optimization utilities
- File issues or share results on the TensorRT LLM GitHub
Acknowledgements
Nikita Korobov, Harrison Zhang, Pamela Peng, Kanghwan Jang, Yuhang He, and Charlotte Mallo

articles.title: Friday Squid Blogging: New Jurassic Squid Predecessors - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Friday Squid Blogging: New Jurassic Squid Predecessors
News story: “Scientists discover a bizarre Jurassic ‘squid’ unlike anything ever seen.”
Scientists have identified the “fattest” belemnite ever discovered, a bizarre, barrel-shaped squid relative that lived in Wyoming’s ancient seas 160 million years ago. The exceptionally rare fossils reveal a creature unlike anything previously known, potentially a predator of smaller squid-like animals and a surprising survivor of a supposedly vanished family.
As usual, you can also use this squid post to talk about the security stories in the news that I haven’t covered.
Clive Robinson • November 6, 2026 7:23 PM
@ Bruce, ALL,
More Apple backdoor censorship?
Apple was in effect the first mobile phone OS developer to put into their OS the foundations of “Client Side Scanning”(CSS) under increasing pressure from US legislators and law enforcement agencies.
Apple received a lot of bad press over it and slid some of it backwards.
Importantly though it emphasised the point that the US Gov had finally accepted the impossibility of NOBUS backdoors in “End to End Encryption”(E2EE) even though it had been repeatedly pointed out by those involved with ICTsec.
Thus the USG move to attack privacy on the other side of the “security end point” via CSS as an “end run attack”.
Something pointed out on this blog back in the very early days of “Secure Messaging Apps” and the weak links in the security chains on consumer and commercial systems.
Hence the argument for taking the “security end point” off the device that is the “communications end point” (and why I gave the basics of the design of how to build a “Deniable Encryption” system on this blog).
Well Apple have a new less obvious nod in the direction of “Client Side Censorship”(CSC).
Investigators have discovered quite deliberate censorship in the user side “autocomplete” text entry system,
https://www.reuters.com/business/retail-consumer/apples-predictive-text-restrictions-include-dictator-trump-sleepy-joe-researcher-2026-11-06/
Not only is it a first step “light-touch censorship” system, it also opens up fingerprinting users via their typing cadence and word / symantec usage.

articles.title: Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds
This is fascinating:
The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening.
It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another.
[…]
It’s sound that’s relevant here, though, and specifically the sound of aeroplanes. Early in his video, Colsto brings up a map of the flights that were in the air at the time the video he’s tracing was recorded. Much of this information is publicly available. Aircraft equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) transmit data about their position, velocity, and altitude, which flight-tracking services collect and make available to the public. While not every plane is tracked, the system provides an enormous amount of information about aircraft movements.
Wicked Lad • November 6, 2026 12:16 PM
At the risk of stating the obvious, it seems this would also be useful in evaluating the likelihood that a video was taken where and when it is purported to have been taken.

articles.title: Moulinex Dolci : la rivale moins chère de la Ninja Creami ne manque pas d'atouts
articles.text:
Au rayon dédié aux glaces, Moulinex propose la Dolci, une machine qui, si elle ne refroidit pas, permet de travailler la texture de nombreuses préparations déjà congelées, de la crème glacée aux sorbets en passant par les milkshakes.
Dans la famille des machines à glace de Moulinex, nous demandons la Dolci. Aux côtés de la Freezi (350 €), le modèle à granités et glaces à l'italienne de la marque qui refroidit, la Dolci s'appuie sur un système de lames pour brasser des préparations préalablement congelées. Une approche qui permet de déguster des recettes dignes d'un artisan glacier, à l'instar de la célèbre Ninja Creami.
Affichée à 230 € (contre 269 € pour la Creami de Ninja), la Dolci propose 10 programmes : sorbet, crème glacée, gelato, yaourt glacé, smoothie, granité, frappé, cocktail, milkshake, ainsi qu'un cycle de rinçage et un mode baptisé Mix in permettant d'incorporer des garnitures à la préparation (brisures de biscuits, par exemple).
La Dolci n'est pas le type d'appareil que l'on utilise au quotidien, surtout une fois la saison estivale passée. Pourtant, avec ses 4,3 kg, ses 38 cm de hauteur, 17 cm de largeur et plus de 30 cm de profondeur, cette belle bête s'avère encombrante à manipuler dès qu'une envie de gourmandise glacée se fait sentir.
Aux lignes arrondies, l'appareil présente un tableau de bord sur sa partie supérieure. Il regroupe les boutons correspondant aux différents programmes pour un rendu visuel très lisible.
Sur la partie inférieure, une porte dissimule l'emplacement destiné au pot de crème glacée. Ce dernier doit être inséré dans un bol extérieur, puis coiffé du couvercle abritant les lames. L'ensemble est ensuite introduit et verrouillé dans la machine, avant de refermer la porte.
Ces manipulations exigent une lecture attentive du mode d'emploi et un peu d'entraînement pour démarrer la machine correctement. Notez d'ailleurs que si les pièces sont mal assemblées, les boutons clignotent et l'appareil refuse de se lancer.
La machine est fournie avec trois pots en Tritan d'une contenance d'environ 470 ml chacun, idéals pour varier les plaisirs. Nous avons réalisé nos tests avec un pot de crème glacée au chocolat et un autre de sorbet à la mangue, tous deux préparés et congelés la veille. Rappelons-le en effet que la Dolci ne produit pas de froid, elle se contente de brasser des préparations.
Après avoir lancé le programme (nous avons fait le test avec les modes Crème glacée et Sorbet), c'est le début du show : le pot monte comme un ascenseur pour entamer le brassage.
La machine a brassé la préparation durant 3 min 15 s avant de la faire redescendre.
Côté texture, le sorbet est sorti granuleux de l’appareil, signe selon le mode d'emploi que la recette manquait de sucre, tandis que la crème glacée au chocolat a présenté une texture plus mousseuse et agréable à déguster.
Les deux préparations se sont toutefois révélées assez collantes sur la cuillère, ce qui n'a pas facilité le service. Précisons à toutes fins utiles que nous avons utilisé une cuillère classique, et non une cuillère à glace spécifique.
Lorsqu'elle active ses lames dans la préparation glacée, la Moulinex Dolci peut faire penser à un blender. Nous avons relevé un niveau sonore de 70 dB, soit à peu près similaire à ce qu'émet la Creami (72 dB) ou la Nutribullet Chill (73 dB). Sur 3 min de brassage, cela nous a paru assez long.
Les pots de glace et le récipient extérieur passent au lave-vaisselle, mais pas le couvercle ni les lames. Une fois le pot vidé, il est possible de lancer le mode rinçage qui lance la machine avec de l'eau pour un premier nettoyage bienvenu.
Si l'on accepte le fait d’avoir à anticiper ses préparations et leur congélation, la Dolci de Moulinex est une machine plutôt facile à utiliser, dotée de nombreux programmes (trop ?). Les textures obtenues se révèlent très agréables en bouche, à condition de prévoir un minimum de sucre dans la recette sous peine de devoir relancer un cycle de brassage, au passage assez bruyant.
Moins onéreuse que sa principale concurrente, la Creami Deluxe de Ninja, pour un usage quasiment similaire, la Dolci de Moulinex semble constituer une offre plus pertinente. Elle mérite néanmoins d'être comparée à la Nutribullet Chill, vendue au même tarif, mais qui présente l'avantage d'être plus compacte.

articles.title: How NVIDIA Open Source Tools Are Helping Researchers Build Next-Generation 6G Networks
articles.text:
A year ago, NVIDIA open sourced its Aerial wireless software, joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless systems.
Today, researchers and developers are using these tools to build 6G-ready networks that do more than just transmit data — receiving signals more effectively, keeping robots and autonomous systems connected when it matters most, and adapting in real time as devices move through the world.
Over the past year, global developer adoption of NVIDIA AI Aerial and NVIDIA Sionna software has grown 10x, while NVIDIA’s open source 5G/6G tools have surpassed 1 million downloads. More than 8,000 research and academic institutions worldwide are using these platforms.
The projects emerging today offer a view of how future networks could look. Each addresses a different challenge, but together point toward a broader ambition for building AI-native 6G networks that deliver connectivity, computing and sensing over a converged software-defined platform for billions of people, machines and agents.
Networks That Help Robots React Faster
A robot picking up an object needs to understand its surroundings and act before they change. When the AI powering that decision runs on a nearby server or in the cloud, the wireless connection becomes part of the response time.
Researchers are exploring a more efficient approach called goal-oriented semantic communications. Instead of sending full images, robots transmit compact descriptions of objects, their positions and their relationships. Transmitting just as much information as needed allows robots to more quickly respond, especially in dynamic environments like workplaces and warehouses.
At King’s College London, researchers connected a camera-equipped robot arm to an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin running NVIDIA Sionna, which supports both software-defined 5G network and edge AI processing. In fruit-packing and cube-stacking experiments with deliberately introduced faults, the approach reduced robot task completion time by up to 52.6% and improved task success compared with sending periodic images.
In addition to quicker responses and less processing overhead, the system also proved more resilient — detecting dropped objects, recovering from unsuccessful actions and, in configurations using a digital twin, checking planned movements for potential collisions before execution.
Networks That Learn to Receive Signals Better
For a firefighter receiving live drone footage or a rescue team searching for a missing person, timely images can help guide urgent decisions. But interference and changing radio conditions can make wireless signals harder to decode, causing errors and retransmissions that delay information from the field.
AI receivers address this challenge by learning to recover information from incoming signals more effectively. Better reception could help responders maintain a clearer, more current view of a fire scene or search area.
SoftBank demonstrated this by integrating a neural receiver into NVIDIA Aerial CUDA-Accelerated RAN (ACAR) and testing it with a commercial 5G smartphone. In controlled tests with interference, the neural receiver delivered higher uplink throughput than a conventional receiver at all 15 tested settings, with a maximum gain of roughly 60%.
Another way to improve reception is to teach receivers about the environments where they operate. Using NVIDIA Aerial Testbed, ETH Zurich researchers found that tuning neural receivers using local measurements reduced block error rates by more than one-third compared with selected pretrained versions.
Networks That Learn When to Save Power
As 6G connects more devices and supports more AI applications, managing energy demand will become increasingly important.
For example, a network may need enough capacity to serve a busy stadium, but demand changes when the crowd leaves. AI can help identify when spare capacity can power down — and when it needs to come back online — so operators can reduce electricity use without dropping connections.
At the University of Leeds, researchers developed a system that predicts network demand 10 minutes ahead and uses those forecasts to guide base station sleep decisions. Before powering down, it checks that neighboring active stations can continue serving affected devices and monitors for changes that require capacity to be restored.
The team tested their approach using a portable, NVIDIA DGX Spark-powered 5G “network-in-a-box” alongside a digital twin for validating decisions against real wireless equipment. The result: researchers reported a 45.6% reduction in RAN power consumption relative to a full-power baseline while maintaining device connectivity.
Networks That Can Be Tested Faster — Before They’re Built
Before deploying a network, researchers need to know how it will perform when hundreds of devices compete for connections or radio signals run into interference. Simulating these conditions helps teams evaluate designs before committing to costly equipment and field trials. But realistic simulations can take hours, limiting how many ideas researchers can explore.
The Centre Tecnològic de Telecomunicacions de Catalunya (CTTC) is accelerating that process by bringing GPU-accelerated radio channel models, running on ACAR, into CTTC’s open source 5G-LENA network simulator. These models calculate how wireless signals travel between antennas and devices — a computation that grows increasingly demanding as simulated networks grow.
In an early evaluation, the approach reduced simulation runtime from approximately three hours to 10-20 minutes, depending on the integration, while preserving the expected statistical behavior and network performance.
Faster simulations let researchers compare more designs, investigate more demanding scenarios and refine ideas sooner. As the industry develops 6G, this could shorten the path from a proposed innovation to a thoroughly evaluated network design — helping teams build better connectivity before deploying it in the real world.
At NVIDIA GTC Washington, D.C., attend 6G Developer Sessions where researchers and developers will showcase more innovations shaping the future of wireless networks.
NVIDIA AI Aerial and NVIDIA Sionna are available on GitHub.

articles.title: Beyond code generation: A developer's guide to agentic engineering
articles.text:
Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering
Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.
This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?
Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.
As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.
Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page
See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.
You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.
- Plan together where your team already works. Use Copilot in Slack or Teams to collaborate with everyone involved—from product managers and designers to analysts and business stakeholders. Bring in context from connected tools so your team can check assumptions, contribute ideas, and refine requirements together.
- Turn agreed-upon requirements into actionable work. Ask Copilot to create GitHub Issues with the context and acceptance criteria needed for implementation, breaking out tasks that can be handled separately.
- Keep routine triage from consuming planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label your issues and estimate task complexity. Assign low-complexity tasks directly to Copilot, then spend your time focusing on harder decisions.
- Give complex work the planning it needs. Use Plan Mode in your preferred Copilot surface to compare approaches and refine an implementation plan. Review and approve the plan before handing it off to Copilot to begin implementation.
What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.
Build: Move more than one task forward at a time
You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.
You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.
- Continue your conversation from another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session across clients, so you can work wherever it’s most convenient for you.
- Let work continue after you close your laptop. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes, keeping execution off your machine and allowing you to leave and return to a session later.
- Work on separate tasks without mixing their edits. The Copilot app gives sessions isolated copies of the repository, so an implementation task and a documentation update don’t share an unfinished working tree.
- Carry project knowledge into each task. Repository instructions capture conventions and validation commands, while shared memory stores useful facts Copilot can reuse across a repository. Copilot Dreaming reviews eligible sessions and pull request feedback to keep memories current and propose instruction or skill updates. That means less time re-explaining how your team works and more consistent help from Copilot across tasks.
- Match the models to the work. Select Copilot Fusion to choose models and reasoning depth for the task, bringing in additional models to review a solution when needed. You set the effort level to balance quality, cost, and response time.
- Follow company rules wherever you work. Enterprise managed settings carry your company’s policies and configured tools across Copilot surfaces, reducing setup differences as you move between clients.
Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.
Verify: Spend your attention where it counts
After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.
That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.
- Stack up smaller, more focused pull requests instead of creating a single, massive change. You and your agents can use stacked pull requests to separate dependent work into smaller pieces. This lets each PR be reviewed on its own, keeps dependencies visible, and unblocks teams by letting them build on top of your work before it merges.
- Catch routine quality issues before they consume review time. GitHub Code Quality checks changes against coding practices and your organization’s standards, catching issues before they reach a human reviewer and saving time for both authors and reviewers.
- Get review help matched to the change. Copilot code review gives automated feedback, with lighter analysis for simple changes and deeper analysis for complex ones. You can set that depth yourself or let Copilot select it for each pull request.
- Check security across more of your codebase. AI Scan finds vulnerabilities in languages and files beyond CodeQL’s coverage. AI secret detection helps identify unstructured secrets, such as passwords, that pattern matching can miss.
- Keep new dependencies within policy. License compliance checks dependency licenses against your company’s rules before merging. GitHub package firewall, currently in public preview for npm, can block downloads that violate configured security policies.
- Resolve findings and follow-up work without babysitting every pull request. Agentic Autofix proposes repairs for security issues, while Agent Merge automatically addresses failing checks, review comments, and merge conflicts—helping you keep your pull requests moving and preparing them for merge. And, if you configure it, Copilot will even merge your pull requests once your verification steps are passing.
Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.
Observe: Learn from what happens after you ship
Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.
Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.
- Check assumptions against real behavior. With access to your observability tools and business data through connectors such as Fabric, Copilot can help investigate which requests or customer groups are affected.
- Capture the finding where someone can act on it. Ask Copilot to draft an issue with supporting evidence and acceptance criteria, including a regression test for the failure you uncovered.
- Carry useful lessons into future work. Review suggested improvements from Dreaming, which uses sessions and repository activity to help refine memories, skills, and code review guidance.
Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up issues, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.
Where to start
Take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?
You don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.
We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”

articles.title: Accelerating Reinforcement Learning Weight Refit with the Reshard Collective | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
During reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, training trajectories are generated on the fly by running inference with the current policy model. For training efficiency, it is common to run inference and training in parallel on separate GPU resources in a disaggregated setup. Although the policy model is updated only on the training GPUs, the system must periodically refresh the weights on the inference GPUs with the latest parameters generated on the training GPUs. This transfer of model weights between training and inference GPUs is called refit.
Refit involves two defining characteristics that pose challenges. First, inference and training have different computational requirements, so the weights are distributed differently across inference and training instances by having different parallel mappings (data, context, tensor, expert, and pipeline parallelism).
Second, because refit must update all model weights on the inference GPUs, the communication payload is on the order of the total size of the model’s weights. This payload is already very large for the latest frontier models and is expected to continue growing. Together, these characteristics mean that refit requires high-performance communication across a wide variety of distributed source and destination layouts.
This post explains how AI training frameworks can address these refit challenges using the Reshard collective, a new type of collective communication primarily designed to accelerate RL weight refit. NCCL M2N Reshard, an open source reference implementation of the Reshard collective, is available through the NVIDIA/nccl-extensions GitHub repo.
Challenges of current weight refit methods as models scale
Existing refit implementations commonly use a gather-and-broadcast approach to handle differences between training and inference layouts.
The typical gather-and-broadcast weight refit sequence for every model parameter is structured as follows:
- Training GPUs all-gather their local shards to reconstruct the complete parameter.
- The complete parameter tensor is broadcast to the inference GPUs.
- Each inference GPU retains the shard required by its local layout.
Using the complete tensor as an intermediate representation makes it straightforward to transfer weights between different layouts. However, an inference GPU receives the full parameter even when it needs only a shard. This process creates redundant communication in both the gathering and broadcasting phases, which is suboptimal.
The size of this communication grows with the model size, which continues to scale. For example, Kimi K3 contains 2.8 trillion parameters, while Qwen 3.8 2.4T A95B contains 2.4 trillion parameters. Assuming BF16 weights at two bytes per parameter, their weight sizes are approximately 5.6 TB and 4.8 TB, respectively.
Accounting for both the all-gather and broadcast stages gives an estimated logical payload of approximately twice the size of the model’s weights (Table 1).
| Model | Size in bytes | Refit payload estimate (all-gather+broadcast) | 
| Kimi K3 | 5.6 TB | ≈11.2 TB | 
| Qwen 3.8 2.4T A95B | 4.8 TB | ≈9.6 TB | 
For today’s largest open weight models, the communication payload already reaches around 10 TB per refit, which must be performed at every training step. As LLMs continue to scale, the overhead associated with this large payload will become even more significant. As a result, a more sophisticated approach is needed to perform weight refit that reduces the actual payload size while properly accounting for diverse weight layouts.
Reformulating refit as a DTensor-to-DTensor transfer problem
To overcome these limitations, start from the principle that refit should transfer only the theoretical minimum amount of weight data. However, achieving this presents several challenges. Training and inference instances can use different parallelism configurations and GPU counts, producing different shard boundaries. A destination shard may therefore need to be assembled from portions of several source shards, and vice versa.
Replication further complicates the mapping since the same weights may be available from multiple source GPUs or required by multiple destination GPUs. It is nontrivial to determine which source GPUs should send which tensor regions to each destination while achieving high performance across all possible configurations.
The key to addressing this challenge is to identify the right abstraction for this unique communication pattern. The team turned to the existing PyTorch distributed tensor (DTensor) abstraction, which is designed to represent tensors that are sharded or replicated across GPUs under different forms of data and model parallelism. The key insight is that weight refit can be reformulated as resharding a DTensor from the training layout to the inference layout, regardless of the parallelism configurations used by the two instances.
A DTensor layout is described by the tensor’s global shape, a device mesh specifying the logical arrangement of GPUs, and placements specifying how the tensor is sharded or replicated across that mesh. Refit can use the source description to specify where the updated weights reside and the destination description to specify which weights each inference GPU needs.
For example, consider an 8 x 8 weight matrix split by rows across two training GPUs and by columns across four inference GPUs. Assuming the tensor is sharded in the row dimension on the training GPUs and sharded in the column dimension on the inference GPUs, each training GPU holds a 4 x 8 shard, while each inference GPU needs an 8 x 2 shard. Each destination can obtain its required shard by receiving a 4 x 2 region from each source. These regions follow directly from the overlap between the source and destination shards, as illustrated in Figure 1.
As the figure shows, any kind of sharded tensor can be easily represented as a DTensor format, and the refit can be redefined as a DTensor-to-DTensor reshard problem. This finding provides the foundation for the Reshard collective.
Reshard collective communication for DTensor-to-DTensor transfers
Reshard is a new type of collective communication call for arbitrary DTensor-to-DTensor transfers. Like all-reduce, reduce-scatter, all-gather, broadcast, and so on, reshard defines a communication pattern that applications can invoke as one operation. It transfers the values of a logical tensor from its source distribution into its destination distribution.
A Reshard call can be specified simply by the source and destination DTensor descriptions. This abstraction not only simplifies the refit problem, but also encapsulates the communication logic in a library, allowing the underlying algorithms to evolve and improve independently of the application.
NCCL M2N Reshard is open source, provided to the community as the first reference implementation of the Reshard collective. Built on NCCL, this implementation transfers a tensor distributed across M source GPUs into the layout required by N destination GPUs. In RL refit, the training GPUs form the source group and the inference GPUs form the destination group.
Figure 2 shows how this implementation accepts the layout descriptions and local buffers to carry out the Reshard operation.
How NCCL M2N Reshard unlocks maximum network bandwidth
NCCL M2N Reshard first derives the exact intersections between source and destination shards, then maps those transfers onto the physical GPU network topology. Instead of sending every source contribution independently to every destination replica, NCCL M2N groups replicas by NVIDIA NVLink domain. Within each domain, it distributes the incoming contributions as evenly as possible across the replica ranks, so each receiving rank receives a distinct subset of the total data over the network.
The receiving ranks then exchange those subsets over NVLink, enabling every replica to assemble the complete shard without duplicating network traffic. If replicas span multiple NVLink domains, one copy of each contribution is forwarded through the domains, and the same balanced local exchange occurs within each domain. Network transfer and NVLink replication are pipelined to hide each other’s latency.
Figure 3 illustrates this data movement scheme for a tensor moving from TP4 on the source to TP2 x DP2 on the destination, with all four destination GPUs in one NVLink domain. With direct point-to-point transfers (Figure 3a), each source shard is sent to both data parallel (DP) replicas. As a result, each shard is transferred twice over the network redundantly. This means that each shard gets roughly half the network bandwidth (assuming each shard saturates the network bandwidth).
NCCL M2N Reshard transfers each source shard across the network just once, supplying each destination GPU with half of its required data (Figure 3b). The destination GPUs exchange the missing half over NVLink. For example, destination GPU 0 receives S0 from source GPU 0 over the network and S1 from destination GPU 2 over NVLink. Network transfers and NVLink exchanges proceed concurrently. This way, each shard gets the full network bandwidth.
Demonstrating the Reshard collective with NVIDIA NeMo RL
To demonstrate the effectiveness of the Reshard collective for weight refit, a reference implementation is provided in the NVIDIA NeMo RL framework. NeMo RL is an open source framework designed to streamline and scale RL post-training. The clear abstraction of the Reshard collective makes the required implementation within the framework relatively simple. For a given parallelism configuration, the framework only needs to provide a DTensor description for each parameter for training and inference instances, which should be straightforward because DTensor was designed for this purpose.
In practice, however, the variety of layer types and the diversity in how training and inference engines shard parameters under each parallelism configuration make it challenging to handle every edge case through the Reshard collective.
To develop an efficient and sustainable design, we built on the key observation that feed-forward projection weights in the transformer block dominate the weight refit payload. In the latest LLMs, these weights account for around 95% of the model’s parameters.
Based on this observation, our design uses a hybrid approach in which dominant feed-forward projection weights take the reshard path, while all other small weights (for example, QKV projection or mamba weights) use the conventional gather-and-broadcast refit path, which is optimized for broad functional coverage. This approach combines efficient reshard communication for most of the payload with the same functional coverage as conventional gather-and-broadcast refit.
The sharding layout can change at runtime as nodes are added or removed during failure recovery. To accommodate changes in GPU membership, frameworks can either destroy and recreate the communication group or use NCCL shrink and grow APIs to adjust the existing communicator group. NeMo RL currently uses the first approach for resiliency support. Resiliency support using NCCL shrink and grow APIs is planned for future updates.
RL weight refit performance benchmark results
Table 2 summarizes reshard-based refit latencies measured using the NeMo RL implementation introduced above. The benchmarks cover a range of models on NVIDIA DGX H100 (NVL8) and NVIDIA DGX GB200 (NVL72) systems. Across various benchmarks, the reshard refit achieves a speedup of 2.7x to 5.7x over conventional gather-and-broadcast refit.
| Platform | Model | Training → inference layout | Gather-and-broadcast refit latency | Reshard refit latency | 
| NVIDIA DGX H100 | Qwen 3 235B | TP4 x PP8 x EP16 → TP8 x DP16 | 6.4 s | 1.9 s | 
| NVIDIA DGX H100 | DeepSeek v3 671B | PP16 x EP16 → TP32 x DP8 | 14.9 s | 2.6 s | 
| NVIDIA DGX GB200 | DeepSeek v3 671B | PP16 x EP16 → TP32 x DP8 | 6.1 s | 2.3 s | 
| NVIDIA DGX GB200 | Nemotron Ultra v3 | TP8 x EP32 x PP2 → TP8 x DP8 | 8.2 s | 2.3 s | 
This new refit is designed for trillion-parameter models. In our refit-only microbenchmark, Reshard refit took only 4.3 seconds for the Qwen3.8 2.4T BF16 model, demonstrating its effectiveness at the trillion-parameter scale for which it was designed.
Get started with reshard weight refit using NeMo RL
The reference implementation in the NVIDIA NeMo RL framework enables you to adopt and extend this approach for your own RL workloads.
To enable the reshard refit path in NeMo RL, use the following configuration:
policy:
  generation:
    colocated:
      enabled: false
    refit_transport: nccl_reshard
The NeMo RL refit guide and NCCL Reshard configuration requirements describe the supported backends, layouts, and precision modes for this feature.
Acknowledgements
We sincerely appreciate the contributions of Ke Wen, Ching-Hsiang Chu, Guyue Huang, Seonjin Na, and Nitin to NCCL M2N Reshard and nccl-reshard weight refit in NeMo RL.

articles.title: 100 Nm et 750 W de puissance : le nouveau moteur Shimano pour vélo électrique veut défier Bosch et DJI
articles.text:
Chez Shimano, les VTT électriques haut de gamme tournaient depuis 2022 sur l’EP801, un moteur de 85 Nm et 600 watts que la marque avait enrichi de nouvelles fonctions fin 2024. Entre-temps, la concurrence est passée à 750 watts, comme le Bosch Performance Line CX, voire bien au-delà : le DJI Avinox M2S grimpe à 1 500 watts et 150 Nm. Shimano a présenté ce vendredi 6 novembre son successeur, l’EP810, dont le site allemand Pedelecs & E-Bikes a relayé la fiche complète. Le moteur est plus léger et plus puissant, et il arrive surtout avec un système qui choisit lui-même le bon rapport et le bon niveau d’aide.
Plus puissant
Ce moteur, le DU-EP810 plus précisément, pèse 2,3 kg pour un couple maximal de 100 Nm et une puissance de pointe de 750 watts. Shimano gagne donc 400 grammes par rapport à l’EP801 (2,7 kg), avec 15 Nm et 150 watts de plus pour les vélos électriques.
Le boîtier est en alliage de magnésium, avec des ailettes de refroidissement pour mieux évacuer la chaleur. Shimano a également revu l’intérieur du moteur pour réduire le bruit mécanique. Shimano promet une puissance régulière jusqu’à 160 tours de pédalier par minute, contre 120 sur l’EP801. On atteint cette cadence en moulinant sur un petit braquet. Selon Shimano, ce moteur plus compact s’intègre plus facilement au cadre et laisse plus de garde au sol. Il reste pourtant plus volumineux que la plupart des moteurs concurrents actuels.
Vitesses et assistance en pilote automatique
Shimano met également en avant son système « True Auto ». Il associe la troisième génération d’Auto Shift, son système de passage de vitesses automatique qui s’appuie sur la transmission électronique Di2, à une nouvelle fonction baptisée Auto Assist. Les deux exploitent les mêmes mesures (cadence, couple, vitesse et pente), si bien que le changement de rapport et l’aide du moteur restent coordonnés.
Le cycliste règle la cadence qu’il préfère directement sur le vélo, sur une échelle de -3 à +3. Le passage automatique fonctionne avec les groupes Di2 XTR, Deore XT, Deore, GRX et Cues. Bosch, de son côté, a étendu sa propre fonction de vitesses automatiques à bien plus de vélos en 2025.
Auto Assist est intégré au mode de conduite TRAIL+ et ajuste en continu l’aide du moteur selon la pente. En montée, Shimano promet une assistance qui augmente progressivement pour garder de l’adhérence, sans faire patiner la roue arrière ni lever la roue avant. En descente, elle baisse, et sur le plat, le moteur consomme moins pour préserver l’autonomie.
Pour le terrain technique et les côtes raides, Shimano ajoute quatre fonctions :
- l’assistance maintenue, qui compense les baisses d’effort passagères sur les pédales ;
- l’assistance prolongée, qui continue de pousser un court instant après l’arrêt du pédalage pour passer un obstacle, avec une durée réglable ;
- Hill Hold, qui se sert de l’assistance à la marche pour garder le vélo immobile en pente sans toucher au frein ;
- Lift & Shift, qui rétrograde quand on soulève la roue arrière et qu’on appuie deux fois sur le bouton de baisse d’assistance, pour repartir en côte sans élan.
Une batterie de 720 Wh et un nouveau protocole sans fil
Côté batterie, Shimano livre une batterie BT-EN827 de 720 Wh, intégrée au tube diagonal. Elle pèse environ 4,1 kg et mesure 420 x 84 x 73 mm, ce qui porte l’ensemble moteur et batterie à environ 6,4 kg. Pour la recharge, on a le choix entre deux chargeurs, l’EC-EN832 de 2 ampères et l’EC-EN834 de 4 ampères.
Au guidon, on retrouve l’ordinateur SC-EN700, intégré au tube supérieur, ou le SC-EM810, un écran couleur qui affiche le rapport engagé, le mode d’assistance, la vitesse, le temps, l’autonomie et la distance. Le commutateur sans fil SW-UT600-LR, proposé en option, dispose de trois boutons pour changer de mode et piloter d’autres fonctions. Un module USB-C, l’EW-USB30-C, permet aussi de recharger un smartphone, mais avec 5 volts et 1,5 ampère, soit 7,5 watts, la recharge reste lente.
Tous les réglages passent par la nouvelle application Shimano Connect, qui regroupe la configuration, les mises à jour des composants et l’enregistrement des sorties à vélo. Shimano annonce une connexion plus rapide et plus stable. Avec les composants compatibles, il est possible de télécharger une mise à jour pendant la sortie et de l’installer plus tard. L’application intègre aussi un verrouillage du système.
La marque lance enfin D-FLY+, un protocole sans fil plus rapide et mieux sécurisé, qui fait dialoguer les composants du vélo entre eux. En revanche, il ne fonctionne pas avec l’ancien D-FLY et reste réservé à l’EP810 et aux futures plateformes.
Pas encore de prix, mais un premier vélo annoncé
Shimano n’a pas communiqué le prix de son nouveau moteur. Selon la marque, les tarifs dépendront du marché et de la configuration, en première monte comme en kit de mise à niveau, et la disponibilité variera selon les régions. Un premier vélo est déjà annoncé avec ce moteur, l’Orbea Rise LT millésime 2027.
Orbea décline ce Rise 2027 en deux versions, SL et LT, à partir de 5 699 euros pour le SL et de 5 999 euros pour le LT. Ce premier vélo montre aussi que les 750 watts ne seront pas présents partout : Orbea limite l’EP810 à 600 watts de puissance de pointe avec son propre logiciel RS, pour 100 Nm de couple. Avant d’acheter un vélo équipé de ce moteur, il faudra donc vérifier la puissance retenue par chaque marque. Honda a lui aussi annoncé son VTT électrique RN0 avec l’EP810.
